What the shekinah glory was to tabernacle and temple, that the Spirit is to the "holy temple," the Church, and to the temple which is the believer's body. <reference osisRef="1co 6:19">1 Corinthians 6:19</reference>. <chapter eID="Exod.40"/><div eID="gen579" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen339" osisID="Exod" type="book"/>
<div canonical="true" osisID="Lev" sID="gen580" type="book"/> <milestone n="" type="x-usfm-toc1"/> <milestone n="" type="x-usfm-toc2"/> <milestone n="" type="x-usfm-toc3"/>
<chapter n="1" osisID="Lev.1" sID="Lev.1"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv20"/><title type="x-s">Book Introduction - Leviticus</title> <div sID="gen581" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="le 1">Read first chapter of Leviticus</reference><div eID="gen581" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen582" type="x-p"/> LEVITICUS stands in the same relation to EXODUS, that the Epistles do to the Gospels. EXODUS is the record of redemption, and lays the foundation of the cleansing, worship, and service of a redeemed people. LEVITICUS gives the detail of the walk, worship, and service of that people. In EXODUS God speaks out of the mount to which approach was forbidden; in LEVITICUS He speaks out of the tabernacle in which He dwells in the midst of His people, to tell them that which befits His holiness in their approach to, and communion with, Himself.<div eID="gen582" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen583" type="x-p"/> The key word of Leviticus is holiness, occurring 87 times. Key verse is <reference osisRef="le 19:2">Leviticus 19:2</reference>.<div eID="gen583" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen584" type="x-p"/> LEVITICUS is in nine chief divisions:<div eID="gen584" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">The Offerings 1-6:7</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The Law of the Offerings6:8-7:38.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">Consecration8:1-9:24</item> <item type="x-indent-1">A Warning Example10:1-20.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">A Holy God Must Have a Cleansed People 11-15.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">Atonement 16,17.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The Relationships of God's People 18-22.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The Feasts of Jehovah, 23.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">Instructions and Warnings, 24-27.</item> </list> <div sID="gen585" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv20"/> <hi type="bold">burnt-sacrifice</hi> <div eID="gen585" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen586" type="x-p"/> The burnt-offering<div eID="gen586" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(1) typifies Christ offering Himself without spot to God in delight to do His Father's will even in death.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(2) it is atoning because the believer has not had this delight in the will of God; and</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(3) substitutionary (<reference osisRef="le 1:4">Leviticus 1:4</reference>) because Christ did it in the sinner's stead. But the thought of penalty is not prominent. ; <reference osisRef="heb 9:11-14">Hebrews 9:11-14</reference>; <reference osisRef="heb 10:5-7"> 10:5-7</reference>; <reference osisRef="ps 40:6-8">Psalms 40:6-8</reference>; <reference osisRef="php 2:8">Philippians 2:8</reference>. The emphatic words <reference osisRef="le 1:3-5">Leviticus 1:3-5</reference> are "burnt-sacrifice," "voluntary," "it shall be accepted for him," and "atonement." The creatures acceptable for sacrifice are five:</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(1) The bullock, or ox, typifies Christ as the patient and enduring Servant <reference osisRef="1co 9:9 1co 9:10">1 Corinthians 9:9,10</reference>; <reference osisRef="heb 12:2 heb 12:3">Hebrews 12:2,3</reference> "obedient unto death" ; <reference osisRef="isa 52:13-15">Isaiah 52:13-15</reference>; <reference osisRef="php 2:5-8">Philippians 2:5-8</reference>. His offering in this character is substitutionary, for this we have not been.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(2) The sheep, or lamb, typifies Christ in unresisting self-surrender to the death of the cross <reference osisRef="isa 53:7">Isaiah 53:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="ac 8:32-35">Acts 8:32-35</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(3) The goat typifies the sinner <reference osisRef="mt 25:33">Matthew 25:33</reference> and, when used sacrificially, Christ, as "numbered with the transgressors" ; <reference osisRef="isa 53:12">Isaiah 53:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="lu 23:33">Luke 23:33</reference> and "made sin," and "a curse" ; <reference osisRef="ga 3:13">Galatians 3:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="2co 5:21">2 Corinthians 5:21</reference> as the sinner's substitute.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(4,5) The turtle-dove or pigeon. Naturally a symbol of mourning innocency <reference osisRef="isa 38:14">Isaiah 38:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="isa 59:11"> 59:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="mt 23:37">Matthew 23:37</reference>; <reference osisRef="heb 7:26">Hebrews 7:26</reference> is associated with poverty in <reference osisRef="le 5:7">Leviticus 5:7</reference> and speaks of Him who for our sakes become poor <reference osisRef="lu 9:58">Luke 9:58</reference> and whose pathway of poverty which began with laying aside "the form of God," ended in the sacrifice through which we became rich ; <reference osisRef="2co 8:9">2 Corinthians 8:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="php 2:6-8">Philippians 2:6-8</reference>. The sacrifice of the poor Man becomes the poor man's sacrifice. <reference osisRef="lu 2:24">Luke 2:24</reference>. These grades of typical sacrifice test the measure of our apprehension of the varied aspects of Christ's one sacrifice on the cross. The mature believer should see Christ crucified in all these aspects. </item> </list>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv21"/><div sID="gen587" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv21"/> <hi type="bold">put his hand upon</hi> <div eID="gen587" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen588" type="x-p"/> The laying of the offerer's hand signified acceptance and identification if himself with his offering. In type it answered to the believer's faith accepting and identifying himself with Christ <reference osisRef="ro 4:5">Romans 4:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="ro 6:3-11"> 6:3-11</reference>. The believer is justified by faith, and his faith is reckoned for righteousness, because his faith identifies him with Christ, who died as his sin-offering ; <reference osisRef="2co 5:21">2 Corinthians 5:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="1pe 2:24">1 Peter 2:24</reference>.<div eID="gen588" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen589" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">atonement</hi><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ex 29:33">Exodus 29:33</reference>")</hi>.

Fire. Essentially as symbol of God's holiness. As such it expresses God in three ways:<div eID="gen589" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(1) In judgment upon that which His holiness utterly condemns (e.g.) <reference osisRef="ge 19:24">Genesis 19:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="mr 9:43-48">Mark 9:43-48</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 20:15">Revelation 20:15</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(2) in the manifestation of Himself, and of that which He approves <reference osisRef="ex 3:2">Exodus 3:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="1pe 1:7">1 Peter 1:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="ex 13:21">Exodus 13:21</reference></item> </list> <div sID="gen590" type="x-p"/> and (3) in purification (e.g) <reference osisRef="1co 3:12-14">1 Corinthians 3:12-14</reference>; <reference osisRef="mal 3:2 mal 3:3">Malachi 3:2,3</reference>. So, in Leviticus, the fire which only manifests the sweet savour of the burnt-, meal-, and peace- offerings, wholly consumes the sin-offering.<div eID="gen590" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen591" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fat</hi> That which burns most quickly -- devotedness, zeal.

<hi type="bold">sweet savour</hi><div eID="gen591" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen592" type="x-p"/> The sweet savour offerings are so called because they typify Christ in His own perfections, and in His affectionate devotion to the Father's will. The non-sweet savour offerings typify Christ as bearing the whole demerit of the sinner. Both are substantial. In our place Christ, in the burnt-offering, makes good our lack of devotedness, and, in the sin- and trespass-offerings, suffers because of our disobediences. <div eID="gen592" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv22"/><div sID="gen593" type="x-p"/> <chapter eID="Lev.1"/>
<div eID="gen593" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen594" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="2" osisID="Lev.2" sID="Lev.2"/>

<hi type="bold">fine flour</hi> <div eID="gen594" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen595" type="x-p"/> The meal-offering. The fine flour speaks of the evenness and balance of the character of Christ; of that perfection in which no quality was in excess, none lacking; the fire, of His testing by suffering, even unto death; frankincense; the fragrance of His life Godward (see) <reference osisRef="ex 30:34">Exodus 30:34</reference> absence of leaven, His character as "the Truth" (see) <reference osisRef="ex 12:8">Exodus 12:8</reference> absence of honey;--His was not that mere natural sweetness which may exist quite apart from grace; oil mingled, Christ as born of the Spirit <reference osisRef="mt 1:18-23">Matthew 1:18-23</reference> oil upon, Christ as baptized with the Spirit ; <reference osisRef="joh 1:32">John 1:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="joh 6:27"> 6:27</reference> the oven, the unseen sufferings of Christ--His inner agonies ; <reference osisRef="heb 2:18">Hebrews 2:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="mt 27:45 mt 27:46">Matthew 27:45,46</reference> the pan, His more evident sufferings (e.g.) <reference osisRef="mt 27:27-31">Matthew 27:27-31</reference> salt, the pungency of the truth of God--that which arrests the action of leaven.

<hi type="bold">leaven</hi><div eID="gen595" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen596" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">honey</hi> <div eID="gen596" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen597" type="x-p"/> For meanings of leaven see Mat 13:.33. Also <reference osisRef="le 7:13">Leviticus 7:13,</reference> <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Le 7:13">Leviticus 7:13</reference>")</hi><div eID="gen597" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen598" type="x-p"/> 2 Honey is mere natural sweetness and could not symbolize the divine graciousness of the Lord Jesus.

<hi type="bold">salt</hi><div eID="gen598" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen599" type="x-p"/> Cf. <reference osisRef="nu 18:19">Numbers 18:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="mr 9:49 mr 9:50">Mark 9:49,50</reference>; <reference osisRef="col 4:6">Colossians 4:6</reference> <div eID="gen599" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv22"/><div sID="gen600" type="x-p"/> <chapter eID="Lev.2"/>
<div eID="gen600" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen601" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="3" osisID="Lev.3" sID="Lev.3"/>

<hi type="bold">peace-offering</hi> <div eID="gen601" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen602" type="x-p"/> The peace-offering. The whole work of Christ in relation to the believer's peace is here in type. He made peace, <reference osisRef="col 1:20">Colossians 1:20</reference> proclaimed peace, <reference osisRef="eph 2:17">Ephesians 2:17</reference> and is our peace, <reference osisRef="eph 2:14">Ephesians 2:14</reference>.<div eID="gen602" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen603" type="x-p"/> In Christ God and the sinner meet in peace; God is propitiated, the sinner reconciled-- both alike satisfied with what Christ has done. But all this at the cost of blood and fire. The details speak of fellowship. This brings in prominently the thought of fellowship with God through Christ. Hence the peace-offering is set forth as affording food for the priests <reference osisRef="le 7:31-34">Leviticus 7:31-34</reference>. Observe that it is the breast (affections) and shoulders (strength) upon which we as priests <reference osisRef="1pe 2:9">1 Peter 2:9</reference> feed in fellowship with the Father. This it is which makes the peace-offering especially a thank-offering. <reference osisRef="le 7:11 le 7:12">Leviticus 7:11,12</reference>.
<hi type="bold">caul</hi> Fat appendage. <chapter eID="Lev.3"/><div eID="gen603" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen604" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="4" osisID="Lev.4" sID="Lev.4"/>

<hi type="bold">sin-offering</hi> <div eID="gen604" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen605" type="x-p"/> The sin-offering, though still Christ, is Christ seen laden with the believer's sin, absolutely in the sinner's place and stead, and not, as in the sweet savour offerings, in His own perfections. It is Christ's death as viewed in <reference osisRef="isa 53:1-12">Isaiah 53:1-12</reference>; <reference osisRef="ps 22:1-31">Psalms 22:1-31</reference>; <reference osisRef="mt 26:28">Matthew 26:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="1pe 2:24">1 Peter 2:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="1pe 3:18"> 3:18</reference>.<div eID="gen605" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen606" type="x-p"/> But note <reference osisRef="le 6:24-30">Leviticus 6:24-30</reference> how the essential holiness of Him who was "made sin for us" <reference osisRef="2co 5:21">2 Corinthians 5:21</reference> is guarded. The sin-offerings are expiatory, substitutional, efficacious <reference osisRef="le 4:12 le 4:29 le 4:35">Leviticus 4:12,29,35</reference> and have in view the vindication of the law through substitutional sacrifice.

<hi type="bold">without the camp</hi><div eID="gen606" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen607" type="x-p"/> Cf. <reference osisRef="ex 29:14">Exodus 29:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="le 16:27">Leviticus 16:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="nu 19:3">Numbers 19:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="heb 13:10-13">Hebrews 13:10-13</reference>. The last passage is the interpretative one. The "camp" was Judaism-- a religion of forms and ceremonies. "Jesus, also, that He might sanctify separate, or set apart for God] the people with or 'through' His own blood, suffered without the gate" temple gate, city gate, i.e. Judaism civil and religious]; <reference osisRef="heb 13:12">Hebrews 13:12</reference> but how does this sanctify, or set apart, a people? "Let us go forth therefore unto Him without the camp Judaism then, Judaized Christianity now--anything religious which denies Him as our sin-offering] bearing His reproach" <reference osisRef="heb 13:13">Hebrews 13:13</reference>. The sin- offering, "burned without the camp," typifies this aspect of the death of Christ. The cross becomes a new altar, in a new place, where, without the smallest merit in themselves, the redeemed gather to offer, as believer-priests, spiritual sacrifices. ; <reference osisRef="heb 13:15">Hebrews 13:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="1pe 2:5">1 Peter 2:5</reference>. The bodies of the sin-offering beasts were not burned without the camp, as some have fancied, because "saturated with sin," and unfit for a holy camp. Rather, an unholy camp was an unfit place for a holy sin-offering. The dead body of our Lord was not "saturated with sin," though in it our sins had been borne <reference osisRef="1pe 2:24">1 Peter 2:24</reference>.
<hi type="bold">atonement</hi><div eID="gen607" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen608" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ex 29:33">Exodus 29:33</reference>")</hi>.

<hi type="bold">atonement</hi><div eID="gen608" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen609" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ex 29:33">Exodus 29:33</reference>")</hi> <chapter eID="Lev.4"/> <div eID="gen609" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen610" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="5" osisID="Lev.5" sID="Lev.5"/>

<hi type="bold">trespass offering</hi> <div eID="gen610" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen611" type="x-p"/> The trespass-offerings have in view rather the injury which sin does than its guilt-- which is the sin-offering aspect. What is due to God's rights in every human being is here meant. <reference osisRef="ps 51:4">Psalms 51:4,</reference> is a perfect expression of this.

<hi type="bold">atonement</hi><div eID="gen611" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen612" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ex 29:33">Exodus 29:33</reference>")</hi>. <chapter eID="Lev.5"/><div eID="gen612" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen613" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="6" osisID="Lev.6" sID="Lev.6"/>

<hi type="bold">The Fire</hi> <div eID="gen613" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen614" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Le 1:8">Leviticus 1:8</reference>")</hi>. Here the fire expresses also the undying devotedness of Christ.

<hi type="bold">reconcile</hi><div eID="gen614" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen615" type="x-p"/> Heb. "kaphar," to cover. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Da 9:24">Daniel 9:24</reference>")</hi> See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:ex 29:33">Exodus 29:33</reference>" <div eID="gen615" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv22"/><div sID="gen616" type="x-p"/> <chapter eID="Lev.6"/>
<div eID="gen616" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen617" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="7" osisID="Lev.7" sID="Lev.7"/>

<hi type="bold">reconcile</hi> <div eID="gen617" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen618" type="x-p"/> Heb. "kaphar," to cover. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Da 9:24">Daniel 9:24</reference>")</hi> See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:ex 29:33">Exodus 29:33</reference>"
<hi type="bold">atonement</hi><div eID="gen618" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen619" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ex 29:33">Exodus 29:33</reference>")</hi>

<hi type="bold">peace-offerings</hi> <div eID="gen619" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen620" type="x-p"/> In the "law of the offerings," the peace-offering is taken out of its place as third of the sweet savour offerings, and placed alone, and after all the non-sweet savour offerings. The explanation is as simple as the fact is beautiful. In revealing the offerings Jehovah works from Himself out to the sinner. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ex 25:10">Exodus 25:10</reference>")</hi>. The whole burnt-offering comes first as meeting what is due to the divine affections, and the trespass-offering last as meeting the simplest aspect of sin-- its injuriousness. But the sinner begins of necessity with that which lies nearest to a newly awakened conscience--a sense, namely, that because of sin he is at enmity with God. His first need, therefore, is peace with God. And that is precisely the Gospel order. Christ's first message is, "Peace" <reference osisRef="joh 20:19">John 20:19</reference> afterward He shows them His hands and His side. It is the order as <reference osisRef="2co 5:18-21">2 Corinthians 5:18-21</reference> first "the word of reconciliation," <reference osisRef="le 7:19">Leviticus 7:19,</reference> then the trespass- and sin-offering, <reference osisRef="le 7:21">Leviticus 7:21</reference>. Experience thus reverses the order of revelation.

<hi type="bold">leaven</hi><div eID="gen620" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen621" type="x-p"/> The use of leaven here is significant. Peace with God is something which the believer shares with God. Christ is our peace-offering <reference osisRef="eph 2:13">Ephesians 2:13</reference>. Any thanksgiving for peace must, first of all, present Him. In verse 12 we have this, in type, and so leaven is excluded. In verse 13 it is the offerer who gives thanks for his participation in the peace, and so leaven fitly signifies, that though having peace with God through the work of another, there is still evil in him. This is illustrated in <reference osisRef="am 4:5">Amos 4:5</reference> where the evil in Israel is before God. <chapter eID="Lev.7"/><div eID="gen621" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen622" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="8" osisID="Lev.8" sID="Lev.8"/>

<hi type="bold">Aaron</hi> <div eID="gen622" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen623" type="x-p"/> The priests did not consecrate themselves, all was done by another, in this instance Moses, acting for Jehovah. The priests simply presented their bodies in the sense of <reference osisRef="ro 12:1">Romans 12:1</reference>.
<hi type="bold">Urim and Thummim</hi> <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ex 28:30">Exodus 28:30</reference>")</hi>. Urim, "lights." Thummim, "perfection."

<hi type="bold">poured of the anointing oil</hi><div eID="gen623" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen624" type="x-p"/> Two important distinctions are made in the case of the high priest, thus confirming his typical relation to Christ the anti-type:<div eID="gen624" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(1) Aaron is anointed before the sacrifices are slain, while in the case of the priests the application of blood precedes the anointing. Christ the sinless One required no preparation for receiving the anointing oil, symbol of the Holy Spirit;</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(2) upon the high priest only was the anointing oil poured. "God giveth not the Spirit by measure unto him" <reference osisRef="joh 3:34">John 3:34</reference>. "Thy God hath anointed Thee with the oil of gladness above Thy fellows." <reference osisRef="heb 1:9">Hebrews 1:9</reference>. </item> </list>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv22"/><div sID="gen625" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv22"/><hi type="bold">reconciliation</hi> Heb. "kaphar," to cover.<div eID="gen625" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen626" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Da 9:24">Daniel 9:24</reference>")</hi>.

<hi type="bold">atonement</hi><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ex 29:33">Exodus 29:33</reference>")</hi><div eID="gen626" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv23"/><div sID="gen627" type="x-p"/> <chapter eID="Lev.8"/>
<div eID="gen627" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen628" type="x-p"/><chapter n="10" osisID="Lev.10" sID="Lev.10"/>

Strange fire. Fire "from before the Lord" had kindled upon the altar of burnt-offering the fire which the care of the priests was to keep burning <reference osisRef="le 6:12">Leviticus 6:12</reference>. No commandment had yet been given <reference osisRef="le 16:12">Leviticus 16:12</reference> how the incense should be kindled. The sin of Nadab and Abihu was in acting in the things of God without seeking the mind of God. It was "will worship" <reference osisRef="col 2:23">Colossians 2:23</reference> which often has a "show of wisdom and humility." It typifies any use of carnal means to kindle the fire of devotion and praise.
Mish-a-el, 'one with God.' El-za-phan, 'God protects.' Uz-zi-el, 'power of God.'
El-e-a-zar, 'God has helped.' Ith-a-mar, 'isle of palms.'

<hi type="bold">atonement</hi><div eID="gen628" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen629" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ex 29:33">Exodus 29:33</reference>")</hi>. <chapter eID="Lev.10"/><div eID="gen629" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen630" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="11" osisID="Lev.11" sID="Lev.11"/>

<hi type="bold">These are the beasts</hi> <div eID="gen630" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen631" type="x-p"/> The dietary regulations of the covenant people must be regarded primarily as sanitary. Israel, it must be remembered, was a nation living on the earth under a theocratic government. Of necessity the divine legislation concerned itself with the social as well as with the religious life of the people. To force upon every word of that legislation a typical meaning is to strain <reference osisRef="1co 10:1-11">1 Corinthians 10:1-11</reference>; <reference osisRef="heb 9:23 heb 9:24">Hebrews 9:23,24</reference> beyond all reasonable interpretation.

<hi type="bold">hare</hi><div eID="gen631" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen632" type="x-p"/> Heb. arnebeth, an unidentified animal, but certainly not a hare, possessing as it is said to, characteristics not possessed by the hare. The supposed error in the text is due entirely to the translators' assumption that the English hare and the ancient "arnebeth" were identical. <chapter eID="Lev.11"/><div eID="gen632" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen633" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="12" osisID="Lev.12" sID="Lev.12"/>

<hi type="bold">atonement</hi> <div eID="gen633" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen634" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ex 29:33">Exodus 29:33</reference>")</hi>. <chapter eID="Lev.12"/><div eID="gen634" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen635" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="13" osisID="Lev.13" sID="Lev.13"/>

<hi type="bold">Leprosy</hi> <div eID="gen635" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen636" type="x-p"/> Leprosy speaks of sin as<div eID="gen636" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(1) in the blood;</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(2) becoming overt in loathsome ways;</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(3) incurable by human means. The anti-type as applied to the people of God is "sin," demanding self-judgment <reference osisRef="1co 11:31">1 Corinthians 11:31</reference> and "sins," demanding confession and cleansing. <reference osisRef="1jo 1:9">1 John 1:9</reference>. </item> </list>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv23"/><div sID="gen637" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv23"/> <hi type="bold">priest</hi> <div eID="gen637" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen638" type="x-p"/> Some have found in the regulations of this chapter concerning an inquest by the priest of a case of leprosy, elaborate provisions for the exercise of discipline in the local church. No little self-righteousness and cruelty have come in thereby. The explicit instructions of the N.T. are the alone and sufficient rule of discipline. <chapter eID="Lev.13"/><div eID="gen638" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen639" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="14" osisID="Lev.14" sID="Lev.14"/>

<hi type="bold">go forth</hi> <div eID="gen639" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen640" type="x-p"/> As a type of Gospel salvation the points are:<div eID="gen640" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(1) The leper does nothing <reference osisRef="ro 4:5 ro 4:5">Romans 4:5,5</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(2) the priest seeks the leper, not the leper the priest <reference osisRef="lu 19:10">Luke 19:10</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(3) "with-out shedding of blood is no remission" <reference osisRef="heb 9:22">Hebrews 9:22</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(4) "and if Christ be not raised, your faith is vain" <reference osisRef="1co 15:17">1 Corinthians 15:17</reference>. </item> </list>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv24"/><div sID="gen641" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv24"/> <hi type="bold">birds</hi> <div eID="gen641" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen642" type="x-p"/> The bird slain, and the live bird, dipped in blood and released, present the two aspects of salvation in <reference osisRef="ro 4:25">Romans 4:25</reference> "delivered for our offences, and raised again for our justification."

<hi type="bold">vessel</hi><div eID="gen642" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen643" type="x-p"/> The earthen vessel typifies the humanity of Christ, as the running water typifies the Holy Spirit as the "Spirit of life" <reference osisRef="ro 8:2">Romans 8:2</reference> "put to death in the flesh, but quickened by the Spirit." <reference osisRef="1pe 3:18">1 Peter 3:18</reference>
Marg<div eID="gen643" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen644" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ex 29:33">Exodus 29:33</reference>")</hi>
<hi type="bold">atonement</hi> <div eID="gen644" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen645" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ex 29:33">Exodus 29:33</reference>")</hi>

<hi type="bold">atonement</hi> <div eID="gen645" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen646" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ex 29:33">Exodus 29:33</reference>")</hi>. <chapter eID="Lev.14"/><div eID="gen646" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen647" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="15" osisID="Lev.15" sID="Lev.15"/>

<hi type="bold">atonement</hi> <div eID="gen647" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen648" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ex 29:33">Exodus 29:33</reference>")</hi>. <chapter eID="Lev.15"/><div eID="gen648" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen649" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="16" osisID="Lev.16" sID="Lev.16"/>

<hi type="bold">goats</hi> <div eID="gen649" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen650" type="x-p"/> The two goats. The offering of the high priest for himself has no anti-type in Christ <reference osisRef="heb 7:26 heb 7:27">Hebrews 7:26,27</reference>. The typical interest centres upon the two goats and the high priest. Typically<div eID="gen650" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(1) all is done by the high priest <reference osisRef="heb 1:3">Hebrews 1:3</reference> "by Himself"), the people only bring the sacrifice ; <reference osisRef="mt 26:47">Matthew 26:47</reference>; <reference osisRef="mt 27:24 mt 27:25"> 27:24,25</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(2) The goat slain (Jehovah's lot) is that aspect of Christ's work which vindicates the holiness and righteousness of God as expressed in the law <reference osisRef="ro 3:24-26">Romans 3:24-26</reference> and is expiatory.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(3) The living goat typifies that aspect of Christ's work which puts away our sins from before God <reference osisRef="heb 9:26">Hebrews 9:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="ro 8:33 ro 8:34">Romans 8:33,34</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(4) The high priest entering the holiest, typifies Christ entering "heaven itself" with "His own blood" for us <reference osisRef="heb 9:11 heb 9:12">Hebrews 9:11,12</reference>. His blood makes that to be a "throne of grace," and "mercy seat" which else must have been a throne of judgment.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(5) For us, the priests of the New Covenant, there is what Israel never had, a rent veil <reference osisRef="mt 27:51">Matthew 27:51</reference>; <reference osisRef="heb 10:19 heb 10:20">Hebrews 10:19,20</reference>. So that, for worship and blessing, we enter, in virtue of His blood, where He is, into the holiest ; <reference osisRef="heb 4:14-16">Hebrews 4:14-16</reference>; <reference osisRef="heb 10:19-22"> 10:19-22</reference>. The atonement of Christ, as interpreted by the O.T. sacrificial types, has these necessary elements:</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(1) It is substitutionary--the offering takes the offerer's place in death.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(2) The law is not evaded but honored--every sacrificial death was an execution of the sentence of the law.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(3) The sinlessness of Him who bore our sins is expressed in every animal sacrifice--it must be without blemish.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(4) The effect of the atoning work of Christ is typified</item> <item type="x-indent-2">(a) in the promises, "it shall be forgiven him"; and (b) in the peace-offering, the expression of fellowship--the highest privilege of the saint. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ex 29:33">Exodus 29:33</reference>")</hi> </item> </list>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv25"/><div sID="gen651" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv25"/> <hi type="bold">Atonement</hi> <div eID="gen651" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen652" type="x-p"/> Atonement. The biblical use and meaning of the word must be sharply distinguished from its use in theology. In theology it is term which covers the whole sacrificial and redemptive work of Christ. In the O.T. atonement is the English word used to translate the Hebrew words which mean "cover," "coverings," or "to cover." Atonement (at-one-ment) is, therefore, not a translation of the hebrew, but a purely theologic concept. The Levitical offerings "covered" the sins of Israel until, and in anticipation of the Cross, but did not "take away" <reference osisRef="heb 10:4">Hebrews 10:4</reference> those sins. These were the "sins done aforetime" ("covered" meantime by the Levitical sacrifices), which God "passed over" <reference osisRef="ro 3:25">Romans 3:25</reference> for which "passing over" God's righteousness was never vindicated until, in the Cross, Jesus Christ was "set forth a propitiation." See "Propitiation," <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ro 3:25">Romans 3:25</reference>")</hi>. It was the Cross, not the Levitical sacrifices which made "at-one-ment." The O.T. sacrifices enabled God to go on with a guilty people because they typified the Cross. To the offerer they were the confession of his desert of death, and the expression of his faith; to God they were the "shadows" <reference osisRef="heb 10:1">Hebrews 10:1</reference> of which Christ was the reality.<div eID="gen652" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen653" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">atonement</hi><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ex 29:33">Exodus 29:33</reference>")</hi>.
<hi type="bold">atonement</hi><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ex 29:33">Exodus 29:33</reference>")</hi>.
<hi type="bold">atonement</hi><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ex 29:33">Exodus 29:33</reference>")</hi>.

<hi type="bold">out unto the altar</hi><div eID="gen653" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen654" type="x-p"/> Dispensationally, for Israel, this is yet future; the High Priest is still in the holiest. When He comes out to His ancient people they will be converted and restored <reference osisRef="ro 11:23-27">Romans 11:23-27</reference>; <reference osisRef="zec 12:10 zec 12:12">Zechariah 12:10,12</reference>; <reference osisRef="zec 13:1"> 13:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 1:7">Revelation 1:7</reference> Meantime, believers of this dispensation as priests <reference osisRef="1pe 2:9">1 Peter 2:9</reference> enter into the holiest where He is. <reference osisRef="heb 10:19-22">Hebrews 10:19-22</reference>.

<hi type="bold">reconciling</hi> Heb. kaphar = covering. See <reference osisRef="da 9:24">Daniel 9:24</reference>. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Da 9:24">Daniel 9:24</reference>")</hi>.
<hi type="bold">atonement</hi> <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ex 29:33">Exodus 29:33</reference>")</hi>.
<hi type="bold">seventh month</hi> i.e. October. <chapter eID="Lev.16"/><div eID="gen654" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen655" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="17" osisID="Lev.17" sID="Lev.17"/>

<hi type="bold">altar</hi> <div eID="gen655" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(1) The value of the "life" is the measure of the value of the "blood." This gives the blood of Christ its inconceivable value. When it was shed the sinless God-man gave His life. "It is not possible that the blood of bulls and of goats could take away sins" <reference osisRef="heb 10:4">Hebrews 10:4</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(2) it is not the blood in the veins of the sacrifice, but the blood upon the altar which is efficacious. The Scripture knows nothing of salvation by the imitation or influence of Christ's life, but only by that life yielded up on the cross.</item> </list> <div sID="gen656" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">blood</hi> <div eID="gen656" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen657" type="x-p"/> The meaning of all sacrifice is here explained. Every offering was an execution of the sentence of the law upon a substitute for the offender, and every such offering pointed forward to that substitutional death of Christ which alone vindicated the righteousness of God in passing over the sins of those who offered the typical sacrifices <reference osisRef="ro 3:24 ro 3:25">Romans 3:24,25</reference>; <reference osisRef="ex 29:36">Exodus 29:36</reference>.<div eID="gen657" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen658" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">atonement</hi> <div eID="gen658" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen659" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ex 29:33">Exodus 29:33</reference>")</hi>. <chapter eID="Lev.17"/><div eID="gen659" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen660" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="18" osisID="Lev.18" sID="Lev.18"/>

<hi type="bold">Molech</hi> <div eID="gen660" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen661" type="x-p"/> Called Moloch. <reference osisRef="ac 7:43">Acts 7:43</reference>. <chapter eID="Lev.18"/><div eID="gen661" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen662" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="19" osisID="Lev.19" sID="Lev.19"/>
<hi type="bold">fear</hi> <div eID="gen662" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen663" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ps 19:9">Psalms 19:9</reference>")</hi>.
<hi type="bold">atonement</hi><div eID="gen663" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen664" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ex 29:33">Exodus 29:33</reference>")</hi>.

<hi type="bold">fear</hi><div eID="gen664" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen665" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ps 19:9">Psalms 19:9</reference>")</hi>. <chapter eID="Lev.19"/><div eID="gen665" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen666" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="21" osisID="Lev.21" sID="Lev.21"/>

<hi type="bold">sanctify</hi> <div eID="gen666" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen667" type="x-p"/> Verse 8 illustrates the O.T. holiness or sanctification--a person set apart for the service of God.<div eID="gen667" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen668" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">sanctify</hi> <div eID="gen668" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen669" type="x-p"/> Heb. "qodesh." <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ge 2:3">Genesis 2:3</reference>")</hi>. <chapter eID="Lev.21"/><div eID="gen669" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen670" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="23" osisID="Lev.23" sID="Lev.23"/>

<hi type="bold">feasts</hi> <div eID="gen670" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen671" type="x-p"/> The feasts of Jehovah. As given to Israel, these were simply seven great religious festivals which were to be observed every year. The first three verses of Lev. 23. do not relate to the feasts but separate the sabbath from the feasts.

<hi type="bold">Passover</hi><div eID="gen671" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen672" type="x-p"/> The Passover, <reference osisRef="le 23:4 le 23:5">Leviticus 23:4,5</reference>. This feast is memorial and brings into view redemption, upon which all blessing rests. Typically, it stands for "Christ our passover, sacrificed for us." <reference osisRef="1co 5:7">1 Corinthians 5:7</reference>.<div eID="gen672" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen673" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">first month</hi> i.e. April.

<hi type="bold">bread</hi><div eID="gen673" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen674" type="x-p"/> The feast of Unleavened Bread, <reference osisRef="le 23:6-8">Leviticus 23:6-8</reference>. This feast speaks of communion with Christ, the unleavened wave-loaf, in the full blessing of His redemption, and of a holy walk. The divine order here is beautiful; first redemption, then a holy walk. ; <reference osisRef="1co 5:6-8">1 Corinthians 5:6-8</reference>; <reference osisRef="2co 7:1">2 Corinthians 7:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="ga 5:7-9">Galatians 5:7-9</reference>.

<hi type="bold">first fruits</hi><div eID="gen674" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen675" type="x-p"/> The feast of Firstfruits, <reference osisRef="le 23:10-14">Leviticus 23:10-14</reference>. This feast is typical of resurrection--first of Christ, then of "them that are Christ's at His coming" ; <reference osisRef="1co 15:23">1 Corinthians 15:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="1th 4:13-18">1 Thessalonians 4:13-18</reference>.

<hi type="bold">fifty days</hi><div eID="gen675" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen676" type="x-p"/> The feast of Pentecost, <reference osisRef="le 23:15-22">Leviticus 23:15-22</reference>. The anti-type is the descent of the Holy Spirit to form the church. For this reason leaven is present, because there is evil in the church ; <reference osisRef="mt 13:33">Matthew 13:33</reference>; <reference osisRef="ac 5:1 ac 5:10">Acts 5:1,10</reference>; <reference osisRef="ac 15:1">Acts 15:1</reference>. Observe, it is now loaves; not a sheaf of separate growths loosely bound together, but a real union of particles making one homogenous body. The descent of the Holy Spirit at Pentecost united the separated disciples into one organism. ; <reference osisRef="1co 10:16 1co 10:17">1 Corinthians 10:16,17</reference>; <reference osisRef="1co 12:12 1co 12:13 1co 12:20"> 12:12,13,20</reference>.

<hi type="bold">wave-loaves</hi><div eID="gen676" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen677" type="x-p"/> The wave-loaves were offered fifty days after the wave-sheaf. This is precisely the period between the resurrection of Christ and the formation of the church at Pentecost by the baptism of the Holy Spirit <reference osisRef="ac 2:1-4">Acts 2:1-4</reference>; <reference osisRef="1co 12:12 1co 12:13">1 Corinthians 12:12,13</reference>. See "Church" ; <reference osisRef="mt 16:18">Matthew 16:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="heb 12:22 heb 12:23">Hebrews 12:22,23</reference>. With the wave-sheaf no leaven was offered, for there was no evil in Christ; but the wave-loaves, typifying the church, are "baken with leaven," for in the church there is still evil.

<hi type="bold">trumpets</hi><div eID="gen677" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen678" type="x-p"/> The feast of Trumpets, <reference osisRef="le 23:23-25">Leviticus 23:23-25</reference>. This feast is a prophetical type and refers to the future regathering of long-dispersed Israel. A long interval elapses between Pentecost and Trumpets, answering to the long period occupied in the pentecostal work of the Holy Spirit in the present dispensation. Study carefully ; <reference osisRef="isa 18:3">Isaiah 18:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="isa 27:13"> 27:13</reference> (with contexts); <reference osisRef="isa 58:1-14">Isaiah 58:1-14</reference> (entire chapter), and ; <reference osisRef="joe 2:1-joe 3:21">Joel 2:1-3:21</reference>; in connection with the "trumpets," and it will be seen that these trumpets, always symbols of testimony, are connected with the regathering and repentance of Israel after the church, or pentecostal period is ended. This feast is immediately followed by the day of atonement.<div eID="gen678" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen679" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">seventh month</hi> <div eID="gen679" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen680" type="x-p"/> i.e. October; also <reference osisRef="le 23:27 le 23:34 le 23:39 le 23:41">Leviticus 23:27,34,39,41</reference>.

<hi type="bold">atonement</hi><div eID="gen680" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen681" type="x-p"/> The day of Atonement, <reference osisRef="le 23:26-32">Leviticus 23:26-32</reference>. The day is the same described in Lev. 16., but here the stress is laid upon the sorrow and repentance of Israel. In other words, the prophetical feature is made prominent, and that looks forward to the repentance of Israel after her regathering under the Palestinian Covenant, <reference osisRef="de 30:1-10">Deuteronomy 30:1-10</reference> preparatory to the second advent of Messiah and the establishment of the kingdom. See the connection between the "trumpet" in <reference osisRef="joe 2:1">Joel 2:1</reference> and the mourning which follows in verses <reference osisRef="joe 2:11-15">Joel 2:11-15</reference>.<div eID="gen681" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen682" type="x-p"/> Also <reference osisRef="zec 12:10-13">Zechariah 12:10-13</reference> in connection with the atonement of <reference osisRef="zec 13:1">Zechariah 13:1</reference>. Historically the "fountain" of <reference osisRef="zec 13:1">Zechariah 13:1</reference> was opened at the crucifixion, but rejected by the Jews of that and the succeeding centuries. After the regathering of Israel the fountain will be efficaciously "opened" to Israel.<div eID="gen682" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen683" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">atonement</hi> <div eID="gen683" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen684" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ex 29:33">Exodus 29:33</reference>")</hi>.

<hi type="bold">booths</hi><div eID="gen684" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen685" type="x-p"/> The feast of Tabernacles, <reference osisRef="le 23:34-44">Leviticus 23:34-44</reference> is (like the Lord's Supper for the church) both memorial and prophetic --memorial as to redemption out of Egypt <reference osisRef="le 23:43">Leviticus 23:43</reference> prophetic as to the kingdom-rest of Israel after her regathering and restoration, when the feast again becomes memorial, not for Israel alone, but for all nations. <reference osisRef="zec 14:16-21">Zechariah 14:16-21</reference>. <chapter eID="Lev.23"/><div eID="gen685" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen686" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="25" osisID="Lev.25" sID="Lev.25"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv26"/><title type="x-s">Book Introduction - Numbers</title> <div sID="gen711" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="nu 1">Read first chapter of Numbers</reference><div eID="gen711" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen712" type="x-p"/> The book derives its name from the fact that it records the enumeration of Israel. Historically, NUMBERS takes up the story where EXODUS left it, and is the book of the wilderness wanderings of the redeemed people consequent upon their failure to enter the land at Kadesh-barnea.<div eID="gen712" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen713" type="x-p"/> Typically, it is the book of service and walk, and thus completes, with the preceding books, a beautiful moral order: GENESIS, the book of the creation and fall; EXODUS, of redemption; LEVITICUS, of worship and fellowship; and NUMBERS, of that which should follow--service and walk.<div eID="gen713" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen714" type="x-p"/> It is important to see that nothing was left to self-will. Every servant was numbered, knew his place in the family, and had his own definitely assigned service. The N.T. parallel is 1 Cor. 12.<div eID="gen714" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen715" type="x-p"/> The second typical lesson is that, tested by wilderness circumstances, Israel utterly failed.<div eID="gen715" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen716" type="x-p"/> NUMBERS is in five chief divisions:<div eID="gen716" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">The Order of the Host, 1:1-10:10</item> <item type="x-indent-1">From Sinai to Kadesh-barnea, 10:11-12:16,</item> <item type="x-indent-1">Israel at Kadesh-barnea, 13:1-19:22,</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The Wilderness Wanderings, 20:1-33:49,</item> <item type="x-indent-1">Closing Instructions, 33:50-36:13.</item> </list> <div sID="gen717" type="x-p"/> The events covered in NUMBERS cover a period of 39 years (Ussher). <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv26"/><hi type="bold">second month</hi><div eID="gen717" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen718" type="x-p"/> i.e. May; also <reference osisRef="nu 1:18">Numbers 1:18</reference>.

<hi type="bold">Moses, saying</hi> <div eID="gen726" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen727" type="x-p"/> There is a beautiful moral order in chapters 6.-7.; separation, <reference osisRef="nu 6:1-12">Numbers 6:1-12,</reference> worship, <reference osisRef="nu 6:13-21">Numbers 6:13-21,</reference> blessing, <reference osisRef="nu 6:22-27">Numbers 6:22-27</reference> service, <reference osisRef="nu 7:1-89">Numbers 7:1-89</reference>. See <reference osisRef="heb 13:12-16">Hebrews 13:12-16</reference>.

<hi type="bold">Nazarite</hi><div eID="gen727" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen728" type="x-p"/> The Nazarite (more accurately Nazirite, one separated) was a person of either sex separated wholly unto the Lord. Abstention from wine, the symbol of mere natural joy <reference osisRef="ps 104:15">Psalms 104:15</reference> was the expression of a devotedness which found all its joy in the Lord (cf) ; <reference osisRef="ps 87:7">Psalms 87:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="ps 97:12"> 97:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="hab 3:18">Habakkuk 3:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="phm 3:1 phm 3:3">Philemon 3:1,3</reference>; <reference osisRef="phm 4:4 phm 4:10"> 4:4,10</reference>. The long hair, naturally a reproach to man <reference osisRef="1co 11:14">1 Corinthians 11:14</reference> was at once the visible sign of the Nazarite's separation, and of his willingness to bear reproach for Jehovah's sake. The type found its perfect fulfilment in Jesus, who was "holy, harmless, undefiled and separate from sinners" <reference osisRef="heb 7:26">Hebrews 7:26</reference> who was utterly separated unto the Father ; <reference osisRef="joh 1:18">John 1:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="joh 6:38"> 6:38</reference> who allowed no mere natural claim to hinder or divert Him. <reference osisRef="mt 12:46-50">Matthew 12:46-50</reference>.

<hi type="bold">atonement</hi><div eID="gen728" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen729" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ex 29:33">Exodus 29:33</reference>")</hi>. <chapter eID="Num.6"/><div eID="gen729" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen730" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="7" osisID="Num.7" sID="Num.7"/>

<hi type="bold">mixt mixed</hi> <div eID="gen743" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen744" type="x-p"/> CF. <reference osisRef="ex 12:38">Exodus 12:38</reference>. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ex 12:38">Exodus 12:38</reference>")</hi>. Unconverted church members, unable to desire or understand Christ as the Bread of God <reference osisRef="ex 16:35">Exodus 16:35</reference>. See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:ex 16:35">Exodus 16:35</reference>" will clamour for things pleasing to the flesh in the work and way of the church: sumptuous buildings, ornate ritual, an easy doctrine. Alas! they lead away the unspiritual believers also.
<hi type="bold">manna</hi><div eID="gen744" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen745" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ex 16:35">Exodus 16:35</reference>")</hi>.

<hi type="bold">spirit that was upon him</hi><div eID="gen745" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen746" type="x-p"/> There was no more power than before--only more machinery. Moses had murmured (<reference osisRef="nu 5:11">Numbers 5:11</reference>) because of the burden that God had laid upon him. God, in distributing the burden, shows that Moses' power had, all along, been in proportion to his burden.

<hi type="bold">two cubits high upon the face of all the earth</hi><div eID="gen746" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen747" type="x-p"/> The correct rendering is, "about two cubits above the face of the earth," that is, within reach of the people that they might slay them for food. The statement is not that the quails were piled up from the face of the earth two cubits deep. The level of their flight was two cubits above the earth.

<hi type="bold">Kibroth-hattaavah</hi><div eID="gen747" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen748" type="x-p"/> i.e. graves of lust. <reference osisRef="nu 33:17">Numbers 33:17</reference> <chapter eID="Num.11"/><div eID="gen748" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen749" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="12" osisID="Num.12" sID="Num.12"/>

<hi type="bold">Kibroth-hattaavah</hi> <div eID="gen749" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen750" type="x-p"/> i.e. graves of lust. <reference osisRef="nu 33:17">Numbers 33:17</reference> <chapter eID="Num.12"/><div eID="gen750" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen751" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="13" osisID="Num.13" sID="Num.13"/>
<hi type="bold">Jehoshua</hi> <div eID="gen751" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen752" type="x-p"/> i.e. Saviour, or Deliverer.

<hi type="bold">Surely</hi><div eID="gen752" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen753" type="x-p"/> Kadesh-barnea is, by the unbelief of Israel there, and the divine comment on that unbelief <reference osisRef="nu 14:22-38">Numbers 14:22-38</reference>; <reference osisRef="de 1:19-40">Deuteronomy 1:19-40</reference>; <reference osisRef="1co 10:1-5">1 Corinthians 10:1-5</reference>; <reference osisRef="heb 3:12-19">Hebrews 3:12-19</reference> invested with immense spiritual significance. The people had faith to sprinkle the blood of atonement <reference osisRef="ex 12:28">Exodus 12:28</reference> and to come out of Egypt (the world), but had not faith to enter their Canaan rest. Therefore, though redeemed, they were a forty years' grief to Jehovah. The spiritual application is made in Heb. <reference osisRef="ex 6:3-11"> 6:3-11</reference>:<div eID="gen753" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen754" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Heb 6:4">Hebrews 6:4</reference>")</hi>. <chapter eID="Num.13"/><div eID="gen754" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen755" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="15" osisID="Num.15" sID="Num.15"/>

<hi type="bold">wandering</hi> <div eID="gen755" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen756" type="x-p"/> The wilderness was part of the necessary discipline of the redeemed people, but not the years of wandering. The latter were due wholly to the unbelief of the people at Kadesh-barnea. The Red Sea, Marah, Elim, Sinai, were God's ways, in development and discipline, and have, of necessity, their counterpart in Christian experience. The Red Sea speaks of the cross as that which--death to Christ but life for us--separates us from Egypt, the world <reference osisRef="ga 6:14">Galatians 6:14</reference> Marah of God's power to turn untoward things into blessings; Elim of God's power to give rest and refreshment by the way; Sinai of God's holiness and our deep inherent evil, the experience of <reference osisRef="ro 7:7-24">Romans 7:7-24</reference> So far the path was and is of God. But from Kadesh-barnea to Jordan all save the grace of God toward an unbelieving people, is for warning, not imitation ; <reference osisRef="1co 10:1-11">1 Corinthians 10:1-11</reference>; <reference osisRef="heb 3:17-19">Hebrews 3:17-19</reference>. There is a present rest of God, of which the Sabbath and Canaan were types, into which believers may, and therefore should, enter by faith <reference osisRef="heb 3:1-heb 4:16">Hebrews 3:1-4:16</reference>.

<hi type="bold">When</hi><div eID="gen756" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen757" type="x-p"/> It is remarkable that just when the people are turning in unbelief from the land, God gives directions for conduct when they shall have entered it. See <reference osisRef="ro 11:29">Romans 11:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="php 1:6">Philippians 1:6</reference>.
<hi type="bold">atonement</hi><div eID="gen757" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen758" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ex 29:33">Exodus 29:33</reference>")</hi>.

<hi type="bold">ribband of blue</hi><div eID="gen758" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen759" type="x-p"/> The ribband of blue. Blue, the heavenly colour, used upon the borders of the priests' garments signified that the servants of God were to be heavenly in obedience and character, and separate from earthly ambitions and desires. <chapter eID="Num.15"/><div eID="gen759" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen760" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="16" osisID="Num.16" sID="Num.16"/>

<hi type="bold">Seek ye the priesthood also</hi> <div eID="gen760" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen761" type="x-p"/> The "gainsaying of Korah" was intrusion into the priest's office ("no man taketh this honour unto himself,") <reference osisRef="heb 5:4">Hebrews 5:4</reference>. It was an attempt to create a priestly order without the divine authority <reference osisRef="heb 5:10">Hebrews 5:10</reference>. The modern analogue is Nicolaitanism <reference osisRef="re 2:6 re 2:15">Revelation 2:6,15</reference> the division of an equal brotherhood <reference osisRef="mt 23:8">Matthew 23:8</reference> into "clergy" and "laity"; a vastly different thing from the due recognition of ministry-gifts ; <reference osisRef="1co 12:4-31">1 Corinthians 12:4-31</reference>; <reference osisRef="eph 4:8 eph 4:11 eph 4:12">Ephesians 4:8,11,12</reference> or of elders and deacons ; <reference osisRef="1ti 3:1-13">1 Timothy 3:1-13</reference>; <reference osisRef="tit 1:5-9">Titus 1:5-9</reference>.

<hi type="bold">atonement</hi><div eID="gen761" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen762" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ex 29:33">Exodus 29:33</reference>")</hi> <chapter eID="Num.16"/> <div eID="gen762" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen763" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="17" osisID="Num.17" sID="Num.17"/>

<hi type="bold">rod of Aaron</hi> <div eID="gen763" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen764" type="x-p"/> Aaron's rod that budded: Type of Christ in resurrection, owned of God as High Priest. Aaron's priesthood had been questioned in the rebellion of Korah, so God Himself will confirm it <reference osisRef="nu 17:5">Numbers 17:5</reference>. Each of the tribe-heads brought a perfectly dead rod; God put life into Aaron's only. So all the authors of religions have died, Christ among them, but only Christ was raised from the dead, and exalted to be a high priest. ; <reference osisRef="heb 4:14">Hebrews 4:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="heb 5:4-10"> 5:4-10</reference>. <div eID="gen764" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv27"/><div sID="gen765" type="x-p"/> <chapter eID="Num.17"/>
<div eID="gen765" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen766" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="18" osisID="Num.18" sID="Num.18"/>

<hi type="bold">bear</hi> <div eID="gen766" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen767" type="x-p"/> i.e. be responsible for every neglect or offence relation to. CF. <reference osisRef="ex 28:38">Exodus 28:38</reference>. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ex 28:38">Exodus 28:38</reference>")</hi>.

<hi type="bold">red heifer</hi><div eID="gen767" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen768" type="x-p"/> The red heifer: Type of the sacrifice of Christ as the ground of the cleansing of the believer from the defilement contracted in his pilgrim walk through this world, and illustration of the method of his cleansing. The order is:<div eID="gen768" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(1) the slaying of the sacrifice;</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(2) the sevenfold sprinkling of the blood, typical public testimony before the eyes of all of the complete and never-to-be-repeated putting away of all the believer's sin as before God. <reference osisRef="heb 9:12-14">Hebrews 9:12-14</reference>; <reference osisRef="heb 10:10-12"> 10:10-12</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(3) the reduction of the sacrifice to ashes which are preserved and become a memorial of the sacrifice;</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(4) the cleansing from defilement (sin has two aspects--guilt and uncleanness) by sprinkling with the ashes mingled with water. Water is a type of both the Spirit and the Word. <reference osisRef="joh 7:37-39">John 7:37-39</reference>. <reference osisRef="eph 5:26">Ephesians 5:26</reference>. The operation typified is this: the Holy Spirit used the Word to convict the believer of some evil allowed in his life to the hindering of his joy, growth, and service. Thus convicted, he remembers that the guilt of his sin has been met by the sacrifice of Christ <reference osisRef="1jo 1:7">1 John 1:7</reference>. Instead, therefore, of despairing, the convicted believer judges and confesses the defiling thing as unworthy a saint, and is forgiven and cleansed ; <reference osisRef="joh 13:3-10">John 13:3-10</reference>; <reference osisRef="1jo 1:7-10">1 John 1:7-10</reference>. </item> </list>

<hi type="bold">speak ye unto the rock before their eyes</hi><div eID="gen774" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen775" type="x-p"/> See <reference osisRef="ex 17:5">Exodus 17:5</reference>. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ex 17:5">Exodus 17:5</reference>")</hi>.<div eID="gen775" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen776" type="x-p"/> The rock (Christ) <reference osisRef="1co 10:4">1 Corinthians 10:4</reference> once smitten, needs not to be smitten (crucified) again. Moses' act exalted himself <reference osisRef="nu 20:10">Numbers 20:10</reference> and implied (in type) that the one sacrifice was ineffectual, thus denying the eternal efficacy of the blood ; <reference osisRef="heb 9:25 heb 9:26">Hebrews 9:25,26</reference>; <reference osisRef="heb 10:3 heb 10:11 heb 10:12"> 10:3,11,12</reference>. The abundant water (grace reaching the need of the people, despite the error of their leader) tells of refreshing and power through the Spirit.
<hi type="bold">angel</hi><div eID="gen776" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen777" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Heb 1:4">Hebrews 1:4</reference>")</hi>.

Henceforth Israel marches or halts, but does not wander.<div eID="gen778" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen779" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Nu 15:1">Numbers 15:1</reference>")</hi>. <chapter eID="Num.20"/><div eID="gen779" type="x-p"/>

<hi type="bold">Hormah</hi> <div eID="gen780" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen781" type="x-p"/> i.e. utter destruction.

<hi type="bold">serpent</hi><div eID="gen781" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen782" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ge 3:14">Genesis 3:14</reference>")</hi>. The serpent is a symbol of sin judged; brass speaks of the divine judgment, as in the brazen altar See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:ex 27:1">Exodus 27:1</reference>", note (2) and self-judgment, as in the laver of brass. The brazen serpent is a type of Christ "made sin for us" ; <reference osisRef="joh 3:14 joh 3:15">John 3:14,15</reference>; <reference osisRef="2co 5:21">2 Corinthians 5:21</reference> in bearing our judgment. Historically, the moment is indicated in the cry: "My God, My God, why hast Thou forsaken Me?" <reference osisRef="mt 27:46">Matthew 27:46</reference>.

<hi type="bold">Then Israel</hi><div eID="gen782" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen783" type="x-p"/> The spiritual order here is beautiful:<div eID="gen783" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(1) atonement <reference osisRef="nu 21:8 nu 21:9">Numbers 21:8,9</reference>; <reference osisRef="joh 3:14 joh 3:15">John 3:14,15</reference></item> <item type="x-indent-1">(2) water, symbol of the Spirit bestowed <reference osisRef="nu 21:16">Numbers 21:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="joh 7:37-39">John 7:37-39</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(3) joy <reference osisRef="nu 21:17 nu 21:18">Numbers 21:17,18</reference>; <reference osisRef="ro 14:17">Romans 14:17</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(4) power <reference osisRef="nu 21:21-24">Numbers 21:21-24</reference>. </item> </list> <chapter eID="Num.21"/>
<div sID="gen784" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="22" osisID="Num.22" sID="Num.22"/>

<hi type="bold">Balaam</hi> <div eID="gen784" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen785" type="x-p"/> Balaam is the typical hireling prophet, seeking only to make a market of his gift. This is "the way of Balaam" <reference osisRef="2pe 2:15">2 Peter 2:15</reference> and characterizes false teachers. The "error" of Balaam" <reference osisRef="jude 1:11">Jude 1:11</reference> was that he could see only the natural morality--a holy God, he reasoned, must curse such a people as Israel. Like all false teachers he was ignorant of the higher morality of vicarious atonement, by which God could be just and yet the justifier of believing sinners <reference osisRef="ro 3:26">Romans 3:26</reference>. The "doctrine of Balaam" <reference osisRef="re 2:14">Revelation 2:14</reference> refers to his teaching Balak to corrupt the people whom he could not curse ; <reference osisRef="nu 31:16">Numbers 31:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="nu 25:1-3"> 25:1-3</reference>; <reference osisRef="jas 4:4">James 4:4</reference>. Spiritually, Balaamism in teaching never rises above natural reasonings; in practice, it is easy world- conformity. Scofield "<reference osisRef="re 2:14">Revelation 2:14</reference>".

<hi type="bold">not go</hi><div eID="gen785" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen786" type="x-p"/> Cf. <reference osisRef="nu 22:12">Numbers 22:12</reference>. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ge 46:3">Genesis 46:3</reference>")</hi>.

<hi type="bold">anger</hi><div eID="gen786" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen787" type="x-p"/> (Cf) <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ge 46:3">Genesis 46:3</reference>")</hi>. In <reference osisRef="nu 22:12">Numbers 22:12</reference> the directive will of Jehovah is made known to Balaam, in <reference osisRef="nu 22:20">Numbers 22:20</reference> Jehovah's permissive will. The prophet is now free to go, but knows the true mind of the Lord about it. The matter is wholly one between Jehovah and His servant. The permission of <reference osisRef="nu 22:20">Numbers 22:20</reference> really constitutes a testing of Balaam. He chose the path of self-will and self- advantage, and Jehovah could not but gravely disapprove. The whole scene, <reference osisRef="nu 22:22-35">Numbers 22:22-35</reference> prepared Balaam for what was to follow.<div eID="gen787" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen788" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">angel</hi> <div eID="gen788" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen789" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Heb 1:4">Hebrews 1:4</reference>")</hi>
<hi type="bold">angel</hi> <div eID="gen789" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen790" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Heb 1:4">Hebrews 1:4</reference>")</hi>

<hi type="bold">utmost</hi> <div eID="gen790" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen791" type="x-p"/> "Utmost part," etc., means the end of the encampment, the "fourth part of Israel" <reference osisRef="nu 23:10">Numbers 23:10</reference>. Balak's thought, as Grant (following Keil) points out, was not at all to permit Balaam to see the whole of the Hebrew host. In bringing Balaam to Pisgah <reference osisRef="nu 22:13 nu 22:14">Numbers 22:13,14</reference>. Balak corrects what, evidently, he thought a blunder. <reference osisRef="nu 23:13 nu 23:14">Numbers 23:13,14</reference>. But when the hireling sees the whole camp he must utter a grander word than before, "He hath not beheld iniquity in Jacob," and that with the nation in full view! What an illustration of the truth of <reference osisRef="ro 4:5-8">Romans 4:5-8</reference>. <div eID="gen791" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv28"/><div sID="gen792" type="x-p"/> <chapter eID="Num.22"/>

Balak's thought, as Grant (following Keil) points out, was not at all to permit Balaam to see the whole of the Hebrew host. In bringing Balaam to Pisgah <reference osisRef="nu 22:13 nu 22:14">Numbers 22:13,14</reference>. Balak corrects what, evidently, he thought a blunder. <reference osisRef="nu 23:13 nu 23:14">Numbers 23:13,14</reference>. But when the hireling sees the whole camp he must utter a grander word than before, "He hath not beheld iniquity in Jacob," and that with the nation in full view! What an illustration of the truth of <reference osisRef="ro 4:5-8">Romans 4:5-8</reference>.

<hi type="bold">and said</hi><div eID="gen794" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen795" type="x-p"/> In the prophecies of Balaam God testifies on behalf of His people rather than (as usual) to them. It is the divine testimony to their standing as a redeemed people in view of the serpent "lifted up," and of the water from the smitten rock. <reference osisRef="nu 21:5-9">Numbers 21:5-9</reference>; <reference osisRef="nu 20:11"> 20:11</reference>. Their state was morally bad, but this was a matter concerning the discipline of God, not His judgment. The interpretation of the prophecies is literal as to Israel, typical as to Christians. Through Christ "lifted up" <reference osisRef="joh 3:14">John 3:14</reference> our standing is eternally secure and perfect, though our state may require the Father's discipline ; <reference osisRef="1co 11:30-32">1 Corinthians 11:30-32</reference>; <reference osisRef="2co 1:4-9">2 Corinthians 1:4-9</reference>; <reference osisRef="2co 1:10-13"> 1:10-13</reference> meantime, against all enemies, God is "for us." <reference osisRef="ro 8:31">Romans 8:31</reference>.

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv28"/><title type="x-s">Book Introduction - Deuteronomy</title> <div sID="gen830" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="de 1">Read first chapter of Deuteronomy</reference><div eID="gen830" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen831" type="x-p"/> DEUTERONOMY consists of the parting counsels of Moses delivered to Israel in view of the impending entrance upon their covenanted possession. It contains a summary of the wilderness wanderings of Israel, which is important as unfolding the moral judgement of God upon those events; repeats the Decalogue to a generation which had grown up in the wilderness; gives needed instruction as the conduct of Israel in the land, and contains the Palestinian Covenant (<reference osisRef="de 30:1-9">Deuteronomy 30:1-9</reference>). The book breathes the sternness of the Law. Key- words, "Thou shalt"; key-verses, <reference osisRef="de 11:26-28">Deuteronomy 11:26-28</reference>.<div eID="gen831" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen832" type="x-p"/> It is important to note that, while the land of promise was unconditionally given Abraham and to his seed in the Abrahamic Covenant (<reference osisRef="ge 13:15">Genesis 13:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="ge 15:7"> 15:7</reference>), it was under the conditional Palestinian Covenant (<reference osisRef="de 28:1-de 30:9">Deuteronomy 28:1-30:9</reference>) that Israel entered the land under Joshua. Utterly violating the conditions of that covenant, the nation was first disrupted (1 Kings 12) and then cast out of the land (<reference osisRef="2ki 17:1-18">2 Kings 17:1-18</reference>; <reference osisRef="2ki 24:1-2ki 25:11"> 24:1-25:11</reference>). But the same covenant unconditionally promises a national restoration of Israel which is yet to be fulfilled <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:De 15:18">De 15:18</reference>")</hi>.<div eID="gen832" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen833" type="x-p"/> DEUTERONOMY is in seven divisions:<div eID="gen833" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">Summary of the history of Israel in the wilderness, 1:1-3:29</item> <item type="x-indent-1">A restatement of the Law, with warnings and exhortations, 4:1 -11:32,</item> <item type="x-indent-1">Instructions, Warnings, and Predictions, 12:1-27:26,</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The great closing prophecies summarizing the history of Israel to the second coming of Christ, and containing the Palestinian Covenant, 28:1-30:20,</item> <item type="x-indent-1">Last counsels to Priests, Levites, and to Joshua, 31,</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The Song of Moses and his parting blessings, 32,33,</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The Death of Moses, 34.</item> </list> <div sID="gen834" type="x-p"/> The time covered by this retrospect is approximately forty years. <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv28"/><hi type="bold">eleven days</hi><div eID="gen834" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen835" type="x-p"/> Prolonged by one act of unbelief to forty years. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Nu 14:23">Numbers 14:23</reference>")</hi>.
<hi type="bold">eleventh</hi><div eID="gen835" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen836" type="x-p"/> i.e. February. <chapter eID="Deut.1"/><div eID="gen836" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen837" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="2" osisID="Deut.2" sID="Deut.2"/>

Between, in <reference osisRef="de 16:9-12">Deuteronomy 16:9-12</reference> comes the Feast of Weeks--the joy of a redeemed people, anticipating a greater blessing yet to come. <hi type="bold">turn thy captivity</hi> <div eID="gen886" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen887" type="x-p"/> The Palestinian Covenant gives the conditions under which Israel entered the land of promise. It is important to see that the nation has never as yet taken the land under the unconditional Abrahamic Covenant, nor has it ever possessed the whole land (cf. <reference osisRef="ge 15:18">Genesis 15:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="nu 34:1-12">Numbers 34:1-12</reference>. The Palestinian Covenant is in seven parts.<div eID="gen887" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen888" type="x-p"/><div eID="gen888" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(1) Dispersion for disobedience, <reference osisRef="de 30:1">Deuteronomy 30:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="de 28:63-68"> 28:63-68</reference> <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ge 15:18">Genesis 15:18</reference>")</hi></item> <item type="x-indent-1">(2) The future repentance of Israel while in the dispersion, <reference osisRef="de 30:2">Deuteronomy 30:2</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(3) The return of the Lord, <reference osisRef="de 30:3">Deuteronomy 30:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="am 9:9-14">Amos 9:9-14</reference>; <reference osisRef="ac 15:14-17">Acts 15:14-17</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(4) Restoration to the land, <reference osisRef="de 30:5">Deuteronomy 30:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="isa 11:11 isa 11:12">Isaiah 11:11,12</reference>; <reference osisRef="jer 23:3-8">Jeremiah 23:3-8</reference>; <reference osisRef="eze 37:21-25">Ezekiel 37:21-25</reference></item> <item type="x-indent-1">(5) National conversion, <reference osisRef="de 30:6">Deuteronomy 30:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="ro 11:26 ro 11:27">Romans 11:26,27</reference>; <reference osisRef="ho 2:14-16">Hosea 2:14-16</reference></item> <item type="x-indent-1">(6) The judgment of Israel's oppressors, <reference osisRef="de 30:7">Deuteronomy 30:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="isa 14:1 isa 14:2">Isaiah 14:1,2</reference>; <reference osisRef="joe 3:1-8">Joel 3:1-8</reference>; <reference osisRef="mt 25:31-46">Matthew 25:31-46</reference></item> <item type="x-indent-1">(7) National prosperity, <reference osisRef="de 30:9">Deuteronomy 30:9</reference>;
