<chapter n="1" osisID="Josh.1" sID="Josh.1"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv29"/><title type="x-s">Book Introduction - Joshua</title> <div sID="gen900" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="jos 1">Read first chapter of Joshua</reference><div eID="gen900" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen901" type="x-p"/> Joshua records the consummation of the redemption of Israel of Israel out of Egypt; for redemption has two parts: "out," and "into" (<reference osisRef="de 6:23">Deuteronomy 6:23</reference>). The key-phrase is "Moses My servant is dead" (<reference osisRef="jos 1:2">Joshua 1:2</reference>). Law, of which Moses is the representative, could never give a sinful people victory (<reference osisRef="heb 7:19">Hebrews 7:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="ro 6:14">Romans 6:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="ro 8:2-4"> 8:2-4</reference>).<div eID="gen901" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen902" type="x-p"/> In a spiritual sense the book of Joshua is the Ephesians of the Old Testament. "The heavenly" of Ephesians is to the Christian what Canaan was to the Israelite and blessing through divine power (<reference osisRef="jos 21:43-55">Joshua 21:43-55</reference>; <reference osisRef="eph 1:3">Ephesians 1:3</reference>)<div eID="gen902" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen903" type="x-p"/> The government, as before, was theocratic; Joshua succeeding Moses as the ruler under God.<div eID="gen903" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen904" type="x-p"/> Joshua falls into four parts:<div eID="gen904" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">The conquest, 1-12.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The partition of the inheritance, 13-21.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">Incipient discord, 22.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">Joshua's last counsels and death, 23,24.</item> </list> <div sID="gen905" type="x-p"/> The events recorded in Joshua cover a period of 26 years (Ussher). <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv29"/><hi type="bold">Every place</hi><div eID="gen905" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen906" type="x-p"/> The law of appropriation. God gives, but we must take. <chapter eID="Josh.1"/><div eID="gen906" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen907" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="2" osisID="Josh.2" sID="Josh.2"/>

<hi type="bold">scarlet line</hi> <div eID="gen907" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen908" type="x-p"/> The scarlet line of Rahab speaks, by its color, of safety through sacrifice. <reference osisRef="heb 9:19 heb 9:22">Hebrews 9:19,22</reference>. <div eID="gen908" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv30"/><div sID="gen909" type="x-p"/> <chapter eID="Josh.2"/>
<div eID="gen909" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen910" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="3" osisID="Josh.3" sID="Josh.3"/>

<hi type="bold">Jordan</hi> <div eID="gen910" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen911" type="x-p"/> The passage of Jordan, type of our death with Christ <reference osisRef="ro 6:6-11">Romans 6:6-11</reference>; <reference osisRef="eph 2:5 eph 2:6">Ephesians 2:5,6</reference>; <reference osisRef="col 3:1-3">Colossians 3:1-3</reference>. <chapter eID="Josh.3"/><div eID="gen911" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen912" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="4" osisID="Josh.4" sID="Josh.4"/>

<hi type="bold">The two memorials</hi> <div eID="gen912" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen913" type="x-p"/> The two memorials. The twelve stones taken out of Jordan and erected by Joshua in Gilgal, and the twelve stones left in Jordan to be overwhelmed by its waters, are memorials marking the distinction between Christ's death under judgment in the believer's place <reference osisRef="ps 42:7">Psalms 42:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="ps 88:7"> 88:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="joh 12:31-33">John 12:31-33</reference> and the believer's perfect deliverance from judgment. The stones in Jordan stand, typically, for <reference osisRef="ps 22:1-8">Psalms 22:1-8</reference>.
<hi type="bold">first month</hi><div eID="gen913" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen914" type="x-p"/> i.e. April. <chapter eID="Josh.4"/><div eID="gen914" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen915" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="5" osisID="Josh.5" sID="Josh.5"/>

<hi type="bold">circumcision</hi> <div eID="gen915" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen916" type="x-p"/> Circumcision is the "sign" of the Abrahamic Covenant <reference osisRef="ge 17:7-14">Genesis 17:7-14</reference>; <reference osisRef="ro 4:11">Romans 4:11</reference>. "The reproach of Egypt" was that, during the later years of the Egyptian bondage, this separating sign had been neglected (cf. <reference osisRef="ex 4:24-26">Exodus 4:24-26</reference> and this neglect had continued during the wilderness wanderings. The N.T. analogue is world conformity; the failure openly to take a believer's place with Christ in death and resurrection. ; <reference osisRef="ro 6:2-11">Romans 6:2-11</reference>; <reference osisRef="ga 6:14-16">Galatians 6:14-16</reference>. Spiritually it is mortifying the deeds of the body through the Spirit. ; <reference osisRef="ro 8:13">Romans 8:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="ga 5:16 ga 5:17">Galatians 5:16,17</reference>; <reference osisRef="col 2:11 col 2:12">Colossians 2:11,12</reference>; <reference osisRef="col 3:5-10"> 3:5-10</reference>.

<hi type="bold">corn</hi><div eID="gen916" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen917" type="x-p"/> The manna is a type of Christ in humiliation, known "after the flesh," giving his flesh that the believer might have life <reference osisRef="joh 6:49-51">John 6:49-51</reference> while the "old corn of the land" is Christ apprehended as risen, glorified, and seated in the heavenlies. Occupation with Christ on earth, "crucified through weakness," tends to a wilderness experience. An experience befitting the believer's place in the heavenlies demands an apprehension of the power of His resurrection ; <reference osisRef="2co 5:16">2 Corinthians 5:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="2co 13:4"> 13:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="php 3:10">Philippians 3:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="eph 1:15-23">Ephesians 1:15-23</reference>. It is the contrast between "milk" and "meat" in Paul's writings. ; <reference osisRef="1co 3:1 1co 3:2">1 Corinthians 3:1,2</reference>; <reference osisRef="heb 5:12-14">Hebrews 5:12-14</reference>; <reference osisRef="heb 6:1-3"> 6:1-3</reference>.

<hi type="bold">holy</hi><div eID="gen917" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen918" type="x-p"/> Trans. "consecrated," <reference osisRef="jos 6:19">Joshua 6:19</reference> in R.V. "holy." <div eID="gen918" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv30"/><div sID="gen919" type="x-p"/> <chapter eID="Josh.5"/>
<div eID="gen919" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen920" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="6" osisID="Josh.6" sID="Josh.6"/>
<hi type="bold">holy</hi> <div eID="gen920" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen921" type="x-p"/> Trans. "consecrated," <reference osisRef="jos 6:19">Joshua 6:19</reference> in R.V. "holy."

<hi type="bold">And it shall come to pass</hi><div eID="gen921" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen922" type="x-p"/> The central truth here is that spiritual victories are won by means and upon principles utterly foolish and inadequate in the view of human wisdom. <reference osisRef="1co 1:17-29">1 Corinthians 1:17-29</reference>; <reference osisRef="2co 10:3-5">2 Corinthians 10:3-5</reference>. <chapter eID="Josh.6"/><div eID="gen922" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen923" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="7" osisID="Josh.7" sID="Josh.7"/>

<hi type="bold">Israel</hi> <div eID="gen923" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen924" type="x-p"/> The sin of Achan and its results teach the great truth of the oneness of the people of God, <reference osisRef="jos 7:11">Joshua 7:11</reference>. "Israel hath sinned." See in illustration ; <reference osisRef="1co 5:1-7">1 Corinthians 5:1-7</reference>; <reference osisRef="1co 12:12-14 1co 12:26"> 12:12-14,26</reference>. <chapter n="1" osisID="Judg.1" sID="Judg.1"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv30"/><title type="x-s">Book Introduction - Judges</title> <div sID="gen943" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="jud 1">Read first chapter of Judges</reference><div eID="gen943" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen944" type="x-p"/> This book takes its name from the thirteen men raised up to deliver Israel in the declension and disunion which followed the death of Joshua. Through these men Jehovah continued His personal government of Israel. The key-verse to the condition of Israel is (<reference osisRef="jud 17:6">Judges 17:6</reference>), "Every man did that which was right in his own eyes." Two facts stand out--the utter failure of Israel; the persistent grace of Jehovah. In the choice of the Judges is illustrated Zechariah's great word (<reference osisRef="zec 4:6">Zechariah 4:6</reference>), "not by might, nor by power, but by My Spirit, saith the Lord"; and Paul's word (<reference osisRef="1co 1:25">1 Corinthians 1:25</reference>), "not many wise men after the flesh, not many mighty, not many noble, are called."<div eID="gen944" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen945" type="x-p"/> The book records seven apostasies, seven servitudes to seven heathen nations, seven deliverances. The spiritual parallel is found in the history of the professing church since the Apostles, in the rise of sects and the lost sense of the unity of the one body (<reference osisRef="1co 12:12 1co 12:13">1 Corinthians 12:12,13</reference>).<div eID="gen945" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen946" type="x-p"/> Judges is in two parts:<div eID="gen946" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">1-16 inclusive; key-verse, Judges2:18.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">17-21; key-verse, Judges21:25.</item> </list> <div sID="gen947" type="x-p"/> The events recorded in Judges cover a period of 305 years (Ussher).<div eID="gen947" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen948" type="x-p"/> <chapter eID="Judg.1"/>
<div eID="gen948" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen949" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="2" osisID="Judg.2" sID="Judg.2"/>

<hi type="bold">Timmathheres</hi><div eID="gen950" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen951" type="x-p"/> Timnathserah. <reference osisRef="jos 19:50">Joshua 19:50</reference>.

<hi type="bold">Ashtaroth</hi><div eID="gen951" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen952" type="x-p"/> Ashtaroth, plural of Ashtoreth <reference osisRef="1ki 11:5">1 Kings 11:5</reference> were figures of Ashtoreth the Phoenician goddess (the Astarte of the Greeks), which were worshipped as idols during times of spiritual declension in Israel. ; <reference osisRef="jud 10:6">Judges 10:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="1sa 7:3 1sa 7:4">1 Samuel 7:3,4</reference>; <reference osisRef="1sa 12:10"> 12:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="1sa 31:10"> 31:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="1ki 11:5 1ki 11:33">1 Kings 11:5,33</reference>; <reference osisRef="2ki 23:13">2 Kings 23:13</reference>. Jeremiah refers <reference osisRef="jer 44:18 jer 44:19">Jeremiah 44:18,19</reference> to Ashtoreth as the "queen of heaven."

<hi type="bold">judges</hi><div eID="gen952" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen953" type="x-p"/> The judges were tribesmen in Israel upon whom the Lord laid the burden of Israel's apostate and oppressed state. They were the spiritual ancestors of the prophets; that is to say, men raised up of God, the theocratic King, to represent Him in the nation. They were patriots and religious reformers because national security and prosperity were inseparably connected with loyalty and obedience to Jehovah. Not one of the chosen deliverers had anything whereof to glory in the flesh. Othniel was but the son of the younger brother of Caleb; Ehud was a left-handed man and an assassin; Shamgar, a rustic with an ox-goad; Deborah, a woman; Gideon, of an obscure family in the smallest tribe, etc. Each of the classes mentioned in <reference osisRef="1co 1:27 1co 1:28">1 Corinthians 1:27,28</reference> is illustrated among the judges.<div eID="gen953" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen954" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">repented</hi> <div eID="gen954" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen955" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Zec 8:14">Zechariah 8:14</reference>")</hi>. <chapter eID="Judg.2"/><div eID="gen955" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen956" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="3" osisID="Judg.3" sID="Judg.3"/>

<hi type="bold">Groves</hi> <div eID="gen956" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen957" type="x-p"/> Groves, like high places, have been associated with idolatrous worship from time immemorial. The Heb. asherah, trans. grove means also the idol enshrined there. <reference osisRef="de 16:21">Deuteronomy 16:21</reference>. This idol seems often to have been a sacred tree, the figure of which is constantly found on Assyrian monuments. In apostate Israel, however, such groves were associated with every form of idolatry, e.g. <reference osisRef="2ki 17:16 2ki 17:17">2 Kings 17:16,17</reference>.<div eID="gen957" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen958" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:1Ki 3:2">1 Kings 3:2</reference>")</hi> and Ashtaroth See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:jud 2:13">Judges 2:13</reference>". <chapter eID="Judg.3"/><div eID="gen958" type="x-p"/>

Announced by an angel <reference osisRef="jud 13:1-21">Judges 13:1-21</reference>. He was a Nazarite ; <reference osisRef="nu 6:1-27">Numbers 6:1-27</reference>; <reference osisRef="jud 13:5">Judges 13:5</reference> who constantly defiled his Nazarite separation through fleshly appetites. Called of God to judge Israel, and endued wonderfully with the Spirit, he wrought no abiding work for Israel, and perished in captivity to his enemies the Philistines. What was real in the man was his mighty faith in Jehovah in a time of doubt and apostasy, and this faith God honoured <reference osisRef="heb 11:32">Hebrews 11:32</reference>. <div eID="gen989" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv30"/><div sID="gen990" type="x-p"/> <chapter eID="Judg.16"/>

Called of God to judge Israel, and endued wonderfully with the Spirit, he wrought no abiding work for Israel, and perished in captivity to his enemies the Philistines. What was real in the man was his mighty faith in Jehovah in a time of doubt and apostasy, and this faith God honoured <reference osisRef="heb 11:32">Hebrews 11:32</reference>.

<hi type="bold">Now know I</hi><div eID="gen992" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen993" type="x-p"/> A striking illustration of all apostasy. With his entire departure from the revealed will of God concerning worship and priesthood, there is yet an exaltation of false priesthood. Saying, "Blessed be thou of Jehovah," Micah's mother makes an idol; and Micah expects the blessing of Jehovah because he has linked his idolatry to the ancient levitical order. <div eID="gen993" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv30"/><div sID="gen994" type="x-p"/> <chapter eID="Judg.17"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv30"/><title type="x-s">Book Introduction - Ruth</title> <div sID="gen1004" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="ru 1">Read first chapter of Ruth</reference><div eID="gen1004" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1005" type="x-p"/> This lovely story should be read in connection with the first half of Judges, as it presents a picture of life in Israel at that time.<div eID="gen1005" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1006" type="x-p"/> Typically, the book may be taken as a foreview of the church (Ruth), as the Gentile bride of Christ, the Bethlehemite who is able to redeem. Ruth also gives a normal Christian experience:<div eID="gen1006" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">Ruth deciding, 1</item> <item type="x-indent-1">Ruth serving, 2.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">Ruth resting, 3.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">Ruth rewarded, 4.</item> </list> <div sID="gen1007" type="x-p"/> The events recorded in Ruth cover a period of 10 years (Ussher) <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv30"/><hi type="bold">famine</hi> <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ge 12:10">Genesis 12:10</reference>")</hi>.<div eID="gen1007" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1008" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Bethlehemjudah</hi> House of Bread and Praise. <chapter eID="Ruth.1"/><div eID="gen1008" type="x-p"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv31"/><title type="x-s">Book Introduction - 1 Samuel</title> <div sID="gen1015" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1sa 1">Read first chapter of 1 Samuel</reference><div eID="gen1015" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1016" type="x-p"/> This book represents the personal history of Samuel, last of the Judges. It records the moral failure of the priesthood under Eli, and of the Judges in Samuel's attempt to make the office hereditary (<reference osisRef="1sa 8:1">1 Samuel 8:1</reference>). In his prophetic office Samuel was faithful, and in him begins the line of writing prophets. Henceforth the prophet, not the priest, is conspicuous in Israel. In this book the theocracy, as exercised through judges, ends (<reference osisRef="1sa 8:7">1 Samuel 8:7</reference>), and the line of kings begins with Saul.<div eID="gen1016" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1017" type="x-p"/> The book is in four parts:<div eID="gen1017" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">The story of Samuel to the death of Eli, 1:1-4:22.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">From the taking of the ark to the demand for a king, 5:1-8:22.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The reign of Saul to the call of David, 9:1-15:35.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">From the call of David to the death of Saul, 16:1-31:13.</item> </list> <div sID="gen1018" type="x-p"/> The events recorded in First Samuel cover a period of 115 years (Ussher). <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv31"/><hi type="bold">Lord of hosts</hi><div eID="gen1018" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1019" type="x-p"/> Jehovah (Lord) of Hosts, Heb. Jehovah Sabaoth. For the distinctive meanings of Jehovah, <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ge 2:4">Genesis 2:4</reference>")</hi>. Sabaoth means simply host or hosts, but with especial reference to warfare or service. In use the two ideas are united; Jehovah is LORD of (warrior) hosts. It is the name, therefore, of Jehovah in manifestation of power. "The Lord of Hosts, He is the King of glory" <reference osisRef="ps 24:10">Psalms 24:10</reference> and accordingly in the Old Testament Scripture this name is revealed in the time of Israel's need. It is never found in the Pentateuch, nor directly in Joshua or Judges, and occurs but rarely in the Psalms; but Jeremiah, the prophet of approaching national judgment, uses the name about eighty times. Haggai in two chapters uses the name fourteen times, Zechariah in fourteen chapters calls upon the Lord of hosts about fifty times. In Malachi the name occurs about twenty five times. In the utmost extremity, the Psalmist twice comforts his heart with the assurance "the Lord of hosts is with us." <reference osisRef="ps 46:7 ps 46:11">Psalms 46:7,11</reference>.<div eID="gen1019" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1020" type="x-p"/> The meanings and uses of this name may thus be summarized:<div eID="gen1020" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(1) The "hosts" are heavenly. Primarily the angels are meant, but the name gathers into itself the idea of all divine or heavenly power as available for the need of God's people <reference osisRef="ge 32:1 ge 32:2">Genesis 32:1,2</reference>; <reference osisRef="isa 6:1-5">Isaiah 6:1-5</reference>; <reference osisRef="1ki 22:19">1 Kings 22:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="lu 2:13-15">Luke 2:13-15</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(2) In use this is the distinctive name of Deity for Israel's help and comfort in the time of her division and failure <reference osisRef="1ki 18:15">1 Kings 18:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="1ki 19:14"> 19:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="isa 1:9">Isaiah 1:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="isa 8:11-14"> 8:11-14</reference>; <reference osisRef="isa 9:13-19"> 9:13-19</reference> ; <reference osisRef="isa 10:24-27"> 10:24-27</reference>; <reference osisRef="isa 31:4 isa 31:5"> 31:4,5</reference>; <reference osisRef="hag 2:4">Haggai 2:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="mal 3:16 mal 3:17">Malachi 3:16,17</reference>; <reference osisRef="jas 5:4">James 5:4</reference>.</item> </list> <div sID="gen1021" type="x-p"/> See other names of Deity, <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ge 1:1">Genesis 1:1</reference>")</hi> See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:ge 2:4">Genesis 2:4</reference>" <reference osisRef="ge 2:7">Genesis 2:7</reference> See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:ge 14:18">Genesis 14:18</reference>" See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:ge 15:2">Genesis 15:2</reference>" See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:ge 17:1">Genesis 17:1</reference>" See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:ge 21:33">Genesis 21:33</reference>" <chapter eID="1Sam.1"/><div eID="gen1021" type="x-p"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv33"/><title type="x-s">Book Introduction - 2 Samuel</title> <div sID="gen1056" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2sa 1">Read first chapter of 2 Samuel</reference><div eID="gen1056" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1057" type="x-p"/> As First Samuel marks the failure of man in Eli, Saul, and even Samuel, so Second Samuel marks the restoration of order through the enthroning of God's king, David. This book also records the establishment of Israel's political centre in Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="2sa 5:6-12">2 Samuel 5:6-12</reference>), and her religious centre in Zion (<reference osisRef="2sa 5:7">2 Samuel 5:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="2sa 6:1-17"> 6:1-17</reference>). When all was thus ordered, Jehovah established the great Davidic Covenant (<reference osisRef="2sa 27:8-17">2 Samuel 27:8-17</reference>) out of which all kingdom truth is henceforth developed. David, in his "last words" (<reference osisRef="2sa 23:1-7">2 Samuel 23:1-7</reference>), describes the millennial kingdom yet to be.<div eID="gen1057" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1058" type="x-p"/> The book is in four parts:<div eID="gen1058" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">From the death of Saul to the anointing of David over Judah, in Hebron, 1:1-27.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">From the anointing in Hebron to the establishment of David over united Israel, 2:1-5:25.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">From the conquest of Jerusalem to the rebellion of Absalom, 6:1-14:33.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">From the rebellion of Absalom to the purchase of the temple-site, 15:1-24:25.</item> </list> <div sID="gen1059" type="x-p"/> The events recorded in 2 Samuel cover a period of 38 years (Ussher). <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv33"/><hi type="bold">stood</hi><div eID="gen1059" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1060" type="x-p"/> Cf. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:1Sa 31:3">1 Samuel 31:3</reference>")</hi>. <chapter eID="2Sam.1"/><div eID="gen1060" type="x-p"/>

<hi type="bold">new cart</hi> <div eID="gen1068" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1069" type="x-p"/> The story of David's new cart and its results is a striking illustration of the spiritual truth that blessing does not follow even the best intentions in the service of God except as that service is rendered in God's way. It is a constant point of failure. God had given explicit directions how the ark should be borne. <reference osisRef="nu 4:1-15">Numbers 4:1-15</reference> but David adopted a Philistine expedient.<div eID="gen1069" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1070" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1sa 6:7 1sa 6:8">1 Samuel 6:7,8</reference>. The church is full of Philistine ways of doing service to Christ. Cf. ; <reference osisRef="1co 1:17-31">1 Corinthians 1:17-31</reference>; <reference osisRef="2co 10:4 2co 10:5">2 Corinthians 10:4,5</reference>. See, also, <reference osisRef="1ch 15:2">1 Chronicles 15:2</reference>. <chapter eID="2Sam.6"/><div eID="gen1070" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen1071" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="7" osisID="2Sam.7" sID="2Sam.7"/>

<hi type="bold">mercy</hi> <div eID="gen1071" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1072" type="x-p"/> Verses 14 and 15 state the principle of judgment within the family of God. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:1Co 11:31">1 Corinthians 11:31</reference>")</hi>. It is always remedial, not penal <reference osisRef="heb 12:5-11">Hebrews 12:5-11</reference>.<div eID="gen1072" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1073" type="x-p"/> Judgment of the wicked is penal, not remedial.

<hi type="bold">The Davidic Covenant</hi><div eID="gen1073" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1074" type="x-p"/> The Davidic Covenant <reference osisRef="2sa 7:8-17">2 Samuel 7:8-17</reference>.<div eID="gen1074" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1075" type="x-p"/> This covenant, upon which the glorious kingdom of Christ "of the seed of David according to the flesh" is to be founded, secures:<div eID="gen1075" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(1) A Davidic "house"; i.e. posterity, family</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(2) A "throne"; i.e. royal authority</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(3) A kingdom; i.e. sphere of rule</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(4) In perpetuity; "for ever"</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(5) And this fourfold covenant has but one condition: disobedience in the Davidic family is to be visited with chastisement; but not to the abrogation of the covenant <reference osisRef="2sa 7:15">2 Samuel 7:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="ps 89:20-37">Psalms 89:20-37</reference>; <reference osisRef="isa 24:5">Isaiah 24:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="isa 54:3"> 54:3</reference>.</item> </list> <div sID="gen1076" type="x-p"/> The chastisement fell; first in the division of the kingdom under Rehoboam, and, finally, in the captivities. <reference osisRef="2ki 25:1-7">2 Kings 25:1-7</reference>. Since that time but one King of the Davidic family has been crowned at Jerusalem and He was crowned with thorns. But the Davidic Covenant confirmed to David by the oath of Jehovah, and renewed to Mary by the angel Gabriel, is immutable <reference osisRef="ps 89:30-37">Psalms 89:30-37</reference> and the Lord God will yet give to that thorn-crowned One "the throne of his father David." ; <reference osisRef="lu 1:31-33">Luke 1:31-33</reference>; <reference osisRef="ac 2:29-32">Acts 2:29-32</reference>; <reference osisRef="ac 15:14-17"> 15:14-17</reference>.<div eID="gen1076" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1077" type="x-p"/> See, for the other seven covenants:<div eID="gen1077" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1078" type="x-p"/> EDENIC, <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ge 1:28">Genesis 1:28</reference>")</hi> ADAMIC, See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:ge 3:15">Genesis 3:15</reference>" NOAHIC, See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:ge 9:1">Genesis 9:1</reference>" ABRAHAMIC, See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:ge 15:18">Genesis 15:18</reference>" MOSAIC, See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:ex 19:25">Exodus 19:25</reference>" PALESTINIAN, See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:de 30:3">Deuteronomy 30:3</reference>" NEW, See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:heb 8:8">Hebrews 8:8</reference>"

<hi type="bold">redeem</hi><div eID="gen1078" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1079" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ex 14:30">Exodus 14:30</reference>")</hi> <div eID="gen1079" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv34"/><div sID="gen1080" type="x-p"/> <chapter eID="2Sam.7"/>
<div eID="gen1080" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1081" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="9" osisID="2Sam.9" sID="2Sam.9"/>

<hi type="bold">kindness</hi> <div eID="gen1081" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1082" type="x-p"/> A lovely picture of salvation by grace.<div eID="gen1082" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(1) What grace is -- kindness to a helpless one for another's sake, <reference osisRef="2sa 1:1-3">2 Samuel 1:1-3</reference>; <reference osisRef="1jo 2:12">1 John 2:12</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(2) Grace gives the highest place, <reference osisRef="2sa 1:11">2 Samuel 1:11</reference>. <reference osisRef="eph 1:1-6">Ephesians 1:1-6</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(3) Grace keeps the saved one, <reference osisRef="2sa 1:13">2 Samuel 1:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="joh 10:28 joh 10:29">John 10:28,29</reference>. </item> </list> <chapter eID="2Sam.9"/>
<div sID="gen1083" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="12" osisID="2Sam.12" sID="2Sam.12"/>

<hi type="bold">sinned</hi> <div eID="gen1083" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1084" type="x-p"/> Here read <reference osisRef="ps 51:1-19">Psalms 51:1-19</reference>. <chapter eID="2Sam.12"/><div eID="gen1084" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen1085" type="x-p"/><chapter n="13" osisID="2Sam.13" sID="2Sam.13"/>

<hi type="bold">But Absalom fled, and went to Talmai</hi> <reference osisRef="1sa 27:8">1 Samuel 27:8</reference>. David, in the years of his wanderings, made a savage raid upon Geshur, and evidently bore away Maacah, daughter of the king of Geshur. Of her was born Absalom, and in him was her wild Bedouin blood, and the blood of a father who had been the reckless chief of a handful of desperate men. ; <reference osisRef="2sa 3:3">2 Samuel 3:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="2sa 23:8-39"> 23:8-39</reference> and whom only the divine love could tame. <reference osisRef="2sa 22:36">2 Samuel 22:36</reference>. In Absalom David reaped from his own sowing. <chapter eID="2Sam.13"/><div eID="gen1085" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen1086" type="x-p"/><chapter n="14" osisID="2Sam.14" sID="2Sam.14"/>
<hi type="bold">revengers</hi> Heb. goel, Redemp. (Kinsman type). <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Isa 59:20">Isaiah 59:20</reference>")</hi>.
<hi type="bold">angel</hi> <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Heb 1:4">Hebrews 1:4</reference>")</hi>.

<hi type="bold">saw not the king's face</hi><div eID="gen1086" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1087" type="x-p"/> Not so had God taught David to forgive. Legalists have thought Absalom's wilfulness to have been due to over-indulgence on the part of David. There is no such intimation in Scripture. Rather it would seem that had David at this time taken Absalom into intimacy, the rebellion might have been averted.

<chapter n="1" osisID="1Kgs.1" sID="1Kgs.1"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv34"/><title type="x-s">Book Introduction - 1 Kings</title> <div sID="gen1112" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1ki 1">Read first chapter of 1 Kings</reference><div eID="gen1112" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1113" type="x-p"/> First Kings records the death of David, the reign of Solomon, the building of the temple, death of Solomon, division of the kingdom under Rehoboam and Jeroboam, and the history of the two kingdoms to the reign of Jehoram over Judah, and Ahaziah over Samaria. Includes the mighty ministry of Elijah.<div eID="gen1113" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1114" type="x-p"/> The book is in seven parts:<div eID="gen1114" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">From the rebellion of Adonijah to the death of David, 1:1-2:11.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">From the accession of Solomon to the dedication of the temple, 2:12-8:66.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">From the division of the kingdom to the death of Jeroboam and Rehoboam, 12:1-14:31.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The kingdoms to the accession of Ahab, 15:1-16:28.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">Accession of Ahab to his death, 16:29-22:40.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">From the reign of Jehoshaphat to the accession of Jehoram over Judah, and Ahaziah over Samaria, 22:41-53.</item> </list> <div sID="gen1115" type="x-p"/> The events recorded in First Kings cover a period of 118 years (Ussher). <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv34"/><hi type="bold">redeemed</hi><div eID="gen1115" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1116" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="ex 14:30">Exodus 14:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="isa 59:20">Isaiah 59:20</reference>. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ex 14:30">Exodus 14:30</reference>")</hi>. See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:isa 59:20">Isaiah 59:20</reference>". <chapter eID="1Kgs.1"/><div eID="gen1116" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen1117" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="2" osisID="1Kgs.2" sID="1Kgs.2"/>

<hi type="bold">grave</hi> <div eID="gen1117" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1118" type="x-p"/> Heb. "Sheol," <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Hab 2:5">Habakkuk 2:5</reference>")</hi>. <chapter eID="1Kgs.2"/><div eID="gen1118" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen1119" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="3" osisID="1Kgs.3" sID="1Kgs.3"/>

<hi type="bold">high places</hi> <div eID="gen1119" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1120" type="x-p"/> Cf. <reference osisRef="le 26:30">Leviticus 26:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="de 12:11-14">Deuteronomy 12:11-14</reference>. The use of commanding elevations for altars seems to have been immemorial and universal. In itself the practice was not evil ; <reference osisRef="ge 12:7 ge 12:8">Genesis 12:7,8</reference>; <reference osisRef="ge 22:2-4"> 22:2-4</reference> ; <reference osisRef="ge 31:54"> 31:54</reference>; <reference osisRef="jud 6:25 jud 6:26">Judges 6:25,26</reference>; <reference osisRef="jud 13:16-23"> 13:16-23</reference>. After the establishment of Mount Moriah and the temple as the centre of divine worship ; <reference osisRef="de 12:5">Deuteronomy 12:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="2ch 7:12">2 Chronicles 7:12</reference> the pentateuchal prohibition of the use of high places <reference osisRef="de 12:11-14">Deuteronomy 12:11-14</reference> which had looked forward to the setting up of such a centre, came into effect, and high places became identified with idolatrous practices. The constant recurrence to the use of high places, even for Jehovistic worship <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:1Ki 15:14">1 Kings 15:14</reference>")</hi> and after the building of the temple, proves how deeply rooted the custom was.<div eID="gen1120" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1121" type="x-p"/> See <reference osisRef="2ki 18:4-22">2 Kings 18:4-22</reference>; <reference osisRef="2ki 23:1-37"> 23:1-37</reference>; <reference osisRef="2ch 33:3 2ch 33:17 2ch 33:19">2 Chronicles 33:3,17,19</reference> Note below refers to "Groves." <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Jud 3:7">Judges 3:7</reference>")</hi>. <chapter eID="1Kgs.3"/><div eID="gen1121" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen1122" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="4" osisID="1Kgs.4" sID="1Kgs.4"/>

<hi type="bold">son of Hur</hi> <div eID="gen1122" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1123" type="x-p"/> Or, Benhur. <div eID="gen1123" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv35"/><div sID="gen1124" type="x-p"/> <chapter eID="1Kgs.4"/>
<div eID="gen1124" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1125" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="6" osisID="1Kgs.6" sID="1Kgs.6"/>

<hi type="bold">the house of the Lord</hi> <div eID="gen1125" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1126" type="x-p"/> The typology of the temple, if indeed it has any typical significance, is most obscure and difficult. The N.T. invariably expounds the typology of the tabernacle, not of the temple. The symbolism of the latter may be revealed in the kingdom-age (see "Kingdom" O.T., <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ge 1:26">Genesis 1:26</reference>")</hi> See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:zec 12:8">Zechariah 12:8</reference>" N.T., ; <reference osisRef="lu 1:32">Luke 1:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="1co 15:28">1 Corinthians 15:28</reference>. In the N.T. the usual Gk. word for sanctuary (naos) is used<div eID="gen1126" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(1) of the temple in Jerusalem <reference osisRef="mt 23:16">Matthew 23:16</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(2) of the believer's body <reference osisRef="1co 3:16 1co 3:17">1 Corinthians 3:16,17</reference>; <reference osisRef="1co 6:19"> 6:19</reference></item> <item type="x-indent-1">(3) of the local church <reference osisRef="2co 6:16">2 Corinthians 6:16</reference> and</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(4) of the true church <reference osisRef="eph 2:21">Ephesians 2:21</reference> But in all these instances the thought is simply of a habitation of God. No reference to the structure of the temple, as in the case of the tabernacle <reference osisRef="heb 9:1-heb 10:39">Hebrews 9:1-10:39</reference>.</item> </list> <div sID="gen1127" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Zif</hi> <div eID="gen1127" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1128" type="x-p"/> Second month, i.e. May.

<hi type="bold">windows of narrow lights</hi><div eID="gen1128" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1129" type="x-p"/> Cf. <reference osisRef="2ch 4:20">2 Chronicles 4:20</reference>. In the holy of holies in the tabernacle no light but the shekinah glory was provided. In many ways Solomon's temple manifests the spiritual deterioration of the people, and Jehovah's condescension to it in grace.
<hi type="bold">they stretched forth</hi> Or, the cherubim stretched forth their wings.
<hi type="bold">Zif</hi><div eID="gen1129" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1130" type="x-p"/> Second month, i.e. May.

<hi type="bold">Bul</hi><div eID="gen1130" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1131" type="x-p"/> Eighth month i.e. November. <div eID="gen1131" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv35"/><div sID="gen1132" type="x-p"/> <chapter eID="1Kgs.6"/>
<div eID="gen1132" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1133" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="7" osisID="1Kgs.7" sID="1Kgs.7"/>

<hi type="bold">Jachin</hi> i.e. He shall establish.<div eID="gen1135" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1136" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Boaz</hi> i.e. in it is strength.

<hi type="bold">shewbread</hi> <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ex 25:30">Exodus 25:30</reference>")</hi> <div eID="gen1136" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv35"/><div sID="gen1137" type="x-p"/> <chapter eID="1Kgs.7"/>
<div eID="gen1137" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1138" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="8" osisID="1Kgs.8" sID="1Kgs.8"/>

<hi type="bold">Then Solomon</hi> <div eID="gen1138" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1139" type="x-p"/> The consecration of the temple illustrates all consecration. The temple, like the believer <reference osisRef="1th 5:23">1 Thessalonians 5:23</reference> was threefold: the court, that which was outward, visible, answered to the body; the holy place, where everything appealed to the sacred emotions, answered to the soul; the holy of holies, the place of communion with God <reference osisRef="ex 25:22">Exodus 25:22</reference> answered to the spirit of man. The ark was the most all- inclusive type of Christ of any one of the vessels of the tabernacle. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ex 25:9">Exodus 25:9</reference>")</hi>. When, therefore, the priests brought the ark into the court, the holy place, and the holy of holies, they were, in type, enthroning Christ over the body, with its powers and appetites; the soul, seat of the emotions and desires; and the mind, seat of the capacity to know and commune with God. See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:ge 1:26">Genesis 1:26</reference>" note 3. In Christian experience this answers to ; <reference osisRef="ro 12:1-3">Romans 12:1-3</reference>; <reference osisRef="eph 5:18">Ephesians 5:18</reference>.
<hi type="bold">Ethanim</hi><div eID="gen1139" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1140" type="x-p"/> Seventh month i.e. October.

<hi type="bold">cloud</hi><div eID="gen1140" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1141" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1ki 8:10 1ki 8:11">1 Kings 8:10,11</reference>. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ex 40:34">Exodus 40:34</reference>")</hi>
<hi type="bold">fear</hi><div eID="gen1141" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1142" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ps 19:9">Psalms 19:9</reference>")</hi>.

<hi type="bold">perfect</hi><div eID="gen1142" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1143" type="x-p"/> The word implies whole-heartedness for God, single-mindedness, sincerity -- not sinless perfection. <chapter eID="1Kgs.8"/><div eID="gen1143" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen1144" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="11" osisID="1Kgs.11" sID="1Kgs.11"/>

<hi type="bold">Rehoboam</hi><div eID="gen1145" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1146" type="x-p"/> called Roboam. <reference osisRef="mt 1:7">Matthew 1:7</reference>. <div eID="gen1146" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv35"/><div sID="gen1147" type="x-p"/> <chapter eID="1Kgs.11"/>

<hi type="bold">saying</hi><div eID="gen1149" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1150" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Jud 8:1">Judges 8:1</reference>")</hi>.

<hi type="bold">eighth month</hi> i.e. November. <reference osisRef="1ki 12:33">1 Kings 12:33</reference>.<div eID="gen1150" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1151" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">altar</hi> See <reference osisRef="1ki 12:25-33">1 Kings 12:25-33</reference>; <reference osisRef="de 12:4-14">Deuteronomy 12:4-14</reference>. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Am 4:4">Amos 4:4</reference>")</hi>. <chapter eID="1Kgs.12"/><div eID="gen1151" type="x-p"/>

<hi type="bold">and an</hi> An impressive illustration of <reference osisRef="ga 1:8 ga 1:9">Galatians 1:8,9</reference>.<div eID="gen1152" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1153" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">angel</hi><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Heb 1:4">Hebrews 1:4</reference>")</hi>. <div eID="gen1153" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv35"/><div sID="gen1154" type="x-p"/> <chapter eID="1Kgs.13"/>

<hi type="bold">Abbijam</hi> <div eID="gen1155" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1156" type="x-p"/> Called Abijah, <reference osisRef="2ch 13:1">2 Chronicles 13:1</reference>.

<hi type="bold">high places</hi><div eID="gen1156" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1157" type="x-p"/> Cf. <reference osisRef="2ch 14:3">2 Chronicles 14:3</reference>. It appears that local sacrifices to Jehovah (though not according to the divine order) were offered in the times of the kings upon "high places" (cf) <reference osisRef="1sa 9:12">1 Samuel 9:12</reference>. Apparently Asa's mother had defiled one of these with an idol, <reference osisRef="1ki 15:13">1 Kings 15:13</reference>. Asa destroyed the idol and the idolatrous (but not the Jehovistic) "high places." But see "high places," <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:1Ki 3:2">1 Kings 3:2</reference>")</hi>.

<hi type="bold">Jehoshaphat</hi><div eID="gen1157" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1158" type="x-p"/> Called Josaphat, <reference osisRef="mt 1:8">Matthew 1:8</reference>. <chapter eID="1Kgs.15"/><div eID="gen1158" type="x-p"/>

(Kinsman type). <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Isa 59:20">Isaiah 59:20</reference>")</hi>. <div eID="gen1159" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv35"/><div sID="gen1160" type="x-p"/> <chapter eID="1Kgs.16"/>

<hi type="bold">Elijah</hi> Heb. "Elijahu," <reference osisRef="lu 1:17">Luke 1:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="lu 4:25"> 4:25</reference> called Elias.<div eID="gen1161" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1162" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Ahab</hi> It was a small thing for a man whose life was passed in Jehovah's presence to stand before Ahab.

<hi type="bold">Zarephath</hi> called Sarepta, <reference osisRef="ob 1:20">Obadiah 1:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="lu 4:26">Luke 4:26</reference>. <chapter eID="1Kgs.17"/><div eID="gen1162" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen1163" type="x-p"/><chapter n="18" osisID="1Kgs.18" sID="1Kgs.18"/>

<hi type="bold">Obadiah</hi> In such a time as the reign of Ahab and Jezebel a believer's true place was by Elijah's side. Obadiah is a warning type of the men of God who adhere to the world while still seeking to serve God. The secret of the Lord, and the power of the Lord were with Elijah, the separated servant. Cf. <reference osisRef="2ti 2:20 2ti 2:21">2 Timothy 2:20,21</reference>.<div eID="gen1163" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1164" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">feared</hi><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ps 19:9">Psalms 19:9</reference>")</hi>. <chapter eID="1Kgs.18"/><div eID="gen1164" type="x-p"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv35"/><title type="x-s">Book Introduction - 2 Kings</title> <div sID="gen1172" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2ki 1">Read first chapter of 2 Kings</reference><div eID="gen1172" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1173" type="x-p"/> This book continues the history of the kingdoms to the captivities. It includes the translation of Elijah and the ministry of Elisha. During this period Amos and Hosea prophesied in Israel, and Obadiah, Joel, Isaiah, Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, and Jeremiah in Judah.<div eID="gen1173" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1174" type="x-p"/> Second Kings is in seven parts:<div eID="gen1174" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">The last ministry and translation of Elijah, 1:1-2:11.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The ministry of Elisha from the translation of Elijah to the anointing of Jehu, 2:12-9:10.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The reign of Jehu over Israel, 9:11-10:36.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The reigns of Athaliah and Jehoash over Judah, 11:1-12:21.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The reigns of Jehoahaz and Joash over Israel, and the last ministry of Elisha, 13:1-25.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">From the death of Elisha to the captivity of Israel, 14:1-17:41.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">From the accession of Hezekiah to the captivity of Judah, 18:1-25:30.</item> </list> <div sID="gen1175" type="x-p"/> The events recorded in Second Kings cover a period of 308 years. (Ussher) <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv35"/><hi type="bold">angel</hi><div eID="gen1175" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1176" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Heb 1:4">Hebrews 1:4</reference>")</hi>.

From this captivity the ten tribes have never been restored to Palestine. A remnant of Judah returned under Zerubbabel, Ezra, and Nehemiah, and individuals out of the ten tribes (called, after the division of Solomon's kingdom, "Israel" in the historical books and Prophets, also "Ephraim" by the latter) went back, but the national restoration is yet to be fulfilled. <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv36"/><title type="x-s">Book Introduction - 1 Chronicles</title> <div sID="gen1236" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1ch 1">Read first chapter of 1 Chronicles</reference><div eID="gen1236" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1237" type="x-p"/> The two books of Chronicles (like the two books of Kings) are but one book in the Jewish canon. Together they cover the period from the death of Saul to the captivities. They were written probably during the Babylonian captivity, and are distinguished from the two books of the Kings in a fuller account of Judah, and in the omission of many details. The blessing of God's earthly people in connection with the Davidic monarchy is probably the typical significance of these books.<div eID="gen1237" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1238" type="x-p"/> First Chronicles is in three parts:<div eID="gen1238" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">Official genealogies, 1:1-9:44.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">From the death of Saul to the accession of David, 10:1-12:24.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">From the accession of David to his death, 13:1-29:30.</item> </list> <div sID="gen1239" type="x-p"/> Excluding the genealogies (Ch 1-9) the events recorded in First Chronicles cover a period of 41 years (Ussher). <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv36"/><hi type="bold">Magog</hi><div eID="gen1239" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1240" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="ge 10:2">Genesis 10:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="eze 38:2">Ezekiel 38:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="eze 39:6"> 39:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 20:8">Revelation 20:8</reference>. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Eze 38:2">Ezekiel 38:2</reference>")</hi>. <chapter eID="1Chr.1"/><div eID="gen1240" type="x-p"/>

<hi type="bold">castle of Zion</hi> <div eID="gen1258" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1259" type="x-p"/> Heb. castle.<div eID="gen1259" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(1) Zion, the ancient Jebusite stronghold, is the southwest eminence in Jerusalem, called in Scripture the city of David, and associated with the Davidic royalty both historically and prophetically <reference osisRef="1ch 11:7">1 Chronicles 11:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="ps 2:6">Psalms 2:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="isa 2:3">Isaiah 2:3</reference>. The word is often used of the whole city of Jerusalem considered as the city of God <reference osisRef="ps 48:2 ps 48:3">Psalms 48:2,3</reference> especially in passages referring to the future kingdom-age ; <reference osisRef="isa 1:27">Isaiah 1:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="isa 2:3"> 2:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="isa 4:1-6"> 4:1-6</reference>; <reference osisRef="joe 3:16">Joel 3:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="zec 1:16 zec 1:17">Zechariah 1:16,17</reference>; <reference osisRef="zec 8:3-8"> 8:3-8</reference>; <reference osisRef="ro 11:26">Romans 11:26</reference>. In <reference osisRef="heb 12:22">Hebrews 12:22</reference> the word is used symbolically of heaven.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(2) In <reference osisRef="de 4:48">Deuteronomy 4:48</reference> the name is given to a projection or peak of Mount Hermon. </item> </list> <chapter eID="1Chr.11"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv37"/><title type="x-s">Book Introduction - 2 Chronicles</title> <div sID="gen1310" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2ch 1">Read first chapter of 2 Chronicles</reference><div eID="gen1310" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1311" type="x-p"/> This book continues the history begun in First Chronicles. It falls into eighteen divisions, by reigns, from Solomon to the captivities; records the division of the kingdom of David under Jeroboam and Rehoboam, and is marked by an ever growing apostasy, broken temporarily by reformations under Asa, 14-16; Jehoshaphat, <reference osisRef="2ch 17:1-19"> 17:1-19</reference>; Joash, 24; Hezekiah, 29-32; and Josiah, 34,35. But the religious state of the people, even at the best, is described in Isaiah 1-5.<div eID="gen1311" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1312" type="x-p"/> The events recorded in Second Chronicles cover a period of 427 years. <chapter n="1" osisID="Ezra.1" sID="Ezra.1"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv38"/><title type="x-s">Book Introduction - Ezra</title> <div sID="gen1397" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="ezr 1">Read first chapter of Ezra</reference><div eID="gen1397" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1398" type="x-p"/> Ezra, the first of the post-captivity books (Ezra, Nehemiah, Esther, Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi), records the return to Palestine under Zerubbabel, by decree of Cyrus, of a Jewish remnant who laid the temple foundations (B.C. 536). Later (B.C. 458) Ezra followed, and restored the law and ritual. But the mass of the nation, and most of the princes, remained by preference in Babylonia and Assyria, where they were prospering. The post-captivity books deal with that feeble remnant which alone had a heart for God.<div eID="gen1398" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1399" type="x-p"/> The book is in two parts:<div eID="gen1399" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">From the decree of Cyrus to the dedication of the restored temple, 1:1-6:22.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The ministry of Ezra, 7:1-10:44.</item> </list> <div sID="gen1400" type="x-p"/> The events recorded in Ezra cover a period of 80 years (Ussher).<div eID="gen1400" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1401" type="x-p"/> <chapter eID="Ezra.1"/>
<div eID="gen1401" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1402" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="2" osisID="Ezra.2" sID="Ezra.2"/>

<hi type="bold">are the children</hi> <div eID="gen1402" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1403" type="x-p"/> Probably individuals from all of the tribes returned to Jerusalem under Zerubbabel, Ezra and Nehemiah, but speaking broadly, the dispersion of the ten tribes (Ephraim- Israel) still continues; nor can they now be positively identified. They are, however, preserved distinct from other peoples and are known to God as such, though they themselves, few in number, know Him not <reference osisRef="de 28:62">Deuteronomy 28:62</reference>; <reference osisRef="isa 11:11-13">Isaiah 11:11-13</reference>; <reference osisRef="ho 3:4">Hosea 3:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="ho 8:8"> 8:8</reference>.<div eID="gen1403" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1404" type="x-p"/> The order of the restoration was as follows:<div eID="gen1404" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(1) The return of the first detachment under Zerubbabel and Jeshua (B.C. 536), Ezra 1.-6., and the books of Haggai and Zechariah;</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(2) the expedition of Ezra (B.C. 458), seventy-eight years later (Ezra 7.-10);</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(3) the commission of Nehemiah (B.C. 444), fourteen years after the expedition of Ezra. <reference osisRef="ne 2:1-5">Nehemiah 2:1-5</reference>. </item> </list>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv38"/><div sID="gen1405" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv38"/> <hi type="bold">Zerubbabel</hi> <div eID="gen1405" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1406" type="x-p"/> Called Zorobabel, <reference osisRef="mt 1:12 mt 1:13">Matthew 1:12,13</reference>.

<hi type="bold">for we seek</hi> <div eID="gen1413" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1414" type="x-p"/> The people of the land sought to hinder the work in three ways:<div eID="gen1414" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(1) by seeking to draw the Jews into an unreal union, <reference osisRef="ezr 4:3">Ezra 4:3</reference>. (cf) <reference osisRef="2ki 17:32">2 Kings 17:32</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(2) by "weakening the hands of the people of Judah," <reference osisRef="ezr 4:4">Ezra 4:4</reference> i.e, by withholding supplies, etc.; and</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(3) by accusations lodged with Ahasuerus and Darius. The first was by far the most subtle and dangerous. The lives of Ezra and Nehemiah afford many illustrations of true separation. <reference osisRef="2co 6:14-18">2 Corinthians 6:14-18</reference>; <reference osisRef="2ti 2:19-21">2 Timothy 2:19-21</reference>. </item> </list>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv39"/><div sID="gen1415" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv39"/> <hi type="bold">Ahasuerus</hi> <div eID="gen1415" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1416" type="x-p"/> The Cambyses of secular history (529-521 BC); not the Ahasuerus of Esther, who is the Xerxes of secular history (485 BC). <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Da 5:31">Daniel 5:31</reference>")</hi>.

<hi type="bold">Artaxerxes</hi><div eID="gen1416" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1417" type="x-p"/> The Artaxerxes of <reference osisRef="ezr 4:7">Ezra 4:7</reference> is identical with Ahasuerus of <reference osisRef="ezr 4:6">Ezra 4:6,</reference> i.e. the Cambyses of profane history. The Artaxerxes of <reference osisRef="ezr 7:1">Ezra 7:1</reference> is the Longimanus of secular history, BC 418. But <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Da 5:31">Daniel 5:31</reference>")</hi>.
<hi type="bold">Give</hi><div eID="gen1417" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1418" type="x-p"/> Chald. make a new decree. <chapter eID="Ezra.4"/><div eID="gen1418" type="x-p"/>

<hi type="bold">your companions</hi> <div eID="gen1421" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1422" type="x-p"/> Chald. "their societies."

<hi type="bold">finished it</hi><div eID="gen1422" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1423" type="x-p"/> The worship of Jehovah was thus re-established in Jerusalem, but the theocracy was not restored. The remnant which returned from the Babylonian captivity lived in the land by Gentile sufferance, though doubtless by the providential care of Jehovah, till Messiah came, and was crucified by soldiers of the fourth Gentile world-empire Rome, <reference osisRef="da 2:40">Daniel 2:40</reference>; <reference osisRef="da 7:7"> 7:7</reference>. Soon after (A.D. 70) Rome destroyed the city and temple. See "Times of the Gentiles" ; <reference osisRef="lu 21:24">Luke 21:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 16:19">Revelation 16:19</reference>.

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv40"/><title type="x-s">Book Introduction - Nehemiah</title> <div sID="gen1437" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="ne 1">Read first chapter of Nehemiah</reference><div eID="gen1437" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1438" type="x-p"/> Fourteen years after the return of Ezra to Jerusalem, Nehemiah led up a company (B.C. 444) and restored the walls and the civil authority. Of those events this book is the record. It is in eight divisions:<div eID="gen1438" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">The journey to Jerusalem, 1:1-2:20</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The building of the wall, 3:1-6:19.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The census, 7:1-73.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The revival, 8:1-11:36.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The census of the priests and Levites, 12:1-26.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">Dedication of the wall, 12:27-43.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">Restoration of the temple worship, 12:44-47.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The legal order restored, 13:1-31.</item> </list> <div sID="gen1439" type="x-p"/> The moral state of the time is disclosed by the prophet Malachi. This book affords many instances of individual faith acting on the written word (e.g. <reference osisRef="ne 1:8 ne 1:9">Nehemiah 1:8,9</reference>; <reference osisRef="ne 13:1"> 13:1</reference>). It is the principle of 2 Timothy 2.<div eID="gen1439" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1440" type="x-p"/> The events recorded in Nehemiah cover a period of 11 years (Ussher). <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv40"/>SCOFIELD REFERENCE NOTES (Old Scofield 1917 Edition)<div eID="gen1440" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1441" type="x-p"/> The Book of Nehemiah<div eID="gen1441" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1442" type="x-p"/> Fourteen years after the return of Ezra to Jerusalem, Nehemiah led up a company (B.C. 444) and restored the walls and the civil authority. Of those events this book is the record. It is in eight divisions:<div eID="gen1442" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1443" type="x-p"/> I. The journey to Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="ne 1:1-ne 2:20"> 1:1-2:20</reference>;<div eID="gen1443" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1444" type="x-p"/> II. The building of the wall, <reference osisRef="ne 3:1-ne 6:19"> 3:1-6:19</reference>.<div eID="gen1444" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1445" type="x-p"/> III. The census, <reference osisRef="ne 7:1-73"> 7:1-73</reference>.<div eID="gen1445" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1446" type="x-p"/> IV. The revival, <reference osisRef="ne 8:1-ne 11:36"> 8:1-11:36</reference>.<div eID="gen1446" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1447" type="x-p"/> V. The census of the priests and Levites, <reference osisRef="ne 12:1-26"> 12:1-26</reference>.<div eID="gen1447" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1448" type="x-p"/> VI. Dedication of the wall, <reference osisRef="ne 12:27-43"> 12:27-43</reference>.<div eID="gen1448" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1449" type="x-p"/> VII. Restoration of the temple worship, <reference osisRef="ne 12:44-47"> 12:44-47</reference>.<div eID="gen1449" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1450" type="x-p"/> VIII. <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv42"/><title type="x-s">Book Introduction - Esther</title> <div sID="gen1499" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="es 1">Read first chapter of Esther</reference><div eID="gen1499" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1500" type="x-p"/> The significance of the Book of Esther is that it testifies to the secret watch care of Jehovah over dispersed Israel. The name of God does not once occur, but in no other book of the Bible is His providence more conspicuous. A mere remnant returned to Jerusalem. The mass of the nation preferred the easy and lucrative life under the Persian rule. But God did not forsake them. What He here does for Judah, He is surely doing for all the covenant people. The book is in seven parts:<div eID="gen1500" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">The Story of Vashti, 1:1-22.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">Esther made queen, 2:1-23.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The conspiracy of Haman, 3:1-15.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The courage of Esther brings deliverance, 4:1-7:10.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The vengeance, 8:1-9:19.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The feast of Purim, 9:20-32.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">Epilogue, 10:1-3.</item> </list> <div sID="gen1501" type="x-p"/> The events recorded in Esther cover a period of 12 years (Ussher). <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv42"/><hi type="bold">chamberlains</hi><div eID="gen1501" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1502" type="x-p"/> Or, enunchs. <chapter eID="Esth.1"/><div eID="gen1502" type="x-p"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv43"/><title type="x-s">Book Introduction - Job</title> <div sID="gen1520" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="job 1">Read first chapter of Job</reference><div eID="gen1520" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1521" type="x-p"/> Job is in form a dramatic poem. It is probably the oldest of the Bible books, and was certainly written before the giving of the law. It would have been impossible, in a discussion covering the whole field of sin, of the providential government of God, and man's relation to Him, to avoid all reference to the law if the law had then been known. Job was a veritable personage (<reference osisRef="eze 14:20">Ezekiel 14:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="jas 5:11">James 5:11</reference>), and the events are historical. The book sheds a remarkable light on the philosophic breadth and intellectual culture of the patriarchal age. The problem is, Why do the godly suffer?<div eID="gen1521" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1522" type="x-p"/> Job is in seven parts:<div eID="gen1522" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">Prologue, 1:1-2:8.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">Job and his wife, 2:9,10.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">Job and his three friends, 2:11-31:40.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">Job and Elihu, 32:1-37:24.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">Jehovah and Job, 38:1-41:34.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">Job's final answer, 42:1-6.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">Epilogue, 42:7-17.</item> </list> <div sID="gen1523" type="x-p"/> The events recorded in Job cover a period within 1 year. <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv43"/><hi type="bold">land of Uz</hi><div eID="gen1523" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1524" type="x-p"/> A region at the south of Edom, and west of the Arabian desert, extending to Chaldea.<div eID="gen1524" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1525" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Uz</hi> See <reference osisRef="jer 25:20">Jeremiah 25:20</reference>.<div eID="gen1525" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1526" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fear</hi><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ps 19:9">Psalms 19:9</reference>")</hi>.
<hi type="bold">sons of God</hi><div eID="gen1526" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1527" type="x-p"/> This scene is in heaven. Cf. <reference osisRef="job 2:1-7">Job 2:1-7</reference>.
<hi type="bold">feareth</hi><div eID="gen1527" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1528" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ps 19:9">Psalms 19:9</reference>")</hi>.

<hi type="bold">Eliphaz</hi> <div eID="gen1537" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1538" type="x-p"/> Eliphaz is a religious dogmatist whose dogmatism rests upon a mysterious and remarkable experience <reference osisRef="job 4:12-16">Job 4:12-16</reference>. Did a spirit ever pass before Job's face? Did Job's hair of his flesh ever stand up? Then let him be meek while one so superior as Eliphaz declares the causes of his misfortunes. Eliphaz says many true things (as do the others), and often rises into eloquence, but he remains hard and cruel, a dogmatist who must be heard because of one remarkable experience.

<hi type="bold">breath</hi><div eID="gen1538" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1539" type="x-p"/> i.e. by His anger, as <reference osisRef="isa 30:33">Isaiah 30:33</reference>; <reference osisRef="ex 15:8">Exodus 15:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="job 1:19">Job 1:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="job 15:30">Job 15:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="isa 11:4">Isaiah 11:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="2th 2:8">2 Thessalonians 2:8</reference>.

<hi type="bold">So these three</hi> <div eID="gen1587" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1588" type="x-p"/> Despite minor differences, Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar have one view of the problem of Job's afflictions. He is a hypocrite. Outwardly good, he is, they hold, really a bad man. Otherwise, according to their conception of God, Job's sufferings would be unjust. Job, though himself the sufferer, will not so accuse the justice of God, and his self-defence is complete. Before God he is guilty, helpless, and undone, and there is no daysman (<reference osisRef="job 32:9">Job 32:9</reference>). Later, his faith is rewarded by a revelation of a coming Redeemer, and of the resurrection (<reference osisRef="job 32:19">Job 32:19</reference>). But Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar are sinners also as before God, and yet they are not afflicted. Job refutes the theory of the three that he is a secret sinner as against the common moralities, but the real problem, Why are the righteous afflicted remains. It is solved in the last chapter.

<hi type="bold">Elihu</hi><div eID="gen1588" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1589" type="x-p"/> Elihu has a far juster and more spiritual conception of the problem than Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar because he has an infinitely higher conception of God. The God of Eliphaz and the others, great though they perceive Him to be in His works, becomes in their thought petty and exacting in His relations with mankind. It is the fatal misconception of all religious externalists and moralizers. Their God is always a small God. Elihu's account of God is noble and true, and it is noteworthy that at the last Jehovah does not class him with Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar (cf) <reference osisRef="job 42:7">Job 42:7</reference> but he is still a dogmatist, and his eloquent discourse is marred by self-assertiveness (e.g) ; <reference osisRef="job 32:8 job 32:9">Job 32:8,9</reference>; <reference osisRef="job 33:3"> 33:3</reference>. Jehovah's judgment of Elihu is that he darkened counsel by words <reference osisRef="job 38:2">Job 38:2</reference> the very charge that Elihu had brought against Job. ; <reference osisRef="job 34:35">Job 34:35</reference>; <reference osisRef="job 35:16"> 35:16</reference>. Furthermore, the discourse of Jehovah is wholly free from the accusations of Job with which even Elihu's lofty discourse abounds.<div eID="gen1589" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1590" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">himself</hi> Heb. his soul. <div eID="gen1590" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv44"/><div sID="gen1591" type="x-p"/> <chapter eID="Job.32"/>
<div eID="gen1591" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1592" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="38" osisID="Job.38" sID="Job.38"/>

<hi type="bold">The Lord answered Job</hi> <div eID="gen1592" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1593" type="x-p"/> The words of jehovah have the effect of bringing Job consciously into His presence. <reference osisRef="job 42:5">Job 42:5</reference>. Hitherto the discussions have been about God, but He has been conceived as absent. Now Job and the Lord are face to face. It is noteworthy that Job does not answer Elihu. Despite his harsh judgment he has spoken so truly about God that Job remains silent. <reference osisRef="job 38:1">Job 38:1</reference> might be paraphrased, "Then Jehovah answered for or on behalf of Job."

<div sID="gen1602" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="42" osisID="Job.42" sID="Job.42"/>

<hi type="bold">Wherefore I abhor myself</hi> <div eID="gen1602" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1603" type="x-p"/> The problem, of which the book of Job is the profound discussion, finds here its solution. Brought into the presence of God, Job is revealed to himself. In no sense a hypocrite, but godly and possessing a faith which all his afflictions could not shake, Job was yet self-righteous and lacking in humility. Chapter 29 fully discloses this. But in the presence of God he anticipates, as it were, the experience of Paul. <reference osisRef="php 3:4-9">Philippians 3:4-9</reference> and the problem is solved. The godly are afflicted that they may be brought to self-knowledge and self-judgment. Such afflictions are not penal for their sins, but remedial and purifying. The book of Job affords a sublime illustration of the truth announced in ; <reference osisRef="1co 11:31 1co 11:32">1 Corinthians 11:31,32</reference>; <reference osisRef="heb 12:7-11">Hebrews 12:7-11</reference>. Best of all, such self-knowledge and self-judgment is the prelude to greater fruitfulness. ; <reference osisRef="job 42:7-17">Job 42:7-17</reference>; <reference osisRef="joh 15:2">John 15:2</reference>. Cf. ; <reference osisRef="jos 5:13 jos 5:14">Joshua 5:13,14</reference>; <reference osisRef="eze 1:28">Ezekiel 1:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="eze 2:1-3">Ezekiel 2:1-3</reference>; <reference osisRef="da 10:5-11">Daniel 10:5-11</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 1:17-19">Revelation 1:17-19</reference>.<div eID="gen1603" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1604" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">repent</hi><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Zec 8:14">Zechariah 8:14</reference>")</hi>. <chapter eID="Job.42"/><div eID="gen1604" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen1519" osisID="Job" type="book"/>

<div canonical="true" osisID="Ps" sID="gen1605" type="book"/> <milestone n="" type="x-usfm-toc1"/> <milestone n="" type="x-usfm-toc2"/> <milestone n="" type="x-usfm-toc3"/> <div sID="gen1606" type="x-p"/>
<chapter n="1" osisID="Ps.1" sID="Ps.1"/>

<div eID="gen1606" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Book Introduction - Psalms</title> <div sID="gen1607" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="ps 1">Read first chapter of Psalms</reference><div eID="gen1607" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1608" type="x-p"/> The simplest description of the five books of Psalms is that they were the inspired prayer- and-praise book of Israel. They are revelations of truth, not abstractly, but in the terms of human experience. The truth revealed is wrought into the emotions, desires, and sufferings of the people of God by the circumstances through which they pass. But those circumstances are such as to constitute an anticipation of analogous conditions through which Christ in His incarnation, and the Jewish remnant in the tribulation (<reference osisRef="Is 10:21">Is 10:21,</reference> refs), should pass; so then many Psalms are prophetic of the sufferings, the faith, and the victory of both. Psalms 22 and 50 are examples. The former--the holy of holies of the Bible-- reveals all that was in the mind of Christ when He uttered the desolate cry, "My God, My God, why hast Thou forsaken Me?" The latter is an anticipation of what will be in the heart of Israel when she shall turn to Jehovah again (<reference osisRef="de 30:1 de 30:2">Deuteronomy 30:1,2</reference>). Other Psalms are directly prophetic of "the sufferings of Christ, and the glories which should follow" (<reference osisRef="lu 24:25-27 lu 24:44">Luke 24:25-27,44</reference>). Psalm 2 is a notable instance, presenting Jehovah's Anointed as rejected and crucified (<reference osisRef="ps 2:1-3">Psalms 2:1-3</reference>; <reference osisRef="ac 4:24-28">Acts 4:24-28</reference>) but afterward set as King in Zion.<div eID="gen1608" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1609" type="x-p"/> The great themes of the Psalms are, Christ, Jehovah, the Law, Creation, the future of Israel, and the exercises of the renewed heart in suffering, in joy, in perplexity. The promises of the Psalms are primarily Jewish, and suited to a people under the law, but are spiritually true in Christian experience also, in the sense that they disclose the mind of God, and the exercises of His heart toward those who are perplexed, afflicted, or cast down.<div eID="gen1609" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1610" type="x-p"/> The imprecatory Psalms are the cry of the oppressed in Israel for justice--a cry appropriate and right in the earthly people of God, and based upon a distinct promise in the Abrahamic Covenant (<hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ge 15:18">Genesis 15:18</reference>")</hi> ), but a cry unsuited to the church, a heavenly people who have taken their place with a rejected and crucified Christ. (<reference osisRef="lu 9:52-55">Luke 9:52-55</reference>).<div eID="gen1610" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1611" type="x-p"/> The Psalms are in five books, each ending in a doxology:<div eID="gen1611" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">Psalms 1-41.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">Psalms 42-72.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">Psalms 73-89.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">Psalms 90-106.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">Psalms 107-150. </item> </list> <chapter eID="Ps.1"/>
<chapter n="2" osisID="Ps.2" sID="Ps.2"/> <div sID="gen1612" type="x-p"/>

<hi type="bold">king</hi> <div eID="gen1612" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1613" type="x-p"/> The second Psalm gives the order of the establishment of the kingdom. It is in six parts:<div eID="gen1613" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(1) The rage of the Gentiles, the vain imagination of "people" (Jews), and the antagonism of rulers against Jehovah's anointed <reference osisRef="ps 2:1-3">Psalms 2:1-3</reference>. The inspired interpretation of this is in <reference osisRef="ac 4:25-28">Acts 4:25-28</reference> which asserts its fulfilment in the crucifixion of Christ.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(2) The derision of Jehovah <reference osisRef="ps 2:4">Psalms 2:4</reference> that men should suppose it possible to set aside His covenant <reference osisRef="2sa 7:8-17">2 Samuel 7:8-17</reference> and oath <reference osisRef="ps 89:34-37">Psalms 89:34-37</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(3) The vexation <reference osisRef="ps 2:5">Psalms 2:5</reference> fulfilled, first in the destruction of Jerusalem, A.D. 70; and in the final dispersion of the Jews at that time; and to be fulfilled more completely in the tribulation <reference osisRef="mt 24:29">Matthew 24:29</reference> which immediately precedes the return of the King. <reference osisRef="mt 24:30">Matthew 24:30</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(4) The establishment of the rejected King upon Zion <reference osisRef="ps 2:6">Psalms 2:6</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(5) The subjection of the earth to the King's rule <reference osisRef="ps 2:7-9">Psalms 2:7-9</reference> and</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(6) the present appeal to the world powers. <reference osisRef="ps 2:10-12">Psalms 2:10-12</reference>. See Psalm 8., next in order of the Messianic Psalms. (Note. Psalms 2. 8. 16. 22. 23. 24. 40. 41. 45. 68. 69. 72. 89. 102. 110. and 118. are considered as Messianic. It is not questioned that many other Psalms also refer to Christ. </item> </list>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv44"/><div sID="gen1614" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv44"/> <hi type="bold">fear</hi> <div eID="gen1614" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1615" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ps 19:9">Psalms 19:9</reference>")</hi>

<hi type="bold">trust</hi> <div eID="gen1615" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1616" type="x-p"/> Trust is the characteristic O.T. word for the N.T. "faith," "believe." It occurs 152 times in the O.T., and is the rendering of Heb. words signifying to take refuge (e.g. <reference osisRef="ru 2:12">Ruth 2:12</reference> "to lean on" (e.g.) <reference osisRef="ps 56:3">Psalms 56:3</reference> "to roll on" (e.g.) <reference osisRef="ps 22:8">Psalms 22:8</reference> "to stay upon" (e.g.) <reference osisRef="job 35:14">Job 35:14</reference>. <div eID="gen1616" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv45"/><div sID="gen1617" type="x-p"/> <chapter eID="Ps.2"/>

1 Gittith= "winepress," and so, of the harvest, in the sense of judgment <reference osisRef="isa 63:3">Isaiah 63:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 19:15">Revelation 19:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="ps 7:1">Psalms 7:1,</reference> to which the title of Psalm 8. properly belongs, is a Psalm of judgment.

<hi type="bold">For thou hast made him a little lower than the angels</hi><div eID="gen1632" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1633" type="x-p"/> In Psa 2. Christ was presented as Jehovah's Son and King, rejected and crucified but yet to reign in Zion. In Psa 8., while His deity is fully recognized (<reference osisRef="ps 8:1">Psalms 8:1</reference>), Psa. 110 with <reference osisRef="mt 22:41-46">Matthew 22:41-46</reference> He is seen as Son of man <reference osisRef="ps 8:4-6">Psalms 8:4-6</reference> who, "made for a little while lower than the angels, " is to have dominion over the redeemed creation <reference osisRef="heb 2:6-11">Hebrews 2:6-11</reference>. The authority here is racial and Adamic, rather than purely divine as in Psa 2., or Davidic as in Psa 89. That which the first man lost, the second man and "last Adam" more than regained. <reference osisRef="heb 2:6-11">Hebrews 2:6-11</reference> in connection with Psa. 8., and <reference osisRef="ro 8:17-21">Romans 8:17-21</reference> show that the "many sons" whom He is bringing to glory, are joint heirs with Him in both the royal right of Psa. 2. and the human right of Heb. 2. See Psa. 16., next in order of the Messianic Psalms.<div eID="gen1633" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1634" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">angel</hi><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Heb 1:4">Hebrews 1:4</reference>")</hi>. <div eID="gen1634" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv45"/><div sID="gen1635" type="x-p"/> <chapter eID="Ps.8"/>
