<hi type="bold">Aijeleth Shahar</hi> <div eID="gen1666" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1667" type="x-p"/> Or, Ay-ys-leth Shachar, "hind of the morning," a title, not a musical instrument.<div eID="gen1667" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1668" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">My God, My God</hi> <div eID="gen1668" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1669" type="x-p"/> Psalms 22., 23., and 24. form a trilogy. In Psalm 22, the good Shepherd gives His life for the sheep <reference osisRef="joh 10:11">John 10:11,</reference> in Psalm 23 the great Shepherd, "brought again from the dead through the blood of the everlasting covenant." <reference osisRef="heb 13:20">Hebrews 13:20</reference> tenderly cares for the sheep; in Psalm 24, the chief Shepherd appears as King of glory to own and reward the sheep <reference osisRef="1pe 5:4">1 Peter 5:4</reference>.

<hi type="bold">All they that see me</hi><div eID="gen1669" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1670" type="x-p"/> Psalm 22. is a graphic picture of death by crucifixion. The bones (of the hands, arms, shoulders, and pelvis) out of joint (<reference osisRef="ps 22:14">Psalms 22:14</reference>) the profuse perspiration caused by intense suffering (v. 14); the action of the heart affected (v.14); strength exhausted, and extreme thirst (<reference osisRef="ps 22:15">Psalms 22:15</reference>); the hands and feet pierced (<reference osisRef="ps 22:16">Psalms 22:16</reference>) partial nudity with hurt to modesty (<reference osisRef="ps 22:17">Psalms 22:17</reference>), are all incidental to that mode of death. The accompanying circumstances are precisely those fulfilled in the crucifixion of Christ. <reference osisRef="ps 22:14-17">Psalms 22:14-17</reference>. The desolate cry of ; <reference osisRef="ps 22:1">Psalms 22:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="mt 27:46">Matthew 27:46,</reference> the periods of light and darkness of ; <reference osisRef="ps 22:2">Psalms 22:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="mt 27:45">Matthew 27:45</reference> the contumely of ; <reference osisRef="ps 22:6-8 ps 22:12-13 ps 22:18">Psalms 22:6-8,12,13,18</reference>; <reference osisRef="mt 27:29-43">Matthew 27:29-43</reference> the casting lots of verse <reference osisRef="ps 22:18">Psalms 22:18</reference> (<reference osisRef="mt 27:35">Matthew 27:35</reference>), all were literally fulfilled. When it is remembered that crucifixion was a Roman, not Jewish form of execution, the proof of inspiration is irresistible.

<hi type="bold">I will declare</hi><div eID="gen1670" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1671" type="x-p"/> At verse 22 the Psalm breaks from crucifixion to resurrection; fulfilled in the "Go to my brethren," etc., of <reference osisRef="joh 20:17">John 20:17</reference>. The risen Christ declares to His brethren the name, "Father."

1 Jeduthun<div eID="gen1724" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1725" type="x-p"/> Jeduthun, a Levite, chief singer and instructor. See <reference osisRef="1ch 9:16">1 Chronicles 9:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="1ch 16:38 1ch 16:41 1ch 16:42"> 16:38,41,42</reference>; <reference osisRef="1ch 25:1 1ch 25:3 1ch 25:6"> 25:1,3,6</reference>; <reference osisRef="2ch 5:12">2 Chronicles 5:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="2ch 35:15"> 35:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="ne 11:17">Nehemiah 11:17</reference>. He is mentioned in Psalms 39,62, 77. Jeduthun was first called Ethan. <div eID="gen1725" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv45"/><div sID="gen1726" type="x-p"/> <chapter eID="Ps.39"/>
<div eID="gen1726" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1727" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="40" osisID="Ps.40" sID="Ps.40"/>

<hi type="bold">I waited</hi> <div eID="gen1727" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1728" type="x-p"/> The 40th Psalm speaks of Messiah, Jehovah's Servant, obedient unto death. The Psalm begins with the joy of Christ in resurrection (<reference osisRef="ps 40:1 ps 40:2">Psalms 40:1,2</reference>). He has been in the horrible pit of the grave, but has been brought up. Verses 3-5 are His resurrection testimony, His "new song." Verses 6 and 7 are retrospective. When sacrifice and offering had become abominable because of the wickedness of the people <reference osisRef="isa 1:10-15">Isaiah 1:10-15</reference> then the obedient Servant came to make the pure offering ; <reference osisRef="ps 40:7-17">Psalms 40:7-17</reference>; <reference osisRef="heb 10:5-17">Hebrews 10:5-17</reference>. See Psalm 41., next in order of the Messianic Psalms.

<div eID="gen1740" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1741" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="45" osisID="Ps.45" sID="Ps.45"/>

<hi type="bold">Shoshannim</hi> <div eID="gen1741" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1742" type="x-p"/> Shoshannim, "lilies," and so, the spring; the Shoshannim Psalms were probably connected with the Passover season, and hence reminders of redemption out of bondage, and of the origins of Israel.<div eID="gen1742" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1743" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">king</hi> <div eID="gen1743" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1744" type="x-p"/> This great psalm of the King, with Psalms 46.-47., obviously looks forward to the advent in glory. The reference in <reference osisRef="heb 1:8 heb 1:9">Hebrews 1:8,9</reference> is not so much to the anointing as an event <reference osisRef="mt 3:16 mt 3:17">Matthew 3:16,17</reference> as to the permanent state of the King. Cf. <reference osisRef="isa 11:1 isa 11:2">Isaiah 11:1,2</reference>.<div eID="gen1744" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1745" type="x-p"/> The divisions are:<div eID="gen1745" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(1) The supreme beauty of the King (<reference osisRef="ps 45:1 ps 45:2">Psalms 45:1,2</reference>);</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(2) the coming of the King in glory <reference osisRef="ps 45:3-5">Psalms 45:3-5</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 19:11-21">Revelation 19:11-21</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(3) the deity of the King and character of His reign <reference osisRef="ps 45:6 ps 45:7">Psalms 45:6,7</reference>; <reference osisRef="heb 1:8 heb 1:9">Hebrews 1:8,9</reference>; <reference osisRef="isa 11:1-5">Isaiah 11:1-5</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(4) as associated with Him in earthly rule, the queen is presented, <reference osisRef="ps 45:9-13">Psalms 45:9-13</reference> and in that relation the King is not called Elohim <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ge 1:1">Genesis 1:1</reference>")</hi> as in verse 6, but Adonai, the husband name of Deity See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:ge 15:2">Genesis 15:2</reference>".</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(5) the virgin companions of the queen, who would seem to be the Jewish remnant. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ro 11:5">Romans 11:5</reference>")</hi>. <reference osisRef="re 14:1-4">Revelation 14:1-4</reference> are next seen <reference osisRef="ps 45:14 ps 45:15">Psalms 45:14,15,</reference> and</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(6) the Psalm closes with a reference to the earthly fame of the King.</item> </list> <div sID="gen1746" type="x-p"/> See Psalm 68., next in order of the Messianic Psalms. <div eID="gen1746" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv45"/><div sID="gen1747" type="x-p"/> <chapter eID="Ps.45"/>
<div eID="gen1747" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1748" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="46" osisID="Ps.46" sID="Ps.46"/>

<hi type="bold">Alamoth</hi> <div eID="gen1748" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1749" type="x-p"/> Alamoth, "soprano," from almah, a virgin. Some have thought the alamoth, "virgins," were a temple choir, singing antiphonally to the sheminith, or male choir. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ps 6:1">Psalms 6:1</reference>")</hi>. But contr, see <reference osisRef="1ch 15:20">1 Chronicles 15:20</reference>. <chapter eID="Ps.46"/><div eID="gen1749" type="x-p"/>

<hi type="bold">redeem</hi> <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Isa 59:20">Isaiah 59:20</reference>")</hi> See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:ex 14:30">Exodus 14:30</reference>"<div eID="gen1754" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1755" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">grave</hi> Heb. "Sheol," <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Hab 2:5">Habakkuk 2:5</reference>")</hi>. <div eID="gen1755" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv45"/><div sID="gen1756" type="x-p"/> <chapter eID="Ps.49"/>
<div eID="gen1756" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1757" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="51" osisID="Ps.51" sID="Ps.51"/>

<hi type="bold">Have</hi> <div eID="gen1757" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1758" type="x-p"/> This Psalm must ever be, in its successive steps, the mould of the experience of a sinning saint who comes back to full communion and service. The steps are:<div eID="gen1758" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(1) sin thoroughly judged before God (vs. 1-6);</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(2) forgiveness and cleansing through the blood (v. 7.f.c.)</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(3) cleansing (v. 7,1,c, to 10.) Cf <reference osisRef="joh 13:4-10">John 13:4-10</reference>; <reference osisRef="eph 5:26">Ephesians 5:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="1jo 1:9">1 John 1:9</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(4) Spirit-filled for joy and power (vs. 11,12);</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(5) service (v. 13);</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(6) worship (vs 14-17);</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(7) the restored saint in fellowship with God, not about self, but about the blessing of Zion. Personally, it was David's pathway to restored communion after his sin with Bathsheba. Dispensationally, it will be the pathway of returning Israel. <reference osisRef="de 30:1-10">Deuteronomy 30:1-10</reference>. </item> </list>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv45"/><div sID="gen1759" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv45"/> <hi type="bold">Hyssop</hi> <div eID="gen1759" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1760" type="x-p"/> Hyssop was the little shrub <reference osisRef="1ki 4:33">1 Kings 4:33</reference> with which the blood and water of purification were applied. ; <reference osisRef="le 14:1-7">Leviticus 14:1-7</reference>; <reference osisRef="nu 19:1-19">Numbers 19:1-19</reference>. Cleansing in Scripture is twofold:<div eID="gen1760" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(1) Of a sinner from the guilt of sin; the blood ("hyssop") aspect;</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(2) of a saint from the defilement of sin--the water ("wash me") aspect;</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(3) Under grace the sinner is purged by blood when he believes <reference osisRef="mt 26:28">Matthew 26:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="heb 1:3">Hebrews 1:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="heb 9:12"> 9:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="heb 10:14"> 10:14</reference>. Both aspects of cleansing, by blood and by water, are brought out in ; <reference osisRef="joh 13:10">John 13:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="eph 5:25 eph 5:26">Ephesians 5:25,26</reference>.</item> </list> <div sID="gen1761" type="x-p"/> "He that is bathed needeth not save to wash his feet"; "Christ loved the church and gave Himself for it redemption by "blood, "hyssop," the "bath"] that He might sanctify and cleanse "it with the washing by the word": answering to the "wash me" of verse 7. <div eID="gen1761" type="x-p"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv46"/><div sID="gen1762" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv46"/> <hi type="bold">Take not</hi> <div eID="gen1762" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1763" type="x-p"/> No believer of this dispensation, aware of the promise of His abiding <reference osisRef="joh 14:16">John 14:16</reference> should pray, "Take not Thy Holy Spirit from me." <reference osisRef="eph 4:30">Ephesians 4:30</reference> but while Christian position is not found here, Christian experience in essence is. <chapter eID="Ps.51"/><div eID="gen1763" type="x-p"/>

<hi type="bold">Let God arise</hi> <div eID="gen1796" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1797" type="x-p"/> The entire Psalm is pervaded by the joy of Israel in the kingdom, but a stricter order of events begins with verse 18. This is quoted <reference osisRef="eph 4:7-16">Ephesians 4:7-16</reference> of Christ's ascension ministry. Verses 21-23 refer to the regathering of Israel, and the destruction of the Beast and his armies.<div eID="gen1797" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(See "Beast," <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Da 7:8">Daniel 7:8</reference>")</hi> )</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(See "Beast," <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Re 19:20">Revelation 19:20</reference>")</hi> ).</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(See "Armageddon" <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Re 16:16">Revelation 16:16</reference>")</hi> , <reference osisRef="re 19:17-19">Revelation 19:17-19</reference>.</item> </list> <div sID="gen1798" type="x-p"/> Verses 24-35 are descriptive of full and universal kingdom blessing.<div eID="gen1798" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(See "Kingdom" (O.T.), <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ge 1:26">Genesis 1:26</reference>")</hi></item> </list> <div sID="gen1799" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Zec 12:8">Zechariah 12:8</reference>")</hi>.<div eID="gen1799" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1800" type="x-p"/> See Psalm 69., next in order of the Messianic Psalms.

<div eID="gen1802" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1803" type="x-p"/><chapter n="69" osisID="Ps.69" sID="Ps.69"/>

<hi type="bold">Shoshannim</hi><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ps 45:1">Psalms 45:1</reference>")</hi>.<div eID="gen1803" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1804" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Save me, O God</hi> <div eID="gen1804" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1805" type="x-p"/> The N.T. quotations from, and references to, this Psalm indicate in what way it adumbrates Christ. It is the psalm of His humiliation and rejection <reference osisRef="ps 69:4 ps 69:7-8 ps 69:10-12">Psalms 69:4,7,8,10-12</reference>. <reference osisRef="ps 69:14-20">Psalms 69:14-20</reference> may well describe the exercises of His holy soul in Gethsemane <reference osisRef="mt 26:36-45">Matthew 26:36-45</reference> while <reference osisRef="ps 69:21">Psalms 69:21</reference> is a direct reference to the cross ; <reference osisRef="mt 27:34 mt 27:48">Matthew 27:34,48</reference>; <reference osisRef="joh 19:28">John 19:28</reference>. The imprecatory verses <reference osisRef="ps 69:22-28">Psalms 69:22-28</reference> are connected <reference osisRef="ro 11:9 ro 11:10">Romans 11:9,10</reference> with the present judicial blindness of Israel, <reference osisRef="ps 69:25">Psalms 69:25</reference> having special reference to Judas. <reference osisRef="ac 1:20">Acts 1:20</reference> who is thus made typical of his generation, which shared his guilt.<div eID="gen1805" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1806" type="x-p"/> See Psalm 72, next in order of the Messianic Psalms.

<hi type="bold">Give the king</hi> <div eID="gen1814" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1815" type="x-p"/> The Psalm as a whole forms a complete vision of Messiah's kingdom so far as the O.T. revelation extended. All David's prayers will find their fruition in the kingdom (<reference osisRef="ps 72:20">Psalms 72:20</reference>); <reference osisRef="2sa 23:1-4">2 Samuel 23:1-4</reference>.<div eID="gen1815" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1816" type="x-p"/> Verse 1 refers to the investiture of the King's Son with the kingdom, of which investiture the formal description is given in <reference osisRef="da 7:13 da 7:14">Daniel 7:13,14</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 5:5-10">Revelation 5:5-10</reference>; <reference osisRef="ps 72:2-7 ps 72:12-14">Psalms 72:2-7,12-14</reference> give the character of the kingdom. (Cf) <reference osisRef="isa 11:3-9">Isaiah 11:3-9</reference>.<div eID="gen1816" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1817" type="x-p"/> The emphatic word is righteousness. The sermon on the Mount describes the kingdom of righteousness. Verses 8-11 speak of the universality of the kingdom. Verse 16 hints at the means by which universal blessing is to be brought in. Converted Israel will be the "handful of corn" <reference osisRef="am 9:9">Amos 9:9</reference> as the King Himself in death and resurrection was the single grain, the "corn of wheat" <reference osisRef="joh 12:24">John 12:24</reference> "To the Jew first" is the order alike of Church and kingdom. ; <reference osisRef="ro 1:16">Romans 1:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="ac 13:46">Acts 13:46</reference>; <reference osisRef="ac 15:16 ac 15:17"> 15:16,17</reference>. It is through restored Israel that the kingdom is to be extended over the earth. <reference osisRef="zec 8:13 zec 8:20-23">Zechariah 8:13,20-23</reference>.<div eID="gen1817" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1818" type="x-p"/> See Psalm 89., next in order of the Messianic Psalms.

<hi type="bold">higher than the kings of the earth</hi><div eID="gen1866" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1867" type="x-p"/> The eighty-ninth Psalm is at once the confirmation and exposition of the Davidic Covenant <reference osisRef="2sa 7:9-14">2 Samuel 7:9-14</reference>. That the covenant itself looks far beyond David and Solomon is sure from <reference osisRef="ps 89:27">Psalms 89:27</reference>. "Higher than the kings of the earth" can only refer to Immanuel. ; <reference osisRef="isa 7:13-15">Isaiah 7:13-15</reference>; <reference osisRef="isa 9:6 isa 9:7"> 9:6,7</reference>; <reference osisRef="mic 5:2">Micah 5:2</reference>.<div eID="gen1867" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1868" type="x-p"/> The Psalm is in four parts:<div eID="gen1868" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(1) The covenant, though springing from the lovingkindness of Jehovah, yet rests upon His oath (vs. 1-4).</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(2) Jehovah is glorified for His power and goodness in connection with the covenant (vs 5-18).</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(3) The response of Jehovah (vs. 19-37). This is in two parts:</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(a), it confirms the covenant (<reference osisRef="ps 89:19-29">Psalms 89:19-29</reference>), but (b), warns that disobedience in the royal posterity of David will be punished with chastening (<reference osisRef="ps 89:30-32">Psalms 89:30-32</reference>). Historically this chastening began in the division of the Davidic kingdom ; <reference osisRef="1ki 11:26-36">1 Kings 11:26-36</reference>; <reference osisRef="1ki 12:16-20"> 12:16-20</reference> and culminated in the captivities and that subordination of Israel to the Gentiles which still continues. See "Gentiles, times of" ; <reference osisRef="lu 21:24">Luke 21:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 16:14">Revelation 16:14</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(4) The plea of the Remnant <reference osisRef="isa 1:9">Isaiah 1:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="ro 11:5">Romans 11:5</reference> who urge the severity and long continuance of the chastening (<reference osisRef="ps 89:38-52">Psalms 89:38-52</reference>).</item> </list> <div sID="gen1869" type="x-p"/> See Psalm 102., next in order of the Messianic Psalms.

<hi type="bold">The Lord said unto my Lord</hi> <div eID="gen1902" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1903" type="x-p"/> The importance of Psalm 110 is attested by the remarkable prominence given to it in the New Testament.<div eID="gen1903" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(1) It affirms the deity of Jesus, thus answering those who deny the full divine meaning of his N.T. title of "Lord." <reference osisRef="mt 22:41-45">Matthew 22:41-45</reference>; <reference osisRef="mr 12:35-37">Mark 12:35-37</reference>; <reference osisRef="lu 20:41-44">Luke 20:41-44</reference>; <reference osisRef="ac 2:34 ac 2:35">Acts 2:34,35</reference>; <reference osisRef="heb 1:13">Hebrews 1:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="heb 10:12 heb 10:13"> 10:12,13</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(2) This Psalm announces the eternal priesthood of Messiah--one of the most important statements of Scripture (<reference osisRef="ps 110:4">Psalms 110:4</reference>).</item> </list> <div sID="gen1904" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ge 14:18">Genesis 14:18</reference>")</hi> See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:heb 5:6">Hebrews 5:6</reference>". ; <reference osisRef="heb 7:1-28">Hebrews 7:1-28</reference>; <reference osisRef="1ti 2:5 1ti 2:6">1 Timothy 2:5,6</reference>; <reference osisRef="joh 14:6">John 14:6</reference>.<div eID="gen1904" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(3) Historically, the Psalm begins with the ascension of Christ <reference osisRef="ps 110:1">Psalms 110:1,</reference>; <reference osisRef="joh 20:17">John 20:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="ac 7:56">Acts 7:56</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 3:21">Revelation 3:21</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(4) Prophetically, the Psalm looks on</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(a) to the time when Christ will appear as the Rod of Jehovah's strength, the Deliverer out of Zion. <reference osisRef="ro 11:25-27">Romans 11:25-27</reference> and the conversion of Israel ; <reference osisRef="ps 110:3">Psalms 110:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="joe 2:27">Joel 2:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="zec 13:9">Zechariah 13:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="de 30:1-9">Deuteronomy 30:1-9</reference> <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:De 30:3">Deuteronomy 30:3</reference>")</hi> , and</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(b) to the judgment upon the Gentile powers which precedes the setting up of the kingdom (<reference osisRef="ps 110:5 ps 110:6">Psalms 110:5,6</reference>); <reference osisRef="joe 3:9-17">Joel 3:9-17</reference>; <reference osisRef="zec 14:1-4">Zechariah 14:1-4</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 19:11-21">Revelation 19:11-21</reference>.</item> </list> <div sID="gen1905" type="x-p"/> See "Armageddon" <reference osisRef="re 16:14">Revelation 16:14</reference> <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Re 19:17">Revelation 19:17</reference>")</hi>. "Israel" <reference osisRef="ge 12:2 ge 12:3">Genesis 12:2,3</reference>. See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:ro 11:26">Romans 11:26</reference>". "Kingdom" See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:zec 12:8">Zechariah 12:8</reference>". See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:1co 15:24">1 Corinthians 15:24</reference>". See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:ps 2:6">Psalms 2:6</reference>". See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:ps 118:22">Psalms 118:22</reference>.<div eID="gen1905" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1906" type="x-p"/> See Psalm 118, last in order of the Messianic Psalms.

See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:1pe 2:8">1 Peter 2:8</reference>".</hi><div eID="gen1925" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1926" type="x-p"/> Psalm 118 looks beyond the rejection of the Stone (Christ) to His final exaltation in the kingdom (<reference osisRef="ps 118:22">Psalms 118:22</reference>).<div eID="gen1926" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1927" type="x-p"/> See Psalm 2, first of the Messianic Psalms.

<hi type="bold">O give thanks unto the Lord</hi><div eID="gen1927" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen1928" type="x-p"/> The Messianic Psalms: Summary. That the Psalms contain a testimony to Christ our Lord Himself affirmed <reference osisRef="lu 24:44">Luke 24:44</reference> and the N.T. quotations from the Psalter point unerringly to those Psalms which have the Messianic character. A close spiritual and prophetic character as surely identifies others. Christ is seen in the Psalms<div eID="gen1928" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(1) in two general character, as suffering (e.g. Psa. 22), and as entering into His kingdom glory (e.g. psa 2.; 24.) Cf <reference osisRef="lu 24:25-27">Luke 24:25-27</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(2) Christ is seen in His person</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(a) as Son of God <reference osisRef="ps 2:7">Psalms 2:7</reference> and very God ; <reference osisRef="ps 45:6 ps 45:7">Psalms 45:6,7</reference>; <reference osisRef="ps 102:25"> 102:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="ps 110:1"> 110:1</reference> (b) as Son of man <reference osisRef="ps 8:4-6">Psalms 8:4-6</reference> (c) as Son of David <reference osisRef="ps 89:3 ps 89:4 ps 89:27 ps 89:29">Psalms 89:3,4,27,29</reference></item> <item type="x-indent-1">(3) Christ is seen in His offices</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(a) as Prophet <reference osisRef="ps 22:22 ps 22:25">Psalms 22:22,25</reference>; <reference osisRef="ps 40:9 ps 40:10"> 40:9,10</reference> (b) as Priest <reference osisRef="ps 110:4">Psalms 110:4</reference> and (c) as King (e.g. Psa 2., 24.)</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(4) Christ is seen in His varied work. As Priest He offers Himself in sacrifice <reference osisRef="ps 22:1-31">Psalms 22:1-31</reference>; <reference osisRef="ps 40:6"> 40:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="heb 10:5-12">Hebrews 10:5-12</reference> and, in resurrection, as the Priest-Shepherd, ever living to make intercession ; <reference osisRef="ps 23:1-6">Psalms 23:1-6</reference>; <reference osisRef="heb 7:21-25">Hebrews 7:21-25</reference>; <reference osisRef="heb 13:20"> 13:20</reference>. As Prophet He proclaims the name of Jehovah as Father ; <reference osisRef="ps 22:22">Psalms 22:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="joh 20:17">John 20:17</reference>. As King He fulfils the Davidic Covenant <reference osisRef="ps 89:1-52">Psalms 89:1-52</reference> and restores alike the dominion of man over creation ; <reference osisRef="ps 8:4-8">Psalms 8:4-8</reference>; <reference osisRef="ro 8:17-21">Romans 8:17-21</reference> and of the Father over all. <reference osisRef="1co 15:25-28">1 Corinthians 15:25-28</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(5) The Messianic Psalms give, also, the inner thoughts, the exercises of soul, of Christ in His earthly experiences. (See, e.g., <reference osisRef="ps 16:8-11">Psalms 16:8-11</reference>; <reference osisRef="ps 22:1-21 ps 40:1-17"> 22:1-21 40:1-17</reference>). </item> </list> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv47"/><div sID="gen1929" type="x-p"/> <chapter eID="Ps.118"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv47"/><title type="x-s">Book Introduction - Proverbs</title> <div sID="gen2002" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="pr 1">Read first chapter of Proverbs</reference><div eID="gen2002" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2003" type="x-p"/> This collection of sententious sayings is divine wisdom applied to the earthly conditions of the people of God. That the Proverbs were Solomon's (<reference osisRef="pr 1:1">Proverbs 1:1</reference>) implies no more than that he gathered into orderly arrangement sayings already current amongst the people, the wisdom of the Spirit, perhaps through many centuries (<reference osisRef="ec 12:9">Ecclesiastes 12:9</reference>). Chapters 25-29 were current in Hezekiah's time (<reference osisRef="ec 25:1">Ecclesiastes 25:1</reference>). Chapters 30 and 31 are by Agur and Lemuel.<div eID="gen2003" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2004" type="x-p"/> The book is in six parts:<div eID="gen2004" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">To sons, 1-7.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The praise of wisdom, 8-9.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The folly of sin, 10-19.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">Warnings and instructions, 20-29.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The words of Agur, 30. The words of King Lemuel, 31.</item> </list> <div sID="gen2005" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv47"/> <hi type="bold">fear</hi> <div eID="gen2005" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2006" type="x-p"/> Also; <reference osisRef="pr 1:29">Proverbs 1:29,</reference> <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ps 19:9">Psalms 19:9</reference>")</hi>

<hi type="bold">foolish son</hi> <div eID="gen2028" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2029" type="x-p"/> A "fool" in Scripture is never a mentally deficient person, but rather one arrogant and self-sufficient; one who orders his life as if there were no God. See, for illustration, <reference osisRef="lu 12:16-20">Luke 12:16-20</reference>. The rich man was not mentally deficient, but he was a "fool" because he supposed that his soul could live on the things in the barn, giving no thought to his eternal wellbeing.

<chapter n="1" osisID="Eccl.1" sID="Eccl.1"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv48"/><title type="x-s">Book Introduction - Ecclesiastes</title> <div sID="gen2071" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="ec 1">Read first chapter of Ecclesiastes</reference><div eID="gen2071" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2072" type="x-p"/> This is the book of man "under the sun," reasoning about life; it is the best man can do, with the knowledge that there is a holy God, and that He will bring every-thing into judgment. The key phrases are "under the sun;" "I perceived"; "I said in my heart." Inspiration sets down accurately what passes, but the conclusions and reasonings are, after all, man's. That those conclusions are just in declaring it "vanity" in view of judgment, to devote life to earthly things, is surely true; but the "conclusion" (<reference osisRef="ec 12:13">Ecclesiastes 12:13</reference>) is legal, the best that man apart from redemption can do, and does not anticipate the Gospel.<div eID="gen2072" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2073" type="x-p"/> Ecclesiastes is in five parts:<div eID="gen2073" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">Theme, 1:1-3.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">Theme proved, 1:4-3:22.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">Theme unfolded in the light of human sufferings, hypocrisies, uncertainties, poverty and riches, 4:1-10:20.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The best thing possible to the natural man apart from God, 11:1-12:12.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The best thing possible to man under the law, 12:13,14.</item> </list> <chapter eID="Eccl.1"/>
<div sID="gen2074" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="3" osisID="Eccl.3" sID="Eccl.3"/>

<hi type="bold">Vanity</hi> <div eID="gen2074" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2075" type="x-p"/> "Vanity," in Ecclesiastes, and usually in Scripture, means, not foolish pride, but the emptiness in final result of all life apart from God. It is to be born, to toil, to suffer, to experience some transitory joy, which is as nothing in view of eternity, to leave it all, and to die. See <reference osisRef="ro 8:20-22">Romans 8:20-22</reference>.

<hi type="bold">fear</hi><div eID="gen2075" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2076" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ps 19:9">Psalms 19:9</reference>")</hi>. <chapter eID="Eccl.3"/><div eID="gen2076" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen2077" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="5" osisID="Eccl.5" sID="Eccl.5"/>
<hi type="bold">angel</hi> <div eID="gen2077" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2078" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Heb 1:4">Hebrews 1:4</reference>")</hi>

<hi type="bold">fear</hi> <div eID="gen2078" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2079" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ps 19:9">Psalms 19:9</reference>")</hi> <chapter eID="Eccl.5"/> <div eID="gen2079" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen2080" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="7" osisID="Eccl.7" sID="Eccl.7"/>
<hi type="bold">good</hi> <div eID="gen2080" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2081" type="x-p"/> Or, as good as an inheritance, yea, better too.

<hi type="bold">Be not righteous</hi><div eID="gen2081" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2082" type="x-p"/> See; <reference osisRef="ec 7:16 ec 7:17">Ecclesiastes 7:16,17</reference> Natural wisdom: be moderately religious and moderately wicked. <chapter eID="Eccl.7"/><div eID="gen2082" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen2083" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="8" osisID="Eccl.8" sID="Eccl.8"/>

<hi type="bold">fear</hi> <div eID="gen2083" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2084" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ps 19:9">Psalms 19:9</reference>")</hi> <chapter eID="Eccl.8"/> <div eID="gen2084" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen2085" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="9" osisID="Eccl.9" sID="Eccl.9"/>

<hi type="bold">there is no work</hi> <div eID="gen2085" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2086" type="x-p"/> Verse 10 is no more a divine revelation concerning the state of the dead than any other conclusion of "the Preacher" <reference osisRef="ec 1:1">Ecclesiastes 1:1</reference> is such a revelation. Reasoning from the standpoint of man "under the sun" the natural man can see no difference between a dead man and a dead lion. <reference osisRef="ec 9:4">Ecclesiastes 9:4</reference>. A living dog is better than either. No one would quote verse 2 as a divine revelation. These reasonings of man apart from divine revelation are set down by inspiration just as the words of Satan ; <reference osisRef="ge 3:4">Genesis 3:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="job 2:4 job 2:5">Job 2:4,5</reference> are so set down. But that life and consciousness continue between death and resurrection is directly affirmed in Scripture. ; <reference osisRef="isa 14:9-11">Isaiah 14:9-11</reference>; <reference osisRef="mt 22:32">Matthew 22:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="mr 9:43-48">Mark 9:43-48</reference>; <reference osisRef="lu 16:19-31">Luke 16:19-31</reference>; <reference osisRef="joh 11:26">John 11:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="2co 5:6-8">2 Corinthians 5:6-8</reference>; <reference osisRef="php 1:21-23">Philippians 1:21-23</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 6:9-11">Revelation 6:9-11</reference>.<div eID="gen2086" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2087" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">grave</hi> Heb. "Sheol," <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Hab 2:5">Habakkuk 2:5</reference>")</hi>.

<hi type="bold">fear</hi><div eID="gen2087" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2088" type="x-p"/> Also; <reference osisRef="de 6:2">Deuteronomy 6:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="de 10:12"> 10:12</reference> <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ps 19:9">Psalms 19:9</reference>")</hi>. <chapter eID="Eccl.9"/><div eID="gen2088" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen2070" osisID="Eccl" type="book"/>
<div canonical="true" osisID="Song" sID="gen2089" type="book"/> <milestone n="" type="x-usfm-toc1"/> <milestone n="" type="x-usfm-toc2"/> <milestone n="" type="x-usfm-toc3"/>
<chapter n="1" osisID="Song.1" sID="Song.1"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv48"/><title type="x-s">Book Introduction - Song</title> <div sID="gen2090" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="so 1">Read first chapter of Song</reference><div eID="gen2090" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2091" type="x-p"/> Nowhere in Scripture does the unspiritual mind tread upon ground so mysterious and incomprehensible as in this book, while the saintliest men and women of the ages have found it a source of pure and exquisite delight. That the love of the divine Bridegroom should follow all the analogies of the marriage relation seems evil only to minds so ascetic that martial desire itself seems to them unholy.<div eID="gen2091" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2092" type="x-p"/> The interpretation is twofold: Primarily, the book is the expression of pure marital love as ordained of God in creation, and the vindication of that love as against both asceticism and lust--the two profanations of the holiness of marriage. The secondary and larger interpretation is of Christ, the Son and His heavenly bride, the Church (<reference osisRef="2co 11:1-4">2 Corinthians 11:1-4</reference> refs).<div eID="gen2092" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2093" type="x-p"/> In this sense the book has six divisions:<div eID="gen2093" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">The bride seen in restful communion with the Bridegroom, 1:1-2:7.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">A lapse and restoration, 2:3-3:5.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">Joy of fellowship, 3:6-5:1.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">Separation of interest--the bride satisfied, the Bridegroom toiling for others, 5:2-5.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The bride seeking and witnessing, 5:6-6:3.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">Unbroken communion, 6:4-8:14.</item> </list> <div sID="gen2094" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv48"/>Verse 6 grave<div eID="gen2094" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2095" type="x-p"/> Hebrew, "Sheol," <chapter eID="Song.1"/><div eID="gen2095" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen2096" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="2" osisID="Song.2" sID="Song.2"/>

<hi type="bold">so is</hi> <div eID="gen2096" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2097" type="x-p"/> How poor are the similes of the bride as compared with those of the Bridegroom. To Him she is a "lily among thorns; she can only say that He is "as the apple tree among the trees of the wood."
<hi type="bold">our wall</hi><div eID="gen2097" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2098" type="x-p"/> "Our wall." The bride had returned to her own home: the Bridegroom seeks her.

<hi type="bold">dove</hi><div eID="gen2098" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2099" type="x-p"/> There is beautiful order here. First we have what the bride is as seen in Christ, "My dove." In herself most faulty; in Him "blameless and harmless" <reference osisRef="php 2:15">Philippians 2:15</reference> the very character of the dove. The bride's place of safety, "in the clefts of the rock"--hidden, so to speak, in the wounds of Christ. Thirdly, her privilege. "Stairs" speaks of access. It is not "secret places," as in A.V., but "the secret of the stairs"--the way and privilege of access to His presence ; <reference osisRef="eph 2:18">Ephesians 2:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="col 3:1">Colossians 3:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="heb 10:19-22">Hebrews 10:19-22</reference>. Fourthly, the order of approach: she is to come near before she speaks, "Let me see thy countenance," then "Let me hear thy voice." Lastly, now that she is near and has spoken, He speaks a tender word of admonition: "Take us the foxes," etc. <chapter eID="Song.2"/><div eID="gen2099" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen2100" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="4" osisID="Song.4" sID="Song.4"/>

<hi type="bold">sister</hi> <div eID="gen2100" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2101" type="x-p"/> The word "sister" here is of infinitely delicate significance, intimating the very whiteness of purity in the midst of an ardour which is, like the shekinah, aglow but unspeakably holy. Sin has almost deprived us of the capacity even to stand with unshod feet before this burning bush. <chapter eID="Song.4"/><div eID="gen2101" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen2102" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="5" osisID="Song.5" sID="Song.5"/>

<hi type="bold">sleep</hi> <div eID="gen2102" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2103" type="x-p"/> The bride is satisfied with her washed feet while the Bridegroom, His "head filled with dew," and His "locks with the drops of night," is toiling for others. See <reference osisRef="lu 6:12">Luke 6:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="lu 14:21-23"> 14:21-23</reference>. The state of the bride is not one of sin, but of neglect of service. She is preoccupied with the graces and perfections which she has in Christ through the Spirit ; <reference osisRef="1co 12:4-11">1 Corinthians 12:4-11</reference>; <reference osisRef="ga 5:22 ga 5:23">Galatians 5:22,23</reference>. It is mysticism, unbalanced by the activities of the Christian warfare. Her feet are washed, her hands drop with sweet smelling myrrh; but He has gone on, and now she must seek Him (cf. <reference osisRef="lu 2:44 lu 2:45">Luke 2:44,45</reference>).

<hi type="bold">I sought him</hi><div eID="gen2103" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2104" type="x-p"/> Observe, it is now the Bridegroom Himself who occupies her heart, not His gifts-- myrrh and washed feet <reference osisRef="joh 13:2-9">John 13:2-9</reference>.

<hi type="bold">fitly set</hi> Heb. "sitting in fulness;" i.e. fitly placed, and set as a precious stone in the foil of a ring. <div eID="gen2104" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv49"/><div sID="gen2105" type="x-p"/> <chapter eID="Song.5"/>
<div eID="gen2105" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2106" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="6" osisID="Song.6" sID="Song.6"/>

<hi type="bold">we may seek him</hi> <div eID="gen2106" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2107" type="x-p"/> So soon as the bride witnesses to the Bridegroom's own personal loveliness, a desire is awakened in the daughters of Jerusalem to seek Him. <chapter eID="Song.6"/><div eID="gen2107" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen2108" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="8" osisID="Song.8" sID="Song.8"/>

<hi type="bold">grave</hi> <div eID="gen2108" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2109" type="x-p"/> Heb. "Sheol," <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Hab 2:5">Habakkuk 2:5</reference>")</hi>

<hi type="bold">We have</hi><div eID="gen2109" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2110" type="x-p"/> The reference here is obscure. <chapter eID="Song.8"/><div eID="gen2110" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen2089" osisID="Song" type="book"/>
<div canonical="true" osisID="Isa" sID="gen2111" type="book"/> <milestone n="" type="x-usfm-toc1"/> <milestone n="" type="x-usfm-toc2"/> <milestone n="" type="x-usfm-toc3"/>
<chapter n="1" osisID="Isa.1" sID="Isa.1"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv49"/><title type="x-s">Book Introduction - Isaiah</title> <div sID="gen2112" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="isa 1">Read first chapter of Isaiah</reference><div eID="gen2112" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2113" type="x-p"/> Isaiah is justly accounted the chief of the writing prophets. He has the more comprehensive testimony and is distinctively the prophet of redemption. Nowhere else in the Scriptures written under the law have we so clear a view of grace. The New Testament Church does not appear (<reference osisRef="Eph 3:3-10">Eph 3:3-10</reference>), but Messiah in His Person and sufferings, and the blessing of the Gentiles through Him, are in full vision.<div eID="gen2113" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2114" type="x-p"/> Apart from his testimony to his own time, which includes warnings of coming judgments upon the great nations of that day, the predictive messages of Isaiah cover seven great themes:<div eID="gen2114" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">Israel in exile and divine judgment upon Israel's oppressors.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The return from Babylon.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The manifestation of Messiah in humiliation (e.g. Chap. 53).</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The blessing of the Gentiles.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The manifestation of Messiah in judgment ("the day of vengeance of our God").</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The reign of David's righteous Branch in the kingdom-age.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The new heavens and the new earth.</item> </list> <div sID="gen2115" type="x-p"/> Isaiah is in two chief divisions:<div eID="gen2115" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">Looking toward the captivities, 1:1-39:8. Key verses, 1:1,2.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">Looking beyond the captivities, 40:1-66:24. Key verses, 40:1,2.</item> </list> <div sID="gen2116" type="x-p"/> These chief divisions fall into subdivisions, as indicated in the text.<div eID="gen2116" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2117" type="x-p"/> The events recorded in Isaiah cover a period of 62 years (Ussher). <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv49"/><hi type="bold">Hear, O heavens</hi><div eID="gen2117" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2118" type="x-p"/> The chapter, down to verse 23, states the case of Jehovah against Judah. Chastening, according to Deut. 28., 29., had been visited upon Israel in the land (vs. 5-8), and now the time of expulsion from the land is near. But just here Jehovah renews the promise of the Palestinian Covenant of future restoration and exaltation <reference osisRef="isa 1:26 isa 1:27">Isaiah 1:26,27</reference>; <reference osisRef="isa 2:1-4"> 2:1-4</reference>.

<hi type="bold">remnant</hi> Remnant. See, <reference osisRef="isa 10:20">Isaiah 10:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="ro 11:5">Romans 11:5</reference> <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ro 11:5">Romans 11:5</reference>")</hi>
<hi type="bold">Bring no more</hi> <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:2Co 8:1">2 Corinthians 8:1</reference>")</hi> <reference osisRef="Is 1:11-17">Is 1:11-17</reference>.

<hi type="bold">thy judges</hi><div eID="gen2118" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2119" type="x-p"/> Under the kingdom the ancient method of administering the theocratic government over Israel is to be restored. Cf. <reference osisRef="jud 2:18">Judges 2:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="mt 19:28">Matthew 19:28</reference>. <chapter eID="Isa.1"/><div eID="gen2119" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen2120" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="2" osisID="Isa.2" sID="Isa.2"/>

<hi type="bold">that the mountain</hi> <div eID="gen2120" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2121" type="x-p"/> A mountain, in Scripture symbolism, means a kingdom <reference osisRef="da 2:35">Daniel 2:35</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 13:1">Revelation 13:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 17:9-11"> 17:9-11</reference>.

<hi type="bold">Day of the Lord</hi> (Day of Jehovah) vs.<div eID="gen2121" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2122" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="isa 2:10-22">Isaiah 2:10-22</reference>; <reference osisRef="isa 4:1-6"> 4:1-6</reference> ; <reference osisRef="isa 11:10-13"> 11:10-13</reference>; <reference osisRef="isa 13:9-16"> 13:9-16</reference> ; <reference osisRef="isa 24:21-23"> 24:21-23</reference>; <reference osisRef="isa 26:20 isa 26:21"> 26:20,21</reference>; <reference osisRef="isa 63:1-6">Isaiah 63:1-6</reference>; <reference osisRef="isa 66:15-24"> 66:15-24</reference>; <reference osisRef="jer 25:29-33">Jeremiah 25:29-33</reference>; <reference osisRef="jer 46:10"> 46:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="eze 30:3">Ezekiel 30:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 19:11-21">Revelation 19:11-21</reference> \ <chapter eID="Isa.2"/><div eID="gen2122" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen2123" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="4" osisID="Isa.4" sID="Isa.4"/>

<hi type="bold">branch</hi> <div eID="gen2123" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2124" type="x-p"/> A name of Christ, used in fourfold way:<div eID="gen2124" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(1) "The Branch of Jehovah" (<reference osisRef="isa 4:2">Isaiah 4:2</reference>), that is, the "Immanuel" character of Christ <reference osisRef="isa 7:14">Isaiah 7:14</reference> to be fully manifested to restored and converted Israel after His return in divine glory <reference osisRef="mt 25:31">Matthew 25:31</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(2) the "Branch of David" <reference osisRef="isa 11:1">Isaiah 11:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="jer 23:5">Jeremiah 23:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="jer 33:15"> 33:15</reference> that is, the Messiah, "of the seed of David according to the flesh" <reference osisRef="ro 1:3">Romans 1:3</reference> revealed in His earthly glory as King of kings, and Lord of lords;</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(3) Jehovah's "Servant, the Branch" <reference osisRef="zec 3:8">Zechariah 3:8</reference> Messiah's humiliation and obedience unto death according to ; <reference osisRef="isa 52:13-15">Isaiah 52:13-15</reference>; <reference osisRef="isa 53:1-12"> 53:1-12</reference>; <reference osisRef="php 2:5-8">Philippians 2:5-8</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(4) the "man whose name is the Branch" <reference osisRef="zec 6:12 zec 6:13">Zechariah 6:12,13</reference> that is His character as Son of man, the "last Adam," the "second Man" <reference osisRef="1co 15:45-47">1 Corinthians 15:45-47</reference> reigning, as Priest-King, over the earth in the dominion given to and lost by the first Adam. Matthew is the Gospel of the "Branch of David"; Mark of "Jehovah's Servant, the Branch"; Luke of "the man whose name is the Branch"; John of "the Branch of Jehovah." </item> </list> <chapter eID="Isa.4"/>
<div sID="gen2125" type="x-p"/><chapter n="5" osisID="Isa.5" sID="Isa.5"/>
<hi type="bold">hell</hi> Heb. "Sheol," <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Hab 2:5">Habakkuk 2:5</reference>")</hi>. <chapter eID="Isa.5"/><div eID="gen2125" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen2126" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="6" osisID="Isa.6" sID="Isa.6"/>

<hi type="bold">seraphims</hi> <div eID="gen2126" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2127" type="x-p"/> Heb. Burners. The word occurs only here. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Eze 1:5">Ezekiel 1:5</reference>")</hi>. The Seraphim are, in many respects, in contrast with the Cherubim, though both are expressive of the divine holiness, which demands that the sinner shall have access to divine presence only through a sacrifice which really vindicates the righteousness of God.<div eID="gen2127" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2128" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ro 3:24">Romans 3:24</reference>")</hi> See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:ro 3:25">Romans 3:25</reference>" See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:ro 3:26">Romans 3:26</reference>" and that the saint shall be cleansed before serving. <reference osisRef="ge 3:22-24">Genesis 3:22-24</reference> illustrates the first; <reference osisRef="isa 6:1-8">Isaiah 6:1-8</reference> the second. The Cherubim may be said to have to do with the altar, the Seraphim with the laver. See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:ps 51:7">Psalms 51:7</reference>" See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:joh 13:10">John 13:10</reference>". The Seraphim appear to be actual angelic beings.

<hi type="bold">tenth</hi><div eID="gen2128" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2129" type="x-p"/> See "Remnant," <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ro 11:5">Romans 11:5</reference>")</hi>.<div eID="gen2129" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2130" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">return</hi> <div eID="gen2130" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2131" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Isa 8:18">Isaiah 8:18</reference>")</hi> <div eID="gen2131" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv50"/><div sID="gen2132" type="x-p"/> <chapter eID="Isa.6"/>
<div eID="gen2132" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2133" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="7" osisID="Isa.7" sID="Isa.7"/>

<hi type="bold">tenth</hi> <div eID="gen2133" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2134" type="x-p"/> See "Remnant," <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ro 11:5">Romans 11:5</reference>")</hi>.<div eID="gen2134" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2135" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">return</hi> <div eID="gen2135" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2136" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Isa 8:18">Isaiah 8:18</reference>")</hi>

<hi type="bold">Ephraim</hi> <div eID="gen2136" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2137" type="x-p"/> In the prophetic books "Ephraim" and "Israel" are the collective names of the ten tribes who, under Jeroboam, established the northern kingdom, subsequently called Samaria <reference osisRef="1ki 16:24">1 Kings 16:24</reference> and were (B.C. 722) sent into an exile which still continues. <reference osisRef="2ki 17:1-6">2 Kings 17:1-6</reference>.<div eID="gen2137" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2138" type="x-p"/> They are distinguished as "the outcasts of Israel" from "the dispersed of Judah." <reference osisRef="isa 11:12">Isaiah 11:12</reference>. "Hidden" in the world <reference osisRef="mt 13:44">Matthew 13:44</reference> they, with Judah, are yet to be restored to Palestine and made one nation again. ; <reference osisRef="jer 23:5-8">Jeremiah 23:5-8</reference>; <reference osisRef="eze 37:11-24">Ezekiel 37:11-24</reference>.
<hi type="bold">Shearjashub</hi><div eID="gen2138" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2139" type="x-p"/> Meaning, a remnant shall return. <reference osisRef="isa 8:3">Isaiah 8:3</reference>.

<hi type="bold">Hear ye now</hi><div eID="gen2139" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2140" type="x-p"/> The prophecy is not addressed to the faithless Ahaz, but to the whole "house of David." The objection that such a far-off event as the birth of Christ could be no "sign" to Ahaz, is, therefore, puerile. It was a continuing prophecy addressed to the Davidic family, and accounts at once for the instant assent of Mary. <reference osisRef="lu 1:38">Luke 1:38</reference>.

<hi type="bold">Butter and honey</hi><div eID="gen2140" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2141" type="x-p"/> Indicating the plainness and simplicity of the life in which the young Immanuel should be brought up. <chapter eID="Isa.7"/><div eID="gen2141" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen2142" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="8" osisID="Isa.8" sID="Isa.8"/>

<hi type="bold">confederacy</hi> <div eID="gen2142" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2143" type="x-p"/> The reference is to the attempt to terrify Judah by the confederacy between Syria and Samaria. <reference osisRef="isa 7:1 isa 7:2">Isaiah 7:1,2</reference>.

<hi type="bold">signs</hi><div eID="gen2143" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2144" type="x-p"/> The primary application here is to the two sons of Isaiah, Maher-shalal-hash-baz= "haste ye, haste ye to the spoil," a "sign" of the coming judgment of the captivity of Judah; Shear-jashub= "a remnant shall return," a "sign" of the return of a remnant of Judah at the end of the seventy years, <reference osisRef="jer 25:11 jer 25:12">Jeremiah 25:11,12</reference>; <reference osisRef="da 9:2">Daniel 9:2</reference>. The larger and final reference is to our Lord <reference osisRef="heb 2:13 heb 2:14">Hebrews 2:13,14</reference>. <chapter eID="Isa.8"/><div eID="gen2144" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen2145" type="x-p"/><chapter n="9" osisID="Isa.9" sID="Isa.9"/>
<hi type="bold">not</hi> Omit, not. Isaiah complains that despite the wickedness of the northern kingdom her afflictions are light, her prosperity great.

<hi type="bold">throne of David</hi><div eID="gen2145" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2146" type="x-p"/> The "throne of David" is a phrase as definite, historic, historically, as "throne of the Caesars," and as little admits of "spiritualizing." <reference osisRef="lu 1:32 lu 1:33">Luke 1:32,33</reference>. See "Kingdom (O.T.). <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Zec 12:8">Zechariah 12:8</reference>")</hi>. "Davidic Covenant," See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:2sa 7:16">2 Samuel 7:16</reference>", <reference osisRef="ac 15:14-16">Acts 15:14-16</reference>.
<hi type="bold">Jacob</hi> <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ge 32:28">Genesis 32:28</reference>")</hi>.

<hi type="bold">For all this his anger</hi><div eID="gen2146" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2147" type="x-p"/> See <reference osisRef="isa 9:17 isa 9:21">Isaiah 9:17,21</reference>; <reference osisRef="isa 5:25"> 5:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="isa 10:4"> 10:4</reference><div eID="gen2147" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2148" type="x-p"/> The context explains. Jehovah's hand is outstretched still because His chastisement is followed by no amendment on the part of Israel. <chapter eID="Isa.9"/><div eID="gen2148" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen2149" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="10" osisID="Isa.10" sID="Isa.10"/>

<hi type="bold">that when</hi> <div eID="gen2149" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2150" type="x-p"/> A permanent method in the divine government of the earth. Israel is always the centre of the divine counsels earthward <reference osisRef="de 32:8">Deuteronomy 32:8</reference>. The Gentile nations are permitted to afflict Israel in chastisement for her national sins, but invariably and inevitably retribution falls upon them. See ; <reference osisRef="ge 15:13 ge 15:14">Genesis 15:13,14</reference>; <reference osisRef="de 30:5-7">Deuteronomy 30:5-7</reference>; <reference osisRef="isa 14:1 isa 14:2">Isaiah 14:1,2</reference>; <reference osisRef="joe 3:1-8">Joel 3:1-8</reference>; <reference osisRef="mic 5:7-9">Micah 5:7-9</reference>; <reference osisRef="mt 25:31-40">Matthew 25:31-40</reference>.

<hi type="bold">that day</hi><div eID="gen2150" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2151" type="x-p"/> "That day": often the equivalent of "the day of the Lord" <reference osisRef="isa 2:10-22">Isaiah 2:10-22</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 19:11-21">Revelation 19:11-21</reference>. The prophecy here passes from the general to the particular, from historic and fulfilled judgments upon Assyria to the final destruction of all Gentile world-power at the return of the Lord in glory. (See "Armageddon," ; <reference osisRef="re 16:14">Revelation 16:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 19:21"> 19:21</reference> "Times of the Gentiles," ; <reference osisRef="lu 21:24">Luke 21:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 16:19">Revelation 16:19,</reference> "The great tribulation," ; <reference osisRef="ps 2:5">Psalms 2:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 7:14">Revelation 7:14,</reference> and <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Isa 13:19">Isaiah 13:19</reference>")</hi> <div eID="gen2151" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv50"/><div sID="gen2152" type="x-p"/> <chapter eID="Isa.10"/>
<div eID="gen2152" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2153" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="11" osisID="Isa.11" sID="Isa.11"/>

<hi type="bold">The Davidic kingdom</hi> <div eID="gen2153" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2154" type="x-p"/> The order of events in Isa. 10., 11., is noteworthy. Isa. 10. gives the distress of the Remnant in Palestine in the great tribulation. <reference osisRef="ps 2:5">Psalms 2:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 7:14">Revelation 7:14</reference> and the approach and destruction of the Gentile host under the Beast. ; <reference osisRef="da 7:8">Daniel 7:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 19:20">Revelation 19:20</reference>. Is. 11. immediately follows with its glorious picture of the kingdom-age. Precisely the same order is found in Re 19., 20. (See "Kingdom," O.T., ; <reference osisRef="ge 1:26-28">Genesis 1:26-28</reference>; <reference osisRef="zec 12:8">Zechariah 12:8</reference> N.T. ; <reference osisRef="lu 1:31-33">Luke 1:31-33</reference>; <reference osisRef="1co 15:28">1 Corinthians 15:28</reference>. Also <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Mt 3:2">Matthew 3:2</reference>")</hi> See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:mt 6:33">Matthew 6:33</reference>".<div eID="gen2154" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2155" type="x-p"/> That nothing of this occurred at the first coming of Christ is evident from a comparison of the history of the times of Christ with this and all the other parallel prophecies. So far from regathering dispersed Israel and establishing peace in the earth, His crucifixion was soon followed (A.D. 70) by the destruction of Jerusalem, and the utter scattering of the Palestinian Jews amongst the nations.<div eID="gen2155" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2156" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">shall come forth a rod</hi> <div eID="gen2156" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2157" type="x-p"/> This chapter is a prophetic picture of the glory of the future kingdom. This is the kingdom announced by John Baptist as "at hand." It was then rejected, but will be set up when David's Son returns in glory <reference osisRef="lu 1:31 lu 1:32">Luke 1:31,32</reference>; <reference osisRef="ac 15:15 ac 15:16">Acts 15:15,16</reference>.<div eID="gen2157" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2158" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Branch</hi> <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Isa 4:2">Isaiah 4:2</reference>")</hi>
<hi type="bold">fear</hi> <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ps 19:9">Psalms 19:9</reference>")</hi>

<hi type="bold">for the earth</hi> <div eID="gen2158" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2159" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Hab 2:14">Habakkuk 2:14</reference>")</hi>

<hi type="bold">an ensign</hi> <div eID="gen2159" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2160" type="x-p"/> (Day of Jehovah) vs. <reference osisRef="isa 2:10-22">Isaiah 2:10-22</reference>; <reference osisRef="isa 4:1-6"> 4:1-6</reference> ; <reference osisRef="isa 11:10-13"> 11:10-13</reference>; <reference osisRef="isa 13:9-16"> 13:9-16</reference> ; <reference osisRef="isa 24:21-23"> 24:21-23</reference>; <reference osisRef="isa 26:20 isa 26:21"> 26:20,21</reference> <reference osisRef="isa 63:1-6"> 63:1-6</reference>; <reference osisRef="isa 66:15-24"> 66:15-24</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 19:11-21">Revelation 19:11-21</reference>. <chapter eID="Isa.11"/><div eID="gen2160" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen2161" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="12" osisID="Isa.12" sID="Isa.12"/>

<hi type="bold">trust</hi> <div eID="gen2161" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2162" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ps 2:12">Psalms 2:12</reference>")</hi> <div eID="gen2162" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv50"/><div sID="gen2163" type="x-p"/> <chapter eID="Isa.12"/>
<div eID="gen2163" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2164" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="13" osisID="Isa.13" sID="Isa.13"/>

<hi type="bold">burden</hi> <div eID="gen2164" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2165" type="x-p"/> A "burden," Heb. massa= a heavy, weighty thing, is a message, or oracle concerning Babylon, Assyria, Jerusalem, etc. It is "heavy" because the wrath of God is in it, and grievous for the prophet to declare.<div eID="gen2165" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2166" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Babylon</hi> <div eID="gen2166" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2167" type="x-p"/> The city, Babylon is not in view here, as the immediate context shows. It is important to note the significance of the name when used symbolically. "Babylon" is the Greek form: invariably in the O.T. Hebrew the word is simply Babel, the meaning of which is confusion, and in this sense the word is used symbolically.<div eID="gen2167" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(1) In the prophets, when the actual city is not meant, the reference is to the "confusion" into which the whole social order of the world has fallen under Gentile world-domination. (See "Times of the Gentiles," <reference osisRef="lu 21:24">Luke 21:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 16:14">Revelation 16:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="isa 13:4">Isaiah 13:4</reference> gives the divine view of the welter of warring Gentile powers. The divine order is given in Isa. 11. Israel in her own land, the centre of the divine government of the world and channel of the divine blessing; and the Gentiles blessed in association with Israel. Anything else is, politically, mere "babel."</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(2) In <reference osisRef="re 14:8-11">Revelation 14:8-11</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 16:19"> 16:19</reference> the Gentile world-system is in view in connection with Armageddon ; <reference osisRef="re 16:14">Revelation 16:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 19:21"> 19:21</reference> while in Re 17. the reference is to apostate Christianity, destroyed by the nations <reference osisRef="re 17:16">Revelation 17:16</reference> headed up under the Beast ; <reference osisRef="da 7:8">Daniel 7:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 19:20">Revelation 19:20</reference> and false prophet. In Isaiah the political Babylon is in view, literally as to the then existing city, and symbolically as to the times of the Gentiles. In the Revelation both the symbolical- political and symbolical-religious Babylon are in view, for there both are alike under the tyranny of the Beast. Religious Babylon is destroyed by political Babylon <reference osisRef="re 17:16">Revelation 17:16</reference> political Babylon by the appearing of the Lord <reference osisRef="re 19:19-21">Revelation 19:19-21</reference>. That Babylon the city is not to be rebuilt is clear from ; <reference osisRef="isa 13:19-22">Isaiah 13:19-22</reference>; <reference osisRef="jer 51:24-26 jer 51:62-64">Jeremiah 51:24-26,62-64</reference>. By political Babylon is meant the Gentile world-system. (See "World," ; <reference osisRef="joh 7:7">John 7:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 13:8">Revelation 13:8</reference>) It may be added that, in Scripture symbolism, Egypt stands for the world as such; Babylon for the world of corrupt power and corrupted religion; Nineveh for the pride, the haughty glory of the world. </item> </list>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv50"/><div sID="gen2168" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv50"/> <hi type="bold">Day of the Lord</hi> <div eID="gen2168" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2169" type="x-p"/> (Day of Jehovah) vs.<div eID="gen2169" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2170" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="isa 2:10-22">Isaiah 2:10-22</reference>; <reference osisRef="isa 4:1-6"> 4:1-6</reference> ; <reference osisRef="isa 11:10-13"> 11:10-13</reference>; <reference osisRef="isa 13:9-16"> 13:9-16</reference> ; <reference osisRef="isa 24:21-23"> 24:21-23</reference>; <reference osisRef="isa 26:20 isa 26:21"> 26:20,21</reference>; <reference osisRef="isa 63:1-6">Isaiah 63:1-6</reference>; <reference osisRef="isa 66:15-24"> 66:15-24</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 19:11-21">Revelation 19:11-21</reference>.

<hi type="bold">And Babylon</hi><div eID="gen2170" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2171" type="x-p"/> Verses 12-16 look forward to the apocalyptic judgments (Re 6.-13.). Verses 17-22 have a near and far view. They predict the destruction of the literal Babylon then existing; with the further statement that, once destroyed, Babylon should never be rebuilt (cf) <reference osisRef="jer 51:61-64">Jeremiah 51:61-64</reference>. All of this has been literally fulfilled. But the place of this prediction in a great prophetic strain looks forward to the destruction of both politico-Babylon and ecclesio- Babylon in the time of the Beast shows that the destruction of the actual Babylon typifies the greater destruction yet to come upon the mystical Babylons. Cf. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Isa 13:1">Isaiah 13:1</reference>")</hi>.<div eID="gen2171" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2172" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Babylon</hi> See note 2; <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Isa 13:1">Isaiah 13:1</reference>")</hi>. <chapter eID="Isa.13"/><div eID="gen2172" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen2173" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="14" osisID="Isa.14" sID="Isa.14"/>

<hi type="bold">hell</hi> <div eID="gen2173" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2174" type="x-p"/> Heb. "Sheol," Also; 15 <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Hab 2:5">Habakkuk 2:5</reference>")</hi>

<hi type="bold">grave</hi> Heb. "Sheol,"<div eID="gen2174" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2175" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Hab 2:5">Habakkuk 2:5</reference>")</hi>

<hi type="bold">son of the morning</hi> <div eID="gen2175" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2176" type="x-p"/> Verses 12-14 evidently refer to Satan, who, as prince of this world-system (see "World," <reference osisRef="joh 7:7">John 7:7</reference> <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Re 13:8">Revelation 13:8</reference>")</hi> is the real unseen ruler of the successive world- powers. Tyre, Babylon, Medo-Persia, Greece, Rome, etc. (see <reference osisRef="eze 28:12-14">Ezekiel 28:12-14</reference> Lucifer, "day-star," can be none other that Satan. This tremendous passage marks the beginning of sin in the universe. When Lucifer said, "I will," sin began. See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:re 20:10">Revelation 20:10</reference>".<div eID="gen2176" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2177" type="x-p"/> See other instances of addressing Satan through another, <reference osisRef="ge 3:15">Genesis 3:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="mt 16:22 mt 16:23">Matthew 16:22,23</reference>.

<hi type="bold">hell</hi><div eID="gen2177" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2178" type="x-p"/> Heb. "Sheol," Also; <reference osisRef="Is 14:9">Is 14:9</reference> <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Hab 2:5">Habakkuk 2:5</reference>")</hi>.

<hi type="bold">Babylon</hi><div eID="gen2178" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2179" type="x-p"/> See note 2; <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Isa 13:1">Isaiah 13:1</reference>")</hi>.

<hi type="bold">whole earth</hi><div eID="gen2179" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2180" type="x-p"/> This universality is significant and marks the whole passage as referring, not merely to a near judgment upon Assyria, but in a yet larger sense to the final crash of the present world-system at the end of the age. (See "Times of the Gentiles," <reference osisRef="lu 21:24">Luke 21:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 16:14">Revelation 16:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="da 2:44 da 2:45">Daniel 2:44,45</reference> "Armageddon," ; <reference osisRef="re 16:14">Revelation 16:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 19:17"> 19:17</reference>. No other such universal catastrophe on the nations is known to Scripture.

<hi type="bold">burden</hi><div eID="gen2180" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2181" type="x-p"/> See note 1; <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Isa 13:1">Isaiah 13:1</reference>")</hi>.
<hi type="bold">come forth</hi><div eID="gen2181" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2182" type="x-p"/> The descendants of Ahaz.

<hi type="bold">trust</hi><div eID="gen2182" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2183" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ps 2:12">Psalms 2:12</reference>")</hi> <div eID="gen2183" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv51"/><div sID="gen2184" type="x-p"/> <chapter eID="Isa.14"/>
<div eID="gen2184" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2185" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="15" osisID="Isa.15" sID="Isa.15"/>

<hi type="bold">Moab</hi> <div eID="gen2185" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2186" type="x-p"/> This "burden" had a precursive fulfilment in Sennacherib's invasion, B.C. 704, three years after the prediction <reference osisRef="isa 16:14">Isaiah 16:14</reference> but the words have a breadth of meaning which includes also the final world-battle. (<hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Re 19:17">Revelation 19:17</reference>")</hi> , <reference osisRef="isa 16:1-5">Isaiah 16:1-5</reference> which is a continuation of this "burden," shows the "tabernacle of David" set up, the next event in order after the destruction of the Beast and his armies. Cf. the order in ; <reference osisRef="isa 10:28-34">Isaiah 10:28-34</reference>; <reference osisRef="isa 11:1-10"> 11:1-10</reference> ; <reference osisRef="ac 15:14-17">Acts 15:14-17</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 19:17-21">Revelation 19:17-21</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 20:1-4"> 20:1-4</reference>.<div eID="gen2186" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2187" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">burden</hi> See note 1; <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Isa 13:1">Isaiah 13:1</reference>")</hi>. <div eID="gen2187" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv51"/><div sID="gen2188" type="x-p"/> <chapter eID="Isa.15"/>

<hi type="bold">thy dead men</hi> <div eID="gen2218" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2219" type="x-p"/> Eliminate the supplied words, men, and, together with. "Body" is in the plural, "bodies." <reference osisRef="isa 26:19-21">Isaiah 26:19-21</reference> with chapter 27., constitute Jehovah's answer to the plaint of Israel, <reference osisRef="isa 26:11-18">Isaiah 26:11-18</reference>. Verse 19 should read: "Thy dead shall live: my dead bodies shall rise" (i.e. the dead bodies of Jehovah's people). The restoration and re-establishment of Israel as a nation is also spoken of as a resurrection <reference osisRef="eze 37:1-11">Ezekiel 37:1-11</reference> and many hold that no more than this is meant in <reference osisRef="isa 26:19">Isaiah 26:19</reference>. But since the first resurrection is unto participation in the kingdom <reference osisRef="re 20:4-6">Revelation 20:4-6</reference> it seems the better view that both meanings are here. <div eID="gen2219" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv51"/><div sID="gen2220" type="x-p"/> <chapter eID="Isa.26"/>

<hi type="bold">And I will camp</hi><div eID="gen2226" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2227" type="x-p"/> Here, as often in prophecy, and especially in Isaiah, the near and far horizons blend. The near view is of Sennacherib's invasion and the destruction of the Assyrian host by the angel of the Lord (Isa. 36., 37.); the far view is that of the final gathering of the Gentile hosts against Jerusalem at the end of the great tribulation <reference osisRef="ps 2:5">Psalms 2:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 7:14">Revelation 7:14</reference> when a still greater deliverance will be wrought. (See "Times of the Gentiles," ; <reference osisRef="lu 21:24">Luke 21:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 16:14">Revelation 16:14</reference>. The same remark applies also to <reference osisRef="isa 28:14-18">Isaiah 28:14-18</reference> where there is a near reference to the Egyptian alliance ("we have made a covenant," etc.), while the reference to the stone <reference osisRef="isa 29:16">Isaiah 29:16</reference> carries the meaning forward to the end-time, and the covenant of unbelieving Israel with the Beast. <reference osisRef="da 9:27">Daniel 9:27</reference>.

<hi type="bold">Comfort</hi> <div eID="gen2257" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2258" type="x-p"/> The first two verses of Isa. 40. give the key-note of the second part of the prophecy of Isaiah. The great theme of this section is Jesus Christ in His sufferings, and the glory that shall follow in the Davidic kingdom. (See "Christ in O.T.," sufferings,) <reference osisRef="ge 4:4">Genesis 4:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="heb 10:18">Hebrews 10:18</reference> glory, ; <reference osisRef="2sa 7:8-15">2 Samuel 7:8-15</reference>; <reference osisRef="zec 12:8">Zechariah 12:8</reference> Since Israel is to be regathered, converted, and made the centre of the new social order when the kingdom is set up, this part of Isaiah appropriately contains glowing prophecies concerning these events. The full view of the redemptive sufferings of Christ (e.g. <reference osisRef="Isa 53">Isa. 53</reference>) leads to the evangelic strain so prominent in this part of Isaiah. (e.g. <reference osisRef="Isa 44:22-23 Isa 55:1-3">Isa 44:22-23, 55:1-3</reference>).<div eID="gen2258" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2259" type="x-p"/> The change in style, about which so much has been said, is no more remarkable than the change of theme. A prophet who was also a patriot would not write of the sins and coming captivity of his people in the same exultant and joyous style which he would use to describe their redemption, blessing, and power. In <reference osisRef="joh 12:37-44">John 12:37-44</reference> quotations from <reference osisRef="Isa 53:6">Isa. 53. and 6</reference>. are both ascribed to Isaiah.

<hi type="bold">circle</hi><div eID="gen2259" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2260" type="x-p"/> A remarkable reference to the sphericity of the earth. See, also, <reference osisRef="isa 42:5">Isaiah 42:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="isa 44:24"> 44:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="isa 51:13"> 51:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="job 9:8">Job 9:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="ps 104:2">Psalms 104:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="jer 10:12">Jeremiah 10:12</reference>. <chapter eID="Isa.40"/><div eID="gen2260" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen2261" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="41" osisID="Isa.41" sID="Isa.41"/>

<hi type="bold">the righteous man from the east</hi> <div eID="gen2261" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2262" type="x-p"/> The reference here seems to be to Cyrus, whose victories and rapid growth in power are here ascribed to the providence of God. <reference osisRef="isa 41:5-7">Isaiah 41:5-7</reference> describe the effect upon the nations of the rise of the Persian power. They heartened each other, and made (<reference osisRef="Is 41:7">Is 41:7</reference>) new idols. At verse 8 the prophet addresses Israel. Since it was their God who raised up Cyrus, they should expect good, not evil, from him (<reference osisRef="isa 41:8-20">Isaiah 41:8-20</reference>). <reference osisRef="isa 41:21-24">Isaiah 41:21-24</reference> form a contemptuous challenge to the idols in whom the nations are trusting.

<hi type="bold">servant</hi><div eID="gen2262" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2263" type="x-p"/> Three servants of Jehovah are mentioned in Isaiah:<div eID="gen2263" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(1) David <reference osisRef="isa 37:35">Isaiah 37:35</reference></item> <item type="x-indent-1">(2) Israel the nation <reference osisRef="isa 41:8-16">Isaiah 41:8-16</reference>; <reference osisRef="isa 43:1-10"> 43:1-10</reference> ; <reference osisRef="isa 44:1-8 isa 44:21"> 44:1-8,21</reference>; <reference osisRef="isa 45:4"> 45:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="isa 48:20"> 48:20</reference></item> <item type="x-indent-1">(3) Messiah <reference osisRef="isa 42:1-12">Isaiah 42:1-12,</reference> Is 49., entire chapter, but note especially <reference osisRef="isa 49:5-7">Isaiah 49:5-7,</reference> where the Servant Christ restores the servant nation; <reference osisRef="isa 50:4-6">Isaiah 50:4-6</reference>; <reference osisRef="isa 52:13-15"> 52:13-15</reference> <reference osisRef="isa 53:1-12"> 53:1-12</reference>. Israel the nation was a faithless servant, but restored and converted will yet thresh mountains. Against the Servant Christ no charge of unfaithfulness or failure is brought. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Isa 42:1">Isaiah 42:1</reference>")</hi>. </item> </list>

(Kinsman type). <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Isa 59:20">Isaiah 59:20</reference>")</hi>. <div eID="gen2265" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv52"/><div sID="gen2266" type="x-p"/> <chapter eID="Isa.41"/>
