<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv61"/><title type="x-s">Book Introduction - Daniel</title> <div sID="gen2617" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="da 1">Read first chapter of Daniel</reference><div eID="gen2617" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2618" type="x-p"/> Daniel, like Ezekiel was a Jewish captive in Babylon. He was of royal or princely descent (<reference osisRef="da 1:3">Daniel 1:3</reference>). For his rank and comeliness he was trained for palace service. In the polluted atmosphere of an oriental court he lived a life of singular piety and usefulness. His long life extended from Nebuchadnezzar to Cyrus. He was a contemporary of Jeremiah, Ezekiel (<reference osisRef="da 14:20">Daniel 14:20</reference>), Joshua, the high priest of the restoration, Ezra, and Zerubbabel.<div eID="gen2618" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2619" type="x-p"/> Daniel is the indispensable introduction to New Testament prophecy, the themes of which are, the apostasy of the Church, the manifestation of the man of sin, the great tribulation, the return of the Lord, the resurrections and the judgments. These, except the first, are Daniel's themes also.<div eID="gen2619" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2620" type="x-p"/> But Daniel is distinctively the prophet of the "times of the Gentiles" (<reference osisRef="lu 21:24">Luke 21:24</reference>), <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Lu 21:24">Luke 21:24</reference>")</hi>. His vision sweeps the whole course of Gentile world-rule to its end in catastrophe, and to the setting up of the Messianic kingdom.<div eID="gen2620" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2621" type="x-p"/> Daniel is in four broad divisions:<div eID="gen2621" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">Introduction. The personal history of Daniel from the conquest of Jerusalem to the second year of Nebuchadnezzar, 1:1-21.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The visions of Nebuchadnezzar and their results, 2:1-4:37.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The personal history of Daniel under Belshazzar and Darius, 5:1-6:28.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The visions of Daniel, 7:1-12:13.</item> </list> <div sID="gen2622" type="x-p"/> The events recorded in Daniel cover a period of 73 years (Ussher). <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv61"/><hi type="bold">and the name</hi><div eID="gen2622" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2623" type="x-p"/> Heb. Jehovah-shammah. See <reference osisRef="ex 17:15">Exodus 17:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="jud 6:24">Judges 6:24</reference>.

<hi type="bold">Daniel</hi><div eID="gen2623" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2624" type="x-p"/> deported 8 years before Ezekiel. <reference osisRef="2ki 24:1 2ki 24:2">2 Kings 24:1,2</reference>; <reference osisRef="2ch 36:5-7">2 Chronicles 36:5-7</reference>; <reference osisRef="jer 25:1">Jeremiah 25:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="jer 52:12-30">Jeremiah 52:12-30</reference>.

<hi type="bold">Belteshazzar</hi><div eID="gen2624" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2625" type="x-p"/> i.e. the king's leader, or attendant. <reference osisRef="da 2:26">Daniel 2:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="da 4:8 da 4:9 da 4:18 da 4:19"> 4:8,9,18,19</reference>; <reference osisRef="da 5:12"> 5:12</reference>. Identical in meaning with Belshazzar.

<hi type="bold">continued</hi><div eID="gen2625" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2626" type="x-p"/> i.e. to see the return of the remnant of Judah at the end of the 70 years, <reference osisRef="jer 25:11 jer 25:12">Jeremiah 25:11,12</reference>; <reference osisRef="jer 29:10"> 29:10</reference>. Daniel actually lived beyond the first year of Cyrus. <reference osisRef="da 10:1">Daniel 10:1</reference>. <div eID="gen2626" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv62"/><div sID="gen2627" type="x-p"/> <chapter eID="Dan.1"/>
<div eID="gen2627" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2628" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="2" osisID="Dan.2" sID="Dan.2"/>

<hi type="bold">continued</hi> <div eID="gen2628" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2629" type="x-p"/> i.e. to see the return of the remnant of Judah at the end of the 70 years, <reference osisRef="jer 25:11 jer 25:12">Jeremiah 25:11,12</reference>; <reference osisRef="jer 29:10"> 29:10</reference>. Daniel actually lived beyond the first year of Cyrus. <reference osisRef="da 10:1">Daniel 10:1</reference>.

<hi type="bold">Chaldeans</hi><div eID="gen2629" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2630" type="x-p"/> i.e. the men having the ancient wisdom; the learned; Chaldeans par excellence (<reference osisRef="da 2:13">Daniel 2:13</reference>). "wise"

<hi type="bold">Syriack</hi><div eID="gen2630" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2631" type="x-p"/> From <reference osisRef="da 2:4-da 7:28">Dan. 2:4 to 7:28</reference> the Book of Daniel is written in Aramaic the ancient language of Syria, and substantially identical with Chaldaic, the language of ancient Babylonia. Upon this fact, together with the occurrence of fifteen Persian, and three Greek words has been based an argument against the historicity of Daniel, and in favour of a date after the conquest of Palestine by Alexander (B.C. 332). It has, however, seemed, with some modern exceptions, to the Hebrew and Christian scholarship of the ages an unanswerable proof rather of the Danielic authorship of the book that, living from boyhood in a land the language of which was Chaldaic, a great part of his writing should be in that tongue. It has often been pointed out that the Chaldaic of Daniel is of high antiquity, as is shown by comparison with that of the Targums. The few words of Persian and Greek in like manner confirm the writer's residence at a court constantly visited by emissaries from those peoples. It is noteworthy that the Aramaic section is precisely that part of Daniel which most concerned the peoples amongst whom he lived, and to whom a prophecy written in Hebrew would have been unintelligible. The language returns to Hebrew in the predictive portions which have to do with the future of Israel. "The Hebrew of Daniel is closely related to that of Ezekiel."--Delitzsch.
<hi type="bold">captain</hi><div eID="gen2631" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2632" type="x-p"/> Or, executioner, <reference osisRef="da 2:24">Daniel 2:24</reference>.

<hi type="bold">revealeth</hi><div eID="gen2632" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2633" type="x-p"/> See margin, <reference osisRef="ge 41:45">Genesis 41:45</reference>. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ge 41:45">Genesis 41:45</reference>")</hi> , ; <reference osisRef="da 4:9">Daniel 4:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="job 15:8">Job 15:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="ps 25:14">Psalms 25:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="pr 3:32">Proverbs 3:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="mt 6:6">Matthew 6:6</reference>.

<hi type="bold">what should come</hi><div eID="gen2633" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2634" type="x-p"/> Times (of the Gentiles), <reference osisRef="da 2:29-45">Daniel 2:29-45</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 16:19">Revelation 16:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="lu 21:24">Luke 21:24</reference>.

<hi type="bold">great image</hi><div eID="gen2634" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2635" type="x-p"/> The monarchy-vision. Nebuchadnezzar's dream, as interpreted by Daniel, gives the course and end of "the times of the Gentiles" <reference osisRef="lu 21:24">Luke 21:24</reference>. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Re 16:19">Revelation 16:19</reference>")</hi> that is, of Gentile world-empire. The four metals composing the image are explained as symbolizing <reference osisRef="da 2:38-40">Daniel 2:38-40</reference> four empires, not necessarily possessing the inhabited earth, but able to do so (<reference osisRef="da 2:38">Daniel 2:38</reference>), and fulfilled in Babylon, Media-Persia, Greece (under Alexander), and Rome. The latter power is seen divided, first into two (the legs), fulfilled in the Eastern and Western Roman empires, and then into ten (the toes) See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:da 7:26">Daniel 7:26</reference>. As a whole, the image gives the imposing outward greatness and splendour of the Gentile world-power.<div eID="gen2635" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2636" type="x-p"/> The smiting Stone <reference osisRef="da 2:34 da 2:35">Daniel 2:34,35</reference> destroys the Gentile world-system (in its final form) by a sudden and irremediable blow, not by the gradual processes of conversion and assimilation; and then, and not before, does the Stone become a mountain which fills "the whole earth." (Cf. <reference osisRef="da 7:26 da 7:27">Daniel 7:26,27</reference>). Such a destruction of the Gentile monarchy-system did not occur at the first advent of Christ. On the contrary, He was put to death by the sentence of an officer of the fourth empire, which was then at the zenith of its power. Since the crucifixion the Roman empire has followed the course marked out in the vision, but Gentile world dominion still continues, and the crushing blow is still suspended. The detail of the end-time is given in <reference osisRef="da 7:1-28">Daniel 7:1-28,</reference> and Re 13.-19. It is important to see<div eID="gen2636" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(1) that Gentile world-power is to end in a sudden catastrophic judgment (see "Armageddon," <reference osisRef="re 16:14">Revelation 16:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 19:21"> 19:21</reference>).</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(2) that it is immediately followed by the kingdom of heaven, and that the God of the heavens does not set up His kingdom till after the destruction of the Gentile world- system. It is noteworthy that Gentile world-dominion begins and ends with a great image. <reference osisRef="da 2:31">Daniel 2:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 13:14 re 13:15">Revelation 13:14,15</reference>. </item> </list>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv62"/><div sID="gen2637" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv62"/> <hi type="bold">mountain</hi> <div eID="gen2637" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2638" type="x-p"/> A mountain is one of the bibical symbols of a kingdom. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Isa 2:2">Isaiah 2:2</reference>")</hi>.
<hi type="bold">wheresoever the children</hi><div eID="gen2638" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2639" type="x-p"/> This is universal dominion. It was never fully realized, but power was given for it.

<hi type="bold">but there shall be</hi><div eID="gen2639" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2640" type="x-p"/> From the "head of gold" (<reference osisRef="da 2:38">Daniel 2:38</reference>) to the "iron" of the "fourth kingdom" (Rome) there is deterioration in fineness, but increase of strength (<reference osisRef="da 2:40">Daniel 2:40</reference>). Then comes the deterioration of the "fourth kingdom" in that very quality, strength.<div eID="gen2640" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(1) Deterioration by division: The kingdom is divided into two, the legs (Eastern and Western empires), and these are again divided into kingdoms, the number of which when the Stone smites the image will be ten toes, <reference osisRef="da 2:42">Daniel 2:42</reference>; cf. <reference osisRef="da 7:23 da 7:24">Daniel 7:23,24</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(2) Deterioration by admixture; the iron of the Roman imperium mixed with the clay of the popular will, fickle and easily moulded. This is precisely what has come to pass in the constitutional monarchies which, the Republic of France and the despotism of Turkey, cover the sphere of ancient Roman rule. </item> </list>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv63"/><div sID="gen2641" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv63"/> <hi type="bold">and in the days</hi> <div eID="gen2641" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2642" type="x-p"/> The passage fixes authoritatively the time relative to other predicted events, when the kingdom of the heavens will be set up. It will be "in the days of those kings," i.e. the days of the ten kings (cf. <reference osisRef="da 7:24-27">Daniel 7:24-27</reference> symbolized by the toes of the image. That condition did not exist at the advent of Messiah, nor was it even possible until the dissolution of the Roman empire, and the rise of the present national world system. See "Kingdom (O.T.)" ; <reference osisRef="ge 1:26">Genesis 1:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="zec 12:8">Zechariah 12:8</reference> "Kingdom (N.T.)" ; <reference osisRef="lu 1:31-33">Luke 1:31-33</reference>; <reference osisRef="1co 15:28">1 Corinthians 15:28,</reference> <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Mt 3:2">Matthew 3:2</reference>")</hi> note (defining "kingdom of heaven"). Verse 45 repeats the method by which the kingdom will be set up. (Cf) See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:da 2:31">Daniel 2:31</reference>" ; <reference osisRef="ps 2:5">Psalms 2:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="ps 2:6"> 2:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="zec 14:1-8">Zechariah 14:1-8</reference>; <reference osisRef="zec 14:9"> 14:9</reference>.

<hi type="bold">Daniel</hi><div eID="gen2642" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2643" type="x-p"/> Cf. <reference osisRef="ge 19:1">Genesis 19:1</reference>. Lot the compromiser with Daniel the inflexible. <div eID="gen2643" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv64"/><div sID="gen2644" type="x-p"/> <chapter eID="Dan.2"/>
<div eID="gen2644" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2645" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="3" osisID="Dan.3" sID="Dan.3"/>

<hi type="bold">an image of gold</hi> <div eID="gen2645" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2646" type="x-p"/> The attempt of this great king of Babylon to unify the religions of his empire by self- deification will be repeated by the beast, the last head of the Gentile world-dominion <reference osisRef="re 13:11-15">Revelation 13:11-15</reference> See note on "Beast, the" <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Da 7:8">Daniel 7:8</reference>")</hi> See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:re 19:20">Revelation 19:20</reference>". It has repeatedly characterized Gentile authority in the earth, e.g. ; <reference osisRef="da 6:7">Daniel 6:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="ac 12:22">Acts 12:22</reference> and the later Roman emperors.
<hi type="bold">Chaldeans</hi><div eID="gen2646" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2647" type="x-p"/> Cf. the conduct of Daniel, <reference osisRef="da 2:24">Daniel 2:24</reference>.

<hi type="bold">and he will deliver us</hi><div eID="gen2647" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2648" type="x-p"/> The three Jews, faithful to God while the nation of Israel far from their land bear no testimony, are a fit type of the Jewish remnant in the last days <reference osisRef="isa 1:9">Isaiah 1:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="ro 11:5">Romans 11:5</reference> who will be faithful in the furnace of the great tribulation ; <reference osisRef="ps 2:5">Psalms 2:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 7:14">Revelation 7:14</reference>.

<hi type="bold">angel</hi><div eID="gen2648" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2649" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Heb 1:4">Hebrews 1:4</reference>")</hi> <div eID="gen2649" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv64"/><div sID="gen2650" type="x-p"/> <chapter eID="Dan.3"/>
<div eID="gen2650" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2651" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="4" osisID="Dan.4" sID="Dan.4"/>

<hi type="bold">dwell</hi> <div eID="gen2651" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2652" type="x-p"/> Nebuchadnezzar, first of the Gentile world-kings in whom the times of the Gentiles <reference osisRef="lu 21:24">Luke 21:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 16:14">Revelation 16:14</reference> began, perfectly comprehended the universality of the sway committed to him <reference osisRef="da 2:37 da 2:38">Daniel 2:37,38</reference> as also did Cyrus <reference osisRef="ezr 1:2">Ezra 1:2</reference>. That they did not actually subject the known earth to their sway is true, but they might have done so. The earth lay in their power.

<hi type="bold">everlasting kingdom</hi><div eID="gen2652" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2653" type="x-p"/> See, <reference osisRef="2sa 7:16">2 Samuel 7:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="ps 89:35-37">Psalms 89:35-37</reference>; <reference osisRef="da 7:13 da 7:14 da 7:27">Daniel 7:13,14,27</reference>; <reference osisRef="lu 1:31-33">Luke 1:31-33</reference>.

<hi type="bold">tree</hi><div eID="gen2653" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2654" type="x-p"/> Symbol of a great king. <reference osisRef="da 4:22">Daniel 4:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="eze 31:1-14">Ezekiel 31:1-14</reference>.
<hi type="bold">watcher</hi><div eID="gen2654" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2655" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="da 4:17 da 4:23">Daniel 4:17,23,</reference> plural in 17.
<hi type="bold">seven</hi><div eID="gen2655" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2656" type="x-p"/> The number of completeness.
<hi type="bold">till thou know</hi><div eID="gen2656" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2657" type="x-p"/> The discipline was effective. Cf. <reference osisRef="da 4:30 da 4:37">Daniel 4:30,37</reference>.

<hi type="bold">I blessed the most High</hi><div eID="gen2657" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2658" type="x-p"/> A progress may be traced in Nebuchadnezzar's apprehension of the true God.<div eID="gen2658" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(1) "God is a God of gods one amongst the national or tribal gods, but greater than they], and a Lord Adonai=Master of kings, and a revealer of secrets" <reference osisRef="da 2:47">Daniel 2:47</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(2) He is still a Hebrew deity, but Master of angels, and a God who responds to faith <reference osisRef="da 3:28">Daniel 3:28</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(3) Here <reference osisRef="da 4:34 da 4:35">Daniel 4:34,35</reference> the king rises into a true apprehension of God. Cf. Darius, <reference osisRef="da 6:25-27">Daniel 6:25-27</reference>. </item> </list> <chapter eID="Dan.4"/>
<div sID="gen2659" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="5" osisID="Dan.5" sID="Dan.5"/>

<hi type="bold">father</hi> <div eID="gen2659" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2660" type="x-p"/> Nebuchadnezzar was "father" of Belshazzar in the biblical sense that David is called "father" of Jesus, <reference osisRef="lu 1:32">Luke 1:32</reference>. Belshazzar was probably a grandson.

<hi type="bold">thy father</hi><div eID="gen2660" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2661" type="x-p"/> Or, grandfather. See note 2, <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Da 5:2">Daniel 5:2</reference>")</hi>.

<hi type="bold">Darius the Median</hi><div eID="gen2661" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2662" type="x-p"/> The biblical order of the monarchs of Daniel's time, and of the period of the captivity and restoration of Judah, is as follows:<div eID="gen2662" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(1) Nebuchadnezzar (B.C. 604-561) with whom the captivity of Judah and the "times of the Gentiles" <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Lu 21:24">Luke 21:24</reference>")</hi> , See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:re 16:19">Revelation 16:19</reference>", began, and who established the first of the four world monarchies. ; <reference osisRef="da 2:37 da 2:38">Daniel 2:37,38</reference>; <reference osisRef="da 7:4"> 7:4</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(2) Belshazzar (prob B.C. 556), the Bel-shar-uzzar of the inscriptions, grandson of Nebuchadnezzar, and son of the victorious general Nabonidus. Belshazzar seems to have reigned as viceroy.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(3) Darius the Mede <reference osisRef="da 5:31">Daniel 5:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="da 6:1-27"> 6:1-27</reference>; <reference osisRef="da 9:1"> 9:1</reference>. Concerning this Darius secular history awaits further discoveries, as formerly in the case of Belshazzar. He has been conjectured to be identical with Gobryas, a Persian general. This Darius was "the son of Ahasuerus, of the seed of the Medes, which was made king over the realm of the Chaldeans" <reference osisRef="da 9:1">Daniel 9:1</reference> "Ahasuerus," more a title than a name, the equivalent of the modern "Majesty," is used in Scripture of at least four personages, and is Persian rather than Median. That Darius the Mede was the "son" (or grandson) of an Ahasuerus proves no more than that he was, probably, through the seed of his mother, of the seed royal not only of Media, but also of Persia. There is but one Darius in Daniel. (See <reference osisRef="da 9:1">Daniel 9:1</reference>.)</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(4) Cyrus, with whose rise to power came fully into existence the Medo-Persian, second of the world-empires <reference osisRef="da 2:39">Daniel 2:39</reference>; <reference osisRef="da 7:5"> 7:5</reference></item> </list> <div sID="gen2663" type="x-p"/> In Daniel's vision of this empire in "the third year of the reign of King Belshazzar" <reference osisRef="da 8:1-4">Daniel 8:1-4</reference> the Median power of Darius is seen as the lesser of the two horns of the ram; the Persian power of Cyrus, under whom the Medo-Persian power was consolidated, as the "higher" horn which "came up last." Under Cyrus, who was prophetically named more than a century before his birth. <reference osisRef="isa 44:28-isa 45:4">Isaiah 44:28-45:4</reference>, the return to Palestine of the Jewish remnant began. <reference osisRef="ezr 1:1-4">Ezra 1:1-4</reference>. See <reference osisRef="da 11:2">Daniel 11:2,</reference> marg. ref. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Da 11:2">Daniel 11:2</reference>")</hi>. <div eID="gen2663" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv64"/><div sID="gen2664" type="x-p"/> <chapter eID="Dan.5"/>
<div eID="gen2664" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2665" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="6" osisID="Dan.6" sID="Dan.6"/>

<hi type="bold">Darius the Median</hi> <div eID="gen2665" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2666" type="x-p"/> The biblical order of the monarchs of Daniel's time, and of the period of the captivity and restoration of Judah, is as follows:<div eID="gen2666" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(1) Nebuchadnezzar (B.C. 604-561) with whom the captivity of Judah and the "times of the Gentiles" <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Lu 21:24">Luke 21:24</reference>")</hi> , See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:re 16:19">Revelation 16:19</reference>", began, and who established the first of the four world monarchies. ; <reference osisRef="da 2:37 da 2:38">Daniel 2:37,38</reference>; <reference osisRef="da 7:4"> 7:4</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(2) Belshazzar (prob B.C. 556), the Bel-shar-uzzar of the inscriptions, grandson of Nebuchadnezzar, and son of the victorious general Nabonidus. Belshazzar seems to have reigned as viceroy.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(3) Darius the Mede <reference osisRef="da 5:31">Daniel 5:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="da 6:1-27"> 6:1-27</reference>; <reference osisRef="da 9:1"> 9:1</reference>. Concerning this Darius secular history awaits further discoveries, as formerly in the case of Belshazzar. He has been conjectured to be identical with Gobryas, a Persian general. This Darius was "the son of Ahasuerus, of the seed of the Medes, which was made king over the realm of the Chaldeans" <reference osisRef="da 9:1">Daniel 9:1</reference> "Ahasuerus," more a title than a name, the equivalent of the modern "Majesty," is used in Scripture of at least four personages, and is Persian rather than Median. That Darius the Mede was the "son" (or grandson) of an Ahasuerus proves no more than that he was, probably, through the seed of his mother, of the seed royal not only of Media, but also of Persia. There is but one Darius in Daniel. (See <reference osisRef="da 9:1">Daniel 9:1</reference>.)</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(4) Cyrus, with whose rise to power came fully into existence the Medo-Persian, second of the world-empires <reference osisRef="da 2:39">Daniel 2:39</reference>; <reference osisRef="da 7:5"> 7:5</reference></item> </list> <div sID="gen2667" type="x-p"/> In Daniel's vision of this empire in "the third year of the reign of King Belshazzar" <reference osisRef="da 8:1-4">Daniel 8:1-4</reference> the Median power of Darius is seen as the lesser of the two horns of the ram; the Persian power of Cyrus, under whom the Medo-Persian power was consolidated, as the "higher" horn which "came up last." Under Cyrus, who was prophetically named more than a century before his birth. <reference osisRef="isa 44:28-isa 45:4">Isaiah 44:28-45:4</reference>, the return to Palestine of the Jewish remnant began. <reference osisRef="ezr 1:1-4">Ezra 1:1-4</reference>. See <reference osisRef="da 11:2">Daniel 11:2,</reference> marg. ref. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Da 11:2">Daniel 11:2</reference>")</hi>. <div eID="gen2667" type="x-p"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv64"/><div sID="gen2668" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv64"/> <hi type="bold">angel</hi> <div eID="gen2668" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2669" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Heb 1:4">Hebrews 1:4</reference>")</hi>.

<hi type="bold">unto all people</hi><div eID="gen2669" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2670" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Da 4:1">Daniel 4:1</reference>")</hi>. <chapter eID="Dan.6"/><div eID="gen2670" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen2671" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="7" osisID="Dan.7" sID="Dan.7"/>

<hi type="bold">great sea</hi> <div eID="gen2671" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2672" type="x-p"/> The "sea" in Scripture imagery stands for the populace, the mere unorganized mass of mankind <reference osisRef="mt 13:47">Matthew 13:47</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 13:1">Revelation 13:1</reference>.

<hi type="bold">three ribs</hi> A reference to the three-fold dominion of the second empire, Media, Persia, Babylonia.<div eID="gen2672" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2673" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">devour</hi> i.e. Lydia, Babylonia, Egypt, etc.
<hi type="bold">leopard</hi><div eID="gen2673" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2674" type="x-p"/> Swiftness of Alexander's conquests.
<hi type="bold">horns</hi><div eID="gen2674" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2675" type="x-p"/> A horn symbolizes a king. Cf. <reference osisRef="re 17:12">Revelation 17:12</reference>.

<hi type="bold">little horn</hi><div eID="gen2675" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2676" type="x-p"/> The vision is of the end of Gentile world-dominion. The former Roman empire (the iron kingdom of <reference osisRef="da 2:33-35 da 2:40-44">Daniel 2:33-35,40-44</reference>; <reference osisRef="da 7:7"> 7:7</reference> will have ten horns (i.e. kings, <reference osisRef="re 17:12">Revelation 17:12</reference> corresponding to the ten toes of the image. As Daniel considers this vision of the ten kings, there rises up amongst them a "little horn" (king), who subdues three of the ten kings so completely that the separate identity of their kingdoms is destroyed. Seven kings of the ten are left, and the "little horn." He is the "king of fierce countenance" typified by that other "king of fierce countenance," Antiochus Epiphanes, <reference osisRef="da 8:23-25">Daniel 8:23-25</reference> the "prince that shall come" of <reference osisRef="da 9:26 da 9:27">Daniel 9:26,27</reference> the "king" of <reference osisRef="da 11:36-45">Daniel 11:36-45</reference> the "abomination" of ; <reference osisRef="da 12:11">Daniel 12:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="mt 24:15">Matthew 24:15</reference> the "man of sin" of <reference osisRef="2th 2:4-8">2 Thessalonians 2:4-8</reference> and the "Beast" of <reference osisRef="re 13:4-10">Revelation 13:4-10</reference>. See "Beast" ; <reference osisRef="da 7:8">Daniel 7:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 19:20">Revelation 19:20</reference>.

<hi type="bold">and they</hi><div eID="gen2676" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2677" type="x-p"/> This scene is identical with that of <reference osisRef="re 5:6-10">Revelation 5:6-10</reference>. There the ascription of praise of the "kings and priests" (cf. <reference osisRef="da 7:18 da 7:18">Daniel 7:18,18,</reference> ref. a) ends with the words, "and we shall reign on the earth." Rev. 6. opens the "vexing" of <reference osisRef="ps 2:5">Psalms 2:5</reference> introductory to setting the king on Zion ; <reference osisRef="ps 2:6">Psalms 2:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 20:4">Revelation 20:4</reference>. The vision <reference osisRef="da 7:9-14">Daniel 7:9-14</reference> reverses the order of events as they will be fulfilled. Verse 13 describes the scene in heaven (cf) <reference osisRef="re 5:6-10">Revelation 5:6-10</reference> which, in fulfilment, precedes the events which Daniel sees in vision in <reference osisRef="da 7:9-12">Daniel 7:9-12</reference>. The historic order will be:<div eID="gen2677" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(1) The investiture of the Son of Man with the kingdom <reference osisRef="da 7:13 da 7:14">Daniel 7:13,14</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 5:6-10">Revelation 5:6-10</reference></item> <item type="x-indent-1">(2) the "vexing" of <reference osisRef="ps 2:5">Psalms 2:5,</reference> fully described in <reference osisRef="mt 24:21 mt 24:22">Matthew 24:21,22</reference> Re 6.-18.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(3) The return of the Son of Man in glory to deliver the "smiting" blow of <reference osisRef="da 2:45">Daniel 2:45</reference>; <reference osisRef="da 7:9-11"> 7:9-11</reference> <reference osisRef="re 19:11-21">Revelation 19:11-21</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(4) The judgement of the nations and the setting up of the kingdom <reference osisRef="da 7:10 da 7:26 da 7:27">Daniel 7:10,26,27</reference>; <reference osisRef="mt 25:31-46">Matthew 25:31-46</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 20:1-6">Revelation 20:1-6</reference>. </item> </list>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv65"/><div sID="gen2678" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv65"/> <hi type="bold">him</hi> <div eID="gen2678" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2679" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="da 7:13 da 7:14">Daniel 7:13,14</reference> is identical with <reference osisRef="re 5:1-7">Revelation 5:1-7</reference> and antedates the fulfilment of <reference osisRef="da 2:34 da 2:35">Daniel 2:34,35</reference>. ; <reference osisRef="da 7:13 da 7:14">Daniel 7:13,14</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 5:1-7">Revelation 5:1-7</reference> describe the investiture of the Son of Man and Son of David with the kingdom authority, while <reference osisRef="da 2:34 da 2:35">Daniel 2:34,35</reference> describes the crushing blow (Armageddon, <reference osisRef="re 16:14">Revelation 16:14</reference> which destroys Gentile world-power, thus clearing the way for the actual setting up of the kingdom of heaven. ; <reference osisRef="da 2:34 da 2:35">Daniel 2:34,35</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 19:19-21">Revelation 19:19-21</reference> are the same event.

<hi type="bold">beasts</hi><div eID="gen2679" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2680" type="x-p"/> The monarch vision of Nebuchadnezzar (Dan. 2) covers the same historic order as the beast vision of Daniel, but with this difference: Nebuchadnezzar saw the imposing outward power and splendour of the "times of the Gentiles" <reference osisRef="lu 21:24">Luke 21:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 16:19">Revelation 16:19</reference> while Daniel saw the true character of Gentile world-government as rapacious and warlike, established and maintained by force. It is remarkable that the heraldic insignia of the Gentile nations are all beasts or birds of prey.

<hi type="bold">saints</hi> vs. <reference osisRef="da 7:18 da 7:22 da 7:25 da 7:27">Daniel 7:18,22,25,27</reference>. That church saints will also share in the rule seems clear from ; <reference osisRef="ac 16:17">Acts 16:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="ro 8:17">Romans 8:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="2ti 2:10-12">2 Timothy 2:10-12</reference>; <reference osisRef="1pe 2:9">1 Peter 2:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 1:6">Revelation 1:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 3:21"> 3:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 5:10"> 5:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 20:4-6"> 20:4-6</reference>.
<hi type="bold">know the truth of the fourth beast</hi> See note 4, <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Da 7:17">Daniel 7:17</reference>")</hi>.

<hi type="bold">and they shall</hi><div eID="gen2680" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2681" type="x-p"/> The end of Gentile world-power.<div eID="gen2681" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(1) In the beast vision of Daniel 7. the fourth beast is declared to be "the fourth kingdom," i.e. the Roman empire, the "iron" kingdom of Dan. 2. The "ten horns" upon the fourth beast (Roman empire), <reference osisRef="da 7:7">Daniel 7:7</reference> are declared to be "ten kings that shall arise" (<reference osisRef="da 7:24">Daniel 7:24</reference>) answering to the ten toes of the image vision of Dan. 2. The ten kingdoms, covering the regions formerly ruled by Rome, will constitute, therefore, the form in which the fourth or Roman empire will exist when the whole fabric of Gentile world-domination is smitten by the "stone cut out without hands" == Christ ; <reference osisRef="da 2:44 da 2:45">Daniel 2:44,45</reference>; <reference osisRef="da 7:9"> 7:9</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(2) But Daniel sees a "little horn" rise up and subdue three of the ten kings <reference osisRef="da 7:24-26">Daniel 7:24-26</reference>. His distinguishing mark is hatred of God and of the Saints. He is not to be confounded with the "little horn" of Dan. 8.--a prophecy fulfilled in Antiochus Epiphanes. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Da 8:9">Daniel 8:9</reference>")</hi>. In Rev. 13, additional particulars of the "little horn" of Dan. 7. are given. See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:re 13:1">Revelation 13:1</reference>". </item> </list>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv66"/><div sID="gen2682" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv66"/><hi type="bold">everlasting kingdom</hi> See, <reference osisRef="2sa 7:16">2 Samuel 7:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="ps 89:35-37">Psalms 89:35-37</reference>; <reference osisRef="da 4:3">Daniel 4:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="da 7:13 da 7:14"> 7:13,14</reference>; <reference osisRef="lu 1:31-33">Luke 1:31-33</reference>. <div eID="gen2682" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv67"/><div sID="gen2683" type="x-p"/> <chapter eID="Dan.7"/>
<div eID="gen2683" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2684" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="8" osisID="Dan.8" sID="Dan.8"/>

<hi type="bold">vision</hi> <div eID="gen2684" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2685" type="x-p"/> The eighth chapter gives details concerning the second and third world-kingdoms: the silver and brass kingdoms of Dan. 2.; the bear and leopard kingdoms of Dan. 7., viz., the Medo-Persian and Macedonian kingdoms of history. At the time of this vision (<reference osisRef="da 8:1">Daniel 8:1</reference>) the first monarchy was nearing its end. Belshazzar was the last king of that monarchy.<div eID="gen2685" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2686" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">third year</hi> About B.C. 530.
<hi type="bold">ram</hi><div eID="gen2686" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2687" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Da 8:20">Daniel 8:20</reference>")</hi>.

<hi type="bold">little horn</hi><div eID="gen2687" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2688" type="x-p"/> The "little horn" here is a prophecy fulfilled in Antiochus Epiphanes, B.C. 175, who profaned the temple and terribly persecuted the Jews. He is not to be confounded with the "little horn" of Dan. 7. who is yet to come, and who will dominate the earth during the great tribulation. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Da 7:8">Daniel 7:8</reference>")</hi> concerning "The Beast". See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:re 19:20">Revelation 19:20</reference>" and "The great tribulation," <reference osisRef="ps 2:5">Psalms 2:5</reference>. See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:re 7:14">Revelation 7:14</reference>". But Antiochus is a remarkable type of the Beast, the terrible "little horn" of the last days. Verses 24,25 go beyond Antiochus and evidently refer to the "little horn" of Dan. 7. Both Antiochus and the Beast, but the Beast pre-eminently, are in view in verses 24,25. That the "little horn" of Dan. 7. cannot be the little horn of <reference osisRef="da 8:9-13 da 8:23">Daniel 8:9-13,23</reference> is evident. The former comes up among the ten horns into which the fourth empire (Roman) is to be divided; the little horn of Dan. 8. comes out of one of the four kingdoms into which the third (Grecian) empire was divided (<reference osisRef="da 8:23">Daniel 8:23</reference>), and in "the latter time" of the four kingdoms <reference osisRef="da 8:22 da 8:23">Daniel 8:22,23</reference>). This was historically true of Antiochus Epiphanes. They are alike in hatred of the Jews and of God, and in profaning the temple. Cf. <reference osisRef="da 7:25">Daniel 7:25</reference> (the Beast) with <reference osisRef="da 8:10-12">Daniel 8:10-12</reference> (Antiochus):<div eID="gen2688" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2689" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">one of them</hi> Anticohus Epiphanes came out of Syria, one of the "four notable" kingdoms into which Alexander's empire was divided.

<hi type="bold">And it waxed great</hi><div eID="gen2689" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2690" type="x-p"/> This passage (<reference osisRef="da 8:10-14">Daniel 8:10-14</reference>) is confessedly the most difficult in prophecy, a difficulty increased by the present state of the text. Historically this was fulfilled in and by Antiochus Epiphanes, but in a more intense and final sense Antiochus but adumbrates the awful blasphemy of the "little horn" of ; <reference osisRef="da 7:8 da 7:24 da 7:25">Daniel 7:8,24,25</reference>; <reference osisRef="da 9:27"> 9:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="da 11:36-45"> 11:36-45</reference>; <reference osisRef="da 12:11"> 12:11</reference>. In Daniel <reference osisRef="da 8:10-14">Daniel 8:10-14</reference> the actions of both "little horns" blend.
<hi type="bold">daily sacrifice</hi><div eID="gen2690" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2691" type="x-p"/> Cf. <reference osisRef="da 9:27">Daniel 9:27</reference> where the Beast comes into view:

<hi type="bold">desolation</hi><div eID="gen2691" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2692" type="x-p"/> Seven times in Daniel the "desolation" is spoken of:<div eID="gen2692" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(1) Of the sanctuary, <reference osisRef="da 8:13">Daniel 8:13</reference> fulfilled by Antiochus Epiphanes, B.C. 175-170.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(2) Of the sanctuary, <reference osisRef="da 9:17">Daniel 9:17</reference> the condition in Daniel's time, when the Jews were in exile and the sanctuary desolate.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(3) Generally, of the land, <reference osisRef="da 9:18">Daniel 9:18</reference> also referring to Daniel's time.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(4) Of the sanctuary, <reference osisRef="da 9:26">Daniel 9:26</reference> fulfilled A.D. 70, in the destruction of city and temple after the cutting off of Messiah. <reference osisRef="lu 21:20">Luke 21:20</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(5,6,7) Of the sanctuary, by the Beast, <reference osisRef="da 9:27">Daniel 9:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="da 11:31"> 11:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="da 12:11"> 12:11</reference> Cf ; <reference osisRef="mt 24:15">Matthew 24:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="mr 13:14">Mark 13:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="2th 2:3 2th 2:8-12">2 Thessalonians 2:3,8-12</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 13:14 re 13:15">Revelation 13:14,15</reference>.</item> </list> <div sID="gen2693" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">one saint</hi> Or, holy one, idem. <reference osisRef="da 4:13 da 4:17">Daniel 4:13,17</reference>. <div eID="gen2693" type="x-p"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv67"/><div sID="gen2694" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv67"/> <hi type="bold">a man</hi> <div eID="gen2694" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2695" type="x-p"/> The theophanies. <reference osisRef="da 10:6 da 10:10 da 10:18"> 10:6,10,18</reference>; <reference osisRef="eze 40:3">Ezekiel 40:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="ge 12:7">Genesis 12:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 1:9">Revelation 1:9</reference>.

<hi type="bold">end</hi><div eID="gen2695" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2696" type="x-p"/> Two "ends" are in view here:<div eID="gen2696" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(1) historically, the end of the third, or Grecian empire of Alexander out of one of the divisions of which the little horn of verse 9 (Antiochus) arose;</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(2) prophetically, the end of the times of the Gentiles <reference osisRef="lu 21:24">Luke 21:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 16:14">Revelation 16:14</reference> when the "little horn" of <reference osisRef="da 7:8 da 7:24-26">Daniel 7:8,24-26</reference> the Beast, will arise--Daniel's final time of the end. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Da 12:4">Daniel 12:4</reference>")</hi>. </item> </list>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv68"/><div sID="gen2697" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv68"/> <hi type="bold">ram</hi> <div eID="gen2697" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2698" type="x-p"/> vs. <reference osisRef="da 8:3 da 8:4">Daniel 8:3,4</reference>.<div eID="gen2698" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2699" type="x-p"/> The "higher" horn which "came up last" is Cyrus, the other "Darius the Mede."
<hi type="bold">first king</hi><div eID="gen2699" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2700" type="x-p"/> i.e. Alexander the Great.

<hi type="bold">four kingdoms</hi><div eID="gen2700" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2701" type="x-p"/> The four empires into which Alexander's empire was divided about B.C. 300; Greece, Asia Minor, including Syria, Egypt, the East.

<hi type="bold">king of fierce countenance</hi><div eID="gen2701" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2702" type="x-p"/> i.e. Antiochus Epiphanes who arose out of Syria, one of the "four kingdoms," B.C. 170. <chapter eID="Dan.8"/><div eID="gen2702" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen2703" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="9" osisID="Dan.9" sID="Dan.9"/>

<hi type="bold">seventy years</hi> <div eID="gen2703" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2704" type="x-p"/> Cf. <reference osisRef="jer 25:11 jer 25:12">Jeremiah 25:11,12</reference>. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Jer 25:11">Jeremiah 25:11</reference>")</hi>.

<hi type="bold">Seventy weeks</hi><div eID="gen2704" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2705" type="x-p"/> These are "weeks" or more accurately, sevens of years; seventy weeks of seven years each. Within these "weeks" the national chastisement must be ended and the nation re- established in everlasting righteousness (<reference osisRef="da 9:24">Daniel 9:24</reference>). The seventy weeks are divided into seven == 49 years; sixty-two = 434 years; one = 7 years (vs. 25-27). In the seven weeks == 49 years, Jerusalem was to be rebuilt in "troublous times." This was fulfilled, as Ezra and Nehemiah record. Sixty-two weeks == 434 years, thereafter Messiah was to come (<reference osisRef="da 9:25">Daniel 9:25</reference>). This was fulfilled in the birth and manifestation of Christ. <reference osisRef="da 9:26">Daniel 9:26</reference> 26 is obviously an indeterminate period. The date of the crucifixion is not fixed. It is only said to be "after" the threescore and two weeks. It is the first event in <reference osisRef="da 9:26">Daniel 9:26</reference>. The second event is the destruction of the city, fulfilled A.D. 70. Then, "unto the end," a period not fixed, but which has already lasted nearly 2000 years. To Daniel was revealed only that wars and desolations should continue (cf. <reference osisRef="mt 24:6-14">Matthew 24:6-14</reference>.) The N.T. reveals, that which was hidden from the O.T. prophets ; <reference osisRef="mt 13:11-17">Matthew 13:11-17</reference>; <reference osisRef="eph 3:1-10">Ephesians 3:1-10</reference> that during this period should be accomplished the mysteries of the kingdom of Heaven <reference osisRef="mt 13:1-50">Matthew 13:1-50</reference> and the out-calling of the Church ; <reference osisRef="mt 16:18">Matthew 16:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="ro 11:25">Romans 11:25</reference>. When the Church- age will end, and the seventieth week begin, is nowhere revealed. Its duration can be but seven years. To make it more violates the principle of interpretation already confirmed by fulfilment. <reference osisRef="da 9:27">Daniel 9:27</reference> deals with the last week. The "he" of <reference osisRef="da 9:27">Daniel 9:27</reference> is the "prince that shall come" of <reference osisRef="da 9:26">Daniel 9:26,</reference> whose people (Rome) destroyed the temple, A.D. 70. He is the same with the "little horn" of chapter 7. He will covenant with the Jews to restore their temple sacrifices for one week (seven years), but in the middle of that time he will break the covenant and fulfil ; <reference osisRef="da 12:11">Daniel 12:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="2th 2:3 2th 2:4">2 Thessalonians 2:3,4</reference>. Between the sixty-ninth week, after which Messiah was cut off, and the seventieth week, within which the "little horn" of Dan. 7. will run his awful course, intervenes this entire Church-age. <reference osisRef="da 9:27">Daniel 9:27</reference> deals with the last three and a half years of the seven, which are identical with the "great tribulation." <reference osisRef="mt 24:15-28">Matthew 24:15-28</reference> "time of trouble" <reference osisRef="da 12:1">Daniel 12:1</reference> hour of temptation" <reference osisRef="re 3:10">Revelation 3:10</reference>. (see "Tribulation," ; <reference osisRef="ps 2:5">Psalms 2:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 7:14">Revelation 7:14</reference>). <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ps 2:5">Psalms 2:5</reference>")</hi>.<div eID="gen2705" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2706" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">make reconciliation</hi> <div eID="gen2706" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2707" type="x-p"/> There is no word in the O.T. properly rendered reconcile. In the A.V. the English word is found <reference osisRef="1sa 29:4">1 Samuel 29:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="2ch 29:24">2 Chronicles 29:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="le 6:30">Leviticus 6:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="le 8:15"> 8:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="le 16:20"> 16:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="eze 45:15 eze 45:17 eze 45:20">Ezekiel 45:15,17,20</reference>; <reference osisRef="da 9:24">Daniel 9:24</reference> but always improperly; atonement is invariably the meaning. Reconciliation is a N.T. doctrine <reference osisRef="ro 5:10">Romans 5:10</reference> <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Col 1:21">Colossians 1:21</reference>")</hi><div eID="gen2707" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2708" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thy people</hi> Cf. <reference osisRef="ho 1:9">Hosea 1:9</reference> The Jews, rejected, are "thy people," i.e. Daniel's, not Jehovah's though yet to be restored.<div eID="gen2708" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2709" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">reconciliation</hi> Heb. kaphar, atonement. See this verse note 1, and see note, <reference osisRef="ex 29:33">Exodus 29:33</reference> <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ex 29:33">Exodus 29:33</reference>")</hi>

<hi type="bold">from the going forth of the commandment</hi><div eID="gen2709" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2710" type="x-p"/> Three decrees concerning Jerusalem are recorded, that of Cyrus, B.C. 536 (Ussher), for the restoration of the "house of the Lord God of Israel" <reference osisRef="2ch 36:22 2ch 36:23">2 Chronicles 36:22,23</reference>; <reference osisRef="ezr 1:1-3">Ezra 1:1-3</reference> that of Darius <reference osisRef="eze 6:3-8">Ezekiel 6:3-8</reference> B.C. 521-486), and that of Artaxerxes in his seventh year. <reference osisRef="eze 7:7">Ezekiel 7:7</reference> say, B.C. 458). Artaxerxes in his twentieth year, B.C. 444 (Hales, Jahn), 446 (A.V.), 454 (Ussher, Hengstenberg), gave permission for the rebuilding of the "city," i.e., "Jerusalem" <reference osisRef="ne 2:1-8">Nehemiah 2:1-8</reference>. The latter decree is, obviously, that from which the "seven weeks" (49 years) run, unless by "the commandment to restore," etc. is meant the divine decree <reference osisRef="da 9:23">Daniel 9:23</reference>. In the present state of biblical chronology the date of the decree of Artaxerxes cannot be unanswerably fixed farther than to say that it was issued between 454 and 444 B.C. In either case we are brought to the time of Christ. Prophetic time is invariably so near as to give full warning, so indeterminate as to give no satisfaction to mere curiosity. (cf) ; <reference osisRef="mt 24:36">Matthew 24:36</reference>; <reference osisRef="ac 1:7">Acts 1:7</reference>. The 434 years reckon, of course, from the end of the seven weeks so that the whole time from "the going forth of the commandment to restore," etc., "unto the Messiah" is sixty-nine weeks of years, or 483 years.

<hi type="bold">abominations</hi><div eID="gen2710" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2711" type="x-p"/> (Cf) <reference osisRef="mt 24:15">Matthew 24:15</reference>. The expression occurs three times in Daniel. In ; <reference osisRef="da 9:27">Daniel 9:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="da 12:11"> 12:11</reference> the reference is to the "Beast," "man of sin"; <reference osisRef="2th 2:3 2th 2:4">2 Thessalonians 2:3,4</reference> and is identical with <reference osisRef="mt 24:15">Matthew 24:15</reference>. In <reference osisRef="da 11:31">Daniel 11:31</reference> the reference is to the act of Antiochus Epiphanes, the prototype of the man of sin, who sacrificed a sow upon the altar, and entered the holy of holies. <div eID="gen2711" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv69"/><div sID="gen2712" type="x-p"/> <chapter eID="Dan.9"/>
<div eID="gen2712" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2713" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="10" osisID="Dan.10" sID="Dan.10"/>

<hi type="bold">abominations</hi> <div eID="gen2713" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2714" type="x-p"/> (Cf) <reference osisRef="mt 24:15">Matthew 24:15</reference>. The expression occurs three times in Daniel. In ; <reference osisRef="da 9:27">Daniel 9:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="da 12:11"> 12:11</reference> the reference is to the "Beast," "man of sin"; <reference osisRef="2th 2:3 2th 2:4">2 Thessalonians 2:3,4</reference> and is identical with <reference osisRef="mt 24:15">Matthew 24:15</reference>. In <reference osisRef="da 11:31">Daniel 11:31</reference> the reference is to the act of Antiochus Epiphanes, the prototype of the man of sin, who sacrificed a sow upon the altar, and entered the holy of holies.
<hi type="bold">first month</hi> i.e. April.

<hi type="bold">His body</hi> The theophanies. <reference osisRef="da 10:10 da 10:18">Daniel 10:10,18</reference>; <reference osisRef="eze 40:3">Ezekiel 40:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="ge 12:7">Genesis 12:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 1:9">Revelation 1:9</reference>. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Da 10:10">Daniel 10:10</reference>")</hi>.<div eID="gen2714" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2715" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">beryl</hi> Chrysolite. Cf. <reference osisRef="eze 1:16">Ezekiel 1:16</reference>.

<hi type="bold">And, behold</hi> vs. <reference osisRef="da 10:10-15">Daniel 10:10-15,</reference> introduce an angel. The theophany begins again at <reference osisRef="da 10:16">Daniel 10:16</reference>.

<hi type="bold">prince of</hi> <reference osisRef="da 10:20">Daniel 10:20</reference>.<div eID="gen2715" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2716" type="x-p"/> The intimation is clear that as the holy angels are sent forth in behalf of the heirs of salvation, so demons are concerned in behalf of the world-system of Satan. <reference osisRef="joh 7:7">John 7:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 13:8">Revelation 13:8</reference>.

<hi type="bold">a man</hi> The theophanies. <reference osisRef="da 8:15">Daniel 8:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="eze 40:3">Ezekiel 40:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="ge 12:7">Genesis 12:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 1:9">Revelation 1:9</reference>. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Da 10:6">Daniel 10:6</reference>")</hi>. See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:da 10:10">Daniel 10:10</reference>". \ <chapter eID="Dan.10"/><div eID="gen2716" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen2717" type="x-p"/><chapter n="11" osisID="Dan.11" sID="Dan.11"/>

The spirit of prophecy here returns to that which more immediately concerned Daniel and his royal masters--the near future of the empire in which he was so great a personage. Four kings were yet to follow in Media-Persia. Then will come Alexander the "mighty king" of Grecia (v.3). The division of Alexander's empire into four parts (v.4) as already predicted <reference osisRef="da 8:22">Daniel 8:22</reference> is foretold. The troublous course of affairs in two parts of the disintegrated Alexandrian empire, Syria and Egypt, is then traced down to verse 20. Here Antiochus Epiphanes, the "little horn" of Chapter 8., occupies the vision down to verse 36. His pollution of the sanctuary is again mentioned. (Cf) <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Da 8:9">Daniel 8:9</reference>")</hi>. From verse 36 the interpretation is of the final "little horn" <reference osisRef="da 7:8 da 7:24-26">Daniel 7:8,24-26,</reference> See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:da 11:35">Daniel 11:35</reference>".<div eID="gen2717" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2718" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">three kings</hi> Ahasuerus, <reference osisRef="ezr 4:6">Ezra 4:6,</reference> Artaxerxes, <reference osisRef="ezr 4:7">Ezra 4:7,</reference> and Darius called "Hystaspes" <reference osisRef="ezr 4:24">Ezra 4:24</reference>.<div eID="gen2718" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2719" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fourth</hi> Xerxes, who invaded Greece BC 483-480.
<hi type="bold">king</hi> Alexander the Great, B.C. 332. See <reference osisRef="da 8:5-8 da 8:21-22">Daniel 8:5-8,21,22</reference>.

<hi type="bold">south</hi> i.e. "south" of Palestine. Egypt is meant.<div eID="gen2719" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2720" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his princes</hi> i.e. One of Alexander's princes; historically Ptolemy Lagidae.<div eID="gen2720" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2721" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he shall</hi> Not the "king of the south" (Ptolemy Lagidae, to whom Egypt was given), but the "king of the north" <reference osisRef="da 11:6">Daniel 11:6,</reference> Seleucus, to whom Syria was given:

<hi type="bold">they shall</hi><div eID="gen2721" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2722" type="x-p"/> i.e. the descendants and successors of Ptolemy Lagidae and Seleucus, not those very personages. The prediction was fulfilled in the marriage of Berenice, daughter of Ptolemy Philadelphus, to Antiochus Theos, third king of Syria, B.C. 285-247.

<hi type="bold">branch of her roots</hi><div eID="gen2722" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2723" type="x-p"/> Ptolemy Euergetes, brother of Berenice, who invaded Syria as described in <reference osisRef="da 11:7-9">Daniel 11:7-9</reference>.

<hi type="bold">but his sons</hi><div eID="gen2723" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2724" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="mt 11:10-19">Matthew 11:10-19,</reference> prophetic foreview of the wars of Egypt and Syria, Palestine, <reference osisRef="da 11:17">Daniel 11:17,</reference> the battleground, B.C. 284-175.
<hi type="bold">king of the north</hi><div eID="gen2724" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2725" type="x-p"/> Antiochus the Great, B.C. 198.
<hi type="bold">daughter of women</hi><div eID="gen2725" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2726" type="x-p"/> Probably a reference to the marriage of Cleopatra to an Egyptian king, Ptolemy Philometor.

<hi type="bold">isles</hi> i.e. of Greece.<div eID="gen2726" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2727" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">prince for his own</hi> <div eID="gen2727" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2728" type="x-p"/> i.e. Historically on of the Scipios: the power of Rome felt in the East for the first time.
<hi type="bold">a raiser of taxes</hi><div eID="gen2728" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2729" type="x-p"/> A reference to the tribute exacted of the son of Antiochus the Great by the Romans.
<hi type="bold">south</hi><div eID="gen2729" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2730" type="x-p"/> Egypt.

<hi type="bold">come toward the south</hi><div eID="gen2730" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2731" type="x-p"/> Antiochus Epiphanes' second expedition against Egypt. Stopped by the mandate of Rome, <reference osisRef="da 11:30">Daniel 11:30,</reference> he turns against the Jews:

<hi type="bold">abomination</hi><div eID="gen2731" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2732" type="x-p"/> This is historic -- the act of Antiochus Epiphanes. <reference osisRef="mt 24:15">Matthew 24:15</reference> refers to <reference osisRef="da 12:11">Daniel 12:11,</reference> <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Da 9:27">Daniel 9:27</reference>")</hi>.
<hi type="bold">strong</hi><div eID="gen2732" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2733" type="x-p"/> e.g. the Maccabees. B.C. 168 and following.

<hi type="bold">the time of the end</hi><div eID="gen2733" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2734" type="x-p"/> Here the prophetic foreview, having traced the history of the two parts of Alexander's empire which had to do with Palestine and the Jews, viz. Syria and Egypt, to the time of Antiochus Epiphanes, and having described his career, overleaps the centuries to "the time of the end," when he of whom Antiochus Epiphanes was a type, the "little horn" of <reference osisRef="da 7:8">Daniel 7:8</reference> the "Beast out of the sea" of <reference osisRef="re 13:4-10">Revelation 13:4-10</reference> shall appear (cf) <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Da 7:8">Daniel 7:8</reference>")</hi>. Prophecy does not concern itself with history as such, but only with history as it affects Israel and the Holy Land. Antiochus Epiphanes was insignificant as compared with historical personages whom the Bible does not mention, but he scourged the covenant people and defiled God's altar, thus coming into prophetic light. From verse 36 the "little horn" of <reference osisRef="da 7:8 da 7:24-26">Daniel 7:8,24-26</reference> fills the scene. His prosperity lasts until "the indignation" (the "time of trouble" of ; <reference osisRef="da 12:1">Daniel 12:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="mt 24:21">Matthew 24:21</reference> is accomplished (<reference osisRef="da 11:36">Daniel 11:36</reference>). This is parallel with ; <reference osisRef="re 17:10-14">Revelation 17:10-14</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 19:19-21"> 19:19-21</reference>. <reference osisRef="da 11:37-45">Daniel 11:37-45</reference> supply details not mentioned in the N.T. The expression "God of his fathers" (<reference osisRef="da 11:37">Daniel 11:37</reference>) has been held to indicate that the "king" is an apostate Jew, but this does not accord with <reference osisRef="da 9:26">Daniel 9:26</reference> which was fulfilled by the Gentile armies of Rome. The "little horn" is an apostate, but from Christianity, not Judaism (cf) <reference osisRef="1jo 2:18 1jo 2:19">1 John 2:18,19</reference>. <reference osisRef="da 11:38-45">Daniel 11:38-45</reference> describe his career. Substituting "the god of forces" (i.e. forces of nature) for the true God (<reference osisRef="da 11:38 da 11:39">Daniel 11:38,39</reference>), he soon presents himself as that god (cf) <reference osisRef="2th 2:3 2th 2:4">2 Thessalonians 2:3,4</reference>. While his career lasts he is an irresistible conqueror <reference osisRef="da 11:40-44">Daniel 11:40-44</reference>). He established his palace in Jerusalem, probably at the time of his supreme act of blasphemous impiety ; <reference osisRef="da 9:27">Daniel 9:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="da 12:11"> 12:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="mt 24:15">Matthew 24:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="2th 2:4">2 Thessalonians 2:4</reference>. From this time begins the great tribulation ; <reference osisRef="da 12:1">Daniel 12:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="mt 24:21">Matthew 24:21</reference> which runs its course during the last half of Daniel's seventieth week, viz. three and one half years ; <reference osisRef="da 7:25">Daniel 7:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="da 12:7 da 12:11"> 12:7,11</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 13:5">Revelation 13:5</reference>. Scofield "<reference osisRef="re 19:20">Revelation 19:20</reference>".

<hi type="bold">he shall exalt</hi><div eID="gen2734" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2735" type="x-p"/> The Beast. <reference osisRef="da 11:36-45">Daniel 11:36-45</reference>; <reference osisRef="da 12:11">Daniel 12:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="da 7:8"> 7:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 19:20">Revelation 19:20</reference>.

<hi type="bold">palace</hi><div eID="gen2735" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2736" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Da 11:2">Daniel 11:2</reference>")</hi>. <div eID="gen2736" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv69"/><div sID="gen2737" type="x-p"/> <chapter eID="Dan.11"/>
<div eID="gen2737" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2738" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="12" osisID="Dan.12" sID="Dan.12"/>

<hi type="bold">thy people</hi> <div eID="gen2738" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2739" type="x-p"/> That is, Daniel's people, the Jews. Cf. <reference osisRef="da 9:15 da 9:16 da 9:20 da 9:24">Daniel 9:15,16,20,24</reference>; <reference osisRef="da 10:14"> 10:14</reference>.

<hi type="bold">end</hi><div eID="gen2739" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2740" type="x-p"/> The "time of the end" in Daniel. The expression, or its equivalent, "in the end," occurs, <reference osisRef="da 8:17-19">Daniel 8:17-19</reference>; <reference osisRef="da 9:26"> 9:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="da 11:35 da 11:40 da 11:45"> 11:35,40,45</reference>; <reference osisRef="da 12:4 da 12:6 da 12:9"> 12:4,6,9</reference>.<div eID="gen2740" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2741" type="x-p"/> Summary:<div eID="gen2741" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(1) The time of the end in Daniel begins with the violation by "the prince that shall come" (i.e. "little horn," "man of sin," "Beast") of his covenant with the Jews for the restoration of the temple and sacrifice <reference osisRef="da 9:27">Daniel 9:27</reference> and his presentation of himself as God ; <reference osisRef="da 9:27">Daniel 9:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="da 11:36-38"> 11:36-38</reference>; <reference osisRef="mt 24:15">Matthew 24:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="2th 2:4">2 Thessalonians 2:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 13:4-6">Revelation 13:4-6</reference> and ends with his destruction by the appearing of the Lord in glory. ; <reference osisRef="2th 2:8">2 Thessalonians 2:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 19:19 re 19:20">Revelation 19:19,20</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(2) The duration of the "time of the end" is three and one half years, coinciding with the last half of the seventieth week of Daniel. <reference osisRef="da 7:25">Daniel 7:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="da 12:7"> 12:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 13:5">Revelation 13:5</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(3) This "time of the end" is the "time of Jacob's trouble." <reference osisRef="jer 30:7">Jeremiah 30:7</reference> "a time of trouble such as never was since there was a nation" <reference osisRef="da 12:1">Daniel 12:1</reference> "great tribulation such as was not from the beginning of the world... nor ever shall be" <reference osisRef="mt 24:21">Matthew 24:21</reference>. The N.T., especially the Book of the Revelation, adds many details. </item> </list>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv69"/><div sID="gen2742" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv69"/> <hi type="bold">many shall be</hi> <div eID="gen2742" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2743" type="x-p"/> A prophecy describing the moral state of the world from Daniel's day to the time of the end. Cf. <reference osisRef="mt 13:24-30 mt 13:36-43 mt 13:47-49">Matthew 13:24-30,36-43,47-49</reference>.
<hi type="bold">abomination</hi><div eID="gen2743" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2744" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Da 9:27">Daniel 9:27</reference>")</hi>.

<hi type="bold">thousand three hundred and five and thirty days</hi><div eID="gen2744" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2745" type="x-p"/> Three periods of "days" date from the "abomination" (i.e. the blasphemous assumption of deity by the Beast, <reference osisRef="da 12:11">Daniel 12:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="mt 24:15">Matthew 24:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="2th 2:4">2 Thessalonians 2:4</reference>.<div eID="gen2745" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(1) Twelve hundred and sixty days to the destruction of the Beast <reference osisRef="da 7:25">Daniel 7:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="da 12:7"> 12:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 13:5">Revelation 13:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 19:19 re 19:20"> 19:19,20</reference>. This is also the duration of the great tribulation <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Da 12:4">Daniel 12:4</reference>")</hi>.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(2) Dating from the same event is a period of 1290 days, and addition of thirty days <reference osisRef="da 12:11">Daniel 12:11</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(3) Again forty-five days are added, and with them the promise of <reference osisRef="da 12:12">Daniel 12:12</reference>. No account is directly given of that which occupies the interval of seventy-five days between the end of the tribulation and the full blessing of verse 12. It is suggested that the explanation may be found in the prophetic descriptions of the events following the battle of Armageddon. ; <reference osisRef="re 16:14">Revelation 16:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 19:21"> 19:21</reference>. The Beast is destroyed, and Gentile world-dominion ended, by the smiting of the "Stone cut out without hands" at the end of the 1260 days, but the scene is, so to speak, filled with the debris of the image which the "wind" must carry away before full blessing comes in <reference osisRef="da 2:35">Daniel 2:35</reference>. </item> </list>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv71"/><title type="x-s">Book Introduction - Hosea</title> <div sID="gen2749" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="ho 1">Read first chapter of Hosea</reference><div eID="gen2749" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2750" type="x-p"/> Hosea was a contemporary of Amos in Israel, and of Isaiah and Micah in Judah, and his ministry continued after the first, or Assyrian, captivity of the northern kingdom <reference osisRef="2ki 15:29">2 Kings 15:29</reference>. His style is abrupt, metaphorical, and figurative.<div eID="gen2750" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2751" type="x-p"/> Israel is Jehovah's adulterous wife, repudiated, but ultimately to be purified and restored. This is Hosea's distinctive message, which may be summed up in his two words, Lo-ammi, "not my people," and Ammi, "my people." Israel is not merely apostate and sinful--that is said also; but her sin takes its character from the exalted relationship into which she has been brought.<div eID="gen2751" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2752" type="x-p"/> The book is in three parts:<div eID="gen2752" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">The dishonoured wife, 1:1-3:5.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The sinful people, 4:1-13:8.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The ultimate blessing and glory of Israel, 13:9-14:9.</item> </list> <div sID="gen2753" type="x-p"/> The events recorded in Hosea cover a period of 60 years (Ussher) <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv71"/><hi type="bold">days</hi><div eID="gen2753" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2754" type="x-p"/> i.e. of the 1260,1290, and 1335 days.

<hi type="bold">my people</hi><div eID="gen2754" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2755" type="x-p"/> "My people" is an expression used in the O.T. exclusively of Israel the nation. It is never used of the patriarchs, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. <reference osisRef="mt 2:6">Matthew 2:6</reference>.

<hi type="bold">Israel</hi><div eID="gen2755" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2756" type="x-p"/> "Israel" in Hosea means the ten tribes forming the northern kingdom as distinguished from "Judah" (the tribes of Judah and Benjamin) forming the southern kingdom which adhered to the Davidic family. (See) <reference osisRef="1ki 12:1-21">1 Kings 12:1-21</reference>. The promise of verse 10 awaits fulfilment. See "Israel" ; <reference osisRef="ge 12:2 ge 12:3">Genesis 12:2,3</reference>; <reference osisRef="ro 11:26">Romans 11:26</reference>. <chapter eID="Hos.1"/><div eID="gen2756" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen2757" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="2" osisID="Hos.2" sID="Hos.2"/>

<hi type="bold">She is not my wife</hi> <div eID="gen2757" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2758" type="x-p"/> That Israel is the wife of Jehovah <reference osisRef="ho 2:16-23">Hosea 2:16-23,</reference> now disowned but yet to be restored, is the clear teaching of the passages. This relationship is not to be confounded with that of the Church of Christ. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Joh 3:29">John 3:29</reference>")</hi>. In the mystery of the Divine tri-unity both are true. The N.T. speaks of the Church as a virgin espoused to one husband <reference osisRef="2co 11:1 2co 11:2">2 Corinthians 11:1,2</reference> which could never be said of an adulterous wife, restored in grace. Israel is, then, to be the restored and forgiven wife of Jehovah, the Church the virgin wife of the Lamb ; <reference osisRef="joh 3:29">John 3:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 19:6-8">Revelation 19:6-8</reference>. Israel Jehovah's earthly wife <reference osisRef="ho 2:23">Hosea 2:23,</reference> the Church the Lamb's heavenly bride, <reference osisRef="re 19:7">Revelation 19:7</reference>. <chapter eID="Hos.2"/><div eID="gen2758" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen2759" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="7" osisID="Hos.7" sID="Hos.7"/>

See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:ex 14:30">Exodus 14:30</reference>". <chapter eID="Hos.7"/><div eID="gen2760" type="x-p"/>

<hi type="bold">redeem</hi> Heb. goel, Redemp. (Kinsman type). <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Isa 59:20">Isaiah 59:20</reference>")</hi>.<div eID="gen2768" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2769" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">death</hi> <reference osisRef="1co 15:55">1 Corinthians 15:55</reference>.<div eID="gen2769" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2770" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">O grave</hi> Heb. "Sheol," also in preceding clause. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Hab 2:5">Habakkuk 2:5</reference>")</hi>. <chapter eID="Hos.13"/><div eID="gen2770" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen2748" osisID="Hos" type="book"/>
<div canonical="true" osisID="Joel" sID="gen2771" type="book"/> <milestone n="" type="x-usfm-toc1"/> <milestone n="" type="x-usfm-toc2"/> <milestone n="" type="x-usfm-toc3"/>
<chapter n="1" osisID="Joel.1" sID="Joel.1"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv72"/><title type="x-s">Book Introduction - Joel</title> <div sID="gen2772" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="joe 1">Read first chapter of Joel</reference><div eID="gen2772" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2773" type="x-p"/> Joel, a prophet of Judah, probably exercised his ministry during the reign of Joash (2Chr 22. to 24.). In his youth he may have known Elijah, and he certainly was a contemporary of Elisha. The plagues of insects, which were the token of the divine chastening, give occasion for the unveiling of the coming "day of the Lord" (<reference osisRef="isa 2:12">Isaiah 2:12,</reference> refs.), in its two aspects of judgment on the Gentiles and blessing for Israel.<div eID="gen2773" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2774" type="x-p"/> Joel is in three chief parts:<div eID="gen2774" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">The plague of insects, 1:1-20.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The day of the Lord, 2:1-3:8.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">Retrospect of the day of the Lord, and full kingdom blessing, 3:9-21.</item> </list> <div sID="gen2775" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv72"/> <hi type="bold">palmerworm</hi> <div eID="gen2775" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2776" type="x-p"/> The palmerworm, locust, etc., are thought to be different forms, at different stages of development, of one insect. The essential fact is that, according to the usual method of the Spirit in prophecy, some local circumstance is shown to be of spiritual significance, and is made the occasion of a far-reaching prophecy (e.g.) <reference osisRef="isa 7:1-14">Isaiah 7:1-14</reference> where the Syrian invasion and the unbelief of Ahaz give occasion to the great prophecy of verse 14. Here in Joel a plague of devouring insects is shown to have spiritual significance <reference osisRef="joe 1:13 joe 1:14">Joel 1:13,14</reference> and is made the occasion of the prophecy of the day of the Lord, not yet fulfilled. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Isa 2:12">Isaiah 2:12</reference>")</hi>. This is more developed in Joel 2., where the literal locusts are left behind, and the future day of Jehovah fills the scene.<div eID="gen2776" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2777" type="x-p"/> The whole picture is of the end-time of this present age, of the "times of the Gentiles" <reference osisRef="lu 21:24">Luke 21:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 16:14">Revelation 16:14</reference> of the battle of Armageddon ; <reference osisRef="re 16:14">Revelation 16:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 19:11-21"> 19:11-21</reference> of the regathering of Israel. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ro 11:26">Romans 11:26</reference>")</hi> and of kingdom blessing. It is remarkable that Joel, coming at the very beginning of written prophecy (B.C. 836), gives the fullest view of the consummation of all written prophecy.<div eID="gen2777" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2778" type="x-p"/> The order of events is:<div eID="gen2778" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(1) The invasion of Palestine from the north by Gentile world-powers headed up under the Beast and false prophet <reference osisRef="joe 2:1-10">Joel 2:1-10</reference> "Armageddon," <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Re 16:14">Revelation 16:14</reference>")</hi>.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(2) the Lord's army and destruction of the invaders <reference osisRef="joe 2:11">Joel 2:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 19:11-21">Revelation 19:11-21</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(3) the repentance of Judah in the land <reference osisRef="joe 2:12-17">Joel 2:12-17</reference> <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:De 30:3">Deuteronomy 30:3</reference>")</hi>.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(4) the answer of Jehovah <reference osisRef="joe 2:18-27">Joel 2:18-27</reference></item> <item type="x-indent-1">(5) the effusion of the Spirit in the (Jewish) "last days" <reference osisRef="joe 2:28 joe 2:29">Joel 2:28,29</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(6) the return of the Lord in glory and the setting up of the kingdom <reference osisRef="joe 2:30-32">Joel 2:30-32</reference>; <reference osisRef="ac 15:15-17">Acts 15:15-17</reference> by the regathering of the nation and judgment of the nations <reference osisRef="joe 3:1-16">Joel 3:1-16</reference></item> <item type="x-indent-1">(7) full and permanent kingdom blessing <reference osisRef="joe 3:17-21">Joel 3:17-21</reference>; <reference osisRef="zec 14:1-21">Zechariah 14:1-21</reference>. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Mt 25:32">Matthew 25:32</reference>")</hi>. </item> </list> <chapter eID="Joel.1"/>
<div sID="gen2779" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="2" osisID="Joel.2" sID="Joel.2"/>

<hi type="bold">his army</hi> <div eID="gen2779" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2780" type="x-p"/> To verse 10 inclusive the invading army is described; at verse 11 Jehovah's army. This "army" is described, <reference osisRef="re 19:11-18">Revelation 19:11-18</reference>. The call to repentance is based upon the Lord's promise of deliverance, <reference osisRef="joe 2:12-17">Joel 2:12-17</reference>. At verses <reference osisRef="joe 2:18-20">Joel 2:18-20</reference> we have the deliverance (<reference osisRef="joe 2:20">Joel 2:20</reference>); see "Armageddon," <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Re 16:14">Revelation 16:14</reference>")</hi> , and kingdom blessing in verses <reference osisRef="joe 2:21-27">Joel 2:21-27</reference>. Verses 28-32 give the outpouring of the Spirit, and verses 29-32 the cosmical signs preceding the day of the Lord. See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:re 19:11">Revelation 19:11</reference>".
<hi type="bold">repenteth</hi><div eID="gen2780" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2781" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Zec 8:14">Zechariah 8:14</reference>")</hi>.

<hi type="bold">afterward</hi><div eID="gen2781" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2782" type="x-p"/> Cf. <reference osisRef="ac 2:17">Acts 2:17</reference> which gives a specific interpretation of "afterward" (Heb. acherith= "latter," "last"). "Afterward" in Joel <reference osisRef="joe 2:28">Joel 2:28</reference> means "in the last days" ( (Greek - <w lemma="strong:G2078">ἔσχατος</w> ), and has a partial and continuous fulfilment during the "last days" which began with the first advent of Christ <reference osisRef="heb 1:2">Hebrews 1:2</reference> but the greater fulfilment awaits the "last days" as applied to Israel. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ac 2:17">Acts 2:17</reference>")</hi> , for phrase, "the last days." See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:ac 2:17">Acts 2:17</reference>".
