From verses 9 to 16 we have a resume of <reference osisRef="joe 2:9-32">Joel 2:9-32</reference>. <chapter eID="Joel.3"/><div eID="gen2787" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen2771" osisID="Joel" type="book"/>
<div canonical="true" osisID="Amos" sID="gen2788" type="book"/> <milestone n="" type="x-usfm-toc1"/> <milestone n="" type="x-usfm-toc2"/> <milestone n="" type="x-usfm-toc3"/>
<chapter n="1" osisID="Amos.1" sID="Amos.1"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv73"/><title type="x-s">Book Introduction - Amos</title> <div sID="gen2789" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="am 1">Read first chapter of Amos</reference><div eID="gen2789" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2790" type="x-p"/> Amos, a Jew, but prophesying (B.C. 776-763) in the northern kingdom (<reference osisRef="am 1:1">Amos 1:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="am 7:14 am 7:15"> 7:14,15</reference>) exercised his ministry during the reign of Jeroboam II, an able but idolatrous king who brought his kingdom to the zenith of its power. Nothing could seem more improbable than the fulfilment of Amos' warnings; yet within fifty years the kingdom was utterly destroyed. The vision of Amos is, however, wider than the northern kingdom, including the whole "house of Jacob."<div eID="gen2790" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2791" type="x-p"/> Amos is in four parts:<div eID="gen2791" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">Judgments on the cities surrounding Palestine, 1:1-2:3.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">Judgements on Judah and Israel, 2:4-16.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">Jehovah's controversy with "the whole family" of Jacob, 3:1-9:10.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The future glory of the Davidic kingdom, 9:11-15.</item> </list> <div sID="gen2792" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv73"/> <hi type="bold">roar</hi> <div eID="gen2792" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2793" type="x-p"/> "Roar," etc. Cf. <reference osisRef="isa 42:13">Isaiah 42:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="jer 25:30-33">Jeremiah 25:30-33</reference>; <reference osisRef="ho 11:10 ho 11:11">Hosea 11:10,11</reference>; <reference osisRef="joe 3:16">Joel 3:16</reference>. It will be found that wherever the phrase occurs it is connected with the destruction of Gentile dominion (see "Times of the Gentiles," <reference osisRef="lu 21:24">Luke 21:24</reference>. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Re 16:19">Revelation 16:19</reference>")</hi> and the blessing of Israel in the kingdom. Without a doubt a near fulfilment upon Syria occurred <reference osisRef="2ki 14:28">2 Kings 14:28</reference> but the expression, "the Lord will roar," looks forward to a vaster fulfilment. See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:joe 1:4">Joel 1:4</reference>". <chapter eID="Amos.1"/><div eID="gen2793" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen2794" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="2" osisID="Amos.2" sID="Amos.2"/>

<hi type="bold">For three</hi> <div eID="gen2794" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2795" type="x-p"/> The judgments on Judah and Israel were fulfilled as to Judah in the 70 years' captivity; as to Israel (the northern kingdom) in the world-wide dispersion which still continues. <div eID="gen2795" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv74"/><div sID="gen2796" type="x-p"/> <chapter eID="Amos.2"/>
<div eID="gen2796" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2797" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="3" osisID="Amos.3" sID="Amos.3"/>

<hi type="bold">whole family</hi> <div eID="gen2797" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2798" type="x-p"/> The language here, and the expression "house of Jacob," <reference osisRef="am 3:13">Amos 3:13</reference> evidently gives the prophecy a wider application than to "Israel," the ten-tribe northern kingdom, though the judgment was, in the event, executed first upon the northern kingdom. <reference osisRef="2ki 17:18-23">2 Kings 17:18-23</reference>.

<hi type="bold">therefore</hi><div eID="gen2798" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2799" type="x-p"/> It is noteworthy that Jehovah's controversy with the Gentile cities which hated Israel is brief: "I will send a fire." But Israel had been brought into the place of privilege and so of responsibility, and the Lord's indictment is detailed and unsparing. Cf. <reference osisRef="mt 11:23">Matthew 11:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="lu 12:47 lu 12:48">Luke 12:47,48</reference>. <chapter eID="Amos.3"/><div eID="gen2799" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen2800" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="4" osisID="Amos.4" sID="Amos.4"/>

<hi type="bold">Beth-el</hi> <div eID="gen2800" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2801" type="x-p"/> Cf. <reference osisRef="1ki 12:25-33">1 Kings 12:25-33</reference>. Any altar at Beth-el, after the establishment of Jehovah's worship at Jerusalem was of necessity divisive and schismatic. <reference osisRef="de 12:4-14">Deuteronomy 12:4-14</reference>. Cf. ; <reference osisRef="joh 4:21-24">John 4:21-24</reference>; <reference osisRef="mt 18:20">Matthew 18:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="heb 13:10-14">Hebrews 13:10-14</reference>.

<hi type="bold">raise</hi><div eID="gen2810" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2811" type="x-p"/> As prophesied and fulfilled, <reference osisRef="2ki 15:10">2 Kings 15:10</reference>. <div eID="gen2811" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv74"/><div sID="gen2812" type="x-p"/> <chapter eID="Amos.7"/>

<hi type="bold">standing</hi> <div eID="gen2813" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2814" type="x-p"/> The position of the Lord (Adonai) is significant. The altar speaks properly of mercy because of judgement executed upon an interposed sacrifice, but when altar and sacrifice are despised the altar becomes a place of judgment. Cf. <reference osisRef="joh 12:31">John 12:31</reference>.

<div eID="gen2818" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Book Introduction - Obadiah</title> <div sID="gen2819" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="ob 1">Read first chapter of Obadiah</reference><div eID="gen2819" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2820" type="x-p"/> Internal evidence seems to fix the date of Obadiah's ministry in the reign of the bloody Athaliah <reference osisRef="2ki 8:16-26">2 Kings 8:16-26</reference>. If this be true, and if the ministry of Joel was during the reign of Joash, then Obadiah is chronologically first of the writing prophets, and first to use the formula, "the day of the Lord." (Cf.) <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Joe 1:4">Joel 1:4</reference>")</hi>.<div eID="gen2820" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2821" type="x-p"/> The book is in four parts:<div eID="gen2821" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">Edom's humiliation, vs. 1-9.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The crowning sin of Edom, vs. 10-14.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The future visitation of Edom in the day of the Lord, vs. Ob1:15,16, (Isa 34.). Isa63:1-6.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The inclusion of Edom in the future kingdom, Ob1:17-21; Nu24:17-19. </item> </list>

<div canonical="true" osisID="Jonah" sID="gen2825" type="book"/> <milestone n="" type="x-usfm-toc1"/> <milestone n="" type="x-usfm-toc2"/> <milestone n="" type="x-usfm-toc3"/>
<chapter n="1" osisID="Jonah.1" sID="Jonah.1"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv75"/><title type="x-s">Book Introduction - Jonah</title> <div sID="gen2826" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="jon 1">Read first chapter of Jonah</reference><div eID="gen2826" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2827" type="x-p"/> The historical character of the man Jonah is vouched for by Jesus Christ <reference osisRef="mt 12:39-41">Matthew 12:39-41</reference> as also that his preservation in the great fish was a "sign" or type of the Lord's own entombment and resurrection. Both are miraculous and both are equally credible. <reference osisRef="2ki 14:25">2 Kings 14:25</reference> records the fulfilment of a prophecy by Jonah. The man himself was a bigoted Jew, unwilling to testify to a Gentile city, and angry that God had spared it. Typically he foreshadows the nation of Israel out of its own land; a trouble to the Gentiles, yet witnessing to them; cast out by them, but miraculously preserved; in their future deepest distress calling upon Jehovah-Saviour, and finding deliverance, and then becoming missionaries to the Gentiles. <reference osisRef="zec 8:7-23">Zechariah 8:7-23</reference>.<div eID="gen2827" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2828" type="x-p"/> He typifies Christ as the Sent One, raised from the dead, and carrying salvation to the Gentiles. The chapter divisions indicate the analysis of Jonah. <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv75"/>SCOFIELD REFERENCE NOTES (Old Scofield 1917 Edition)<div eID="gen2828" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2829" type="x-p"/> Book Introduction<div eID="gen2829" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2830" type="x-p"/> The Book of Jonah<div eID="gen2830" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2831" type="x-p"/> The historical character of the man Jonah is vouched for by Jesus Christ <reference osisRef="mt 12:39-41">Matthew 12:39-41</reference> as also that his preservation in the great fish was a "sign" or type of the Lord's own entombment and resurrection. Both are miraculous and both are equally credible. <reference osisRef="2ki 14:25">2 Kings 14:25</reference> records the fulfilment of a prophecy by Jonah. The man himself was a bigoted Jew, unwilling to testify to a Gentile city, and angry that God had spared it. Typically he foreshadows the nation of Israel out of its own land; a trouble to the Gentiles, yet witnessing to them; cast out by them, but miraculously preserved; in their future deepest distress calling upon Jehovah-Saviour, and finding deliverance, and then becoming missionaries to the Gentiles. <reference osisRef="zec 8:7-23">Zechariah 8:7-23</reference>.<div eID="gen2831" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2832" type="x-p"/> He typifies Christ as the Sent One, raised from the dead, and carrying salvation to the Gentiles. The chapter divisions indicate the analysis of Jonah.

<hi type="bold">great fish</hi><div eID="gen2835" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2836" type="x-p"/> No miracle of Scripture has called forth so much unbelief. The issue is not between the doubter and this ancient record, but between the doubter and the Lord Jesus Christ. <reference osisRef="mt 12:39 mt 12:40">Matthew 12:39,40</reference>. Science, "falsely so called" <reference osisRef="1ti 6:20">1 Timothy 6:20</reference> failing to take account of the fact that it deals only with the outward phenomena of a fallen race, and of an earth under a curse <reference osisRef="ge 3:17-19">Genesis 3:17-19</reference> is intolerant of miracles. To faith, and to true science, miracle is what might be expected of divine love, interposing God in a physically and morally disordered universe. <reference osisRef="ro 8:19-23">Romans 8:19-23</reference>.<div eID="gen2836" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2837" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">prepared</hi> <div eID="gen2837" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2838" type="x-p"/> Four prepared things. <reference osisRef="jon 4:6 jon 4:7 jon 4:8">Jonah 4:6,7,8</reference> <div eID="gen2838" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv76"/><div sID="gen2839" type="x-p"/> <chapter eID="Jonah.1"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv77"/><title type="x-s">Book Introduction - Micah</title> <div sID="gen2856" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="mic 1">Read first chapter of Micah</reference><div eID="gen2856" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2857" type="x-p"/> Micah, a contemporary of Isaiah, prophesied during the reigns of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah over Judah, and of Pekahiah, Pekah, and Hoshea over Israel <reference osisRef="2ki 15:23-30">2 Kings 15:23-30</reference>; <reference osisRef="2ki 17:1-6"> 17:1-6</reference>. He was a prophet in Judah <reference osisRef="jer 26:17-19">Jeremiah 26:17-19</reference> but the book called by his name chiefly concerns Samaria.<div eID="gen2857" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2858" type="x-p"/> Micah falls into three prophetic strains, each beginning, "Hear":<div eID="gen2858" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">1:1-2:13</item> <item type="x-indent-1">3:1-5:15</item> <item type="x-indent-1">6:1-7:20</item> </list> <div sID="gen2859" type="x-p"/> The events recorded Micah cover a period of 40 years (Ussher). <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv77"/><hi type="bold">Nineveh</hi> <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Na 1:1">Nahum 1:1</reference>")</hi>

<hi type="bold">Therefore</hi><div eID="gen2859" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2860" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="mic 1:6-16">Micah 1:6-16</reference> the Assyrian invasion is described. Cf. <reference osisRef="2ki 17:1-18">2 Kings 17:1-18</reference>. This is the local circumstance which gives rise to the prophecy of the greater invasion in the last days. <reference osisRef="mic 4:9-13">Micah 4:9-13</reference> and of the Lord's deliverance at Armageddon. ; <reference osisRef="re 16:14">Revelation 16:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 19:17"> 19:17</reference>. <chapter eID="Mic.1"/><div eID="gen2860" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen2861" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="2" osisID="Mic.2" sID="Mic.2"/>

<hi type="bold">remnant</hi> <div eID="gen2861" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2862" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Jer 15:21">Jeremiah 15:21</reference>")</hi> <chapter eID="Mic.2"/> <div eID="gen2862" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen2863" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="3" osisID="Mic.3" sID="Mic.3"/>

<hi type="bold">Therefore</hi> <div eID="gen2863" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2864" type="x-p"/> Prediction of the destruction of Jerusalem, fulfilled A.D. 70. Cf. <reference osisRef="da 9:26">Daniel 9:26</reference> <div eID="gen2864" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv78"/><div sID="gen2865" type="x-p"/> <chapter eID="Mic.3"/>
<div eID="gen2865" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2866" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="4" osisID="Mic.4" sID="Mic.4"/>

<hi type="bold">mountain</hi> <div eID="gen2866" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2867" type="x-p"/> General predictions concerning the kingdom. In Scripture a mountain is the symbol of a great earth power <reference osisRef="da 2:35">Daniel 2:35,</reference> hills, of smaller power. The prediction asserts<div eID="gen2867" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(1) the ultimate establishment of the kingdom, with Jerusalem for the capital (<reference osisRef="mic 4:1">Micah 4:1</reference>);</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(2) the universality of the future kingdom (<reference osisRef="mic 4:2">Micah 4:2</reference>);</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(3) its character--peace (<reference osisRef="mic 4:3">Micah 4:3</reference>);</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(4) its effect--prosperity (<reference osisRef="mic 4:4">Micah 4:4</reference>) 4). Cf. ; <reference osisRef="isa 2:1-5">Isaiah 2:1-5</reference>; <reference osisRef="isa 11:1-12"> 11:1-12</reference></item> </list> <div sID="gen2868" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">it shall be exalted</hi> See "remnant" <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Jer 15:21">Jeremiah 15:21</reference>")</hi>

<hi type="bold">redeem</hi><div eID="gen2868" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2869" type="x-p"/> Heb. "goel," Redemp. (Kinsman type). <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Isa 59:20">Isaiah 59:20</reference>")</hi>. <div eID="gen2869" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv78"/><div sID="gen2870" type="x-p"/> <chapter eID="Mic.4"/>
<div eID="gen2870" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2871" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="5" osisID="Mic.5" sID="Mic.5"/>

<hi type="bold">Now</hi> <div eID="gen2871" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2872" type="x-p"/> The "word of the Lord that came to Micah" <reference osisRef="mic 4:1">Micah 4:1</reference> having described the future kingdom <reference osisRef="mic 4:1-8">Micah 4:1-8</reference> and glanced at the Babylonian captivities <reference osisRef="mic 4:9-10">Micah 4:9-10</reference> goes forward into the last days to refer to the great battle (see "Armageddon,") <reference osisRef="re 16:14">Revelation 16:14,</reference> <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Re 19:17">Revelation 19:17</reference>")</hi> which immediately precedes the setting up of the Messianic kingdom (see "Kingdom (O.T.)," <reference osisRef="ge 1:26">Genesis 1:26</reference> See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:zec 12:8">Zechariah 12:8</reference>" also, "Kingdom (N.T.), ; <reference osisRef="lu 1:31-33">Luke 1:31-33</reference>; <reference osisRef="1co 15:28">1 Corinthians 15:28</reference>.<div eID="gen2872" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2873" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="mic 5:1 mic 5:2">Micah 5:1,2</reference> forms a parenthesis in which the "word of the Lord" goes back from the time of the great battle (yet future) to the birth and rejection of the King, Messiah-Christ <reference osisRef="mt 27:24 mt 27:25 mt 27:37">Matthew 27:24,25,37</reference>. This is followed by the statement that He will "give them up until the time that she which travaileth hath brought forth" (<reference osisRef="mic 5:3">Micah 5:3</reference>). There is a twofold "travail" of Israel:<div eID="gen2873" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(1) that which brings forth the "man child" (Christ) <reference osisRef="re 12:1 re 12:2">Revelation 12:1,2</reference> and</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(2) that which, in the last days, brings forth a believing "remnant" out of the still dispersed and unbelieving nation <reference osisRef="mic 5:3">Micah 5:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="jer 30:6-14">Jeremiah 30:6-14</reference>; <reference osisRef="mic 4:10">Micah 4:10</reference>. Both aspects are combined in Isa. 66. In <reference osisRef="mic 5:7">Micah 5:7</reference> we have the "man-child" (Christ) of <reference osisRef="re 12:1 re 12:2">Revelation 12:1,2</reference> in <reference osisRef="mic 5:8-24">Micah 5:8-24</reference> the remnant, established in kingdom blessing. The meaning of <reference osisRef="mic 5:3">Micah 5:3</reference> is that, from the rejection of Christ at His first coming Jehovah will give Israel up till the believing remnant appears; then He stands and feeds in His proper strength as Jehovah (<reference osisRef="mic 5:4">Micah 5:4</reference>); He is the defence of His people as in <reference osisRef="mic 4:3 mic 4:11-13">Micah 4:3,11-13</reference> and afterward the remnant go as missionaries to Israel and to all the world. ; <reference osisRef="mic 5:7 mic 5:8">Micah 5:7,8</reference>; <reference osisRef="zec 8:23">Zechariah 8:23</reference>. </item> </list>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv78"/><div sID="gen2874" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv78"/> <hi type="bold">everlasting</hi> <div eID="gen2874" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2875" type="x-p"/> Cf. <reference osisRef="isa 7:13 isa 7:14">Isaiah 7:13,14</reference>; <reference osisRef="isa 9:6 isa 9:7"> 9:6,7</reference>. The "child" was born in Bethlehem, but the "Son" was "from everlasting."
<hi type="bold">remnant</hi><div eID="gen2875" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2876" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Jer 15:21">Jeremiah 15:21</reference>")</hi>

<hi type="bold">remnant</hi> <div eID="gen2876" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2877" type="x-p"/> The ministry of the Jewish remnant <reference osisRef="isa 1:9">Isaiah 1:9</reference> <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ro 11:5">Romans 11:5</reference>")</hi> has a twofold aspect, "a dew from the Lord"; "a lion among the beasts." Turning to the Lord in the great tribulation <reference osisRef="ps 2:5">Psalms 2:5</reference>. See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:re 7:14">Revelation 7:14</reference>", the remnant takes up the beautiful gospel of the kingdom. See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:re 14:6">Revelation 14:6</reference>" and proclaims it under awful persecution "unto all nations, for a witness." <reference osisRef="mt 24:14">Matthew 24:14</reference>. The result is seen in <reference osisRef="re 7:4-14">Revelation 7:4-14</reference> This is the "dew" aspect, and is followed by the "day of the Lord" ; <reference osisRef="isa 2:10-22">Isaiah 2:10-22</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 19:11-21">Revelation 19:11-21</reference>. In the morning of which the kingdom is set up in power. Again there is a world-wide preaching to Jew and Gentile, but now it is the word that the King is on His holy hill of Zion (Psa. 2.), and the unrepentant will be broken with His rod of iron. <reference osisRef="ps 2:6-9">Psalms 2:6-9</reference>. The preaching is given in <reference osisRef="ps 2:10-12">Psalms 2:10-12</reference>. This is the "lion" aspect of the remnant's testimony. <reference osisRef="re 2:26-28">Revelation 2:26-28</reference>. The full kingdom-age of blessing follows the "rod of iron" aspect. <chapter eID="Mic.5"/><div eID="gen2877" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen2878" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="6" osisID="Mic.6" sID="Mic.6"/>

<hi type="bold">redeemed</hi> <div eID="gen2878" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2879" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Isa 59:20">Isaiah 59:20</reference>")</hi>. See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:ex 14:30">Exodus 14:30</reference>". <chapter eID="Mic.6"/><div eID="gen2879" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen2880" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="7" osisID="Mic.7" sID="Mic.7"/>
<hi type="bold">trust</hi> <div eID="gen2880" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2881" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ps 2:12">Psalms 2:12</reference>")</hi>.

<hi type="bold">Therefore</hi><div eID="gen2881" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2882" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="mic 7:7-20">Micah 7:7-20</reference> is, primarily, the confession and intercession of the prophet, who identifies himself with Israel. Cf. <reference osisRef="da 9:3-19">Daniel 9:3-19</reference>. Intercession was a test of the prophetic office ; <reference osisRef="jer 27:18">Jeremiah 27:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="ge 20:7">Genesis 20:7</reference> But Micah's prayer voices also the heart exercise of the remnant in the last days. Such is prophecy, an intermingling of the near and the far. (Cf) ; <reference osisRef="ps 22:1">Psalms 22:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="mt 27:46">Matthew 27:46</reference>.

<hi type="bold">remnant</hi><div eID="gen2882" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2883" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Jer 15:21">Jeremiah 15:21</reference>")</hi> <chapter eID="Mic.7"/> <div eID="gen2883" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen2855" osisID="Mic" type="book"/>
<div canonical="true" osisID="Nah" sID="gen2884" type="book"/> <milestone n="" type="x-usfm-toc1"/> <milestone n="" type="x-usfm-toc2"/> <milestone n="" type="x-usfm-toc3"/>
<chapter n="1" osisID="Nah.1" sID="Nah.1"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv79"/><title type="x-s">Book Introduction - Nahum</title> <div sID="gen2885" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="na 1">Read first chapter of Nahum</reference><div eID="gen2885" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2886" type="x-p"/> Nahum prophesied during the reign of Hezekiah, probably about one hundred and fifty years after Jonah. He has but one subject--the destruction of Nineveh. According to Diodorus Siculus, the city was destroyed nearly a century later, precisely as here predicted. The prophecy is one continuous strain which does not yield to analysis. The moral theme is: the holiness of Jehovah which must deal with sin in judgment. <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv79"/><hi type="bold">Nineveh</hi><div eID="gen2886" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2887" type="x-p"/> Nineveh stands in Scripture as the representative of apostate religious Gentiledom, as Babylon represents the confusion into which the Gentile political world-system has fallen <reference osisRef="da 2:41-43">Daniel 2:41-43,</reference> <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Isa 13:1">Isaiah 13:1</reference>")</hi> , Under the preaching of Jonah, B.C. 862, the city and king had turned to God (Elohim), <reference osisRef="jon 3:3-10">Jonah 3:3-10</reference> But in the time of Nahum, more than a century later, the city had wholly apostatized from God. It is this which distinguishes Nineveh from all the other ancient Gentile cities, and which makes her the suited symbol of the present religious Gentile world-system in the last day. Morally, Nineveh is described in <reference osisRef="ro 1:21-23">Romans 1:21-23</reference>. The chief deity of apostate Nineveh was the bull-god, with the face of a man and the wings of a bird: "an image made like to corruptible man, and to birds, and four-footed beasts."<div eID="gen2887" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2888" type="x-p"/> The message of Nahum, uttered about one hundred years before the destruction of Nineveh, is, therefore, not a call to repentance, but an unrelieved warning of judgment: "He will make an utter end: affliction shall not rise up the second time." <reference osisRef="na 1:9">Nahum 1:9</reference>; see, also, <reference osisRef="na 3:10">Nahum 3:10</reference>. For there is no remedy for apostasy but utter judgment, and a new beginning. Cf. ; <reference osisRef="isa 1:4-5 isa 1:24-28">Isaiah 1:4,5,24-28</reference>; <reference osisRef="heb 6:4-8">Hebrews 6:4-8</reference>; <reference osisRef="pr 29:1">Proverbs 29:1</reference>.<div eID="gen2888" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2889" type="x-p"/> It is the way of God; apostasy is punished by catastrophic destruction. Of this the flood and the destruction of Nineveh are witnesses. The coming destruction of apostate Christendom is foreshadowed by these. (Cf) <reference osisRef="da 2:34 da 2:35">Daniel 2:34,35</reference>; <reference osisRef="lu 17:26 lu 17:27">Luke 17:26,27</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 19:17-21">Revelation 19:17-21</reference>.<div eID="gen2889" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2890" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">burden</hi> See note 1, <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Isa 13:1">Isaiah 13:1</reference>")</hi>

<hi type="bold">God is jealous</hi><div eID="gen2890" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2891" type="x-p"/> The great ethical lesson of Nahum is that the character of God makes Him not only "slow to anger," and "a stronghold to them that trust Him," but also one who "will not at all acquit the wicked." He can be "just, and the justifier of him which believeth in Jesus" <reference osisRef="ro 3:26">Romans 3:26</reference> but only because His holy law has been vindicated in the cross.

<hi type="bold">he knoweth them that trust</hi> <reference osisRef="ps 1:6">Psalms 1:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="2ti 2:19">2 Timothy 2:19</reference> <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ps 2:12">Psalms 2:12</reference>")</hi>. <hi type="bold">Nineveh</hi><div eID="gen2891" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2892" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Na 1:1">Nahum 1:1</reference>")</hi>

<hi type="bold">No,</hi> <div eID="gen2892" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2893" type="x-p"/> Or, No-Amon. <reference osisRef="jer 46:25">Jeremiah 46:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="eze 30:15 eze 30:16">Ezekiel 30:15,16</reference> <chapter eID="Nah.1"/><div eID="gen2893" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen2884" osisID="Nah" type="book"/>
<div canonical="true" osisID="Hab" sID="gen2894" type="book"/> <milestone n="" type="x-usfm-toc1"/> <milestone n="" type="x-usfm-toc2"/> <milestone n="" type="x-usfm-toc3"/>
<chapter n="1" osisID="Hab.1" sID="Hab.1"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv80"/><title type="x-s">Book Introduction - Habakkuk</title> <div sID="gen2895" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="hab 1">Read first chapter of Habakkuk</reference><div eID="gen2895" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2896" type="x-p"/> It seems most probable that Habakkuk prophesied in the latter years of Josiah. Of the prophet himself nothing is known. To him the character of Jehovah was revealed in terms of the highest spirituality. He alone of the prophets was more concerned that the holiness of Jehovah should be vindicated than that Israel should escape chastisement. Written just upon the eve of the captivity, Habakkuk was God's testimony to Himself as against both idolatry and pantheism.<div eID="gen2896" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2897" type="x-p"/> The book is in five parts:<div eID="gen2897" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">Habakkuk's perplexity in view of the sins of Israel and the silence of God, 1:1-4. Historically this was the time of Jehovah's forbearance because of Josiah's repentance (2Ki22:18-20).</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The answer of Jehovah to the prophet's perplexity1:5-11.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The prophet, thus answered, utters the testimony to Jehovah, 1:12-17; but he will watch for further answers, 2:1.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">To the watching prophet comes the response of the "vision," 2:20.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">All ends in Habakkuk's sublime Psalm of the Kingdom.</item> </list> <div sID="gen2898" type="x-p"/> As a whole the Book of Habakkuk raise and answers the question of God's consistency with Himself in view of permitted evil. The prophet thought that the holiness of God forbade him to go on with evil Israel. The answer of Jehovah announces a Chaldean invasion (<reference osisRef="hab 1:6">Habakkuk 1:6</reference>), and a world- wide dispersion <reference osisRef="hab 1:5">Habakkuk 1:5</reference>). But Jehovah is not mere wrath; "He delighteth in mercy" (<reference osisRef="mic 7:18">Micah 7:18</reference>), and introduces into His answers to the perplexed prophet the great promises, ; <reference osisRef="mic 1:5">Micah 1:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="mic 2:3 mic 2:4 mic 2:14 mic 2:20"> 2:3,4,14,20</reference>. <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv80"/><hi type="bold">burden</hi> See note 1, <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Isa 13:1">Isaiah 13:1</reference>")</hi>.

<hi type="bold">for I will work</hi><div eID="gen2898" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2899" type="x-p"/> Verse 5 anticipates the dispersion "among the nations" (cf) <reference osisRef="de 28:64-67">Deuteronomy 28:64-67</reference>. While Israel as a nation is thus dispersed, Jehovah will "work a work" which Israel "will not believe." <reference osisRef="ac 13:37-41">Acts 13:37-41,</reference> interprets this prediction of the redemptive work of Christ. It is significant that Paul quotes this to Jews of the dispersion in the synagogue at Antioch. <chapter eID="Hab.1"/><div eID="gen2899" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen2900" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="2" osisID="Hab.2" sID="Hab.2"/>

<hi type="bold">run that readeth it</hi> <div eID="gen2900" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2901" type="x-p"/> Not, as usually quoted, "that he that runneth may read," but, "that he may run that readeth"; i.e. as a messenger of the "vision." Cf. <reference osisRef="zec 2:4 zec 2:5">Zechariah 2:4,5</reference>

<hi type="bold">appointed time</hi><div eID="gen2901" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2902" type="x-p"/> To the watching prophet comes the response of the "vision" <reference osisRef="hab 2:2-20">Habakkuk 2:2-20</reference>). Three elements are to be distinguished:<div eID="gen2902" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(1) The moral judgment of Jehovah upon the evils practised by dispersed Israel (Hab 5-13,15-19).</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(2) The future purpose of God that, practised by dispersed Israel (<reference osisRef="hab 2:5-13 hab 2:15-19">Habakkuk 2:5-13,15-19</reference>).</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(2) The future purpose of God that, "the earth shall be filled with the knowledge of the glory of Jehovah, as the waters cover the sea" (<reference osisRef="hab 2:14">Habakkuk 2:14</reference>). That this revelation awaits the return of the Lord in glory is shown</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(a) by the parallel passage in <reference osisRef="isa 11:9-12">Isaiah 11:9-12</reference> and</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(b) by the quotation of verse 3 in <reference osisRef="heb 10:37 heb 10:38">Hebrews 10:37,38</reference> where the "it" of the "vision" becomes "he" and refers to the return of the Lord. It is then, after the "vision" is fulfilled, that "the knowledge of the glory," etc, shall fill the earth. But</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(3) meantime, "the just shall live by his faith." This great evangelic word is applied to Jew and Gentile in <reference osisRef="ro 1:17">Romans 1:17</reference> to the Gentiles in <reference osisRef="ga 3:11-14">Galatians 3:11-14</reference> and to Hebrews (especially) in <reference osisRef="heb 10:38">Hebrews 10:38</reference>. This opening of life to faith alone, makes possible not only the salvation of the Gentiles during the dispersion of Israel "among the nations" ; <reference osisRef="hab 1:5">Habakkuk 1:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="ga 3:11-14">Galatians 3:11-14</reference> but also makes possible a believing remnant in Israel while the nation, as such, is in blindness and unbelief, <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ro 11:1">Romans 11:1</reference>")</hi> with neither priesthood nor temple, and consequently unable to keep the ordinances of the law. Such is Jehovah! In disciplinary government His ancient Israel is cast out of the land and judicially blinded <reference osisRef="2co 3:12-15">2 Corinthians 3:12-15</reference> but in covenanted mercy the individual Jew may resort to the simple faith of Abraham ; <reference osisRef="ge 15:6">Genesis 15:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="ro 4:1-5">Romans 4:1-5</reference> and be saved. But this does not set aside the Palestinian See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:de 30:3">Deuteronomy 30:3</reference>" and Davidic See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:2sa 7:16">2 Samuel 7:16</reference>". Covenants, for "the earth shall be filled," etc. (<reference osisRef="hab 2:14">Habakkuk 2:14</reference>),and Jehovah will again be in His temple (<reference osisRef="hab 2:20">Habakkuk 2:20</reference>). Cf. ; <reference osisRef="hab 2:14 hab 2:20">Habakkuk 2:14,20</reference>; <reference osisRef="ro 11:25-27">Romans 11:25-27</reference> </item> </list>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv81"/><div sID="gen2903" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv81"/> <hi type="bold">hell</hi> <div eID="gen2903" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2904" type="x-p"/> Sheol is, in the O.T., the place to which the dead go.<div eID="gen2904" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(1) Often, therefore, it is spoken of as the equivalent of the grave, merely, where all human activities cease; the terminus toward which all human life moves (e.g. <reference osisRef="ge 42:38">Genesis 42:38</reference> grave <reference osisRef="job 14:13">Job 14:13</reference> grave <reference osisRef="ps 88:3">Psalms 88:3</reference> grave</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(2) To the man "under the sun," the natural man, who of necessity judges from appearances, sheol seems no more than the grave-- the end and total cessation, not only of the activities of life, but of life itself. <reference osisRef="ec 9:5 ec 9:10">Ecclesiastes 9:5,10</reference></item> <item type="x-indent-1">(3) But Scripture reveals sheol as a place of sorrow <reference osisRef="2sa 22:6">2 Samuel 22:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="ps 18:5 ps 116:3">Psalms 18:5, 116:3</reference>; in which the wicked are turned <reference osisRef="ps 9:17">Psalms 9:17</reference> and where they are fully conscious ; <reference osisRef="isa 14:9-17">Isaiah 14:9-17</reference>; <reference osisRef="eze 32:21">Ezekiel 32:21</reference> see, especially, <reference osisRef="jon 2:2">Jonah 2:2</reference> what the belly of the great fish was to Jonah that sheol is to those who are therein). The sheol of the O.T. and hades of the N.T. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Lu 16:23">Luke 16:23</reference>")</hi> are identical. </item> </list>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv82"/><div sID="gen2905" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv82"/><hi type="bold">is it not</hi> Or, it is not of the LORD, etc., i.e. though permitted in His providence, not His plan. Cf. <reference osisRef="mic 4:2-4">Micah 4:2-4</reference>.

<hi type="bold">For the earth shall be filled</hi><div eID="gen2905" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2906" type="x-p"/> Cf. <reference osisRef="isa 11:9">Isaiah 11:9</reference> which fixes the time when "the earth," etc. It is when David's righteous Branch has set up the kingdom. (See "Kingdom (O.T.)," ; <reference osisRef="2sa 7:9">2 Samuel 7:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="zec 12:8">Zechariah 12:8</reference> also, "Kingdom (N.T.)," ; <reference osisRef="lu 1:31-33">Luke 1:31-33</reference>; <reference osisRef="1co 15:28">1 Corinthians 15:28</reference>. Habakkuk's phrase marks an advance on that of Isaiah. In the latter it is "the knowledge of the Lord." That, in a certain sense, is being diffused now; but in Habakkuk it is "the knowledge of the glory of the Lord," and that cannot be till He is manifested in glory ; <reference osisRef="mt 24:30">Matthew 24:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="mt 25:31"> 25:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="lu 9:26">Luke 9:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="2th 1:7">2 Thessalonians 1:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="2th 2:8"> 2:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="jude 1:14">Jude 1:14</reference>. The transfiguration was a foreview of this. <reference osisRef="lu 9:26-29">Luke 9:26-29</reference>.

<hi type="bold">trusteth</hi> <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ps 2:12">Psalms 2:12</reference>")</hi> <div eID="gen2906" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv83"/><div sID="gen2907" type="x-p"/> <chapter eID="Hab.2"/>
<div eID="gen2907" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2908" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="3" osisID="Hab.3" sID="Hab.3"/>

<hi type="bold">Prayer</hi> <div eID="gen2908" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2909" type="x-p"/> Prayer in the O.T. is in contrast with prayer in the N.T. in two respects:<div eID="gen2909" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(1) In the former the basis of prayer is a covenant of God, or an appeal to his revealed character as merciful, gracious, etc. In the latter the basis is relationship: "When ye pray, say, Our Father" <reference osisRef="mt 6:9">Matthew 6:9</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(2) A comparison, e.g. of the prayers of Moses and Paul, will show that one was praying for an earthly people whose dangers and blessings were earthly; the other for a heavenly people whose dangers and blessings were spiritual. </item> </list>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv83"/><div sID="gen2910" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv83"/> <hi type="bold">Cushan</hi> <div eID="gen2910" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2911" type="x-p"/> Or, Ethiopia.
<hi type="bold">at the light</hi><div eID="gen2911" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2912" type="x-p"/> Or, thine arrows walked in the light, etc.

<hi type="bold">Although</hi><div eID="gen2912" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2913" type="x-p"/> i.e. despite the afflictions of Israel in dispersion, the prophet will rejoice because of the Lord, as yet to return to His temple. <chapter eID="Hab.3"/><div eID="gen2913" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen2894" osisID="Hab" type="book"/>
<div canonical="true" osisID="Zeph" sID="gen2914" type="book"/> <milestone n="" type="x-usfm-toc1"/> <milestone n="" type="x-usfm-toc2"/> <milestone n="" type="x-usfm-toc3"/>
<chapter n="1" osisID="Zeph.1" sID="Zeph.1"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv84"/><title type="x-s">Book Introduction - Zephaniah</title> <div sID="gen2915" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="zep 1">Read first chapter of Zephaniah</reference><div eID="gen2915" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2916" type="x-p"/> This prophet, a contemporary of Jeremiah, exercised his ministry during the reign of Josiah. It was a time of revival (2Ki. 22), but the captivity was impending, nevertheless, and Zephaniah points out the moral state which, despite the superficial revival under Josiah (<reference osisRef="jer 2:11-13">Jeremiah 2:11-13</reference>), made it inevitable.<div eID="gen2916" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2917" type="x-p"/> Zephaniah is in four parts:<div eID="gen2917" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">The coming invasion of Nebuchadnezzar a figure of the day of the Lord, 1:1-2:3.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">Predictions of judgment on certain peoples, 2:4-15.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The moral state of Israel for which the captivity was to come, 3:1-7.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The judgment of the nations followed by kingdom blessing under Messiah, 3:8-20.</item> </list> <div sID="gen2918" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv84"/> <hi type="bold">Chemarims</hi> <div eID="gen2918" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2919" type="x-p"/> i.e. idolatrous priests. Cf. <reference osisRef="2ki 23:5">2 Kings 23:5</reference>.
<hi type="bold">Malcham</hi><div eID="gen2919" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2920" type="x-p"/> An idol of the Ammonites, same as Molech, or Milcom.

<hi type="bold">for the day of the Lord</hi><div eID="gen2920" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2921" type="x-p"/> As in the other Prophets, the approaching invasion of Nebuchadnezzar is treated as an adumbration of the true day of the Lord in which all earth-judgments will culminate, to be followed by the restoration and blessing of Israel and the nations in the kingdom. See "Day of the Lord" <reference osisRef="isa 2:10-22">Isaiah 2:10-22</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 19:11-21">Revelation 19:11-21</reference> "Israel" ; <reference osisRef="ge 12:2 ge 12:3">Genesis 12:2,3</reference>; <reference osisRef="ro 11:26">Romans 11:26</reference>. CF. Joel 1.,2.

<hi type="bold">Maktesh</hi><div eID="gen2921" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2922" type="x-p"/> Lit. The Mortar, a depression in Jerusalem where the bazaars were. <div eID="gen2922" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv85"/><div sID="gen2923" type="x-p"/> <chapter eID="Zeph.1"/>
<div eID="gen2923" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2924" type="x-p"/><chapter n="2" osisID="Zeph.2" sID="Zeph.2"/>
<hi type="bold">desired</hi> Lit. that hath not shame. Cf. <reference osisRef="jer 3:3">Jeremiah 3:3</reference>.
<hi type="bold">remnant</hi><div eID="gen2924" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2925" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Jer 15:21">Jeremiah 15:21</reference>")</hi>.

<hi type="bold">Nineveh</hi><div eID="gen2925" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2926" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Na 1:1">Nahum 1:1</reference>")</hi>. <chapter eID="Zeph.2"/><div eID="gen2926" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen2927" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="3" osisID="Zeph.3" sID="Zeph.3"/>
<hi type="bold">trusted</hi> <div eID="gen2927" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2928" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ps 2:12">Psalms 2:12</reference>")</hi>
<hi type="bold">fear</hi> <div eID="gen2928" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2929" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ps 19:9">Psalms 19:9</reference>")</hi>

<hi type="bold">then will I turn</hi> <div eID="gen2929" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2930" type="x-p"/> In Zephaniah the conversion of "the peoples" is stated out of the usual prophetic order, in which the blessing of Israel and the setting up of the kingdom precedes the conversion of the Gentiles. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Zec 12:1">Zechariah 12:1</reference>")</hi>. See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:zec 12:8">Zechariah 12:8</reference>". But the passage gives clear testimony as to when the conversion of the nations will occur. It is after the smiting of the nations. Cf. <reference osisRef="isa 11:9">Isaiah 11:9</reference> with context; <reference osisRef="da 2:34 da 2:35">Daniel 2:34,35</reference>; <reference osisRef="ps 2:5-8">Psalms 2:5-8</reference>; <reference osisRef="ac 15:15-17">Acts 15:15-17</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 19:19-re 20:6">Revelation 19:19-20:6</reference>.
<hi type="bold">trust</hi><div eID="gen2930" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2931" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ps 2:12">Psalms 2:12</reference>")</hi>.
<hi type="bold">remnant</hi><div eID="gen2931" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2932" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Jer 15:21">Jeremiah 15:21</reference>")</hi>

<hi type="bold">the midst of thee</hi> <div eID="gen2932" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2933" type="x-p"/> That this, and all like passages in the Prophets (see "Kingdom (O.T.)," <reference osisRef="ge 1:26">Genesis 1:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="zec 12:8">Zechariah 12:8</reference> cannot refer to anything which occurred at the first coming of Christ is clear from the context. The precise reverse was true. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Isa 11:1">Isaiah 11:1</reference>")</hi>. <chapter eID="Zeph.3"/><div eID="gen2933" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen2914" osisID="Zeph" type="book"/>
<div canonical="true" osisID="Hag" sID="gen2934" type="book"/> <milestone n="" type="x-usfm-toc1"/> <milestone n="" type="x-usfm-toc2"/> <milestone n="" type="x-usfm-toc3"/>
<chapter n="1" osisID="Hag.1" sID="Hag.1"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv85"/><title type="x-s">Book Introduction - Haggai</title> <div sID="gen2935" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="hag 1">Read first chapter of Haggai</reference><div eID="gen2935" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2936" type="x-p"/> Haggai was a prophet of the restored remnant after the 70 years' captivity. The circumstances are detailed in Ezra and Nehemiah. To hearten, rebuke, and instruct that feeble and divided remnant was the task of Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi. The theme of Haggai is the unfinished temple, and his mission to admonish and encourage the builders.<div eID="gen2936" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2937" type="x-p"/> The divisions of the book are marked by the formula, "came the word of the Lord by Haggai":<div eID="gen2937" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">The event which drew out the prophecy, 1:1,2.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The divine displeasure because of the interrupted work, 1:3-15.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The temples--Solomon's, the restoration temple, and the kingdom-age temple, 2:1-9.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">Uncleanness and chastening, 2:10-19.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The final victory, 2:20-23 (see) Re19:17-20; 14:19,20; Zec14:1-3.</item> </list> <div sID="gen2938" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv85"/> <hi type="bold">sixth month</hi> <div eID="gen2938" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2939" type="x-p"/> i.e. September, also <reference osisRef="hag 1:15">Haggai 1:15</reference>.
<hi type="bold">fear</hi><div eID="gen2939" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2940" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ps 19:9">Psalms 19:9</reference>")</hi>

<hi type="bold">remnant</hi> <div eID="gen2940" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2941" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Jer 15:21">Jeremiah 15:21</reference>")</hi>. <chapter eID="Hag.1"/><div eID="gen2941" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen2942" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="2" osisID="Hag.2" sID="Hag.2"/>
<hi type="bold">seventh month</hi> <div eID="gen2942" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2943" type="x-p"/> i.e. October.

<hi type="bold">house in her first glory</hi><div eID="gen2943" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2944" type="x-p"/> The prophet calls upon the old men who remembered Solomon's temple to witness to the new generation how greatly that structure exceeded the present in magnificence; and then utters a prophecy (<reference osisRef="hag 1:7-9">Haggai 1:7-9</reference>) which can only refer to the future kingdom temple described by Ezekiel. It is certain that the restoration temple and all subsequent structures, including Herod's, were far inferior in costliness and splendour to Solomon's. The present period is described in <reference osisRef="ho 3:4 ho 3:5">Hosea 3:4,5</reference>. Verse 6 is quoted in <reference osisRef="heb 12:26 heb 12:27">Hebrews 12:26,27</reference>. Verse 7: "I will shake all nations," refers to the great tribulation and is followed by the coming of Christ in glory, as in <reference osisRef="mt 24:29 mt 24:30">Matthew 24:29,30</reference>. "The desire of all nations" is Christ. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Mal 3:1">Malachi 3:1</reference>")</hi>.

<hi type="bold">latter house</hi><div eID="gen2944" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2945" type="x-p"/> In a sense all the temples (i.e Solomon's; Ezra's; Herod's; that which will be used by the unbelieving Jews under covenant with the Beast <reference osisRef="da 9:27">Daniel 9:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="mt 24:15">Matthew 24:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="2th 2:3 2th 2:4">2 Thessalonians 2:3,4</reference> and Ezekiel's future kingdom temple Ez 40.-47.), are treated as one "house"-- the "house of the Lord," since they all profess to be that. For that reason Christ purified the temple of His day, erected though it was by an Idumean usurper to please the Jews. <reference osisRef="mt 21:12 mt 21:13">Matthew 21:12,13</reference>.<div eID="gen2945" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2946" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">glory</hi> Or, the future glory of this house shall be greater than the former.

<hi type="bold">holy flesh</hi> <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Jer 11:15">Jeremiah 11:15</reference>")</hi>. <chapter eID="Hag.2"/><div eID="gen2946" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen2934" osisID="Hag" type="book"/>
<div canonical="true" osisID="Zech" sID="gen2947" type="book"/> <milestone n="" type="x-usfm-toc1"/> <milestone n="" type="x-usfm-toc2"/> <milestone n="" type="x-usfm-toc3"/>
<chapter n="1" osisID="Zech.1" sID="Zech.1"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv86"/><title type="x-s">Book Introduction - Zechariah</title> <div sID="gen2948" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="zec 1">Read first chapter of Zechariah</reference><div eID="gen2948" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2949" type="x-p"/> Zechariah, like Haggai, was a prophet to the remnant which returned after the 70 years. There is much of symbol in Zechariah, but these difficult passages are readily interpreted in the light of the whole body of related prophecy. The great Messianic passages are, upon comparison with the other prophecies of the kingdom, perfectly clear. Both advents of Christ are in Zechariah's prophecy <reference osisRef="zec 9:9">Zechariah 9:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="mt 21:1-11">Matthew 21:1-11</reference> <reference osisRef="zec 14:3 zec 14:4">Zechariah 14:3,4</reference>. More than Haggai or Malachi, Zechariah gives the mind of God about the Gentile world-powers surrounding the restored remnant. He has given them their authority <reference osisRef="da 2:27-40">Daniel 2:27-40</reference> and will hold them to account; the test, as always, being their treatment of Israel. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ge 15:18">Genesis 15:18</reference>")</hi> note 3, clause 6; <reference osisRef="zec 2:8">Zechariah 2:8</reference>. Zechariah, therefore, falls into three broad divisions:<div eID="gen2949" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">Symbolic visions in the light of the Messianic hope, 1:1-6:15.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The mission from Babylon, 7:, 8.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">Messiah in rejection and afterwards in power, 9-14.</item> </list> <div sID="gen2950" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv86"/> <hi type="bold">eighth month</hi> <div eID="gen2950" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2951" type="x-p"/> i.e. November.
<hi type="bold">Sebat</hi><div eID="gen2951" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2952" type="x-p"/> Eleventh month i.e. February.

<hi type="bold">I saw</hi><div eID="gen2952" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2953" type="x-p"/> The "man" (<reference osisRef="zec 1:8">Zechariah 1:8</reference>) is the "my lord," "the angel that talked with me" (<reference osisRef="zec 1:9">Zechariah 1:9</reference>), and "the angel of the Lord" (<reference osisRef="zec 1:10 zec 1:11">Zechariah 1:10,11</reference>). The "man" "stood among the myrtle trees" (<reference osisRef="zec 1:8">Zechariah 1:8</reference>). The prophet addresses him as "my lord" (cf) <reference osisRef="ge 19:2">Genesis 19:2</reference> but when the "man" answers he perceives that he has addressed an angel--"the angel that talked with me" (<reference osisRef="zec 1:9">Zechariah 1:9</reference>). In <reference osisRef="zec 1:10">Zechariah 1:10</reference> the being of the vision is again "the man that stood among the myrtle trees." In <reference osisRef="zec 1:11">Zechariah 1:11</reference> he is called "the angel of the Lord," and to him the (riders on the) "red horses, speckled with white" say: "We have walked to and fro," etc. Then (<reference osisRef="zec 1:12">Zechariah 1:12</reference>) "the angel of the Lord" (i.e. the "man," "my lord," "the angel that talked with me") intercedes for the land against a world at ease. The date of the intercession was at the end of the 70 years' captivity of Judah. <reference osisRef="zec 1:9-12">Zechariah 1:9-12</reference>.<div eID="gen2953" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2954" type="x-p"/> Taken as a whole <reference osisRef="zec 1:8-17">Zechariah 1:8-17</reference> Zechariah's first vision reveals Judah in dispersion; Jerusalem under adverse possession; and the Gentile nations at rest about it. This condition still continues, and Jehovah's answer to the intercession of the angel sweeps on to the end-time of Gentile domination, when "the Lord shall yet comfort Zion," etc. (<reference osisRef="zec 1:16 zec 1:17">Zechariah 1:16,17</reference>).<div eID="gen2954" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2955" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="isa 40:1-5">Isaiah 40:1-5</reference>. See "Kingdom (O.T.)" <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ge 1:26">Genesis 1:26</reference>")</hi> See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:zec 12:8">Zechariah 12:8</reference>".<div eID="gen2955" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2956" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">red horse</hi> Cf. <reference osisRef="re 6:4">Revelation 6:4</reference>. The whole Gentile period is characterized by the red horse, i.e. "sword." ; <reference osisRef="da 9:26">Daniel 9:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="mt 24:6 mt 24:7">Matthew 24:6,7</reference>.
<hi type="bold">angel</hi><div eID="gen2956" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2957" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Heb 1:4">Hebrews 1:4</reference>")</hi>.
<hi type="bold">angel</hi><div eID="gen2957" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2958" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Heb 1:4">Hebrews 1:4</reference>")</hi>

<hi type="bold">horn</hi> <div eID="gen2958" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2959" type="x-p"/> A "horn" is the symbol of a Gentile king <reference osisRef="da 7:24">Daniel 7:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 17:12">Revelation 17:12</reference> and the vision is of the four world empires ; <reference osisRef="da 2:36-44">Daniel 2:36-44</reference>; <reference osisRef="da 7:3-7"> 7:3-7</reference> which have "scattered Judah, Israel, and Jerusalem" (v.19)
<hi type="bold">angel</hi><div eID="gen2959" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2960" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Heb 1:4">Hebrews 1:4</reference>")</hi>

<hi type="bold">And the Lord</hi> <div eID="gen2960" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2961" type="x-p"/> The word charash, trans. "carpenter," is lit. carver, engraver. <reference osisRef="zec 1:21">Zechariah 1:21</reference> makes it plain that, whatever the four carvers may be, they are used to "fray," or carve away (Heb. charad) in the sense of diminishing, enfeebling, the great Gentile world-powers. They may stand for Jehovah's "four sore judgments," the sword, famine, evil beasts, and pestilence <reference osisRef="eze 14:21">Ezekiel 14:21</reference> the four horses of Rev. 6. <div eID="gen2961" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv87"/><div sID="gen2962" type="x-p"/> <chapter eID="Zech.1"/>
<div eID="gen2962" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2963" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="2" osisID="Zech.2" sID="Zech.2"/>

<hi type="bold">again</hi> <div eID="gen2963" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2964" type="x-p"/> As in <reference osisRef="zec 1:8-11">Zechariah 1:8-11,</reference> the "man" of <reference osisRef="zec 2:1">Zechariah 2:1</reference> 1 is "the angel that talked with me" of <reference osisRef="zec 1:3">Zechariah 1:3</reference>. The measuring-line (or reed) is used by Ezekiel <reference osisRef="eze 40:3 eze 40:5">Ezekiel 40:3,5</reference> as a symbol of preparation for rebuilding the city and temple in the kingdom-age. Here also it has that meaning, as the context (<reference osisRef="zec 2:4-13">Zechariah 2:4-13</reference>) shows. The subject of the vision is the restoration of nation and city. In no sense has this prophecy been fulfilled. The order is:<div eID="gen2964" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(1) The Lord in glory in Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="zec 2:5">Zechariah 2:5</reference> (cf. <reference osisRef="mt 24:29 mt 24:30">Matthew 24:29,30</reference>)</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(2) the restoration of Israel, <reference osisRef="zec 2:6">Zechariah 2:6</reference>;</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(3) the judgment of Jehovah upon the nations, <reference osisRef="zec 2:8">Zechariah 2:8,</reference> "after the glory" <reference osisRef="mt 25:31 mt 25:32">Matthew 25:31,32</reference></item> <item type="x-indent-1">(4) the full blessing of the earth in the kingdom, <reference osisRef="zec 2:10-13">Zechariah 2:10-13,</reference> See "Kingdom (O.T.)" <reference osisRef="ge 1:26">Genesis 1:26</reference>. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Zec 12:8">Zechariah 12:8</reference>")</hi>. "Israel," ; <reference osisRef="ge 12:2">Genesis 12:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="ro 11:26">Romans 11:26</reference>. </item> </list>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv87"/><div sID="gen2965" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv87"/> <hi type="bold">angel</hi> <div eID="gen2965" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2966" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Heb 1:4">Hebrews 1:4</reference>")</hi>. <div eID="gen2966" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv88"/><div sID="gen2967" type="x-p"/> <chapter eID="Zech.2"/>
<div eID="gen2967" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2968" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="3" osisID="Zech.3" sID="Zech.3"/>

<hi type="bold">Joshua</hi> <div eID="gen2968" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2969" type="x-p"/> The fifth vision discloses:<div eID="gen2969" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(1) The change from self-righteousness to the righteousness of God <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ro 3:21">Romans 3:21</reference>")</hi> of which Paul's experience, <reference osisRef="php 3:1-9">Philippians 3:1-9</reference> is the illustration, as it is also the foreshadowing of the conversion of Israel.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(2) In type, the preparation of Israel for receiving Jehovah's "BRANCH" <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Isa 4:2">Isaiah 4:2</reference>")</hi>. The refusal of the Jews to abandon self-righteousness for the righteousness of God blinded them to the presence of the BRANCH in their midst at His first advent <reference osisRef="ro 10:1-4">Romans 10:1-4</reference>; <reference osisRef="ro 11:7 ro 11:8"> 11:7,8</reference> Cf. <reference osisRef="zec 6:12-15">Zechariah 6:12-15</reference> which speaks of the manifestation of the BRANCH in glory (v. 13) as the Priest-King, when Israel will receive Him. See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:heb 5:6">Hebrews 5:6</reference>".</item> </list> <div sID="gen2970" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">angel</hi><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Heb 1:4">Hebrews 1:4</reference>")</hi>.

<hi type="bold">clothed</hi> See, <reference osisRef="isa 64:6">Isaiah 64:6</reference> Contra: <reference osisRef="php 3:1-9">Philippians 3:1-9</reference>.<div eID="gen2970" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2971" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">angel</hi><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Heb 1:4">Hebrews 1:4</reference>")</hi>.
<hi type="bold">clothe</hi><div eID="gen2971" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2972" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ge 3:21">Genesis 3:21</reference>")</hi>.
<hi type="bold">angel</hi><div eID="gen2972" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2973" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Heb 1:4">Hebrews 1:4</reference>")</hi>.
<hi type="bold">BRANCH</hi><div eID="gen2973" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2974" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Isa 4:2">Isaiah 4:2</reference>")</hi>.

<hi type="bold">stone</hi><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:1Pe 2:8">1 Peter 2:8</reference>")</hi>.<div eID="gen2974" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2975" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">seven eyes</hi> Cf. <reference osisRef="zec 4:10">Zechariah 4:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 5:6">Revelation 5:6</reference>.

<hi type="bold">that day</hi><div eID="gen2975" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2976" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="zec 3:10">Zechariah 3:10</reference> marks the time of fulfilment as in the future kingdom. It speaks of a security which Israel has never known since the captivity, nor will know till the kingdom comes. (Cf. <reference osisRef="isa 11:1-9">Isaiah 11:1-9</reference>). <div eID="gen2976" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv88"/><div sID="gen2977" type="x-p"/> <chapter eID="Zech.3"/>
<div eID="gen2977" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2978" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="4" osisID="Zech.4" sID="Zech.4"/>

<hi type="bold">angel</hi> <div eID="gen2978" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2979" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">that talked</hi> <div eID="gen2979" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2980" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">angel</hi><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Heb 1:4">Hebrews 1:4</reference>")</hi>.<div eID="gen2980" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2981" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that talked</hi><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Zec 1:8">Zechariah 1:8</reference>")</hi>.

<hi type="bold">And I said</hi><div eID="gen2981" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2982" type="x-p"/> The vision of the candlestick and olive trees (lit. trees of oil) is, as we know, from <reference osisRef="re 11:3-12">Revelation 11:3-12</reference> a prophecy to be fulfilled in the last days of the present age. That which marks the ministry of the "two witnesses" <reference osisRef="re 11:3 re 11:4">Revelation 11:3,4</reference> is power. (Cf <reference osisRef="zec 4:6">Zechariah 4:6</reference>). In measure this power would rest upon Zerubbabel, who, having begun the restoration temple of Zechariah's time, would finish it (v.9) laying the "headstone" amid the shoutings of the people. The whole scene forms a precursive fulfilment of the ministry of the two witnesses of Rev. 11. and of the coming of the true "headstone," Prince Messiah, of whom prince Zerubbabel is a type. Oil is a uniform symbol of the Spirit. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ac 2:4">Acts 2:4</reference>")</hi>. Joshua and Zerubbabel were doubtless the two olive trees for that day, as the two witnesses of Rev. 11. may, in turn, but point to Christ as Priest-King in the kingdom- age. <reference osisRef="zec 6:12 zec 6:13">Zechariah 6:12,13</reference>.

<hi type="bold">eyes</hi><div eID="gen2982" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2983" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Zec 3:9">Zechariah 3:9</reference>")</hi> <div eID="gen2983" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv88"/><div sID="gen2984" type="x-p"/> <chapter eID="Zech.4"/>
<div eID="gen2984" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2985" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="5" osisID="Zech.5" sID="Zech.5"/>

<hi type="bold">flying roll</hi> <div eID="gen2985" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2986" type="x-p"/> A "roll," in Scripture symbolism, means the written word whether of God or man <reference osisRef="eze 6:2">Ezekiel 6:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="jer 36:2 jer 36:4 jer 36:6">Jeremiah 36:2,4,6,</reference> etc: <reference osisRef="eze 3:1-3">Ezekiel 3:1-3</reference>. Zechariah's eighth vision is of the rebuke of sin by the word of God. The two sins mentioned really transgress both tables of the law. To steal is to set aside our neighbor's right; to swear is to set aside God's claim to reverence. As always the law can only curse (<reference osisRef="zec 5:3">Zechariah 5:3</reference>); <reference osisRef="ga 3:10-14">Galatians 3:10-14</reference>.
<hi type="bold">earth</hi><div eID="gen2986" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2987" type="x-p"/> Lit. land, i.e. Palestine.

<hi type="bold">What is it</hi><div eID="gen2987" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2988" type="x-p"/> In the vision of the ephah local and prophetic elements are to be distinguished. The elements are: an ephah or measure; a woman in the ephah; a sealing weight upon the mouth of the ephah confining the woman, and the stork-winged women whose only function is to bear the ephah and woman away into Babylonia (Shinar). The thing thus symbolized was "through all the land" (v.6).<div eID="gen2988" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2989" type="x-p"/> Symbolically, a "measure" (or "cup") stands for something which has come to the full, so that God must judge it <reference osisRef="2sa 8:2">2 Samuel 8:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="jer 51:13">Jeremiah 51:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="hab 3:6 hab 3:7">Habakkuk 3:6,7</reference>; <reference osisRef="mt 7:2">Matthew 7:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="mt 23:32"> 23:32</reference>. A woman, in the bad ethical sense, is always a symbol of that which, religiously, is out of its place. The "woman" in <reference osisRef="mt 13:33">Matthew 13:33</reference> is dealing with doctrine, a sphere forbidden to her <reference osisRef="1ti 2:12">1 Timothy 2:12</reference>. In Thyatira a woman is suffered to teach <reference osisRef="re 2:20">Revelation 2:20</reference>. The Babylon phase of the apostate church is symbolized by an unchaste woman, sodden with the greed and luxury of commercialism. ; <reference osisRef="re 17:1-6">Revelation 17:1-6</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 18:3 re 18:11-20"> 18:3,11-20</reference>.<div eID="gen2989" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2990" type="x-p"/> The local application of Zechariah's ninth vision is, therefore, evident. The Jews then in the land had been in captivity in Babylon. Outwardly they had put away idolatry, but they had learned in Babylon that insatiate greed of gain <reference osisRef="ne 5:1-9">Nehemiah 5:1-9</reference>; <reference osisRef="mal 3:8">Malachi 3:8</reference> that intense commercial spirit which had been foreign to Israel as a pastoral people, but which was thenceforward to characterize them through the ages. These things were out of place in God's people and land. Symbolically He judged them as belonging to Babylon and sent them there to build a temple--they could have no part in His. The "woman" was to be "set there upon her own base" (<reference osisRef="zec 5:11">Zechariah 5:11</reference>). It was Jehovah's moral judgment upon Babylonism in His own land and people.<div eID="gen2990" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2991" type="x-p"/> Prophetically, the application to the Babylon of the Revelation is obvious. The professing Gentile church at that time condoning every iniquity of the rich, doctrinally a mere "confusion," as the name indicates, and corrupted to the core by commercialism, wealth, and luxury, falls under the judgment of God (Rev. 18.).<div eID="gen2991" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2992" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">earth</hi> <div eID="gen2992" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2993" type="x-p"/> Lit. land, i.e. Palestine.
<hi type="bold">angel</hi><div eID="gen2993" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2994" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Heb 1:4">Hebrews 1:4</reference>")</hi>.

<hi type="bold">Shinar</hi><div eID="gen2994" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2995" type="x-p"/> i.e. Babylonia. <reference osisRef="da 1:2">Daniel 1:2</reference> <div eID="gen2995" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv88"/><div sID="gen2996" type="x-p"/> <chapter eID="Zech.5"/>
<div eID="gen2996" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2997" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="6" osisID="Zech.6" sID="Zech.6"/>

<hi type="bold">four chariots</hi> <div eID="gen2997" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2998" type="x-p"/> The interpretation of the tenth vision must be governed by the authoritative declaration of <reference osisRef="zec 6:5">Zechariah 6:5</reference>. That which is symbolized by the four chariots with their horses is not the four world-empires of Daniel, but "the four spirits of heaven which go forth from standing before the Lord of all the earth" (<reference osisRef="zec 6:5">Zechariah 6:5</reference>). These "spirits" are angels ; <reference osisRef="lu 1:19">Luke 1:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="heb 1:14">Hebrews 1:14</reference> and are most naturally interpreted of the four angels of ; <reference osisRef="re 7:1-3">Revelation 7:1-3</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 9:14 re 9:15"> 9:14,15</reference>. These have also a ministry earthward, and of like nature with the "spirits" of <reference osisRef="zec 6:1-8">Zechariah 6:1-8</reference>. viz. judgment. The symbol (chariots and horses) is in perfect harmony with this. Always in Scripture symbolism they stand for the power of God earthward in judgment. ; <reference osisRef="jer 46:9 jer 46:10">Jeremiah 46:9,10</reference>; <reference osisRef="joe 2:3-11">Joel 2:3-11</reference> <reference osisRef="na 3:1-7">Nahum 3:1-7</reference>. The vision, then, speaks of the Lord's judgments upon the Gentile nations north and south in the day of the Lord ; <reference osisRef="isa 2:10-22">Isaiah 2:10-22</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 19:11-21">Revelation 19:11-21</reference>.
<hi type="bold">angel</hi><div eID="gen2998" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2999" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Heb 1:4">Hebrews 1:4</reference>")</hi>

<hi type="bold">crowns</hi> <div eID="gen2999" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3000" type="x-p"/> Following the earth-judgments symbolized in the horsed chariots (<reference osisRef="zec 6:1-8">Zechariah 6:1-8</reference>) comes the manifestation of Christ in His kingdom glory (<reference osisRef="zec 6:9-15">Zechariah 6:9-15</reference>). This is the invariable prophetic order: first the judgments of the day of the Lord ; <reference osisRef="isa 2:10-22">Isaiah 2:10-22</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 19:11-21">Revelation 19:11-21</reference> then the kingdom (cf) ; <reference osisRef="ps 2:5">Psalms 2:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="ps 2:6"> 2:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="isa 3:24-26">Isaiah 3:24-26</reference>; <reference osisRef="isa 4:2-6"> 4:2-6</reference> ; <reference osisRef="isa 10:33 isa 10:34"> 10:33,34</reference>; <reference osisRef="isa 11:1-10"> 11:1-10</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 19:19-21">Revelation 19:19-21</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 20:4-6"> 20:4-6</reference>. This is set forth symbolically by the crowning of Joshua, which was not a vision, but actually done (cf) ; <reference osisRef="isa 8:3 isa 8:4">Isaiah 8:3,4</reference>; <reference osisRef="eze 37:16-22">Ezekiel 37:16-22</reference>. The fulfilment in the BRANCH will infinitely transcend the symbol. He "shall bear the glory" ; <reference osisRef="zec 6:13">Zechariah 6:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="mt 16:27">Matthew 16:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="mt 24:30"> 24:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="mt 25:31"> 25:31</reference> as the Priest-King on His own throne (<reference osisRef="zec 6:12 zec 6:13">Zechariah 6:12,13</reference>; <reference osisRef="heb 7:1-3">Hebrews 7:1-3</reference>). Christ is now a Priest, but still in the holiest within the veil ; <reference osisRef="le 16:15">Leviticus 16:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="heb 9:11-14 heb 9:24">Hebrews 9:11-14,24</reference> and seated on the Father's throne <reference osisRef="re 3:21">Revelation 3:21</reference>. He has not yet come out to take His own throne <reference osisRef="heb 9:28">Hebrews 9:28</reference>. The crowns made for the symbolical crowning of Joshua were to be laid up in the temple as a memorial to keep alive this larger hope of Israel.

<hi type="bold">BRANCH</hi><div eID="gen3000" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3001" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Isa 4:2">Isaiah 4:2</reference>")</hi> <chapter eID="Zech.6"/> <div eID="gen3001" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen3002" type="x-p"/><chapter n="7" osisID="Zech.7" sID="Zech.7"/>
Marg<div eID="gen3002" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3003" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ninth month, Chisleu</hi> i.e. December.

<hi type="bold">they</hi><div eID="gen3003" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3004" type="x-p"/> "They," i.e. of the captivity in Babylon. The mission of these Jews of the captivity concerned a fast day instituted by the Jews in commemoration of the destruction of Jerusalem, wholly of their own will, and without warrant from the word of God. In the beginning there was doubtless sincere contrition in the observance of the day; now it had become a mere ceremonial. The Jews of the dispersion would be rid of it, but seek authority from the priests. The whole matter, like much in modern pseudo-Christianity, was extra-Biblical, formal, and futile. Jehovah takes the occasion to send a divine message to the dispersion. That message is in five parts:<div eID="gen3004" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(1) Their fast was a mere religious form; they should rather have given heed to the "former prophets" (vs. 4-7; Cf. <reference osisRef="isa 1:12">Isaiah 1:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="mt 15:1-10">Matthew 15:1-10</reference></item> <item type="x-indent-1">(2) they are told why their 70 years' prayer has not been answered (<reference osisRef="zec 7:8-14">Zechariah 7:8-14</reference>); cf. ; <reference osisRef="ps 66:18">Psalms 66:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="isa 1:14-17">Isaiah 1:14-17</reference></item> <item type="x-indent-1">(3) the unchanged purpose of Jehovah, and the blessing of Israel in the kingdom <reference osisRef="zec 8:1-8">Zechariah 8:1-8</reference> cf. a like order in ; <reference osisRef="isa 1:24-31">Isaiah 1:24-31</reference>; <reference osisRef="isa 2:1-4"> 2:1-4</reference></item> <item type="x-indent-1">(4) the messengers of the captivity are exhorted to hear the prophets of "these days," i.e, Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi, and to do justly; then all their fasts and feasts will become gladness and joy <reference osisRef="zec 8:9-19">Zechariah 8:9-19</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(5) they are assured that Jerusalem is yet to be the religious centre of the earth <reference osisRef="zec 8:20-23">Zechariah 8:20-23</reference>; <reference osisRef="isa 2:1-3">Isaiah 2:1-3</reference>; <reference osisRef="zec 14:16-21">Zechariah 14:16-21</reference>. </item> </list>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv88"/><div sID="gen3005" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv88"/> <hi type="bold">fifth month</hi> <div eID="gen3005" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3006" type="x-p"/> i.e. August. <chapter eID="Zech.7"/><div eID="gen3006" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen3007" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="8" osisID="Zech.8" sID="Zech.8"/>

<hi type="bold">holy mountain</hi> <div eID="gen3007" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3008" type="x-p"/> Holiness, Sanctification, Summary: In the O.T. the words consecration, dedication, sanctification, and holiness are various renderings of one Hebrew word, are used of persons and of things, and have an identical meaning, i.e. set apart for God. Only when used of God himself (e.g. <reference osisRef="le 11:45">Leviticus 11:45</reference>), or of the holy angels (e.g. <reference osisRef="da 4:13">Daniel 4:13</reference>) is any inward ; <reference osisRef="le 11:45">Leviticus 11:45</reference>; <reference osisRef="da 4:13">Daniel 4:13</reference> moral quality necessarily implied. Doubtless a priest or other person set apart to the service of God, whose whole will and desire went with his setting apart, experienced progressively an inner detachment from evil; but that aspect is distinctively of the N.T., not of the O.T. <reference osisRef="mt 4:5">Matthew 4:5</reference>.

<hi type="bold">these days</hi><div eID="gen3008" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3009" type="x-p"/> The "remnant" in <reference osisRef="zec 8:6 zec 8:11 zec 8:12">Zechariah 8:6,11,12</reference> refers to the remnant of Judah which returned from Babylon, and among whom Zechariah was prophesying. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ro 11:5">Romans 11:5</reference>")</hi>.<div eID="gen3009" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3010" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">remnant</hi> <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Jer 15:21">Jeremiah 15:21</reference>")</hi>
<hi type="bold">residue</hi> <div eID="gen3010" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3011" type="x-p"/> Or, remnant.

<hi type="bold">repented</hi><div eID="gen3011" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3012" type="x-p"/> Repentance (O.T.), Summary: In the O.T., repentance is the English word used to translate the Heb. nacham, to be "eased" or "comforted." It is used of both God and man. Notwithstanding the literal meaning of nacham, it is evident, from a study of all the passages, that the sacred writers use it in the sense of metanoia in the N.T.--a change of mind. <reference osisRef="mt 3:2">Matthew 3:2</reference> <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ac 17:30">Acts 17:30</reference>")</hi>. As in the N.T., such change of mind is often accompanied by contrition and self-judgment. When applied to God the word is used phenomenally according to O.T. custom. God seems to change His mind. The phenomena are such as, in the case of man, would indicate a change of mind.

<hi type="bold">fourth month</hi> i.e. July.<div eID="gen3012" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3013" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fifth month</hi> i.e. August.<div eID="gen3013" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3014" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">seventh month</hi> i.e. October.<div eID="gen3014" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3015" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">tenth month</hi> i.e. January.
