<hi type="bold">those days</hi><div eID="gen3015" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3016" type="x-p"/> i.e. in the days when Jerusalem has been made the centre of the earth's worship. <reference osisRef="zec 8:23">Zechariah 8:23</reference> explains: the Jew (see "Remnant," ; <reference osisRef="isa 1:9">Isaiah 1:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="ro 11:5">Romans 11:5</reference> will then be the missionary, and to the very "nations" now called "Christian"!<div eID="gen3016" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3017" type="x-p"/> For Another Point of View: See Topic 301242 <div eID="gen3017" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv89"/><div sID="gen3018" type="x-p"/> <chapter eID="Zech.8"/>
<div eID="gen3018" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3019" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="9" osisID="Zech.9" sID="Zech.9"/>

<hi type="bold">burden</hi> <div eID="gen3019" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3020" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Isa 13:1">Isaiah 13:1</reference>")</hi> , note 1.

<hi type="bold">because of him</hi><div eID="gen3020" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3021" type="x-p"/> There seems to be a reference here to the advance and return of Alexander (<reference osisRef="zec 9:13">Zechariah 9:13</reference>) after the battle of Issus, who subdued the cities mentioned in <reference osisRef="zec 9:1-6">Zechariah 9:1-6,</reference> and afterward returned to Greece without harming Jerusalem. But the greater meaning converges on the yet future last days <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ac 2:17">Acts 2:17</reference>")</hi> as the last clause of verse <reference osisRef="zec 9:8">Zechariah 9:8</reference> shows, for many oppressors have passed through Jerusalem since the days of Alexander.

<hi type="bold">behold, thy King</hi><div eID="gen3021" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3022" type="x-p"/> The events following this manifestation of Christ as King are recorded in the Gospels. The real faith of the multitude who cried, "Hosanna" is given in <reference osisRef="mt 21:11">Matthew 21:11</reference> and so little was Jesus deceived by His apparent reception as King, that He wept over Jerusalem and announced its impending destruction (fulfilled A.D. 70; <reference osisRef="lu 19:38-44">Luke 19:38-44</reference>. The same multitude soon cried, "Crucify Him."

<hi type="bold">And I will cut off</hi><div eID="gen3022" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3023" type="x-p"/> Having introduced the King in <reference osisRef="zec 9:9">Zechariah 9:9,</reference>; <reference osisRef="zec 9:10">Zechariah 9:10</reference> and the verses which follow look forward to the end-time and kingdom. Except in verse 9, this present age is not seen in Zechariah.

Marg<div eID="gen3023" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3024" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">prisoners</hi> Cf. <reference osisRef="isa 24:17-23">Isaiah 24:17-23</reference>; <reference osisRef="zec 9:21 zec 9:23">Zechariah 9:21,23</reference> fix the time as the day of the LORD. <reference osisRef="re 19:11-21">Revelation 19:11-21</reference>.

Marg<div eID="gen3024" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3025" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">strong hold</hi> See context, <reference osisRef="zec 9:14">Zechariah 9:14</reference>. Also, <reference osisRef="jer 16:19">Jeremiah 16:19</reference>. <div eID="gen3025" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv89"/><div sID="gen3026" type="x-p"/> <chapter eID="Zech.9"/>
<div eID="gen3026" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3027" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="10" osisID="Zech.10" sID="Zech.10"/>

<hi type="bold">later rain</hi> <div eID="gen3027" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3028" type="x-p"/> Cf. <reference osisRef="ho 6:3">Hosea 6:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="joe 2:23-32">Joel 2:23-32</reference>; <reference osisRef="zec 12:10">Zechariah 12:10</reference>. There is both a physical and spiritual meaning: Rain as of old will be restored to Palestine, but, also, there will be a mighty effusion of the Spirit upon restored Israel.

<hi type="bold">came</hi><div eID="gen3028" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3029" type="x-p"/> The tense is future: "From him Judah shall be the cornerstone <reference osisRef="ex 17:6">Exodus 17:6</reference>. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:1Pe 2:8">1 Peter 2:8</reference>")</hi> from him the nail <reference osisRef="isa 22:23 isa 22:24">Isaiah 22:23,24</reference> from him the battle-bow," etc. The whole scene is of the events which group about the deliverance of the Jews in Palestine in the time of the northern invasion under the "Beast" ; <reference osisRef="da 7:8">Daniel 7:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 19:20">Revelation 19:20</reference> and "Armageddon," ; <reference osisRef="re 16:14">Revelation 16:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 19:17"> 19:17</reference>.<div eID="gen3029" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3030" type="x-p"/> The final deliverance is wholly effected by the return of the Lord <reference osisRef="re 19:11-21">Revelation 19:11-21,</reference> but previously He strengthens the hard-pressed Israelites ; <reference osisRef="mic 4:13">Micah 4:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="zec 9:13-15">Zechariah 9:13-15</reference>; <reference osisRef="zec 10:5-7"> 10:5-7</reference> ; <reference osisRef="zec 12:2-6"> 12:2-6</reference>; <reference osisRef="zec 14:14"> 14:14</reference>.<div eID="gen3030" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3031" type="x-p"/> That there may have been a precursive fulfilment in the Maccabean victories can neither be affirmed nor denied from Scripture.

<hi type="bold">redeemed</hi><div eID="gen3031" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3032" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="isa 59:20">Isaiah 59:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="ex 14:30">Exodus 14:30</reference>. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Isa 59:20">Isaiah 59:20</reference>")</hi>. See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:ex 14:30">Exodus 14:30</reference>" <chapter eID="Zech.10"/><div eID="gen3032" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen3033" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="11" osisID="Zech.11" sID="Zech.11"/>

<hi type="bold">two staves</hi> <div eID="gen3033" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3034" type="x-p"/> The scene belongs to the first advent. Beauty and Bands--literally "graciousness and union"; the first signifying God's attitude toward His people Israel, in sending His Son <reference osisRef="mt 21:37">Matthew 21:37</reference> the second, His purpose to reunite Judah and Ephraim <reference osisRef="eze 37:15-22">Ezekiel 37:15-22</reference>. Christ, at His first advent, came with grace <reference osisRef="joh 1:17">John 1:17</reference> to offer union <reference osisRef="mt 4:17">Matthew 4:17</reference> and was sold for thirty pieces of silver <reference osisRef="zec 11:12 zec 11:13">Zechariah 11:12,13</reference>. "Beauty" (i.e. graciousness) was "cut in sunder" (<reference osisRef="zec 8:10 zec 8:11">Zechariah 8:10,11</reference>), signifying that Judah was abandoned to the destruction foretold in <reference osisRef="zec 11:1-6">Zechariah 11:1-6</reference> and fulfilled A.D. 70. After the betrayal of the Lord for thirty pieces of silver (<reference osisRef="zec 11:12 zec 11:13">Zechariah 11:12,13</reference>) "Bands" (i.e. union) was broken (<reference osisRef="zec 11:14">Zechariah 11:14</reference>), signifying the abandonment, for the time, of the purpose to reunite Judah and Israel. The order of Zech. 11. is,<div eID="gen3034" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(1) the wrath against the land (<reference osisRef="zec 11:1-6">Zechariah 11:1-6</reference>), fulfilled in the destruction of Jerusalem after the rejection of Christ <reference osisRef="lu 19:41-44">Luke 19:41-44</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(2) the cause of that wrath in the sale and rejection of Christ vs. (<reference osisRef="zec 11:7-14">Zechariah 11:7-14</reference>);</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(3) the rise of the "idol shepherd," the Beast <reference osisRef="da 7:8">Daniel 7:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 19:20">Revelation 19:20</reference> and his destruction (<reference osisRef="zec 11:15-17">Zechariah 11:15-17</reference>).</item> </list> <div sID="gen3035" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">the one</hi> <div eID="gen3035" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3036" type="x-p"/> The O.T. Parables: Summary. A parable is a similitude used to teach or enforce a truth. The O.T. parables fall into three classes:<div eID="gen3036" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(1) The story-parable, of which <reference osisRef="jud 9:7-15">Judges 9:7-15</reference> is an instance;</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(2) parabolic discourses; e.g. <reference osisRef="isa 5:1-7">Isaiah 5:1-7</reference></item> <item type="x-indent-1">(3) parabolic actions; e.g. <reference osisRef="eze 37:16-22">Ezekiel 37:16-22</reference> </item> </list>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv89"/><div sID="gen3037" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv89"/> <hi type="bold">poor</hi> <div eID="gen3037" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3038" type="x-p"/> The "poor of the flock": i.e. the "remnant according to the election of grace" <reference osisRef="ro 11:5">Romans 11:5</reference> those Jews who did not wait for the manifestation of Christ in glory, but believed on Him at His first coming, and since. Of them it is said that they "waited upon Me," and "knew." Neither the Gentiles nor the Gentile church, corporately, are in view: only the believers out of Israel during this age. The church, corporately, is not in O.T. prophecy <reference osisRef="eph 3:8-10">Ephesians 3:8-10</reference>.

<hi type="bold">And the Lord</hi><div eID="gen3038" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3039" type="x-p"/> The reference to the Beast is obvious; no other personage of prophecy in any sense meets the description. He who came in His Father's name was rejected: the alternative is one who comes in his own name <reference osisRef="joh 5:43">John 5:43</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 13:4-8">Revelation 13:4-8</reference>. <div eID="gen3039" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv90"/><div sID="gen3040" type="x-p"/> <chapter eID="Zech.11"/>
<div eID="gen3040" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3041" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="12" osisID="Zech.12" sID="Zech.12"/>

<hi type="bold">burden</hi> <div eID="gen3041" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3042" type="x-p"/> Zech. 12.-14. from one prophecy the general theme of which is the return of the Lord and the establishment of the kingdom. The order is:<div eID="gen3042" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(1) The siege of Jerusalem preceding the battle of Armageddon (<reference osisRef="zec 12:1-3">Zechariah 12:1-3</reference>);</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(2) the battle itself (<reference osisRef="zec 12:4-9">Zechariah 12:4-9</reference>);</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(3) the "latter rain" in the pouring out of the Spirit and the personal revelation of Christ to the family of David and the remnant in Jerusalem, not merely as the glorious Deliverer, but as the One whom Israel pierced and has long rejected (<reference osisRef="zec 12:10">Zechariah 12:10</reference>);</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(4) the godly sorrow which follows that revelation (<reference osisRef="zec 12:11-14">Zechariah 12:11-14</reference>);</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(5) the cleansing fountain <reference osisRef="zec 13:1">Zechariah 13:1</reference> then to be effectually "opened" to Israel. </item> </list>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv91"/><div sID="gen3051" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv91"/> <hi type="bold">and the mount of Olives</hi> <div eID="gen3051" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3052" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="zec 14:5">Zechariah 14:5</reference> implies that the cleavage of the Mount of Olives is due to an earthquake, and this is confirmed by ; <reference osisRef="isa 29:6">Isaiah 29:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 16:19">Revelation 16:19</reference>. In both passages the context, as in <reference osisRef="zec 14:1-3">Zechariah 14:1-3</reference> associates the earthquake with the Gentile invasion under the Beast ; <reference osisRef="da 7:8">Daniel 7:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 19:20">Revelation 19:20</reference>. Surely, in a land seamed by seismic disturbances it should not be difficult to believe that another earthquake might cleave the little hill called the Mount of Olives. Not one of the associated events of Zech. 14 occurred at the first coming of Christ, closely associated though He then was with the Mount of Olives.

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv90"/><div sID="gen3043" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv90"/><hi type="bold">David</hi> Kingdom in O.T., Summary:<div eID="gen3043" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3044" type="x-p"/> I. Dominion over the earth before the call of Abraham<div eID="gen3044" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(1) Dominion over creation was given to the first man and woman <reference osisRef="ge 1:26 ge 1:28">Genesis 1:26,28</reference>. Through the fall this dominion was lost, Satan becoming "prince of this world" ; <reference osisRef="mt 4:8-10">Matthew 4:8-10</reference>; <reference osisRef="joh 14:30">John 14:30</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(2) After the flood, the principle of human government was established under the covenant with Noah <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ge 9:1">Genesis 9:1</reference>")</hi>. Biblically this is still the charter of all Gentile government.</item> </list> <div sID="gen3045" type="x-p"/> II. The Theocracy in Israel. The call of Abraham involved, with much else, the creation of a distinctive people through whom great purposes of God toward the race might be worked out (see "Israel" <reference osisRef="ge 12:1-3">Genesis 12:1-3</reference>; <reference osisRef="ro 11:26">Romans 11:26</reference>).<div eID="gen3045" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3046" type="x-p"/> Among these purposes is the establishment of a universal kingdom. The order of the development of Divine rule in Israel is:<div eID="gen3046" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(1) The mediatorship of Moses <reference osisRef="ex 3:1-10">Exodus 3:1-10</reference>; <reference osisRef="ex 19:9"> 19:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="ex 24:12"> 24:12</reference></item> <item type="x-indent-1">(2) The leadership of Joshua <reference osisRef="jos 1:1-5">Joshua 1:1-5</reference></item> <item type="x-indent-1">(3) The institution of Judges <reference osisRef="jud 2:16-18">Judges 2:16-18</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(4) The popular rejection of the Theocracy, and choice of a king-- Saul, <reference osisRef="1sa 8:1-7">1 Samuel 8:1-7</reference>; <reference osisRef="1sa 9:12-17"> 9:12-17</reference>.</item> </list> <div sID="gen3047" type="x-p"/> III. The Davidic kingdom<div eID="gen3047" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(1) The divine choice of David <reference osisRef="1sa 16:1-13">1 Samuel 16:1-13</reference></item> <item type="x-indent-1">(2) The giving of the Davidic Covenant <reference osisRef="2sa 7:8-16">2 Samuel 7:8-16</reference>; <reference osisRef="ps 89:3-4 ps 89:20-21 ps 89:28-37">Psalms 89:3,4,20,21,28-37</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(3) The exposition of the David Covenant by the prophets <reference osisRef="isa 1:25 isa 1:26">Isaiah 1:25,26</reference>; <reference osisRef="zec 12:6-8">Zechariah 12:6-8</reference>.</item> </list> <div sID="gen3048" type="x-p"/> See marg. "Kingdom" and refs. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Isa 1:25">Isaiah 1:25</reference>")</hi> The kingdom as described by the prophets is:<div eID="gen3048" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-2">(a) Davidic, to be established under an heir of David, who is to be born of a virgin, therefore truly man, but also "Immanuel," "the mighty God, the everlasting Father, the Prince of Peace" <reference osisRef="isa 7:13 isa 7:14">Isaiah 7:13,14</reference>; <reference osisRef="isa 9:6 isa 9:7"> 9:6,7</reference> ; <reference osisRef="isa 11:1"> 11:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="jer 23:5">Jeremiah 23:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="eze 34:23">Ezekiel 34:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="eze 37:24"> 37:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="ho 3:4 ho 3:5">Hosea 3:4,5</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-2">(b) A kingdom heavenly in origin, principle, and authority <reference osisRef="da 2:34 da 2:35 da 2:44 da 2:45">Daniel 2:34,35,44,45</reference> but set up on the earth, with Jerusalem as the capital ; <reference osisRef="isa 2:2-4">Isaiah 2:2-4</reference>; <reference osisRef="isa 4:3 isa 4:5"> 4:3,5</reference> ; <reference osisRef="isa 24:23"> 24:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="isa 33:20"> 33:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="isa 62:1-7"> 62:1-7</reference>; <reference osisRef="jer 23:5">Jeremiah 23:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="jer 31:38-40"> 31:38-40</reference>; <reference osisRef="joe 3:1 joe 3:16 joe 3:17">Joel 3:1,16,17</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-2">(c) The kingdom is to be established first over regathered, restored, and converted Israel, and then to become universal <reference osisRef="ps 2:6-8">Psalms 2:6-8</reference>; <reference osisRef="ps 22:1-3 ps 124:1-10"> 22:1-3 124:1-10</reference>; <reference osisRef="isa 1:2 isa 1:3">Isaiah 1:2,3</reference>; <reference osisRef="isa 11:1 isa 11:10-13 isa 60:12"> 11:1,10-13 60:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="jer 23:5-8">Jeremiah 23:5-8</reference>; <reference osisRef="jer 30:7-11">Jeremiah 30:7-11</reference>; <reference osisRef="eze 20:33-40">Ezekiel 20:33-40</reference>; <reference osisRef="eze 37:21-25"> 37:21-25</reference>; <reference osisRef="zec 9:10">Zechariah 9:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="zec 14:16-19"> 14:16-19</reference></item> <item type="x-indent-2">(d) The moral characteristics of the kingdom are to be righteousness and peace. The meek, not the proud, will inherit the earth; longevity will be greatly increased; the knowledge of the Lord will be universal; beast ferocity will be removed; absolute equity will be enforced; and outbreaking sin visited with instant judgment; while the enormous majority of earth's inhabitants will be saved <reference osisRef="isa 11:4 isa 11:6-9">Isaiah 11:4,6-9</reference>; <reference osisRef="isa 65:20"> 65:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="ps 2:9">Psalms 2:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="isa 26:9">Isaiah 26:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="zec 14:16-21">Zechariah 14:16-21</reference>. The N.T. <reference osisRef="re 20:1-5">Revelation 20:1-5,</reference> adds a detail of immense significance--the removal of Satan from the scene. It is impossible to conceive to what heights of spiritual, intellectual, and physical perfection humanity will attain in this, its coming age of righteousness and peace. ; <reference osisRef="isa 11:4-9">Isaiah 11:4-9</reference>; <reference osisRef="ps 72:1-10">Psalms 72:1-10</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-2">(e) The kingdom is to be established by power, not persuasion, and is to follow divine judgment upon the Gentile world-powers <reference osisRef="ps 2:4-9">Psalms 2:4-9</reference>; <reference osisRef="isa 9:7">Isaiah 9:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="da 2:35 da 2:44 da 2:45">Daniel 2:35,44,45</reference>; <reference osisRef="da 7:26 da 7:27"> 7:26,27</reference>; <reference osisRef="zec 14:1-19">Zechariah 14:1-19</reference> <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Zec 6:11">Zechariah 6:11</reference>")</hi>.</item> <item type="x-indent-2">(f) The restoration of Israel and the establishment of the kingdom are connected with an advent of the Lord, yet future <reference osisRef="de 30:3-5">Deuteronomy 30:3-5</reference>; <reference osisRef="ps 2:1-9">Psalms 2:1-9</reference>; <reference osisRef="zec 14:4">Zechariah 14:4</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-2">(g) The chastisement reserved for disobedience in the house of David <reference osisRef="2sa 7:14">2 Samuel 7:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="ps 89:30-33">Psalms 89:30-33</reference> fell in the captivities and world-wide dispersion, since which time, though a remnant returned under prince Zerubbabel, Jerusalem has been under the overlordship of Gentile. But the Davidic Covenant has not been abrogated <reference osisRef="ps 89:33-37">Psalms 89:33-37</reference> but is yet to be fulfilled. <reference osisRef="ac 15:14-17">Acts 15:14-17</reference>.</item> </list> <div sID="gen3049" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">angel</hi> <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Heb 1:4">Hebrews 1:4</reference>")</hi> <hi type="bold">And it shall come to pass</hi> <div eID="gen3049" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3050" type="x-p"/> Zech. 13 now returns to the subject of <reference osisRef="zec 12:10">Zechariah 12:10</reference>. <reference osisRef="zec 13:8 zec 13:9">Zechariah 13:8,9</reference> refer to the sufferings of the remnant ; <reference osisRef="isa 1:9">Isaiah 1:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="ro 11:5">Romans 11:5</reference> preceding the great battle. Zech. 14. is a recapitulation of the whole matter. The order is:<div eID="gen3050" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(1) The gathering of the nation, <reference osisRef="zec 13:2">Zechariah 13:2</reference> (see "Armageddon," <reference osisRef="re 16:14">Revelation 16:14</reference> <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Re 19:11">Revelation 19:11</reference>")</hi></item> <item type="x-indent-1">(2) the deliverance, <reference osisRef="zec 13:3">Zechariah 13:3</reference>;</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(3) the return of Christ to the Mount of Olives, and the physical change of the scene, <reference osisRef="zec 13:4-8">Zechariah 13:4-8</reference>;</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(4) the setting up of the kingdom, and full earthly blessing, <reference osisRef="zec 13:9-21">Zechariah 13:9-21</reference>. </item> </list>

<hi type="bold">king over all the earth</hi><div eID="gen3052" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3053" type="x-p"/> The final answer to the prayer of <reference osisRef="mt 6:10">Matthew 6:10</reference>. CF. ; <reference osisRef="da 2:44 da 2:45">Daniel 2:44,45,</reference>; <reference osisRef="da 7:24-27"> 7:24-27</reference>. See "Kingdom (N.T.)" ; <reference osisRef="lu 1:31-33">Luke 1:31-33</reference>; <reference osisRef="1co 15:28">1 Corinthians 15:28</reference>. <chapter eID="Zech.12"/><div eID="gen3053" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen2947" osisID="Zech" type="book"/>
<div canonical="true" osisID="Mal" sID="gen3054" type="book"/> <milestone n="" type="x-usfm-toc1"/> <milestone n="" type="x-usfm-toc2"/> <milestone n="" type="x-usfm-toc3"/>
<chapter n="1" osisID="Mal.1" sID="Mal.1"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv92"/><title type="x-s">Book Introduction - Malachi</title> <div sID="gen3055" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="mal 1">Read first chapter of Malachi</reference><div eID="gen3055" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3056" type="x-p"/> MALACHI "my messenger," the last of the prophets to the restored remnant after the 70 years' captivity, probably prophesied in the time of confusion during Nehemiah's absence (<reference osisRef="ne 13:6">Nehemiah 13:6</reference>). The burden of his message is, the love of Jehovah, the sins of the priests and of the people, and the day of the Lord. Malachi, like Zechariah, sees both advents and predicts two forerunners (<reference osisRef="mal 3:1">Malachi 3:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="mal 4:5-6"> 4:5-6</reference>). As a whole, Malachi gives the moral judgement of God on the remnant restored by his grace under Ezra and Nehemiah. He had established his house among them, but their worship was formal and insincere.<div eID="gen3056" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3057" type="x-p"/> The book is in four natural divisions:<div eID="gen3057" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">The love of God for Israel, 1:1-5</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The sins of the priests rebuked1:6-2:9</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The sins of the people rebuked2:10-3:18</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The day of the Lord4:1-6</item> </list> <div sID="gen3058" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv92"/> <hi type="bold">Edom</hi> <div eID="gen3058" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3059" type="x-p"/> i.e. Esau's descendants. See <reference osisRef="ge 25:30">Genesis 25:30</reference>.

<hi type="bold">if then I be a father</hi><div eID="gen3059" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3060" type="x-p"/> Cf. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Isa 63:16">Isaiah 63:16</reference>")</hi>. The relationship here is national, not personal <reference osisRef="jer 3:18 jer 3:19">Jeremiah 3:18,19</reference> here, apparently, the Jews were calling Jehovah, "Father," but yielding Him no filial obedience. See ; <reference osisRef="joh 8:37-39">John 8:37-39</reference>; <reference osisRef="ro 9:1-8">Romans 9:1-8</reference>.

<hi type="bold">Who is there</hi><div eID="gen3060" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3061" type="x-p"/> Or, I would that one among you would shut the doors of the temple that no more vain fire should kindle on mine altar. Cf. <reference osisRef="isa 1:11-15">Isaiah 1:11-15</reference>.

<hi type="bold">For from the raising</hi> i.e. So it would have been had Israel been true. <reference osisRef="isa 45:5 isa 45:6">Isaiah 45:5,6</reference>. So it shall be despite Israel's failure. <chapter eID="Mal.1"/><div eID="gen3061" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen3062" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="2" osisID="Mal.2" sID="Mal.2"/>

<hi type="bold">curse</hi> <div eID="gen3062" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3063" type="x-p"/> Cf. <reference osisRef="de 28:3-14">Deuteronomy 28:3-14</reference> and <reference osisRef="de 28:15-35">Deuteronomy 28:15-35</reference>. Israel's distinctive blessings should turn to curses.

<hi type="bold">Have we not all one</hi><div eID="gen3063" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3064" type="x-p"/> Cf. <reference osisRef="ac 17:24-29">Acts 17:24-29</reference>. In both instances the reference is to creation, not the new birth.

<hi type="bold">spirit</hi><div eID="gen3064" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3065" type="x-p"/> Summary of the O.T. doctrine of the Holy Spirit:<div eID="gen3065" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(1) The personality and Deity of the Holy Spirit appear from the attributes ascribed to Him, and from His works.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(2) He is revealed as sharing the work of creation and therefore omnipotent <reference osisRef="ge 1:2">Genesis 1:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="job 26:13">Job 26:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="job 33:4"> 33:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="ps 104:30">Psalms 104:30</reference> as omnipresent <reference osisRef="ps 139:7">Psalms 139:7</reference> as striving with men <reference osisRef="ge 6:3">Genesis 6:3</reference> as enlightening <reference osisRef="job 32:8">Job 32:8</reference> enduing with constructive skill ; <reference osisRef="ex 28:3">Exodus 28:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="ex 31:3"> 31:3</reference> giving physical strength <reference osisRef="jud 14:6 jud 14:19">Judges 14:6,19</reference> executive ability and wisdom ; <reference osisRef="jud 3:10">Judges 3:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="jud 6:34"> 6:34</reference>; <reference osisRef="jud 11:29"> 11:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="jud 13:25"> 13:25</reference> enabling men to receive and utter divine revelations ; <reference osisRef="nu 11:25">Numbers 11:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="2sa 23:2">2 Samuel 23:2</reference> and, generally, as empowering the servants of God ; <reference osisRef="ps 51:12">Psalms 51:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="joe 2:28">Joel 2:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="mic 3:8">Micah 3:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="zec 4:6">Zechariah 4:6</reference></item> <item type="x-indent-1">(3) He is called holy <reference osisRef="ps 51:11">Psalms 51:11</reference> good <reference osisRef="ps 143:10">Psalms 143:10</reference> the Spirit of judgment and burning <reference osisRef="isa 4:4">Isaiah 4:4</reference> of Jehovah, of wisdom, understanding, counsel, might, good, knowledge, the fear of the Lord <reference osisRef="isa 11:2">Isaiah 11:2</reference> and of grace and supplications <reference osisRef="zec 12:10">Zechariah 12:10</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(4) In the O.T. the Spirit acts in free sovereignty, coming upon men and even upon a dumb beast as He will, nor are the conditions set forth (as in the N.T.) by complying with which any one may receive the Spirit. The indwelling of every believer by the abiding Spirit is a N.T. blessing consequent upon the death and resurrection of Christ <reference osisRef="joh 7:39">John 7:39</reference>; <reference osisRef="joh 16:7"> 16:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="ac 2:33">Acts 2:33</reference>; <reference osisRef="ga 3:1-6">Galatians 3:1-6</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(5) The O.T. contains prediction of a future pouring out of the Spirit upon Israel <reference osisRef="ex 37:14">Exodus 37:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="ex 39:29"> 39:29</reference> and upon "all flesh" <reference osisRef="joe 2:28 joe 2:29">Joel 2:28,29</reference>. The expectation of Israel, therefore, was twofold--of the coming of Messiah-Immanuel, and of such an effusion of the Spirit as the prophets described. See <reference osisRef="mt 1:18">Matthew 1:18</reference>. </item> </list> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv93"/><div sID="gen3066" type="x-p"/> <chapter eID="Mal.2"/>
<div eID="gen3066" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3067" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="3" osisID="Mal.3" sID="Mal.3"/>

<hi type="bold">Lord</hi> <div eID="gen3067" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3068" type="x-p"/> The f.c. of <reference osisRef="mal 3:1">Malachi 3:1</reference> is quoted of John the Baptist ; <reference osisRef="mt 11:10">Matthew 11:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="mr 1:2">Mark 1:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="lu 7:27">Luke 7:27</reference> but the second clause, "the Lord whom ye see," etc., is nowhere quoted in the N.T. The reason is obvious: in everything save the fact of Christ's first advent, the latter clause awaits fulfilment <reference osisRef="hab 2:20">Habakkuk 2:20</reference>. <reference osisRef="mal 3:2-5">Malachi 3:2-5</reference> speak of judgment, not of grace. Malachi, in common with other O.T. prophets, saw both advents of Messiah blended in one horizon, but did not see the separating interval described in Mt. 13. consequent upon the rejection of the King <reference osisRef="mt 13:16 mt 13:17">Matthew 13:16,17</reference>. Still less was the Church-age in his vision ; <reference osisRef="eph 3:3-6">Ephesians 3:3-6</reference>; <reference osisRef="col 1:25-27">Colossians 1:25-27</reference>. "My messenger" <reference osisRef="mal 3:1">Malachi 3:1</reference> is John the Baptist; the "messenger of the covenant" is Christ in both of His advents, but with especial reference to the events which are to follow His return.

<hi type="bold">they</hi> remnant, <reference osisRef="ro 9:25-29">Romans 9:25-29,</reference> <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Jer 15:21">Jeremiah 15:21</reference>")</hi><div eID="gen3068" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3069" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">feared</hi><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ps 19:9">Psalms 19:9</reference>")</hi>.

God
Summary of the O.T. revelation of Deity: God is revealed in the O.T. (1) through His names, as follows:
Class English Form Hebrew Equivalent Primary God El, Elah, or Elohim (Genesis 1:1) LORD Jehovah (Genesis 2:4) Lord Adon or Adonai (Genesis 15:2) Compound (with El = God) Almighty God El Shaddai (Genesis 17:1) Most High, or most high God El Elyon (Genesis 14:18) everlasting God El Olam (Genesis 21:33) Compound (with Jehovah = Lord) LORD God Jehovah Elohim (Genesis 2:4) Lord GOD Adonai Jehovah (Genesis 15:2) LORD of hosts Jehovah Sabaoth (1 Samuel 1:3)
The trinity is suggested by the three times repeated groups of threes. This is not an arbitrary arrangement, but inheres in the O.T. itself.
This revelation of God by His name is invariably made in connection with some particular need of His people, and there can be no need of man to which these names do not answer as showing that man's true resource is in God. Even human failure and sin but evoke new and fuller revelations of the divine fulness.
(2) The O.T. Scriptures reveal the existence of a Supreme Being, the Creator of the universe and of man, the Source of all life and of all intelligence, who is to be worshipped and served by men and angels. This Supreme Being is One, but, in some sense not fully revealed in the O.T., is a unity in plurality. This is shown by the plural name, Elohim, by the use of the plural pronoun in the interrelation of deity as evidenced in Genesis 1:26; 3:22; Psalms 110:1; Isaiah 6:8. That this plurality is really a Trinity is intimated in the three primary names of Deity, and in the threefold ascription of the Seraphim in Isaiah 6:3 That the interrelation of Deity is that of Father and Son is directly asserted ; Psalms 2:7; Hebrews 1:5 and the Spirit is distinctly recognized in His personality, and to Him are ascribed all the divine attributes (e.g. ; Genesis 1:2; Numbers 11:25; 24:2; Judges 3:10; 6:34; 11:29; 13:25; 14:6,19; Judges 15:14; 2 Samuel 23:2; Job 26:13; 33:4; Psalms 106:33; 139:7; Isaiah 40:7; Isaiah 59:19; 63:10. (See Scofield "Malachi 2:15"). (3) The future incarnation is intimated in the theophanies, or appearances of God in human form (e.g. Genesis 18:1,13,17-22; 32:24-30 and distinctly predicted in the promises connected with redemption (e.g. Genesis 3:15 and with the Davidic Covenant Isa 7:13-14, 9:6-7; Jeremiah 23:5,6.
The revelation of Deity in the N.T. so illuminates that of the O.T. that the latter is seen to be, from Genesis to Malachi, the foreshadowing of the coming incarnation of God in Jesus the Christ. In promise, covenant, type, and prophecy the O.T. points forward to Him.
(4) The revelation of God to man is one of authority and redemption. He requires righteousness from man, but saves the unrighteous through sacrifice; and in His redemptive dealings with man all the divine persons and attributes are brought into manifestation. The O.T. reveals the justice of God equally with His mercy, but never in opposition to His mercy. The flood, e.g., was an unspeakable mercy to unborn generations. From Genesis to Malachi He is revealed as the seeking God who has no pleasure in the death of the wicked, and who heaps up before the sinner every possible motive to persuade to faith and obedience. (5) In the experience of the O.T. men of faith their God inspires reverence but never slavish fear; and they exhaust the resources of language to express their love and adoration in view of His loving-kindness and tender mercy. This adoring love of His saints is the triumphant answer to those who pretend to find the O.T. revelation of God cruel and repellent. It is in harmony, not contrast, with the N.T. revelation of God in Christ. (6) Those passages which attribute to God bodily parts and human emotions (e.g. Exodus 33:11,20; Deuteronomy 29:20; 2 Chronicles 16:9; Genesis 6:6,7; Jeremiah 15:6) are metaphorical and mean that in the infinite being of God exists that which answers to these things--eyes, a hand, feet, etc.; and the jealousy and anger attributed to Him are the emotions of perfect Love in view of the havoc of sin. (7) In the O.T. revelation there is a true sense in which, wholly apart from sin or infirmity, God is like His creature man Genesis 1:27 and the supreme and perfect revelation of God, toward which the O.T. points, is a revelation in and through a perfect Man.

<hi type="bold">fear</hi> See note, <reference osisRef="ps 19:9">Psalms 19:9</reference> <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ps 19:9">Psalms 19:9</reference>")</hi>.<div eID="gen3075" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3076" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Sun of righteousness</hi><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ge 1:16">Genesis 1:16</reference>")</hi>.

SCOFIELD REFERENCE NOTES (Old Scofield 1917 Edition)<div eID="gen3076" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3077" type="x-p"/> From Malachi to Matthew<div eID="gen3077" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3078" type="x-p"/> The close of the Old Testament canon left Israel in two great divisions. The mass of the nation were dispersed throughout the Persian Empire, more as colonists than captives. A remnant, chiefly of the tribe of Judah, with Zerubbabel, a prince of the Davidic family, and the survivors of the priests and Levites, had returned to the land under the permissive decrees of Cyrus and his successors<div eID="gen3078" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3079" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Da 5:31">Daniel 5:31</reference>")</hi> See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:da 9:25">Daniel 9:25</reference>" and had established again the temple worship. Upon this remnant the interest of the student of Scripture centres; and this interest concerns both their political and religious history.<div eID="gen3079" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3080" type="x-p"/> I. Politically, the fortunes of the Palestinian Jews followed, with one exception--the Maccabean revolt--the history of the Gentile world-empires foretold by Daniel (Dan. 2., 7.)<div eID="gen3080" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(1) The Persian rule continued about one hundred years after the close of the O.T. canon, and seems to have been mild and tolerant, allowing the high priest, along with his religious functions, a measure of civil power, but under the overlordship of the governors of Syria. The sources of the history of the Jewish remnant during the Persian period were purely legendary when Josephus wrote. During this period the rival worship of Samaria <reference osisRef="joh 4:19 joh 4:20">John 4:19,20</reference> was established.</item> </list> <div sID="gen3081" type="x-p"/> Palestine suffered much from the constant wars between Persia and Egypt, lying as it did "between the anvil and the hammer."<div eID="gen3081" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(2) In 333 B.C. Syria fell under the power of the third of the world-empires, the Graeco-Macedonian of Alexander. That conqueror, as Josephus related, was induced to treat the Jews with much favour; but, upon the breaking up of his empire, Judaea again fell between the hammer and anvil of Syria and Egypt, falling first under the power of Syria, but later under Egypt as ruled by the Ptolemaic kings. During this period (B.C. 320-198) great numbers of Jews were established in Egypt, and the Septuagint translation of the O.T. was made (B.C. 285).</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(3) In B.C. 198 Judaea was conquered by Antiochus the Great, and annexed to Syria. At this time the division of the land into the five provinces familiar to readers of the Gospels, Galilee, Samaria, Judaea (often collectively called Judaea), Trachonitis and Peraea, was made. The Jews at first were permitted to live under their own laws under the high priest and a council. About B.C. 180 the land became the dowry of Cleopatra, a Syrian princess married to Ptolemy Philometor, king of Egypt, but on the death of Cleopatra was reclaimed by Antiochus Epiphanes (the "little horn" of <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Da 8:9">Daniel 8:9</reference>")</hi> after a bloody battle. In 170 B.C., Antiochus, after repeated interferences with the temple and priesthood, plundered Jerusalem, profaned the temple, and enslaved great numbers of the inhabitants. December 25, B.C. 168, Antiochus offered a sow upon the great altar, and erected an altar to Jupiter. This is the "desolation" of <reference osisRef="da 8:13">Daniel 8:13</reference> type of the final "abomination of desolation" of <reference osisRef="mt 24:15">Matthew 24:15</reference>. The temple worship was forbidden, and the people compelled to eat swine's flesh.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(4) The excesses of Antiochus provoked the revolt of the Maccabees, one of the most heroic pages of history. Mattathias, the first of the Maccabees, a priest of great sanctity and energy of character, began the revolt. He did little more than to gather a band of godly and determined Jews pledged to free the nation and restore the ancient worship, and was succeeded by his son Judas, known in history as Maccabaeus, from the Hebrew word for hammer. He was assisted by four brothers of whom Simon is best known.</item> </list> <div sID="gen3082" type="x-p"/> In B.C. 165 Judas regained possession of Jerusalem, purified and rededicated the temple, an event celebrated in the Jewish Feast of the Dedication. The struggle with Antiochus and his successor continued. Judas was slain in battle, his brother Jonathan succeeding. In him the civil and priestly authority were united (B.C. 143). Under Jonathan, his brother Simon, and his nephew John Hyrcanus, the Hasmonean line of priest-rulers was established, under sufferance of other powers. They possessed none of the Maccabean virtues.<div eID="gen3082" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(5) A civil war followed, which was terminated by the Roman conquest of Judaea and Jerusalem by Pompey (B.C. 63), who left Hyrcanus, the last of the Hasmoneans, a nominal sovereignty, Antipater, an Idumean, wielding the actual power. B.C. 47 Antipater was made procurator of Judaea by Julius Caesar, and appointed his son, Herod, governor of Galilee. After the murder of Caesar disorder ensued in Judaea, and Herod fled to Rome. There he was appointed (B.C. 40) king of the Jews, and returning, he conciliated the people by his marriage (B.C. 38) with Mariamne, the beautiful grand- daughter of Hyrcanus, and appointed her brother, the Maccabean Aristobulus III., high priest. Herod was king when Jesus Christ was born.</item> </list> <div sID="gen3083" type="x-p"/> II. The religious history of the Jews during the long period from Malachi (B.C. 397) to Christ followed, as to outer ceremonial, the high-priestly office, and the temple worship, the course of the troublous political history, and is of scant interest.<div eID="gen3083" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3084" type="x-p"/> Of greater moment are the efforts and means by which the real faith of Israel was kept alive and nurtured.<div eID="gen3084" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(1) The tendency to idolatry seems to have been destroyed by the Jews' experience and observation of it during the captivity. Deprived of temple and priest, and of the possibility of continuing a ceremonial worship, the Jewish people were thrown back upon that which was fundamental in their faith, the revelation of God as One, the Creator, to be conceived of as having made man in His own image, and therefore as having such analogies to the nature and life of man as to be comprehensible by man, while remaining the Eternal Spirit, God. This conception of God, enforced by the mighty ministries of the pre-exilic and exilic prophets, finally prevailed over all idolatrous conceptions, and this ministry was continued amongst the returned remnant by Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi. The high ethics of the older prophets, their stern rebuke of mere formalism, and their glowing prophecies of the ultimate restoration of Israel in national and religious supremacy under Messiah, were all repeated by the three prophets of the restoration.</item> </list> <div sID="gen3085" type="x-p"/> The problem was to keep alive this exalted ideal in the midst of outward persecutions and sordid and disgraceful divisions within.<div eID="gen3085" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(2) The organic means to this end was the synagogue, an institution which formed no part of the biblical order of the national life. Its origin is obscure. Probably, during the captivity, the Jews, deprived of the temple and its rites, met on the Sabbath day for prayer. This would give opportunity for the reading of the Scriptures. Such meetings would require some order of procedure, and some authority for the restraint of disorder. The synagogue doubtless grew out of the necessities of the situation in which the Jews were placed, but it served the purpose of maintaining familiarity with the inspired writings, and upon these the spiritual life of the true Israel <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ro 9:6">Romans 9:6</reference>")</hi> was nourished.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(3) But during this period, also, was created that mass of tradition, comment and interpretation, known as Mishna, Gemara (forming the Talmud), Halachoth, Midrashim and Kabbala, so superposed upon the Law that obedience was transferred from the Law itself to the traditional interpretation.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(4) During this period also rose the two great sects know to the Gospel narratives as Pharisees and Sadducees. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Mt 3:7">Matthew 3:7</reference>")</hi> notes 2,3 The Herodians were a party rather than a sect.</item> </list> <div sID="gen3086" type="x-p"/> Amongst such a people, governed, under the suzerainty of Rome, by an Idumean usurper, rent by bitter and unspiritual religious controversies, and maintaining an elaborate ritual, appeared Jesus, the Son and Christ of God. <chapter eID="Mal.4"/><div eID="gen3086" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen3054" osisID="Mal" type="book"/>
