<hi type="bold">Jupiter</hi> Latin for Gr. Zeus, the national god of the Greeks.<div eID="gen4207" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4208" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Mercurius</hi> Gr. Hermes.

<hi type="bold">ordained</hi><div eID="gen4208" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4209" type="x-p"/> (Greek - <w lemma="strong:G3097">μάγος</w>, to designate by stretching out (or pointing with) the hand). <chapter eID="Acts.14"/><div eID="gen4209" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen4210" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="15" osisID="Acts.15" sID="Acts.15"/>
<hi type="bold">Phenice</hi> <div eID="gen4210" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4211" type="x-p"/> Phoenicia.

<hi type="bold">my mouth</hi><div eID="gen4211" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4212" type="x-p"/> See, <reference osisRef="mt 16:19">Matthew 16:19</reference>. Peter used the keys first for the Jews on the day of Pentecost; secondly, in the house of Cornelius for the Gentiles, <reference osisRef="ac 15:14">Acts 15:14,</reference> But Paul was distinctively the apostle to the Gentiles. <reference osisRef="ga 2:7 ga 2:8">Galatians 2:7,8</reference>.

<hi type="bold">Men and brethren</hi><div eID="gen4212" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4213" type="x-p"/> Dispensationally, this is the most important passage in the N.T. It gives the divine purpose for this age, and for the beginning of the next.<div eID="gen4213" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(1) The taking out from among the Gentiles of a people for His name, the distinctive work of the present, or church-age. The church is the ecclesia--the "called-out assembly." Precisely this has been in progress since Pentecost. The Gospel has never anywhere converted all, but everywhere has called out some.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(2) "After this viz. the out-calling I will return." James quotes from <reference osisRef="am 9:11 am 9:12">Amos 9:11,12</reference>. The verses which follow in Amos describe the final regathering of Israel, which the other prophets invariably connect with the fulfilment of the Davidic Covenant (e.g.) ; <reference osisRef="isa 11:1 isa 11:10-12">Isaiah 11:1,10-12</reference>; <reference osisRef="jer 23:5-8">Jeremiah 23:5-8</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(3) "And will build again the tabernacle of David," i.e. re-establish the Davidic rule over Israel <reference osisRef="2sa 7:8-17">2 Samuel 7:8-17</reference>; <reference osisRef="lu 1:31-33">Luke 1:31-33</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(4) "That the residue of men Israelites may seek after the Lord" cf <reference osisRef="zec 12:7 zec 12:8">Zechariah 12:7,8</reference>; <reference osisRef="zec 13:1 zec 13:2"> 13:1,2</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(5) "And all the Gentiles," etc. cf <reference osisRef="mic 4:2">Micah 4:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="zec 8:21 zec 8:22">Zechariah 8:21,22</reference>. This is also the order of <reference osisRef="ro 11:24-27">Romans 11:24-27</reference>. </item> </list>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv122"/><div sID="gen4214" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv122"/> <hi type="bold">at the first</hi> <div eID="gen4214" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4215" type="x-p"/> Lit. for the first time, i.e. in the house of Cornelius. <reference osisRef="ac 15:8-11">Acts 15:8-11</reference>; <reference osisRef="ac 10:34-48"> 10:34-48</reference> <reference osisRef="ac 11:12-18"> 11:12-18</reference>.

<hi type="bold">tabernacle of David</hi><div eID="gen4215" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4216" type="x-p"/> Kingdom (N.T.) vs. <reference osisRef="ac 15:14-17">Acts 15:14-17</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 3:21">Revelation 3:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="lu 1:31-33">Luke 1:31-33</reference>; <reference osisRef="1co 15:34">1 Corinthians 15:34</reference>.

<hi type="bold">Lord</hi><div eID="gen4216" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4217" type="x-p"/> Jehovah. vs. <reference osisRef="ac 15:16 ac 15:17">Acts 15:16,17</reference>; <reference osisRef="am 9:11 am 9:12">Amos 9:11,12</reference>.

<hi type="bold">Wherefore</hi><div eID="gen4217" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4218" type="x-p"/> The scope of the decision goes far beyond the mere question of circumcision. The whole question of the relation of the law to Gentile believers had been put in issue (<reference osisRef="ac 15:5">Acts 15:5</reference>), and their exemption is declared in the decision (<reference osisRef="ac 15:19 ac 15:24">Acts 15:19,24</reference>). The decision might be otherwise stated in the terms of <reference osisRef="ro 6:14">Romans 6:14</reference>. "Ye are not under the law, but under grace." Gentile believers were to show grace by abstaining from the practices offensive to godly Jews.<div eID="gen4218" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4219" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="ac 15:20 ac 15:21 ac 15:28 ac 15:29">Acts 15:20,21,28,29</reference> cf ; <reference osisRef="ro 14:12-17">Romans 14:12-17</reference>; <reference osisRef="1co 8:1-13">1 Corinthians 8:1-13</reference>
<hi type="bold">prophets</hi><div eID="gen4219" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4220" type="x-p"/> See, <reference osisRef="1co 14:3">1 Corinthians 14:3</reference> defines the N.T. gift of prophecy.
<hi type="bold">Barnabas</hi><div eID="gen4220" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4221" type="x-p"/> And is heard of no more in the Bible story. <chapter eID="Acts.15"/><div eID="gen4221" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen4222" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="16" osisID="Acts.16" sID="Acts.16"/>
<hi type="bold">suffered</hi> <div eID="gen4222" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4223" type="x-p"/> R.V. adds "of Jesus", as in the best authorities.
<hi type="bold">prayed him</hi><div eID="gen4223" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4224" type="x-p"/> beseeching him. Here the Gospel turns toward Europe.

<hi type="bold">we</hi><div eID="gen4224" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4225" type="x-p"/> The change here from "they," as in the preceding verses, to "we" indicates that at Troas Luke, the narrator, joined Paul's company.
<hi type="bold">colony</hi><div eID="gen4225" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4226" type="x-p"/> i.e. a Roman colony.
<hi type="bold">was wont</hi><div eID="gen4226" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4227" type="x-p"/> might legally, i.e. a legal meeting-place for Jews where there was no synagogue.
<hi type="bold">spirit</hi><div eID="gen4227" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4228" type="x-p"/> (Greek - <w lemma="strong:G1">Α</w>," "a Python)."

<hi type="bold">most high God</hi> <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Mt 7:22">Matthew 7:22</reference>")</hi>. This marks the "spirit", <reference osisRef="ac 16:18">Acts 16:18,</reference> as being a demon.<div eID="gen4228" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4229" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">salvation</hi> See note, <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ro 1:16">Romans 1:16</reference>")</hi>.

<hi type="bold">drew</hi><div eID="gen4229" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4230" type="x-p"/> (Greek - <w lemma="strong:G1">Α</w>," probably by the feet). Cf. <reference osisRef="ac 14:19">Acts 14:19</reference>.
<hi type="bold">magistrates</hi><div eID="gen4230" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4231" type="x-p"/> (Greek - <w lemma="strong:G1">Α</w>," Roman magistrates).
<hi type="bold">prayed</hi><div eID="gen4231" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4232" type="x-p"/> Lit. were praying and singing hymns.
<hi type="bold">saved</hi><div eID="gen4232" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4233" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ro 1:16">Romans 1:16</reference>")</hi>.
<hi type="bold">serjeants</hi><div eID="gen4233" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4234" type="x-p"/> (Greek - <w lemma="strong:G1">Α</w>)." <chapter eID="Acts.16"/><div eID="gen4234" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen4235" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="17" osisID="Acts.17" sID="Acts.17"/>

<hi type="bold">Christ</hi> <div eID="gen4235" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4236" type="x-p"/> The Christ, i.e. that, according to the Scriptures, the Messiah must die and rise again. That Jesus was the Messiah was the second part of his argument.

<hi type="bold">drew</hi><div eID="gen4236" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4237" type="x-p"/> dragged. See margin ref., <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ac 16:19">Acts 16:19</reference>")</hi>.

<hi type="bold">Therefore</hi> Illustrates <reference osisRef="joh 5:46">John 5:46</reference>. Believing the O.T. they believed the Gospel.<div eID="gen4237" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4238" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">honourable</hi> Greek women of honourable estate.
<hi type="bold">stirred</hi><div eID="gen4238" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4239" type="x-p"/> provoked within him as he beheld the city full of idols.

<hi type="bold">Epicureans</hi> Disciples of Epicurus, B.C. 342-271, who abandoned as hopeless the search by reason for pure truth, cf. <reference osisRef="joh 18:38">John 18:38</reference> seeking instead true pleasure through experience.<div eID="gen4239" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4240" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Stoicks</hi> Disciples of Zeno, B.C. 280, and Chrysippus, B.C. 240. This philosophy was founded on human self-sufficiency, inculcated stern self-repression, the solidarily of the race, and the unity of Deity. Epicureans and Stocis divided the apostolic world.
<hi type="bold">Areopagus</hi><div eID="gen4240" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4241" type="x-p"/> Mars' hill.
<hi type="bold">blood</hi><div eID="gen4241" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4242" type="x-p"/> "blood" is not in the best manuscripts. R.V. omits.
<hi type="bold">For we</hi><div eID="gen4242" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4243" type="x-p"/> Found in the sritings of Aratus and Cleanthes.

<hi type="bold">offspring of God</hi><div eID="gen4243" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4244" type="x-p"/> (Greek - <w lemma="strong:G1085">γένος</w> = "race)." The reference is to the creation-work of God in which He made man (i.e. mankind, the race in Adam) in his own likeness, <reference osisRef="ge 1:26 ge 1:27">Genesis 1:26,27,</reference> thus rebuking the thought that "the Godhead is like unto gold," etc. The word "Father" is not used, not does the passage affirm anything concerning fatherhood or sonship, which are relationships based on faith, and the new birth.<div eID="gen4244" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4245" type="x-p"/> Cf <reference osisRef="joh 1:12 joh 1:13">John 1:12,13</reference>; <reference osisRef="ga 3:26">Galatians 3:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="ga 4:1-7"> 4:1-7</reference>; <reference osisRef="joh 5:1">John 5:1</reference>.

<hi type="bold">Repent</hi><div eID="gen4245" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4246" type="x-p"/> Repentance is the trans. of a (Greek - <w lemma="strong:G1085">γένος</w> ("metanoia-metanoeo") meaning "to have another mind," "to change the mind," and is used in the N).T. to indicate a change of mind in respect of sin, of God, and of self. This change of mind may, especially in the case of Christians who have fallen into sin, be preceded by sorrow <reference osisRef="2co 7:8-11">2 Corinthians 7:8-11</reference> but sorrow for sin, though it may "work" repentance, is not repentance. The son in <reference osisRef="mt 21:28 mt 21:29">Matthew 21:28,29</reference> illustrates true repentance.<div eID="gen4246" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4247" type="x-p"/> Saving faith: <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Heb 11:39">Hebrews 11:39</reference>")</hi> includes and implies that change of mind which is called repentance.

<hi type="bold">world</hi><div eID="gen4247" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4248" type="x-p"/> "oikoumene" = inhabited earth. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Lu 2:1">Luke 2:1</reference>")</hi>. <chapter eID="Acts.17"/><div eID="gen4248" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen4249" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="18" osisID="Acts.18" sID="Acts.18"/>
<hi type="bold">pressed</hi> <div eID="gen4249" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4250" type="x-p"/> Or, constrained by the Word. Cf. <reference osisRef="2co 5:14">2 Corinthians 5:14</reference>.
<hi type="bold">Justus</hi><div eID="gen4250" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4251" type="x-p"/> Titus Justus.

<hi type="bold">cared for</hi><div eID="gen4251" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4252" type="x-p"/> Contra. <reference osisRef="joh 19:13-16">John 19:13-16</reference>; <reference osisRef="ac 24:26 ac 24:27">Acts 24:26,27</reference>.

<hi type="bold">instructed</hi><div eID="gen4252" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4253" type="x-p"/> taught by word of mouth, or, hearsay, i.e. not by revelation. Cf. <reference osisRef="ga 1:11 ga 1:12">Galatians 1:11,12</reference>.<div eID="gen4253" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4254" type="x-p"/> The N.T. Scriptures were not then written.

<hi type="bold">that Jesus</hi><div eID="gen4254" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4255" type="x-p"/> Apollos' ministry seems to have gone no further; Jesus was the long expected Messiah. Of Paul's doctrine of justification through the blood, and sanctification through the Spirit, he seems at that time to have known nothing. See <reference osisRef="ac 19:3-6">Acts 19:3-6</reference>. <div eID="gen4255" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv123"/><div sID="gen4256" type="x-p"/> <chapter eID="Acts.18"/>
<div eID="gen4256" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4257" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="19" osisID="Acts.19" sID="Acts.19"/>

<hi type="bold">Have</hi> <div eID="gen4257" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4258" type="x-p"/> Not as in A.V., "since ye believed," but as in R.V. and marg.: "Did ye receive the Holy Spirit when ye believed?" Paul was evidently impressed by the absence of spirituality and power in these so-called disciples. Their answer brought out the fact that they were Jewish proselytes, disciples of John the Baptist, looking backward to an accomplished redemption. <reference osisRef="ro 8:9">Romans 8:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="1co 6:19">1 Corinthians 6:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="eph 1:13">Ephesians 1:13</reference>.

<hi type="bold">overcame</hi> The sons of Sceva sought to imitate a power to which they were strangers, only to their own confusion. This striking witness from another side caused fear to fall on all.<div eID="gen4258" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4259" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">prevailed</hi> <reference osisRef="lu 11:21 lu 11:22">Luke 11:21,22</reference>; <reference osisRef="1jo 4:4">1 John 4:4</reference>.

<hi type="bold">spirit</hi><div eID="gen4259" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4260" type="x-p"/> i.e. in his own mind. Cf. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ac 20:22">Acts 20:22</reference>")</hi>.
<hi type="bold">about the way</hi><div eID="gen4260" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4261" type="x-p"/> concerning the Way, i.e. Christ. <reference osisRef="joh 14:6">John 14:6</reference>.

<hi type="bold">world</hi><div eID="gen4261" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4262" type="x-p"/> "oikoumene" = inhabited earth. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Lu 2:1">Luke 2:1</reference>")</hi>.

<hi type="bold">Diana</hi><div eID="gen4262" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4263" type="x-p"/> Gr. Artemis. Not anciently of the Greek pantheon, but an Eastern goddess. Cf. <reference osisRef="jud 2:13">Judges 2:13</reference>. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Jud 2:13">Judges 2:13</reference>")</hi>.<div eID="gen4263" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4264" type="x-p"/> But "Diana of the Ephesians" was rather a particular image of Artemis, reputed to have fallen from heaven; <reference osisRef="ac 19:35">Acts 19:35</reference>. <chapter eID="Acts.19"/><div eID="gen4264" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen4265" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="20" osisID="Acts.20" sID="Acts.20"/>
<hi type="bold">we</hi> <div eID="gen4265" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4266" type="x-p"/> From the use of the pronoun, Luke here rejoins the apostle.

<hi type="bold">first day</hi><div eID="gen4266" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4267" type="x-p"/> It was the breaking of bread for which the disciples were assembled. The passage indicates the use by the apostolic churches of the first day, not the seventh. Cf. <reference osisRef="1co 16:2">1 Corinthians 16:2</reference>.

<hi type="bold">spirit</hi><div eID="gen4267" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4268" type="x-p"/> Cf. <reference osisRef="ac 21:4">Acts 21:4</reference>. In <reference osisRef="ac 20:22">Acts 20:22</reference> Paul's own spirit <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:1Th 5:23">1 Thessalonians 5:23</reference>")</hi> is meant; in <reference osisRef="ac 21:4">Acts 21:4</reference> the Holy Spirit. Paul's motive in going to Jerusalem seems to have been his great affection for the Jews <reference osisRef="ro 9:1-5">Romans 9:1-5</reference> and his hope that gifts of the Gentile churches, sent by him to the poor saints at Jerusalem <reference osisRef="ro 15:25-28">Romans 15:25-28</reference> would open the hearts of the law-bound Jewish believers to the "gospel of the grace of God" <reference osisRef="ac 20:24">Acts 20:24</reference>.

<hi type="bold">neither</hi><div eID="gen4268" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4269" type="x-p"/> Or, I hold not my life of any account, as unto myself, in comparison with accomplishing my course. See, <reference osisRef="1co 9:26">1 Corinthians 9:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="php 3:13 php 3:14">Philippians 3:13,14</reference>. <reference osisRef="2ti 4:7 2ti 4:8">2 Timothy 4:7,8</reference>.

<hi type="bold">wolves</hi><div eID="gen4269" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4270" type="x-p"/> The two sources of the apostasy: false teachers from without, <reference osisRef="2co 11:13-15">2 Corinthians 11:13-15</reference>; <reference osisRef="2pe 2:1-3">2 Peter 2:1-3</reference> ambitious leaders from within, ; <reference osisRef="3jo 1:9 3jo 1:10">3 John 1:9,10</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 2:6 re 2:15">Revelation 2:6,15</reference>. Also, ; <reference osisRef="1ti 1:20">1 Timothy 1:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="1jo 2:19">1 John 2:19</reference>.

<hi type="bold">It is more</hi><div eID="gen4270" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4271" type="x-p"/> See, <reference osisRef="lu 14:12">Luke 14:12</reference>. <chapter eID="Acts.20"/><div eID="gen4271" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen4272" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="21" osisID="Acts.21" sID="Acts.21"/>

<hi type="bold">go up to</hi> <div eID="gen4272" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4273" type="x-p"/> Lit. set foot in. Not, as in <reference osisRef="ac 20:23">Acts 20:23</reference> a warning of danger, but now an imperative command. See <reference osisRef="ac 22:17 ac 22:18">Acts 22:17,18</reference>.

<hi type="bold">vow</hi><div eID="gen4273" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4274" type="x-p"/> Probably according to <reference osisRef="nu 6:1-7">Numbers 6:1-7</reference>. Cf. <reference osisRef="col 2:14-17">Colossians 2:14-17</reference>.

<hi type="bold">charges with them</hi> Lit. spend something on them.<div eID="gen4274" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4275" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">walkest orderly</hi> Lit. art keeping in the ranks, guarding the law. Cf. <reference osisRef="ro 10:1-12">Romans 10:1-12</reference>.

<hi type="bold">Paul took</hi><div eID="gen4275" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4276" type="x-p"/> Contra. <reference osisRef="ac 21:4">Acts 21:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="ga 2:2-6">Galatians 2:2-6</reference>. See, ; <reference osisRef="ro 3:9-10 ro 3:19-20 ro 3:28">Romans 3:9,10,19,20,28</reference>; <reference osisRef="ro 4:3-5"> 4:3-5</reference> ; <reference osisRef="ro 5:1 ro 5:2"> 5:1,2</reference>; <reference osisRef="ro 6:14"> 6:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="ro 7:1-4 ro 7:6"> 7:1-4,6</reference>; <reference osisRef="ro 8:3 ro 8:4"> 8:3,4</reference>; <reference osisRef="ga 2:15 ga 2:16 ga 2:18 ga 2:19">Galatians 2:15,16,18,19</reference>; <reference osisRef="ga 3:10 ga 3:24 ga 3:25"> 3:10,24,25</reference> ; <reference osisRef="ga 4:9-11 ga 4:21-31"> 4:9-11,21-31</reference>; <reference osisRef="php 3:7-9">Philippians 3:7-9</reference>; <reference osisRef="heb 9:14 heb 9:15 heb 9:28">Hebrews 9:14,15,28</reference>; <reference osisRef="heb 10:1-4 heb 10:17-18"> 10:1-4,17,18</reference> <reference osisRef="heb 13:11-14"> 13:11-14</reference>
<hi type="bold">drew</hi><div eID="gen4276" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4277" type="x-p"/> See, <reference osisRef="ac 14:19">Acts 14:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="ac 16:19"> 16:19</reference>.

<hi type="bold">chief</hi><div eID="gen4277" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4278" type="x-p"/> (Greek - <w lemma="strong:G5506">χιλίαρχος</w>, the Roman tribune). There were six such "chief captains" in each legion of 6000 men. <chapter eID="Acts.21"/><div eID="gen4278" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen4279" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="22" osisID="Acts.22" sID="Acts.22"/>
<hi type="bold">voice</hi> <div eID="gen4279" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4280" type="x-p"/> Cf. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ac 9:7">Acts 9:7</reference>")</hi>.
<hi type="bold">sins</hi><div eID="gen4280" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4281" type="x-p"/> Sin. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ro 3:23">Romans 3:23</reference>")</hi>.
<hi type="bold">when I was</hi><div eID="gen4281" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4282" type="x-p"/> i.e. probably on his first visit to Jerusalem after his conversion.

<hi type="bold">freedom</hi> citizenship.<div eID="gen4282" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4283" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">was free born</hi> am a Roman born, i.e. of a father who had obtained citizenship.
<hi type="bold">examined him</hi><div eID="gen4283" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4284" type="x-p"/> Or, tortured him. <chapter eID="Acts.22"/><div eID="gen4284" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen4285" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="23" osisID="Acts.23" sID="Acts.23"/>
<hi type="bold">Sadducees</hi> <div eID="gen4285" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4286" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Mt 3:7">Matthew 3:7</reference>")</hi>.

<hi type="bold">scribes</hi><div eID="gen4286" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4287" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Mt 2:4">Matthew 2:4</reference>")</hi>. <chapter eID="Acts.23"/><div eID="gen4287" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen4288" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="24" osisID="Acts.24" sID="Acts.24"/>

<hi type="bold">world</hi> <div eID="gen4288" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4289" type="x-p"/> "oikoumene" = inhabited earth. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Lu 2:1">Luke 2:1</reference>")</hi>.
<hi type="bold">the governor</hi><div eID="gen4289" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4290" type="x-p"/> Felix made procurator over Judaea, A.D. 53.
<hi type="bold">of that way</hi><div eID="gen4290" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4291" type="x-p"/> concerning the Way. See, <reference osisRef="joh 14:6">John 14:6</reference>.

<hi type="bold">righteousness</hi> <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ro 10:10">Romans 10:10</reference>")</hi>.<div eID="gen4291" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4292" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">trembled</hi> becoming afraid; (Greek - <w lemma="strong:G1719">ἔμφοβος</w>," afraid).

<hi type="bold">But after</hi> But when two years were fulfilled, Felix was succeeded by Porcius Festus; and desiring to gain favour with the Jews, Felix left Paul in bonds. <div eID="gen4292" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv123"/><div sID="gen4293" type="x-p"/> <chapter eID="Acts.24"/>
<div eID="gen4293" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4294" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="25" osisID="Acts.25" sID="Acts.25"/>
<hi type="bold">more than ten</hi> <div eID="gen4294" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4295" type="x-p"/> Or, as some copies read, no more than eight or ten days.

<hi type="bold">Agrippa</hi><div eID="gen4295" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4296" type="x-p"/> This (<reference osisRef="ac 5:13">Acts 5:13</reference>) was Herod Agrippa II., son of the Herod Agrippa I. of <reference osisRef="ac 12:1">Acts 12:1,</reference> and great-grandson of Herod the Great. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Mt 2:1">Matthew 2:1</reference>")</hi>.<div eID="gen4296" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4297" type="x-p"/> Bernice, or Berenice, was the sister of Herod Agrippa II. <reference osisRef="ac 5:13">Acts 5:13</reference>. <chapter eID="Acts.25"/><div eID="gen4297" type="x-p"/>

<hi type="bold">his own hired house</hi><div eID="gen4316" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4317" type="x-p"/> It has been much disputed whether Paul endured two Roman imprisonments, from A.D. 62 to 68 or one. The tradition from Clement to Eusebius favours two imprisonments with a year of liberty between. Erdman (W.J.) has pointed out the leaving of Trophimus sick at Miletus, mentioned in <reference osisRef="2ti 4:20">2 Timothy 4:20</reference> could not have been an occurrence of Paul's last journey to Jerusalem, for then Trophimus was not left ; <reference osisRef="ac 20:4">Acts 20:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="ac 21:29"> 21:29</reference> nor of the journey to Rome to appear before Caesar, for then he did not touch at Miletus. To make this incident possible there must have been a release from the first imprisonment, and an interval of ministry and travel. <chapter eID="Acts.28"/><div eID="gen4317" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen4071" osisID="Acts" type="book"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv123"/><title type="x-s">Book Introduction - Romans</title> <div sID="gen4319" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="ro 1">Read first chapter of Romans</reference><div eID="gen4319" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4320" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">WRITER</hi>: The Apostle Paul (<reference osisRef="ro 1:1">Romans 1:1</reference>).<div eID="gen4320" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4321" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">DATE</hi>: Romans, the sixth in chronological order of Paul's Epistles, was written from Corinth during the apostle's third visit to that city. <reference osisRef="2co 13:1">2 Corinthians 13:1</reference> in A.D. 60. The Epistle has its occasion in the intention of the apostle soon to visit Rome. Naturally, he would wish to announce before his coming the distinctive truths which had been revealed to and through him. He would desire the Christians in Rome to have his own statement of the great doctrines of grace so bitterly assailed everywhere by legalistic teachers.<div eID="gen4321" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4322" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">THEME</hi>: The theme of Romans is "the Gospel of God" (<reference osisRef="ro 1:1">Romans 1:1</reference>), the very widest possible designation of the whole body of redemption truth, for it is He with whom is "no respect of persons"; and who is not "the God of the Jews only," but "of the Gentiles also" ; <reference osisRef="ro 2:11">Romans 2:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="ro 3:29"> 3:29</reference>. Accordingly, "all the world" is found guilty <reference osisRef="ro 3:19">Romans 3:19,</reference> and a redemption is revealed as wide as the need, upon the alone condition of faith. Not only does Romans embody in the fullest way the doctrines of grace in relation to salvation, but in three remarkable chapters (9-11.) the great promises to Israel are reconciled with the promises concerning the Gentiles, and the fulfilment of the former shown to await the completion of the church and coming of the Deliverer out of Zion <reference osisRef="ro 11:25-27">Romans 11:25-27</reference>. The key-phrase is "the righteousness of God" ; <reference osisRef="ro 1:17">Romans 1:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="ro 3:21 ro 3:22"> 3:21,22</reference>.<div eID="gen4322" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4323" type="x-p"/> The Epistle, exclusive of the introduction (<reference osisRef="ro 1:1-17"> 1:1-17</reference>), is in seven parts.<div eID="gen4323" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">The whole world guilty before God, 1:18-3:20.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">Justification through the righteousness of God by faith, the Gospel remedy for guilt, 3:21-5:11.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">Crucifixion with Christ, the resurrection life of Christ, and the walk in the Spirit, the Gospel provision for inherent sin, 5:12-8:13.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The full result in blessing of the Gospel, 8:14-39.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">Parenthesis: the Gospel does not abolish the covenant promises to Israel, 9:1-11:36.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">Christian life and service, 12:1-15:33.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The outflow of Christian love, 16:1-27.</item> </list> <div sID="gen4324" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv123"/> <hi type="bold">seed</hi> <div eID="gen4324" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4325" type="x-p"/> See note on the Davidic descent of Christ, <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Lu 3:23">Luke 3:23</reference>")</hi>.

<hi type="bold">for obedience</hi><div eID="gen4325" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4326" type="x-p"/> unto obedience to faith, i.e. faith as a principle, or method of divine dealing. Cf. <reference osisRef="ro 10:1-11">Romans 10:1-11</reference>.

<hi type="bold">world</hi><div eID="gen4326" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4327" type="x-p"/> kosmos = mankind. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Mt 4:8">Matthew 4:8</reference>")</hi>.

<hi type="bold">salvation</hi><div eID="gen4327" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4328" type="x-p"/> The Heb. and (Greek - <w lemma="strong:G219">ἀλεκτοροφωνία</w>, safety, preservation, healing, and soundness). Salvation is the great inclusive word of the Gospel, gathering into itself all the redemptive acts and processes: as justification, redemption, grace, propitiation, imputation, forgiveness, sanctification, and glorification. Salvation is in three tenses:<div eID="gen4328" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(1) The believer has been saved from the guilt and penalty of sin <reference osisRef="lu 7:50">Luke 7:50</reference>; <reference osisRef="1co 1:18">1 Corinthians 1:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="2co 2:15">2 Corinthians 2:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="eph 2:5 eph 2:8">Ephesians 2:5,8</reference>; <reference osisRef="2ti 1:9">2 Timothy 1:9</reference> and is safe.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(2) the believer is being saved from the habit and dominion of sin <reference osisRef="ro 6:14">Romans 6:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="php 1:19">Philippians 1:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="php 2:12 php 2:13"> 2:12,13</reference>; <reference osisRef="2th 2:13">2 Thessalonians 2:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="ro 8:2">Romans 8:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="ga 2:19 ga 2:20">Galatians 2:19,20</reference>; <reference osisRef="2co 3:18">2 Corinthians 3:18</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(3) The believer is to be saved in the sense of entire conformity to Christ. <reference osisRef="ro 13:11">Romans 13:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="heb 10:36">Hebrews 10:36</reference>; <reference osisRef="1pe 1:5">1 Peter 1:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="1jo 3:2">1 John 3:2</reference>. Salvation is by grace through faith, is a free gift, and wholly without works ; <reference osisRef="ro 3:27 ro 3:28">Romans 3:27,28</reference>; <reference osisRef="ro 4:1-8"> 4:1-8</reference> ; <reference osisRef="ro 6:23"> 6:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="eph 2:8">Ephesians 2:8</reference>. The divine order is: first salvation, then works ; <reference osisRef="eph 2:9 eph 2:10">Ephesians 2:9,10</reference>; <reference osisRef="tit 3:5-8">Titus 3:5-8</reference>. </item> </list>

<hi type="bold">righteousness of God</hi><div eID="gen4351" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4352" type="x-p"/> The righteousness of God is neither an attribute of God, not the changed character of the believer, but Christ Himself, who fully met in our stead and behalf every demand of the law, and who is, but the act of God called imputation <reference osisRef="le 25:50">Leviticus 25:50</reference>; <reference osisRef="jas 2:23">James 2:23,</reference> "made unto us.. righteousness" <reference osisRef="1co 1:30">1 Corinthians 1:30</reference>.<div eID="gen4352" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4353" type="x-p"/> "The believer in Christ is now, by grace, shrouded under so complete and blessed a righteousness that the law from Mt. Sinai can find neither fault nor diminution therein. This is that which is called the righteousness of God by faith."--Bunyan.<div eID="gen4353" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4354" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2co 5:21">2 Corinthians 5:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="ro 4:6">Romans 4:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="ro 10:4"> 10:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="php 3:9">Philippians 3:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="ro 3:26">Romans 3:26</reference>

<hi type="bold">sinned</hi><div eID="gen4354" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4355" type="x-p"/> Sin, Summary: The literal meanings of the Heb. and (Greek - <w lemma="strong:G219">ἀλεκτοροφωνία</w> sin," "sinner," etc)., disclose the true nature of sin in its manifold manifestations. Sin is transgression, an overstepping of the law, the divine boundary between good and evil <reference osisRef="ps 51:1">Psalms 51:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="lu 15:29">Luke 15:29,</reference> iniquity, an act inherently wrong, whether expressly forbidden or not; error, a departure from right ; <reference osisRef="ps 51:9">Psalms 51:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="ro 3:23">Romans 3:23,</reference> missing the mark, a failure to meet the divine standard; trespass, the intrusion of self-will into the sphere of divine authority <reference osisRef="eph 2:1">Ephesians 2:1,</reference> lawlessness, or spiritual anarchy <reference osisRef="1ti 1:9">1 Timothy 1:9,</reference> unbelief, or an insult to the divine veracity <reference osisRef="joh 16:9">John 16:9</reference>.<div eID="gen4355" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4356" type="x-p"/> Sin originated with Satan <reference osisRef="isa 14:12-14">Isaiah 14:12-14,</reference> entered the world through Adam <reference osisRef="ro 5:12">Romans 5:12,</reference> was, and is, universal, Christ alone excepted ; <reference osisRef="ro 3:23">Romans 3:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="1pe 2:22">1 Peter 2:22,</reference> incurs the penalties of spiritual and physical death ; <reference osisRef="ge 2:17">Genesis 2:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="ge 3:19"> 3:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="eze 18:4 eze 18:20">Ezekiel 18:4,20</reference>; <reference osisRef="ro 6:23">Romans 6:23</reference> and has no remedy but in the sacrificial death of Christ ; <reference osisRef="heb 9:26">Hebrews 9:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="ac 4:12">Acts 4:12</reference> availed of by faith <reference osisRef="ac 13:38 ac 13:39">Acts 13:38,39</reference>. Sin may be summarized as threefold: An act, the violation of, or want of obedience to the revealed will of God; a state, absence of righteousness; a nature, enmity toward God.

<hi type="bold">Redemption</hi><div eID="gen4356" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4357" type="x-p"/> Redemption, "to deliver by paying a price." The N.T. doctrine. The N.T. records the fulfilment of the O.T. types and prophecies of redemption through the sacrifice of Christ. The completed truth is set forth in the three words which are translated redemption<div eID="gen4357" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(1) agorazo, "to purchase in the market." The underlying thought is of a slave-market. The subjects of redemption are "sold under sin" <reference osisRef="ro 7:14">Romans 7:14</reference> but are, moreover, under sentence of death ; <reference osisRef="eze 18:4">Ezekiel 18:4,</reference>; <reference osisRef="joh 3:18 joh 3:19">John 3:18,19</reference>; <reference osisRef="ro 3:19">Romans 3:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="ga 3:10">Galatians 3:10,</reference> and the purchase price is the blood of the Redeemer who dies in their stead ; <reference osisRef="ga 3:13">Galatians 3:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="2co 5:21">2 Corinthians 5:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="mt 20:28">Matthew 20:28,</reference>; <reference osisRef="mr 10:45">Mark 10:45</reference>; <reference osisRef="1ti 2:6">1 Timothy 2:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="1pe 1:18">1 Peter 1:18</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(2) exagorazo, "to buy out of the market." The redeemed are never again to be exposed to sale;</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(3) lutroo, "to loose," "to set free by paying a price" <reference osisRef="joh 8:32">John 8:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="ga 4:4 ga 4:5 ga 4:31">Galatians 4:4,5,31</reference>; <reference osisRef="ga 5:13"> 5:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="ro 8:21">Romans 8:21</reference>. Redemption is by sacrifice and by power <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ex 14:30">Exodus 14:30</reference>")</hi> Christ paid the price, the Holy Spirit makes deliverance actual in experience <reference osisRef="ro 8:2">Romans 8:2</reference>.</item> </list> <div sID="gen4358" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Isa 59:20">Isaiah 59:20</reference>")</hi>. See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:ro 1:16">Romans 1:16</reference>".<div eID="gen4358" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4359" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">grace</hi> Grace (in salvation), <reference osisRef="ro 4:4-16">Romans 4:4-16</reference>; <reference osisRef="ro 3:24"> 3:24</reference>. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Joh 1:17">John 1:17</reference>")</hi>.

<hi type="bold">propitiation</hi><div eID="gen4359" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4360" type="x-p"/> Lit. a propitiatory sacrifice, through faith by his blood; (Greek - <w lemma="strong:G2435">ἱλαστήριον</w>, "place of propitiation)." The word occurs, <reference osisRef="1jo 2:2">1 John 2:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="1jo 4:10"> 4:10</reference> as the trans. of hilasmos, "that which propitiates," "a propitiatory sacrifice." Hilasterion is used by the Septuagint, and <reference osisRef="heb 9:5">Hebrews 9:5</reference> for "mercy-seat." The mercy-seat was sprinkled with atoning blood in the day of atonement <reference osisRef="le 16:14">Leviticus 16:14</reference> in token that the righteous sentence of the law had been (typically) carried out, so that what must else have been a judgment-seat could righteously be a mercy-seat ; <reference osisRef="heb 9:11-15">Hebrews 9:11-15</reference>; <reference osisRef="heb 4:14-16"> 4:14-16,</reference> a place of communion <reference osisRef="ex 25:21 ex 25:22">Exodus 25:21,22</reference>.<div eID="gen4360" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4361" type="x-p"/> In fulfilment of the type, Christ is Himself the hilasmos, "that which propitiates," and the hilasterion, "the place of propitiation" --the mercy-seat sprinkled with His own blood-- the token that in our stead He so honoured the law by enduring its righteous sentence that God, who ever foresaw the cross, is vindicated in having "passed over" sins from Adam to Moses <reference osisRef="ro 5:13">Romans 5:13</reference> and the sins of believers under the old covenant <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ex 29:33">Exodus 29:33</reference>")</hi> and just in justifying sinners under the covenant. There is no thought in propitiation of placating a vengeful God, but of doing right by His holy law and so making it possible for Him righteously to show mercy.<div eID="gen4361" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4362" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">remission</hi> passing over of sins done aforetime, i.e. since Adam. Cf. <reference osisRef="heb 9:15">Hebrews 9:15</reference>.

<hi type="bold">righteousness</hi><div eID="gen4362" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4363" type="x-p"/> "His righteousness" here is God's consistency with His own law and holiness in freely justifying a sinner who believes in Christ; that is, one in whose behalf Christ has met every demand of the law <reference osisRef="ro 10:4">Romans 10:4</reference>.

<hi type="bold">Justification</hi><div eID="gen4363" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4364" type="x-p"/> Justification, Summary: Justification and righteousness are inseparably united in Scripture by the fact that the same word (dikaios, "righteous"; dikaioo, "to justify") is used for both. The believing sinner is justified because Christ, having borne his sins on the cross, has been "made unto him righteousness" <reference osisRef="1co 1:30">1 Corinthians 1:30</reference>. Justification originates in grace ; <reference osisRef="ro 3:24">Romans 3:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="tit 3:4 tit 3:5">Titus 3:4,5</reference> is through the redemptive and propitiatory work of Christ, who has vindicated the law ; <reference osisRef="ro 3:24 ro 3:25">Romans 3:24,25</reference>; <reference osisRef="ro 5:9"> 5:9</reference> is by faith, not works ; <reference osisRef="ro 3:28-30">Romans 3:28-30</reference>; <reference osisRef="ro 4:5"> 4:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="ro 5:1"> 5:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="ga 2:16">Galatians 2:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="ga 3:8 ga 3:24"> 3:8,24</reference> and may be defined as the judicial act of God whereby He justly declares righteous one who believes on Jesus Christ. It is the Judge Himself <reference osisRef="ro 8:31-34">Romans 8:31-34</reference> who thus declares. The justified believer has been in court, only to learn that nothing is laid to his charge. <reference osisRef="ro 8:1 ro 8:33 ro 8:34">Romans 8:1,33,34</reference>.

<hi type="bold">Do we then</hi><div eID="gen4364" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4365" type="x-p"/> The sinner establishes the law in its right use and honour by confessing his guilt, and acknowledging that by it he is justly condemned. Christ, on the sinner's behalf, establishes the law by enduring its penalty, death. Cf. <reference osisRef="mt 5:17 mt 5:18">Matthew 5:17,18</reference>. <div eID="gen4365" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv125"/><div sID="gen4366" type="x-p"/> <chapter eID="Rom.3"/>

Christ, on the sinner's behalf, establishes the law by enduring its penalty, death. Cf. <reference osisRef="mt 5:17 mt 5:18">Matthew 5:17,18</reference>.

<hi type="bold">works</hi><div eID="gen4368" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4369" type="x-p"/> Cf. <reference osisRef="jas 2:24">James 2:24</reference>. These are two aspects of one truth. Paul speaks of that which justifies man before God, viz.: faith alone, wholly apart from works; James of the proof before men, that he who professes to have justifying faith really has it. Paul speaks of what God sees--faith; James of what men see--works, as the visible evidence of faith. Paul draws his illustration from <reference osisRef="ge 15:6">Genesis 15:6</reference> James from <reference osisRef="ge 22:1-19">Genesis 22:1-19</reference>. James' key phrase is "ye see" <reference osisRef="jas 2:24">James 2:24</reference> for men cannot see faith except as manifested through works.

<hi type="bold">Reconciliation</hi><div eID="gen4386" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4387" type="x-p"/> See Ro 5: 10,11 <reference osisRef="2co 5:18-20">2 Corinthians 5:18-20</reference>; <reference osisRef="col 1:21">Colossians 1:21</reference>.

The "wherefore" relates back to <reference osisRef="ro 3:19-23">Romans 3:19-23</reference> and may be regarded as a continuation of the discussion of the universality of sin, interrupted ; <reference osisRef="ro 3:24-ro 5:11">Romans 3:24-5:11</reference>; by the passage on justification and its results.<div eID="gen4387" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4388" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">have sinned</hi> <div eID="gen4388" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4389" type="x-p"/> The first sin wrought the moral ruin of the race. The demonstration is simple.<div eID="gen4389" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(1) Death is universal (<reference osisRef="ro 4:12 ro 4:14">Romans 4:12,14</reference>), all die: sinless infants, moral people, religious people, equally with the depraved. For a universal effect there must be a universal cause; that cause is a state of universal sin (<reference osisRef="ro 5:12">Romans 5:12</reference>).</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(2) But this universal state must have had a cause. It did. The consequence of Adam's sin was that "the many were made sinners" (<reference osisRef="ro 5:19">Romans 5:19</reference>)--"By the offence of one judgment came upon all men unto condemnation" (<reference osisRef="ro 5:18">Romans 5:18</reference>).</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(3) Personal sins are not meant here. From Adam to Moses death reigned (<reference osisRef="ro 5:14">Romans 5:14</reference>), although, there being no law, personal guilt was not imputed (<reference osisRef="ro 5:13">Romans 5:13</reference>). Accordingly, from <reference osisRef="ge 4:7">Genesis 4:7</reference> to <reference osisRef="ex 29:14">Exodus 29:14</reference> the sin-offering is not once mentioned. Then, since physical death from Adam to Moses was not due to the sinful acts of those who die (<reference osisRef="ro 5:13">Romans 5:13</reference>), it follows that it was due to a universal sinful state, or nature, and that state is declared to be out inheritance from Adam.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(4) the moral state of fallen man is described in Scripture <reference osisRef="ge 6:5">Genesis 6:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="1ki 8:46">1 Kings 8:46</reference>; <reference osisRef="ps 14:1-3">Psalms 14:1-3</reference>; <reference osisRef="ps 39:5"> 39:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="jer 17:9">Jeremiah 17:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="mt 18:11">Matthew 18:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="mr 7:20 mr 7:23">Mark 7:20,23</reference>; <reference osisRef="ro 1:21">Romans 1:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="ro 2:1-29"> 2:1-29</reference>; <reference osisRef="ro 3:9-19"> 3:9-19</reference> ; <reference osisRef="ro 7:24"> 7:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="ro 8:7"> 8:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="joh 3:6">John 3:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="1co 2:14">1 Corinthians 2:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="2co 3:14">2 Corinthians 3:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="2co 4:4"> 4:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="ga 5:19-21">Galatians 5:19-21</reference>; <reference osisRef="eph 2:1-3 eph 2:11-12">Ephesians 2:1-3,11,12</reference>; <reference osisRef="eph 4:18-22"> 4:18-22</reference>; <reference osisRef="col 1:21">Colossians 1:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="heb 3:13">Hebrews 3:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="jas 4:14">James 4:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="1co 15:22">1 Corinthians 15:22</reference>. </item> </list>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv125"/><div sID="gen4390" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv125"/> <hi type="bold">Adam to Moses</hi> <div eID="gen4390" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4391" type="x-p"/> Broadly, the contrast is: Adam: sin, death; Christ: righteousness, life. Adam drew down into his ruin the old creation <reference osisRef="ro 8:19-22">Romans 8:19-22</reference> of which he was lord and head. Christ brings into moral unity with God, and into eternal life, the new creation of which he is Lord and Head. <reference osisRef="eph 1:22 eph 1:23">Ephesians 1:22,23</reference>. Even the animal and material creation, cursed for man's sake. <reference osisRef="ge 3:17">Genesis 3:17</reference> will be delivered by Christ. ; <reference osisRef="isa 11:6-9">Isaiah 11:6-9</reference>; <reference osisRef="ro 8:19-22">Romans 8:19-22</reference>.
<hi type="bold">one many</hi><div eID="gen4391" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4392" type="x-p"/> the one the many died.

<hi type="bold">old self</hi><div eID="gen4403" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4404" type="x-p"/> The expression occurs elsewhere, in <reference osisRef="eph 4:22">Ephesians 4:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="col 3:9">Colossians 3:9</reference> and always means the man of old, corrupt human nature, the inborn tendency to evil in all men. In <reference osisRef="ro 6:6">Romans 6:6</reference> it is the natural man himself; in ; <reference osisRef="eph 4:22">Ephesians 4:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="col 3:9">Colossians 3:9</reference> his ways. Positionally, in the reckoning of God, the old man is crucified, and the believer is exhorted to make this good in experience, reckoning it to be so by definitely "putting off" the old man and "putting on" the new ; <reference osisRef="col 3:8-14">Colossians 3:8-14</reference>; <reference osisRef="4:24"> 4:24</reference>, <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Eph 4:24">Ephesians 4:24</reference>")</hi> , note 3.

<hi type="bold">What then</hi><div eID="gen4408" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4409" type="x-p"/> The old relation to the law and sin, and the new relation to Christ and life are illustrated by the effect of death upon servitude <reference osisRef="ro 6:16-23">Romans 6:16-23</reference> and marriage <reference osisRef="ro 7:1-6">Romans 7:1-6</reference>.<div eID="gen4409" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(1) The old servitude was nominally to the law, but, since the law had no delivering power, the real master continued to be sin in the nature. The end was death. The law could not give life, and "sin" (here personified as the old self) is in itself deathful. But death in another form, ie., crucifixion with Christ, has intervened to free the servant from his double bondage to sin (<reference osisRef="ro 6:6 ro 6:7">Romans 6:6,7</reference>), and to the law <reference osisRef="ro 7:4 ro 7:6">Romans 7:4,6</reference></item> <item type="x-indent-1">(2) This effect of death is further illustrated by widowhood. Death dissolves the marriage relation <reference osisRef="ro 7:1-3">Romans 7:1-3</reference>. As natural death frees a wife from the law of her husband, so crucifixion with Christ sets the believer free from the law. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ga 3:24">Galatians 3:24</reference>")</hi> </item> </list>

<hi type="bold">married</hi> joined.<div eID="gen4419" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4420" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="eph 5:31">Ephesians 5:31,</reference> same Greek word.<div eID="gen4420" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4421" type="x-p"/> Bride (of Christ). <reference osisRef="2co 11:1-3">2 Corinthians 11:1-3</reference>; <reference osisRef="joh 3:29">John 3:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 19:6-8">Revelation 19:6-8</reference>.

<hi type="bold">newness</hi><div eID="gen4421" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4422" type="x-p"/> Cf. <reference osisRef="ro 2:29">Romans 2:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="2co 3:6">2 Corinthians 3:6</reference>. "The letter" is a Paulinism for the law, as "spirit" in these passages is his word for the relationships and powers of new life in Christ Jesus. In 2 Cor. 3. a series is presented of contrast of law with "spirit," of the old covenant and the new. The contrast is not between two methods of interpretation, literal, and spiritual, but between two methods of divine dealing: one through the law, the other through the Holy Spirit.
<hi type="bold">sin</hi><div eID="gen4422" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4423" type="x-p"/> Sin. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ro 3:23">Romans 3:23</reference>")</hi>.
<hi type="bold">sin</hi><div eID="gen4423" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4424" type="x-p"/> Sin. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ro 5:21">Romans 5:21</reference>")</hi>.

<hi type="bold">when the commandment</hi><div eID="gen4424" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4425" type="x-p"/> The passage (vs 7-25) is autobiographical. Paul's religious experience was in three strongly marked phases:<div eID="gen4425" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(1) He was a godly Jew under the law. That the passage does not refer to that period is clear from his own explicit statements elsewhere. At that time he held himself to be "blameless" as concerned the law <reference osisRef="php 3:6">Philippians 3:6</reference>. He had "lived in all good conscience" <reference osisRef="ac 23:1">Acts 23:1</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(2) With his conversion came new light upon the law itself. He now perceived it to be "spiritual" (<reference osisRef="ro 7:14">Romans 7:14</reference>). He now saw that, so far from having kept it, he was condemned by it. He had supposed himself to be "alive," but now the commandment really "came" (<reference osisRef="ro 7:9">Romans 7:9</reference>) and he "died." Just when the apostle passed through the experience of <reference osisRef="ro 7:7-25">Romans 7:7-25</reference> we are not told. Perhaps during the days of physical blindness at Damascus <reference osisRef="ac 9:9">Acts 9:9,</reference> perhaps in Arabia <reference osisRef="ga 1:17">Galatians 1:17</reference>.</item> </list> <div sID="gen4426" type="x-p"/> It is the experience of a renewed man, under the law, and still ignorant of the delivering power of the Holy Spirit <reference osisRef="ro 8:2">Romans 8:2</reference>.<div eID="gen4426" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(3) With the great revelations afterward embodied in Galatians and Romans, the apostle's experience entered it third phase. He now knew himself to be "dead to the law by the body of Christ," and, in the power of the indwelling Spirit, "free from the law of sin and death" <reference osisRef="ro 8:2">Romans 8:2</reference> while "the righteousness of the law" was wrought in him (not by him) while he walked after the Spirit <reference osisRef="ro 8:4">Romans 8:4,</reference> Romans 7. is the record of past conflicts and defeats experience as a renewed man under law.</item> </list> <div sID="gen4427" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sin</hi> Sin. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ro 5:21">Romans 5:21</reference>")</hi>.
<hi type="bold">sin</hi><div eID="gen4427" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4428" type="x-p"/> Sin. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ro 5:21">Romans 5:21</reference>")</hi>.

<hi type="bold">sin/sinful</hi><div eID="gen4428" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4429" type="x-p"/> Sin. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ro 5:21">Romans 5:21</reference>")</hi>.

<hi type="bold">carnal</hi><div eID="gen4429" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4430" type="x-p"/> Cf. <reference osisRef="1co 3:1 1co 3:4">1 Corinthians 3:1,4</reference>. "Carnal" = "fleshly" is Paul's word for the Adamic nature, and for the believer who "walks," i.e. lives, under the power of it. "Natural" is his characteristic word for the unrenewed man <reference osisRef="1co 2:14">1 Corinthians 2:14</reference> as "spiritual" designates the renewed man who walks in the Spirit ; <reference osisRef="1co 3:1">1 Corinthians 3:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="ga 6:1">Galatians 6:1</reference>.<div eID="gen4430" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4431" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sin</hi> Sin. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ro 5:21">Romans 5:21</reference>")</hi>.

<hi type="bold">I do I allow not</hi><div eID="gen4431" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4432" type="x-p"/> The apostle personifies the strife of the two natures in the believer, the old or Adamic nature, and the divine nature received through the new birth <reference osisRef="1pe 1:23">1 Peter 1:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="2pe 1:4">2 Peter 1:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="ga 2:20">Galatians 2:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="col 1:27">Colossians 1:27</reference>. The "I" which is Saul of Tarsus, and the "I" which is Paul the apostle are at strife, and "Paul" is in defeat. In Chapter 8, this strife is effectually taken up on the believer's behalf by the Holy Spirit ; <reference osisRef="ro 8:2">Romans 8:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="ga 5:16 ga 5:17">Galatians 5:16,17</reference> and Paul is victorious.<div eID="gen4432" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4433" type="x-p"/> Contra, <reference osisRef="eph 6:12">Ephesians 6:12</reference> where the conflict is not fleshly, but spiritual.
<hi type="bold">sin</hi><div eID="gen4433" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4434" type="x-p"/> Sin. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ro 5:21">Romans 5:21</reference>")</hi>.
<hi type="bold">sin</hi> Sin. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ro 5:21">Romans 5:21</reference>")</hi>.

<hi type="bold">law</hi><div eID="gen4434" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4435" type="x-p"/> Six "laws" are to be distinguished in Romans: The law of Moses, which condemns <reference osisRef="ro 3:19">Romans 3:19</reference> "law" as a principle <reference osisRef="ro 3:21">Romans 3:21</reference> the law of faith, which excludes self-righteousness <reference osisRef="ro 3:27">Romans 3:27</reference> the law of sin in the members, which is victorious over the law of the mind <reference osisRef="ro 7:21 ro 7:23 ro 7:25">Romans 7:21,23,25</reference> the law of the mind, which consents to the law of Moses but cannot do it because of the law of sin in the members <reference osisRef="ro 7:16 ro 7:23">Romans 7:16,23</reference> and the "law of the Spirit," having power to deliver the believer from the law of sin which is in his members, and his conscience from condemnation by the Mosaic law. Moreover the Spirit works in the yielded believer the very righteousness which Moses' law requires <reference osisRef="ro 8:2 ro 8:4">Romans 8:2,4</reference>.
<hi type="bold">sin</hi><div eID="gen4435" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4436" type="x-p"/> Sin. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ro 5:21">Romans 5:21</reference>")</hi>.

<hi type="bold">For they are not all Israel</hi><div eID="gen4451" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4452" type="x-p"/> The distinction is between Israel after the flesh, the mere natural posterity of Abraham, and Israelites who, through faith, are also Abraham's spiritual children. <hi type="bold">righteousness</hi><div eID="gen4465" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4466" type="x-p"/> The word "righteousness" here, and in the passages having marginal references to this, means legal, or self-righteousness; the futile effort of man to work out under law a character which God can approve.<div eID="gen4466" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4467" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Re 19:8">Revelation 19:8</reference>")</hi>.<div eID="gen4467" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4468" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">righteousness</hi> Cf. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ro 3:21">Romans 3:21</reference>")</hi>.

<hi type="bold">righteousness</hi><div eID="gen4469" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4470" type="x-p"/> Righteousness here, and in the passages which refer to <reference osisRef="ro 10:10">Romans 10:10,</reference> means that righteousness of God which is judicially reckoned to all who believe on the Lord Jesus Christ; believers are the righteous.<div eID="gen4470" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4471" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ro 3:21">Romans 3:21</reference>")</hi>.

<hi type="bold">cast</hi> <div eID="gen4476" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4477" type="x-p"/> That Israel has not been forever set aside is the theme of this chapter.<div eID="gen4477" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(1) The salvation of Paul proves that there is still a remnant (<reference osisRef="ro 11:1">Romans 11:1</reference>)</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(2) The doctrine of the remnant proves it (<reference osisRef="ro 11:2-6">Romans 11:2-6</reference>).</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(3) The present national unbelief was foreseen (<reference osisRef="ro 11:7-10">Romans 11:7-10</reference>).</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(4) Israel's unbelief is the Gentile opportunity (<reference osisRef="ro 11:11-25">Romans 11:11-25</reference>).</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(5) Israel is judicially broken off from the good olive tree, Christ (<reference osisRef="ro 11:17-22">Romans 11:17-22</reference>).</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(6) They are to be grafted in again (<reference osisRef="ro 11:23 ro 11:24">Romans 11:23,24</reference>).</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(7) The promised Deliverer will come out of Zion and the nation will be saved (<reference osisRef="ro 11:25-29">Romans 11:25-29</reference>). That the Christian now inherits the distinctive Jewish promises is not taught in Scripture. The Christian is of the heavenly seed of Abraham ; <reference osisRef="ge 15:5 ge 15:6">Genesis 15:5,6</reference>; <reference osisRef="ga 3:29">Galatians 3:29</reference> and partakes of the spiritual blessings of the Abrahamic Covenant.</item> </list> <div sID="gen4478" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ge 15:18">Genesis 15:18</reference>")</hi> but Israel as a nation always has it own place, and is yet to have its greatest exaltation as the earthly people of God. See "Israel" <reference osisRef="ge 12:2">Genesis 12:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="ro 11:26">Romans 11:26</reference> "Kingdom" ; <reference osisRef="ge 1:26-28">Genesis 1:26-28</reference>; <reference osisRef="zec 12:8">Zechariah 12:8</reference>.<div eID="gen4478" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4479" type="x-p"/> For Another Point of View: See Topic 301242 <div eID="gen4479" type="x-p"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv127"/><div sID="gen4480" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv127"/> <hi type="bold">Remnant</hi> <div eID="gen4480" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4481" type="x-p"/> Remnant, Summary: In the history of Israel, a "remnant" may be discerned, a spiritual Israel within the national Israel. In Elijah's time 7,000 had not bowed the knee to Baal <reference osisRef="1ki 19:18">1 Kings 19:18</reference>. In Isaiah's time it was the "very small remnant" for whose sake God still forbore to destroy the nation <reference osisRef="isa 1:9">Isaiah 1:9</reference>. During the captivities the remnant appears in Jews like Ezekiel, Daniel, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, Esther, and Mordecai. At the end of the 70 years of Babylonian captivity it was the remnant which returned under Ezra and Nehemiah. At the advent of our Lord, John the Baptist, Simeon, Anna, and "them that looked for redemption in Jerusalem" <reference osisRef="lu 2:38">Luke 2:38</reference> were the remnant. During the church-age the remnant is composed of believing Jews <reference osisRef="ro 11:4 ro 11:5">Romans 11:4,5</reference>. But the chief interest in the remnant is prophetic. During the great tribulation a remnant out of all Israel will turn to Jesus as Messiah, and will become His witnesses after the removal of the church <reference osisRef="re 7:3-8">Revelation 7:3-8</reference>. Some of these will undergo martyrdom <reference osisRef="re 6:9-11">Revelation 6:9-11</reference> some will be spared to enter the millennial kingdom <reference osisRef="zec 12:6-zec 13:9">Zechariah 12:6-13:9</reference>. Many of the Psalms express, prophetically, the joys and sorrows of the tribulation remnant.<div eID="gen4481" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4482" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">remnant</hi> Remnant. See, <reference osisRef="isa 1:9">Isaiah 1:9</reference>.<div eID="gen4482" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4483" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">grace</hi> Grace (in salvation). vs. <reference osisRef="2co 8:9">2 Corinthians 8:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="ro 3:24">Romans 3:24</reference> See note, <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Joh 1:17">John 1:17</reference>")</hi>.

<hi type="bold">fullness</hi><div eID="gen4488" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4489" type="x-p"/> The "fullness of the Gentiles" is the completion of the purpose of God in this age, viz. the outcalling from among the Gentiles of a people for Christ's name, "the church which is His body" <reference osisRef="eph 1:22 eph 1:23">Ephesians 1:22,23</reference> Cf ; <reference osisRef="ac 15:14">Acts 15:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="eph 4:11-13">Ephesians 4:11-13</reference>; <reference osisRef="1co 12:12 1co 12:13">1 Corinthians 12:12,13</reference>. It must be distinguished from "the times of the Gentiles" <reference osisRef="lu 21:24">Luke 21:24</reference>.<div eID="gen4489" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4490" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">mystery</hi> See note,<div eID="gen4490" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4491" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Mt 13:11">Matthew 13:11</reference>")</hi>.

<hi type="bold">Jacob</hi><div eID="gen4491" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4492" type="x-p"/> Summary: Israel, so named from the grandson of Abraham, was chosen for a fourfold mission:<div eID="gen4492" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(1) To witness to the unity of God in the midst of universal idolatry <reference osisRef="de 6:4">Deuteronomy 6:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="isa 43:10 isa 43:12">Isaiah 43:10,12,</reference></item> <item type="x-indent-1">(2) to illustrate to the nations the blessedness of serving the true God <reference osisRef="de 33:26-29">Deuteronomy 33:26-29</reference>; <reference osisRef="1ch 17:20 1ch 17:21">1 Chronicles 17:20,21</reference>; <reference osisRef="ps 144:15">Psalms 144:15</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(3) to receive, preserve, and transmit the Scripture <reference osisRef="de 4:5-8">Deuteronomy 4:5-8</reference>; <reference osisRef="ro 3:1 ro 3:2">Romans 3:1,2</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(4) to produce, as to His humanity, the Messiah <reference osisRef="ge 3:15">Genesis 3:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="ge 12:3"> 12:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="ge 22:18"> 22:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="ge 28:10-14"> 28:10-14</reference>; <reference osisRef="ge 49:10"> 49:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="2sa 7:12-16">2 Samuel 7:12-16</reference>; <reference osisRef="isa 7:14">Isaiah 7:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="isa 9:6"> 9:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="mt 1:1">Matthew 1:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="ro 1:3">Romans 1:3</reference>. According to the prophets, Israel, regathered from all nations, restored to her own land and converted, is yet to have her greatest earthly exaltation and glory. See "Kingdom (O.T.)" ; <reference osisRef="ge 1:26">Genesis 1:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="zec 12:8">Zechariah 12:8</reference>.</item> </list> <div sID="gen4493" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Zec 12:8">Zechariah 12:8</reference>")</hi> N.T. <reference osisRef="lu 1:31-33">Luke 1:31-33</reference>; <reference osisRef="1co 15:24">1 Corinthians 15:24</reference>.<div eID="gen4493" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4494" type="x-p"/> "Davidic Covenant" <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:2Sa 7:16">2 Samuel 7:16</reference>")</hi>.<div eID="gen4494" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4495" type="x-p"/> For Another Point of View: See Topic 301242 <div eID="gen4495" type="x-p"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv129"/><title type="x-s">Book Introduction - 1 Corinthians</title> <div sID="gen4520" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1co 1">Read first chapter of 1 Corinthians</reference><div eID="gen4520" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4521" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">WRITER</hi>: The Apostle Paul. His relation to the church at Corinth is set forth in <reference osisRef="ac 18:1-18">Acts 18:1-18</reference> and in the Epistles to the Corinthians.<div eID="gen4521" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4522" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">DATE</hi>: First Corinthians was written in A.D. 59, at the close of Paul's three year's residence in Ephesus. <reference osisRef="ac 20:31">Acts 20:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="1co 16:5-8">1 Corinthians 16:5-8</reference>.<div eID="gen4522" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4523" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">THEME</hi>: The subjects treated are various, but may all be classified under the general theme, Christian conduct. Even the tremendous revelation of the truth concerning resurrection is made to bear upon that theme <reference osisRef="1co 15:58">1 Corinthians 15:58</reference>. The occasion of the Epistle was a letter on inquiry from Corinth concerning marriage, and the use of meats offered to idols ; <reference osisRef="1co 7:1">1 Corinthians 7:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="1co 8:1-13"> 8:1-13</reference> but the apostle was much more exercised by reports of the deepening divisions and increasing contentions in the church, and of a case of incest which had not been judged ; <reference osisRef="1co 1:10-12">1 Corinthians 1:10-12</reference>; <reference osisRef="1co 5:1"> 5:1</reference>.<div eID="gen4523" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4524" type="x-p"/> The factions were not due to heresies, but to the carnality of the restless Corinthians, and to their Greek admiration of "wisdom" and eloquence. The abomination of human leadership in the things of God is here rebuked. Minor disorders were due to vanity, yielding to a childish delight in tongue and the sign gifts, rather than to sober instruction (<reference osisRef="1co 14:1-28">1 Corinthians 14:1-28</reference>). Paul defends his apostleship because it involved the authority of the doctrine revealed through him.<div eID="gen4524" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4525" type="x-p"/> A rigid analysis of First Corinthians is not possible, The Epistle is not a treatise, but came from the Spirit through the apostle's grief, solicitude, and holy indignation. The following analysis may, however, be helpful.<div eID="gen4525" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">Introduction: The believer's standing in grace, 1:1-9</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The contrast of their present factious state, 1:10-4:21.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">Immorality rebuked; discipline enjoined, 5:1-6,8.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The sanctity of the body, and Christian marriage, 6:9-7,40.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">Meats, and the limitations of Christian liberty, 8:1-11:1.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">Christian order and the Lord's Supper, 11:2-34</item> <item type="x-indent-1">Spiritual gifts in relation to the body, the church, and Christian ministry, 12:1-14,40.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The resurrection of the dead, 15:1-58</item> <item type="x-indent-1">Special directions and greetings, 16:1-24.</item> </list> <div sID="gen4526" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv129"/> <hi type="bold">them</hi> <div eID="gen4526" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4527" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1co 1:2-9">1 Corinthians 1:2-9,</reference> in contrast with 1Co 10-13, illustrate a distinction constantly made in the Epistles between the believer's position in Christ Jesus, in the family of God, and his walk, or actual state. Christian position in grace is the result of the work of Christ, and is fully entered the moment that Christ is received by faith ; <reference osisRef="joh 1:12 joh 1:13">John 1:12,13</reference>; <reference osisRef="ro 8:1 ro 8:15-17">Romans 8:1,15-17</reference>; <reference osisRef="1co 1:2 1co 1:30">1 Corinthians 1:2,30</reference>; <reference osisRef="1co 12:12 1co 12:13"> 12:12,13</reference>; <reference osisRef="ga 3:26">Galatians 3:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="eph 1:3-14">Ephesians 1:3-14</reference>; <reference osisRef="eph 2:4-9"> 2:4-9</reference>; <reference osisRef="1pe 2:9">1 Peter 2:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 1:6">Revelation 1:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 5:9 re 5:10"> 5:9,10</reference>. The weakest, most ignorant, and fallible believer has precisely the same relationships in grace as the most illustrious saint. All the after work of God in his behalf, the application of the word to walk and conscience ; <reference osisRef="joh 17:17">John 17:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="eph 5:26">Ephesians 5:26</reference> the divine chastenings ; <reference osisRef="1co 11:32">1 Corinthians 11:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="heb 12:10">Hebrews 12:10,</reference> the ministry of the Spirit <reference osisRef="eph 4:11 eph 4:12">Ephesians 4:11,12</reference> the difficulties and trials of the path <reference osisRef="1pe 4:12 1pe 4:13">1 Peter 4:12,13</reference> and the final transformation at the appearing of Christ <reference osisRef="1jo 3:2">1 John 3:2</reference> have for their object to make the believer's character conform to his exalted position in Christ. He grows in grace, not into grace.

<hi type="bold">for the grace</hi><div eID="gen4527" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4528" type="x-p"/> Grace (imparted). <reference osisRef="1co 3:10">1 Corinthians 3:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="ro 6:1">Romans 6:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="2pe 3:18">2 Peter 3:18</reference>.

<hi type="bold">coming</hi><div eID="gen4528" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4529" type="x-p"/> Three words are used in connection with the return of the Lord:<div eID="gen4529" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(1) Parousia, "personal presence," also used by Paul of the "coming" of Stephanas <reference osisRef="1co 16:17">1 Corinthians 16:17</reference> of Titus <reference osisRef="2co 7:6 2co 7:7">2 Corinthians 7:6,7</reference> and of his own "coming" to Philippi <reference osisRef="php 1:26">Philippians 1:26</reference>. The word means simply personal presence, and is used of the return of the Lord as that event relates to the blessing of the saints ; <reference osisRef="1co 15:23">1 Corinthians 15:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="1th 4:14 1th 4:17">1 Thessalonians 4:14,17</reference> and to the destruction of the man of sin <reference osisRef="2th 2:8">2 Thessalonians 2:8</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(2) Apokalupsis, "unveiling," "revelation." The use of this word emphasizes the visibility of the Lord's return. It is used of the Lord <reference osisRef="2th 1:7">2 Thessalonians 1:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="1pe 1:7 1pe 1:13">1 Peter 1:7,13</reference>; <reference osisRef="1pe 4:13"> 4:13</reference> of the sons of God in connection with the Lord's return <reference osisRef="ro 8:19">Romans 8:19</reference> and of the man of sin <reference osisRef="2th 2:3 2th 2:6 2th 2:8">2 Thessalonians 2:3,6,8</reference> and always implies visibility.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(3) Epiphaneia, "appearing," trans. "brightness" <reference osisRef="2th 2:8">2 Thessalonians 2:8</reference> A.V.; "manifestation," R.V.), and means simply an appearing. It is used of both advents. ; <reference osisRef="2ti 1:10">2 Timothy 1:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="2th 2:8">2 Thessalonians 2:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="1ti 6:14">1 Timothy 6:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="2ti 4:1 2ti 4:8">2 Timothy 4:1,8</reference>; <reference osisRef="tit 2:13">Titus 2:13</reference>.</item> </list> <div sID="gen4530" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">coming</hi> (Greek - revelation, unveiling).

<hi type="bold">day of our Lord Jesus</hi><div eID="gen4530" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4531" type="x-p"/> The expression "day of Christ," occurs in the following passages: <reference osisRef="1co 1:8">1 Corinthians 1:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="1co 5:5"> 5:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="2co 1:14">2 Corinthians 1:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="php 1:6 php 1:10">Philippians 1:6,10</reference>; <reference osisRef="php 2:16"> 2:16</reference>. A.V. has "day of Christ," <reference osisRef="2th 2:2">2 Thessalonians 2:2</reference> incorrectly, for "day of the Lord" ; <reference osisRef="isa 2:12">Isaiah 2:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 19:11-21">Revelation 19:11-21</reference> The "day of Christ" relates wholly to the reward and blessing of saints at his coming, as "day of the Lord" is connected with judgment.

<hi type="bold">words</hi><div eID="gen4545" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(1) The writers of Scripture invariably affirm, where the subject is mentioned by them at all, that the words of their writings are divinely taught. This, of necessity, refers to the original documents, not to translations and versions; but the labours of competent scholars have brought our English versions to a degree of perfection so remarkable that we may confidently rest upon them as authoritative.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(2) <reference osisRef="1co 2:9-14">1 Corinthians 2:9-14</reference> gives the process by which a truth passes from the mind of God to the minds of His people.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(a) The unseen things of God are undiscoverable by the natural man (<reference osisRef="1co 2:9">1 Corinthians 2:9</reference>). (b) These unseen things God has revealed to chosen men (<reference osisRef="1co 2:10-12">1 Corinthians 2:10-12</reference>). (c) The revealed things are communicated in Spirit-taught words (<reference osisRef="1co 2:13">1 Corinthians 2:13</reference>). This implies neither mechanical dictation nor the effacement of the writer's personality, but only that the Spirit infallibly guides in the choice of words from the writer's own vocabulary (<reference osisRef="1co 2:13">1 Corinthians 2:13</reference>). (d) These Spirit-taught words, in which the revelation has been expressed, are discerned, as to their true spiritual content, only by the spiritual among believers ; <reference osisRef="1co 2:15 1co 2:16">1 Corinthians 2:15,16</reference>; <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Re 22:19">Revelation 22:19</reference>")</hi>. </item> </list>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv130"/><div sID="gen4546" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv130"/> <hi type="bold">natural man</hi> <div eID="gen4546" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4547" type="x-p"/> Paul divides men into three classes: psuchikos, "of the senses" <reference osisRef="jas 3:15">James 3:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="jude 1:19">Jude 1:19</reference> or "natural," i.e. the Adamic man, unrenewed through the new birth <reference osisRef="joh 3:3 joh 3:5">John 3:3,5</reference> pneumatikos, "spiritual," i.e. the renewed man as Spirit-filled and walking in the Spirit in full communion with God <reference osisRef="eph 5:18-20">Ephesians 5:18-20</reference> and sarkikos, "carnal," "fleshly," i.e. the renewed man who, walking "after the flesh," remains a babe in Christ <reference osisRef="1co 3:1-4">1 Corinthians 3:1-4</reference>. The natural man may be learned, gentle, eloquent, fascinating, but the spiritual content of Scripture is absolutely hidden from him; and the fleshly, or carnal, Christian is able to comprehend only its simplest truths, "milk" <reference osisRef="1co 3:2">1 Corinthians 3:2</reference>. <div eID="gen4547" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv131"/><div sID="gen4548" type="x-p"/> <chapter eID="1Cor.2"/>

<hi type="bold">fell in one day</hi><div eID="gen4599" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4600" type="x-p"/> Cf. <reference osisRef="nu 25:9">Numbers 25:9</reference>. A discrepancy has been imagined. <reference osisRef="1co 10:8">1 Corinthians 10:8</reference>. gives the number of deaths in "one day"; <reference osisRef="nu 25:9">Numbers 25:9,</reference> the total number of deaths "in the plague." Some discrepant statements concerning numbers are, however, found in the existing manuscripts of the Hebrew Scriptures. These are most naturally ascribed to the fact that the Hebrews used letters in the place of numerals. The letters for Koph to Tau express hundreds up to four hundred. Five certain Hebrew letters, written in a different form, carry hundreds up to nine hundred, while thousands are expressed by two dots over the proper unit letter: e.g. the letter Teth, used alone, stands for 9; with two dots it stands for nine thousand. Error in transcription of Hebrew numbers thus becomes easy, preservation of numerical accuracy difficult.
