<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv158"/><title type="x-s">Book Introduction - 1 Peter</title> <div sID="gen5226" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1pe 1">Read first chapter of 1 Peter</reference><div eID="gen5226" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5227" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">WRITER</hi>: The Apostle Peter (<reference osisRef="1pe 1:1">1 Peter 1:1</reference>)<div eID="gen5227" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5228" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">DATE</hi>: Probably A.D. 60. That "Babylon" refers to the former city on the Euphrates, or to Rome, cannot be inferred from <reference osisRef="1pe 5:13">1 Peter 5:13</reference>. The text is obscure.<div eID="gen5228" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5229" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">THEME</hi>: While Peter undoubtedly has scattered Jewish believers in mind, his Epistles comprehend Gentile believers also (<reference osisRef="1pe 2:10">1 Peter 2:10</reference>). The present Epistle, written from a church on Gentile ground (<reference osisRef="1pe 5:13">1 Peter 5:13</reference>), presents all the foundational truths of the Christian faith, with special emphasis on the atonement. The distinctive note of First Peter is preparation for victory over suffering. The last-name word occurs about fifteen times, and is the key-word to the Epistle.<div eID="gen5229" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5230" type="x-p"/> The Epistle is in three parts:<div eID="gen5230" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">Christian suffering and conduct in the light of full salvation, 1:1-2:8</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The believer's life in view of his sevenfold position, and of the vicarious suffering of Christ, 2:9-4:19</item> <item type="x-indent-1">Christian service in the light of the coming of the Chief Shepherd, 5:1-14</item> </list> <div sID="gen5231" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv158"/> <hi type="bold">sins</hi> <div eID="gen5231" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5232" type="x-p"/> Sin. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ro 3:23">Romans 3:23</reference>")</hi>.

<hi type="bold">Elect</hi><div eID="gen5232" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5233" type="x-p"/> Election, Summary: In both Testaments the Hebrew and Greek words are rendered "elect," "election," "choose," "chosen." In all cases they mean, simply, "chosen," or "to choose"; and are used of both human and divine choices.<div eID="gen5233" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(1) In the latter use election is: (a) corporate, as of the nation of Israel, or the church <reference osisRef="isa 45:4">Isaiah 45:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="eph 1:4">Ephesians 1:4</reference> and (b) individual <reference osisRef="1pe 1:2">1 Peter 1:2</reference></item> <item type="x-indent-1">(2) Election is according to the foreknowledge of God <reference osisRef="1pe 1:2">1 Peter 1:2</reference> and wholly of grace, apart from human merit ; <reference osisRef="ro 9:11">Romans 9:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="ro 11:5 ro 11:6"> 11:5,6</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(3) Election proceeds from the divine volition <reference osisRef="joh 15:16">John 15:16</reference>.</item> </list> <div sID="gen5234" type="x-p"/> Election is, therefore:<div eID="gen5234" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-2">(1) The sovereign act of God in grace whereby certain are chosen from among mankind for Himself. <reference osisRef="joh 15:19">John 15:19</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-2">(2) The sovereign act of God whereby certain elect persons are chosen for distinctive service for Him. <reference osisRef="lu 6:13">Luke 6:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="ac 9:15">Acts 9:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="1co 1:27 1co 1:28">1 Corinthians 1:27,28</reference> </item> </list>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv159"/><div sID="gen5235" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv159"/> <hi type="bold">might</hi> <div eID="gen5235" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5236" type="x-p"/> Suffering, in First Peter, is set in the light of:<div eID="gen5236" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(1) assured salvation, <reference osisRef="1pe 1:2-5">1 Peter 1:2-5</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(2) the greater glory at Christ's appearing, <reference osisRef="1pe 1:7">1 Peter 1:7</reference>;</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(3) Christ's sufferings and coming glories, <reference osisRef="1pe 1:11">1 Peter 1:11</reference></item> <item type="x-indent-1">(4) the believer's association with Him in both, <reference osisRef="1pe 2:20 1pe 2:21">1 Peter 2:20,21</reference>; <reference osisRef="1pe 3:17 1pe 3:18"> 3:17,18</reference> <reference osisRef="1pe 4:12 1pe 4:13"> 4:12,13</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(5) the purifying effect of suffering, <reference osisRef="1pe 1:7">1 Peter 1:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="1pe 4:1 1pe 4:2"> 4:1,2</reference>; <reference osisRef="1pe 5:10"> 5:10</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(6) that Christ is now glorified in the believer's patient suffering, <reference osisRef="1pe 4:16">1 Peter 4:16</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(7) that suffering is disciplinary, <reference osisRef="1pe 4:17-19">1 Peter 4:17-19</reference>; <reference osisRef="1co 11:31 1co 11:32">1 Corinthians 11:31,32</reference>; <reference osisRef="heb 12:5-13">Hebrews 12:5-13</reference>. </item> </list>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv160"/><div sID="gen5237" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv160"/> <hi type="bold">salvation</hi> <div eID="gen5237" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5238" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ro 1:16">Romans 1:16</reference>")</hi>.

<hi type="bold">for the grace</hi><div eID="gen5238" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5239" type="x-p"/> Grace (in salvation). <reference osisRef="1pe 5:12">1 Peter 5:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="ro 3:24">Romans 3:24</reference> <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Joh 1:17">John 1:17</reference>")</hi>.
<hi type="bold">redeemed</hi><div eID="gen5239" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5240" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ro 3:24">Romans 3:24</reference>")</hi>.

<hi type="bold">foreordained</hi><div eID="gen5240" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5241" type="x-p"/> The divine order is foreknowledge, election, predestination. That foreknowledge determines the election or choice is clear from <reference osisRef="1pe 1:2">1 Peter 1:2</reference> and predestination is the bringing to pass of the election. "election looks back to foreknowledge; predestination forward to the destiny." But Scripture nowhere declares what it is in the divine foreknowledge which determines the divine election and predestination. The foreknown are elected, and the elect are predestinated, and this election is certain to every believer by the mere fact that he believes <reference osisRef="1th 1:4 1th 1:5">1 Thessalonians 1:4,5</reference><div eID="gen5241" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5242" type="x-p"/> See Predestination <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Eph 1:5">Ephesians 1:5</reference>")</hi>. <chapter eID="1Pet.1"/><div eID="gen5242" type="x-p"/>
<div sID="gen5243" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="2" osisID="1Pet.2" sID="1Pet.2"/>

<hi type="bold">stone of stumbling</hi> <div eID="gen5243" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5244" type="x-p"/> Christ crucified is the Rock:<div eID="gen5244" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(1) Smitten that the Spirit of life may flow from Him to all who will drink <reference osisRef="ex 17:6">Exodus 17:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="1co 10:4">1 Corinthians 10:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="joh 4:13 joh 4:14">John 4:13,14</reference>; <reference osisRef="joh 7:37-39"> 7:37-39</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(2) To the church the foundation and chief corner Stone <reference osisRef="eph 2:20">Ephesians 2:20</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(3) To the Jews at His first coming a "stumbling stone" <reference osisRef="ro 9:32 ro 9:33">Romans 9:32,33</reference>; <reference osisRef="1co 1:23">1 Corinthians 1:23</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(4) to Israel at His second coming the "headstone of the corner" <reference osisRef="zec 4:7">Zechariah 4:7</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(5) To the Gentile world-power the smiting "stone cut out without hands" <reference osisRef="da 2:34">Daniel 2:34</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(6) In the divine purpose the Stone which, after the destruction of Gentile world- power, is to grow and fill the earth.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(7) To unbelievers the crushing Stone of judgment. <reference osisRef="mt 21:44">Matthew 21:44</reference>. </item> </list>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv161"/><div sID="gen5245" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv161"/> <hi type="bold">priesthood</hi> <div eID="gen5245" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5246" type="x-p"/> The New Testament priesthood, Summary:<div eID="gen5246" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(1) Until the law was given the head of each family was the family priest <reference osisRef="ge 8:20">Genesis 8:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="ge 26:25"> 26:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="ge 31:54"> 31:54</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(2) When the law was proposed, the promise to perfect obedience was that Israel would be unto God "a kingdom of priests" <reference osisRef="ex 19:6">Exodus 19:6</reference>. but Israel violated the law, and God shut up the priestly office to the Aaronic family, appointing the tribe of Levi to minister to them, thus constituting the typical priesthood <reference osisRef="ex 28:1">Exodus 28:1</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(3) In the dispensation of grace, all believers are unconditionally constituted a "kingdom of priests" <reference osisRef="1pe 2:9">1 Peter 2:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 1:6">Revelation 1:6</reference> the distinction which Israel failed to achieve by works. The priesthood of the believer is, therefore, a birthright; just as every descendant of Aaron was born to the priesthood <reference osisRef="heb 5:1">Hebrews 5:1</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(4) The chief privilege of a priest is access to God. Under law the high priest only could enter "the holiest of all," and that but once a year <reference osisRef="heb 9:7">Hebrews 9:7,</reference> but when Christ died, the veil, type of Christ's human body <reference osisRef="heb 10:20">Hebrews 10:20</reference> was rent, so that now the believer-priests, equally with Christ the High Priest, have access to God in the holiest <reference osisRef="heb 10:19-22">Hebrews 10:19-22</reference>.</item> </list> <div sID="gen5247" type="x-p"/> The high Priest is corporeally there <reference osisRef="heb 4:14-16">Hebrews 4:14-16</reference>; <reference osisRef="heb 9:24"> 9:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="heb 10:19-22"> 10:19-22</reference>.<div eID="gen5247" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(5) In the exercise of his office the New Testament believer-priest is</item> <item type="x-indent-2">(1) a sacrificer who offers a threefold sacrifice: (a) his own living body. <reference osisRef="ro 12:1">Romans 12:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="php 2:17">Philippians 2:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="2ti 4:6">2 Timothy 4:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="1jo 3:16">1 John 3:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="jas 1:27">James 1:27</reference> (b) praise to God, "the fruit of the lips that make mention of His name" (R.V.), to be offered "continually" ; <reference osisRef="heb 13:15">Hebrews 13:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="ex 25:22">Exodus 25:22</reference> "I will commune with thee from above the mercy seat"); (c) his substance ; <reference osisRef="heb 13:16">Hebrews 13:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="ro 12:13">Romans 12:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="ga 6:6">Galatians 6:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="3jo 1:5-8">3 John 1:5-8</reference>; <reference osisRef="heb 13:2">Hebrews 13:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="ga 6:10">Galatians 6:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="tit 3:14">Titus 3:14</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-2">(2) The N.T. priest is also an intercessor <reference osisRef="1ti 2:1">1 Timothy 2:1</reference>; <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv163"/><title type="x-s">Book Introduction - 2 Peter</title> <div sID="gen5275" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2pe 1">Read first chapter of 2 Peter</reference><div eID="gen5275" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5276" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">WRITER</hi>: The Apostle Peter (<reference osisRef="2pe 1:1">2 Peter 1:1</reference>)<div eID="gen5276" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5277" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">DATE</hi>: Probably A.D. 66<div eID="gen5277" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5278" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">THEME</hi>: Second Peter and Second Timothy have much in common. In both, the writers are aware that martyrdom is near (<reference osisRef="2ti 4:6">2 Timothy 4:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="2pe 1:14">2 Peter 1:14</reference> with ; <reference osisRef="joh 21:18 joh 21:19">John 21:18,19</reference>); both are singularly sustained and joyful; both foresee the apostasy in which the history of the professing church will end. Paul finds that apostasy in its last stage when the so-called laity <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Re 2:6">Revelation 2:6</reference>")</hi> , have become infected (<reference osisRef="2ti 3:1-5">2 Timothy 3:1-5</reference>; <reference osisRef="2ti 4:3 2ti 4:4"> 4:3,4</reference>); Peter traces the origin of the apostasy to false teachers (<reference osisRef="2pe 2:1-3 2pe 2:15-19">2 Peter 2:1-3,15-19</reference>). In Peter the false teachers deny redemption truth (<reference osisRef="2pe 2:1">2 Peter 2:1</reference>); we shall find in First John a deeper depth--denial of the truth concerning Christ's person (<reference osisRef="1jo 4:1-5">1 John 4:1-5</reference>). In Jude all phases of the apostasy are seen. But in none of these Epistles is the tone one of dejection or pessimism. God and His promises are still the resource of the believer.<div eID="gen5278" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5279" type="x-p"/> The Epistle is in four divisions:<div eID="gen5279" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">The great Christian virtues, 1:1-14</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The Scriptures exalted, 1:15-21</item> <item type="x-indent-1">Warnings concerning apostate teachers, 2:1-22</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The second coming of Christ and the day of Jehovah, 3:1-18</item> </list> <div sID="gen5280" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv163"/> <hi type="bold">grace</hi> <div eID="gen5280" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5281" type="x-p"/> Grace (imparted). <reference osisRef="ro 6:1">Romans 6:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="2pe 3:18">2 Peter 3:18</reference>

<hi type="bold">holy mount</hi><div eID="gen5283" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5284" type="x-p"/> Where the reference is to things, the meaning of "holy" or "sanctified" is, simply, set apart for the use of God, or rendered sacred by the divine presence.

<hi type="bold">whereunto</hi><div eID="gen5284" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5285" type="x-p"/> That is, made more sure by fulfilment in part. Fulfilled prophecy is a proof of inspiration because the Scripture predictions of future events were uttered so long before the events transpired that no merely human sagacity or foresight could have anticipated them, and these predictions are so detailed, minute, and specific, as to exclude the possibility that they were mere fortunate guesses. Hundreds of predictions concerning Israel, the land of Canaan, Babylon, Assyria, Egypt, and numerous personages--so ancient, so singular, so seemingly improbable, as well as so detailed and definite that no mortal could have anticipated them--have been fulfilled by the elements, and by men who were ignorant of them, or who utterly disbelieved them, or who struggled with frantic desperation to avoid their fulfilment. It is certain, therefore, that the Scriptures which contain them are inspired. "Prophecy came not in olden time by the will of man; but holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost" <reference osisRef="2pe 1:21">2 Peter 1:21</reference>.<div eID="gen5285" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5286" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a more sure</hi> Or, the word of prophecy made more sure.<div eID="gen5286" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5287" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dark place</hi> Or, squalid place. <reference osisRef="ps 119:105">Psalms 119:105</reference>; <reference osisRef="joh 1:4 joh 1:9">John 1:4,9</reference>.

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv164"/><title type="x-s">Book Introduction - 1 John</title> <div sID="gen5305" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1jo 1">Read first chapter of 1 John</reference><div eID="gen5305" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5306" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">WRITER</hi>: The Apostle John, as unbroken tradition affirms, and as internal evidence and comparison with the Gospel of John prove.<div eID="gen5306" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5307" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">DATE</hi>: Probably A.D. 90<div eID="gen5307" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5308" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">THEME</hi>: First John is a family letter from the Father to His "little children" who are in the world. With the possible exception of the Song, it is the most intimate of the inspired writings. The world is viewed as without. The sin of a believer is treated as a child's offence against his Father, and is dealt with as a family matter (<reference osisRef="1jo 1:9">1 John 1:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="1jo 2:1"> 2:1</reference>). The moral government of the universe is not in question. The child's sin as an offence against the law had been met in the Cross, and "Jesus Christ the righteous" is now his "Advocate with the Father." John's Gospel leads across the threshold of the Father's house; his first Epistle makes us at home there. A tender word is used for "children," teknia, "born ones," or "bairns." Paul is occupied with our public position as sons; John with our nearness as born-ones of the Father.<div eID="gen5308" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5309" type="x-p"/> First John is in two principal divisions.<div eID="gen5309" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">The family with the Father, 1:1-3:24.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The family and the world, 4:1-5:21.</item> </list> <div sID="gen5310" type="x-p"/> There is a secondary analysis in each division of which occurs the phrase, "My little children," as follows:<div eID="gen5310" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">Introductory, the incarnation, 1:1,2.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The little children and fellowship1:3-2:14</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The little children and secular and "religious" world2:15-28.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">How the little children may know each other, 2:29-3:10</item> <item type="x-indent-1">How the little children must live together, 3:11-24.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">Parenthetic: How the little children may know false teachers, 4:1-6.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The little children assured and warned, 4:7-5:21.</item> </list> <div sID="gen5311" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv164"/><hi type="bold">grace</hi> Grace (imparted). Summary (see "Grace,") <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Joh 1:17">John 1:17</reference>")</hi> grace is not only dispensationally a method of divine dealing in salvation<div eID="gen5311" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5312" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Joh 1:17">John 1:17</reference>")</hi> but is also the method of God in the believer's life and service. As saved, he is "not under the law, but under grace" <reference osisRef="ro 6:14">Romans 6:14</reference>. Having by grace brought the believer into the highest conceivable position. <reference osisRef="eph 1:6">Ephesians 1:6</reference>. God ceaselessly works through grace, to impart to, and perfect in him, corresponding graces ; <reference osisRef="joh 15:4 joh 15:5">John 15:4,5</reference>; <reference osisRef="ga 5:22 ga 5:23">Galatians 5:22,23</reference>.<div eID="gen5312" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5313" type="x-p"/> Grace, therefore, stands connected with service <reference osisRef="ro 12:6">Romans 12:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="ro 15:15 ro 15:16"> 15:15,16</reference>; <reference osisRef="1co 1:3-7">1 Corinthians 1:3-7</reference>; <reference osisRef="1co 3:10"> 3:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="1co 15:10"> 15:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="2co 12:9 2co 12:10">2 Corinthians 12:9,10</reference>; <reference osisRef="ga 2:9">Galatians 2:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="eph 3:7 eph 3:8">Ephesians 3:7,8</reference>; <reference osisRef="eph 4:7">Ephesians 4:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="php 1:7">Philippians 1:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="2ti 2:1 2ti 2:2">2 Timothy 2:1,2</reference>; <reference osisRef="1pe 4:10">1 Peter 4:10</reference> with Christian growth ; <reference osisRef="2co 1:12">2 Corinthians 1:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="eph 4:29">Ephesians 4:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="col 3:16">Colossians 3:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="col 4:6"> 4:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="2th 1:12">2 Thessalonians 1:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="heb 4:16">Hebrews 4:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="heb 12:28 heb 12:29"> 12:28,29</reference>; <reference osisRef="heb 13:9"> 13:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="jas 4:6">James 4:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="1pe 1:2">1 Peter 1:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="1pe 3:7"> 3:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="1pe 5:5 1pe 5:10"> 5:5,10</reference>; <reference osisRef="2pe 3:18">2 Peter 3:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="jude 1:4">Jude 1:4</reference> and with giving ; <reference osisRef="2co 4:15">2 Corinthians 4:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="2co 8:1 2co 8:6 2co 8:7 2co 8:19"> 8:1,6,7,19</reference>; <reference osisRef="2co 9:14"> 9:14</reference><div eID="gen5313" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5314" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">grace</hi> Grace (imparted). <reference osisRef="ro 6:1">Romans 6:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="2pe 3:18">2 Peter 3:18</reference>.

<hi type="bold">light</hi><div eID="gen5314" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5315" type="x-p"/> What it is to "walk in the light" is explained by <reference osisRef="1jo 1:8-10">1 John 1:8-10</reference>. "All things...are made manifest by the light" <reference osisRef="eph 5:13">Ephesians 5:13</reference> The presence of God brings the consciousness of sin in the nature <reference osisRef="1jo 1:8">1 John 1:8</reference> and sins in the life <reference osisRef="1jo 1:9 1jo 1:10">1 John 1:9,10</reference>. The blood of Christ is the divine provision for both. To walk in the light is to live in fellowship with the Father and the Son. Sin interrupts, but confession restores that fellowship. Immediate confession keeps the fellowship unbroken.<div eID="gen5315" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5316" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">light</hi> <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ex 27:20">Exodus 27:20</reference>")</hi> <chapter eID="1John.1"/> <div eID="gen5316" type="x-p"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv166"/><title type="x-s">Book Introduction - 2 John</title> <div sID="gen5349" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2jo 1">Read first chapter of 2 John</reference><div eID="gen5349" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5350" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">WRITER</hi>: The Apostle John.<div eID="gen5350" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5351" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">DATE</hi>: Probably A.D. 90.<div eID="gen5351" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5352" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">THEME</hi>: Second John gives the essentials of the personal walk of the believer in a day when "many deceivers are entered into the world" (<reference osisRef="2jo 1:7">2 John 1:7</reference>). The key phrase is "the truth," by which John means the body of revealed truth, the Scriptures. The Bible as the only authority for doctrine and life, is the believer's resource in a time of declension and apostasy.<div eID="gen5352" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5353" type="x-p"/> The Epistle in three divisions:<div eID="gen5353" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">The pathway of truth and love, vs. 1-6</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The peril of unscriptural ways, vs. 7-11</item> <item type="x-indent-1">Superscription, vs. 12,13</item> </list> <div sID="gen5354" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv166"/> <hi type="bold">that we love one another</hi> <div eID="gen5354" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5355" type="x-p"/> Law (of Christ), Summary: The new "law of Christ" is the divine love, as wrought into the renewed heart by the Holy Spirit <reference osisRef="ro 5:5">Romans 5:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="heb 10:16">Hebrews 10:16</reference> and outflowing in the energy of the Spirit, unforced and spontaneous, toward the objects of the divine love ; <reference osisRef="2co 5:14-20">2 Corinthians 5:14-20</reference>; <reference osisRef="1th 2:7 1th 2:8">1 Thessalonians 2:7,8</reference>. It is, therefore, " the law of liberty" ; <reference osisRef="jas 1:25">James 1:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="jas 2:12"> 2:12</reference> in contrast with the external law of Moses. Moses' law demands love, ; <reference osisRef="le 19:18">Leviticus 19:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="de 6:5">Deuteronomy 6:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="lu 10:27">Luke 10:27</reference> Christ's law is love ; <reference osisRef="ro 5:5">Romans 5:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="1jo 4:7 1jo 4:19 1jo 4:20">1 John 4:7,19,20</reference> and so takes the place of the external law by fulfilling it ; <reference osisRef="ro 13:10">Romans 13:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="ga 5:14">Galatians 5:14</reference>. It is the "law written in the heart" under the New Covenant.<div eID="gen5355" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5356" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Heb 8:8">Hebrews 8:8</reference>")</hi>.

<hi type="bold">world</hi><div eID="gen5356" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5357" type="x-p"/> kosmos = mankind. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Mt 4:8">Matthew 4:8</reference>")</hi>.

<hi type="bold">transgresseth</hi><div eID="gen5357" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5358" type="x-p"/> Sin. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ro 3:23">Romans 3:23</reference>")</hi>. <chapter eID="2John.1"/><div eID="gen5358" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen5348" osisID="2John" type="book"/>

<chapter n="1" osisID="3John.1" sID="3John.1"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv167"/><title type="x-s">Book Introduction - 3 John</title> <div sID="gen5360" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="3jo 1">Read first chapter of 3 John</reference><div eID="gen5360" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5361" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">WRITER</hi>: The Apostle John.<div eID="gen5361" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5362" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">DATE</hi>: Probably about A.D. 90.<div eID="gen5362" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5363" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">THEME</hi>: The aged Apostle had written to a church which allowed one Diotrephes to exercise an authority common enough in later ages, but wholly new in the primitive churches. Diotrephes had rejected the apostolic letters and authority. It appears also that he had refused the ministry of the visiting brethren (<reference osisRef="3jo 1:10">3 John 1:10</reference>), and cast out those that had received them. Historically, this letter marks the beginning of that clerical and priestly assumption over the churches in which the primitive church order disappeared. This Epistle reveals, as well, the believer's resource in such a day. No longer writing as an apostle, but as an elder, John addresses this letter, not to the church as such, but to a faithful man in the church for the comfort and encouragement of those who were standing fast in the primitive simplicity. Second John conditions the personal walk of the Christian in a day of apostasy; Third John the personal responsibility in such a day of the believer as a member of the local church. The key-phrase is "the truth" (see 2 John, Introduction).<div eID="gen5363" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5364" type="x-p"/> There are three divisions:<div eID="gen5364" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">Personal greetings, vs. 1-4</item> <item type="x-indent-1">Instructions concerning ministering brethren, vs. 5-8</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The apostate leader and the good Demetrius, vs. 9-14 </ol></item> </list> <chapter eID="3John.1"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen5359" osisID="3John" type="book"/>
<div canonical="true" osisID="Jude" sID="gen5365" type="book"/> <milestone n="" type="x-usfm-toc1"/> <milestone n="" type="x-usfm-toc2"/> <milestone n="" type="x-usfm-toc3"/>
<chapter n="1" osisID="Jude.1" sID="Jude.1"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv167"/><title type="x-s">Book Introduction - Jude</title> <div sID="gen5366" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="jude 1">Read first chapter of Jude</reference><div eID="gen5366" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5367" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">WRITER</hi>: Jude, the brother of James (<reference osisRef="jude 1:1">Jude 1:1</reference>)<div eID="gen5367" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5368" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">DATE</hi>: Probably A.D. 66<div eID="gen5368" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5369" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">THEME</hi>: It is not so much Jude who speaks, as the constraining Spirit (<reference osisRef="jude 1:3">Jude 1:3</reference>) and the theme is, "Contending for the faith" (<reference osisRef="lu 18:8">Luke 18:8</reference>), <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Lu 18:8">Luke 18:8</reference>")</hi>. In this brief letter the apostasy (See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:2th 2:3">2 Thessalonians 2:3</reference>") of the professing church is predicted, and the cause and course described. As in Second Timothy and Second Peter the apostasy is treated as having already set in.<div eID="gen5369" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5370" type="x-p"/> The Epistle is in five divisions:<div eID="gen5370" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">Introduction vs. 1,2</item> <item type="x-indent-1">Occasion of the Epistle, vs. 3,4</item> <item type="x-indent-1">Apostasy is possible, vs. 5-7</item> <item type="x-indent-1">Apostate teachers described, vs. 8-19</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The saints assured and comforted, vs. 20-25</item> </list> <div sID="gen5371" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv167"/> <hi type="bold">preserved</hi> <div eID="gen5371" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5372" type="x-p"/> Assurance is the believer's full conviction that, through the work of Christ alone, received by faith, he is in possession of a salvation in which he will be eternally kept. And this assurance rests only upon the Scripture promises to him who believes.

<hi type="bold">salvation</hi> <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ro 1:16">Romans 1:16</reference>")</hi>.<div eID="gen5372" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5373" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">it was needful</hi> Lit. constraint was upon me, i.e. of the Spirit.
<hi type="bold">saved</hi><div eID="gen5373" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5374" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ro 1:16">Romans 1:16</reference>")</hi>.

<hi type="bold">great day</hi><div eID="gen5374" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5375" type="x-p"/> The judgment of the fallen angels. The "great day" is the day of the Lord <reference osisRef="isa 2:9-22">Isaiah 2:9-22</reference>. As the final judgment upon Satan occurs after the thousand years, and preceding the final judgment <reference osisRef="re 20:10">Revelation 20:10</reference> it is congruous to conclude, as to the time, that other fallen angels are judged with him ; <reference osisRef="2pe 2:4">2 Peter 2:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 20:10">Revelation 20:10</reference>. Christians are associated with Christ in this judgment. For association with angels at judgment <reference osisRef="1co 6:3">1 Corinthians 6:3</reference>.<div eID="gen5375" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5376" type="x-p"/> For other information <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Re 20:12">Revelation 20:12</reference>")</hi>.<div eID="gen5376" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5377" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">angels</hi><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Heb 1:4">Hebrews 1:4</reference>")</hi>.

<hi type="bold">Cain</hi><div eID="gen5377" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5378" type="x-p"/> Cain (cf) <reference osisRef="ge 4:1">Genesis 4:1</reference> type of the religious natural man, who believes in a God, and in "religion," but after his own will, and who rejects redemption by blood. Compelled as a teacher of religion to explain atonement, the apostate teacher explains it away.<div eID="gen5378" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5379" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">error of Balaam</hi> <div eID="gen5379" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5380" type="x-p"/> Balaam, the "error" of Balaam must be distinguished from his "way" <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:2Pe 2:15">2 Peter 2:15</reference>")</hi> and his "doctrine" See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:re 2:14">Revelation 2:14</reference>".<div eID="gen5380" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5381" type="x-p"/> The "error" of Balaam was that, reasoning from natural morality and seeing the evil in Israel, he supposed a righteous God must curse them. He was blind to the higher morality of the Cross, through which God maintains and enforces the authority and awful sanctions of His law, so that He can be just and the justifier of a believing sinner. The "reward" of <reference osisRef="jude 1:11">Jude 1:11</reference> may not be money, but popularity, or applause.<div eID="gen5381" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5382" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Core</hi> <div eID="gen5382" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5383" type="x-p"/> See Nu 16. The sin of Korah was denial of the authority of Moses as God's chosen spokesman, and intrusion into the priest's office.<div eID="gen5383" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5384" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">gainsaying</hi> antilogia = against the Word.
<hi type="bold">sinners</hi><div eID="gen5384" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5385" type="x-p"/> Sin. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ro 3:23">Romans 3:23</reference>")</hi>.

<hi type="bold">flesh</hi><div eID="gen5385" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5386" type="x-p"/> Flesh, Summary: "Flesh," in the ethical sense, is the whole natural or unregenerate man, spirit, soul, and body, as centered upon self, prone to sin, and opposed to God <reference osisRef="ro 7:18">Romans 7:18</reference>. The regenerate man is not "in the sphere of the flesh," but in the sphere of the Spirit <reference osisRef="ro 8:9">Romans 8:9</reference> but the flesh is still in him, and he may, according to his choice, "walk after the flesh" or "in the Spirit" ; <reference osisRef="1co 3:1-4">1 Corinthians 3:1-4</reference>; <reference osisRef="ga 5:16 ga 5:17">Galatians 5:16,17</reference>. In the first case he is a "carnal," in the second a "spiritual," Christian. Victory over the flesh will be the habitual experience of the believer who walks in the Spirit ; <reference osisRef="ro 8:2 ro 8:4">Romans 8:2,4</reference>; <reference osisRef="ga 5:16 ga 5:17">Galatians 5:16,17</reference>. <chapter eID="Jude.1"/><div eID="gen5386" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen5365" osisID="Jude" type="book"/>
<div canonical="true" osisID="Rev" sID="gen5387" type="book"/> <milestone n="" type="x-usfm-toc1"/> <milestone n="" type="x-usfm-toc2"/> <milestone n="" type="x-usfm-toc3"/>
<chapter n="1" osisID="Rev.1" sID="Rev.1"/>

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv168"/><title type="x-s">Book Introduction - Revelation</title> <div sID="gen5388" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="re 1">Read first chapter of Revelation</reference><div eID="gen5388" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5389" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">WRITER</hi>: The Apostle John (<reference osisRef="re 1:1"> 1:1</reference>)<div eID="gen5389" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5390" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">DATE</hi>: A.D. 96<div eID="gen5390" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5391" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">THEME</hi>: The theme of the Revelation is Jesus Christ (<reference osisRef="re 1:1"> 1:1</reference>), presented in a threefold way:<div eID="gen5391" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">As to time: "which is, and which was, and which is to come" (1:4);</item> <item type="x-indent-1">As to relationships--the churches (1:9-3:22), to the tribulation (4:1-19:21), to the kingdom (20:1-22:21);</item> <item type="x-indent-1">In His offices--High Priest (8:3-6), Bridegroom (19:7-9), King-Judge (20:1-15).</item> </list> <div sID="gen5392" type="x-p"/> But while Christ is thus the central theme of the book, all of the events move toward one consummation, the bringing in of the covenanted kingdom. The key-phrase is the prophetic declaration of the "great voices in heaven" (<reference osisRef="re 11:15">Revelation 11:15</reference>), lit, "The world kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ has come." The book is, therefore, a prophecy (<reference osisRef="re 1:3">Revelation 1:3</reference>).<div eID="gen5392" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5393" type="x-p"/> The three major divisions of Revelation must be clearly held if the interpretation is to be sane and coherent. John was commanded to "write" concerning three classes of "things" (<reference osisRef="re 1:19">Revelation 1:19</reference>):<div eID="gen5393" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">Things past, "the things thou hast seen," i.e. the Patmos vision, 1:1-20.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">Things present, "the things which are," i.e. things then existing--obviously the churches. The temple had been destroyed, the Jews dispersed: the testimony of God had been committed to the Churches (<reference osisRef="1ti 3:15">1 Timothy 3:15</reference>). Accordingly we have seven messages to seven representative churches, <reference osisRef="1ti 2:1 1ti 3:22"> 2:1-3:22</reference>. It is noteworthy that the church is not mentioned in chapters 5-18.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">Things future, "things which shall be hereafter," lit. "after these," i.e. after the church period ends, 4:1-22:21. The third major division, as Erdman (W.J.) has pointed out, falls into a series of six sevens, with parenthetical passages, making, with the church division, seven sevens.</item> </list> <div sID="gen5394" type="x-p"/> The six sevens are:<div eID="gen5394" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">The seals, 4:1-8:1.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The seven trumpets, 8:2-11:19.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The seven personages, 12:1-14,20.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The seven vials (bowls), 15:1-16:21.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The seven dooms, 17:1-20:15.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The seven new things, 21:1-22:21.</item> </list> <div sID="gen5395" type="x-p"/> The parenthetical passages are:<div eID="gen5395" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">The Jewish remnant and the tribulation saints, 7:1-17.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The angel, the little book, the two witnesses, 10:1-11:14.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The Lamb, the Remnant, and the everlasting Gospel, 14:1-13.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The gathering of the kings at Armageddon, 16:13-16.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">The four alleluias in heaven, 19:1-6. These passages do not advance the prophetic narrative. Looking backward and forward they sum up results accomplished, and speak of results yet to come as if they had already come. In Re14:1, for example, the Lamb and Remnant are seen prophetically on Mount Sion, though they are not actually there till Re20:4-6.</ol></item> </list> <div sID="gen5396" type="x-p"/> The end of the church period (2-3.) is left indeterminate. It will end by the fulfilment of <reference osisRef="1th 4:14-17">1 Thessalonians 4:14-17</reference>. Chapters 4-19. are believed to synchronize with Daniel's Seventieth Week (<hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Da 9:24">Daniel 9:24</reference>"</hi>). The great tribulation begins at the middle of the week," and continues three and a half years (<reference osisRef="re 11:3-re 19:21">Revelation 11:3-19:21</reference>). The tribulation is brought to an end by the appearing of the Lord and the battle of Armageddon (<reference osisRef="mt 24:29 mt 24:30">Matthew 24:29,30</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 19:11-21">Revelation 19:11-21</reference>). The kingdom follows (<reference osisRef="re 20:4 re 20:5">Revelation 20:4,5</reference>); after this the "little season" (<reference osisRef="re 20:7-15">Revelation 20:7-15</reference>), and then eternity.<div eID="gen5396" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5397" type="x-p"/> Interpreters of the Revelation should bear in mind two important passages: <reference osisRef="1pe 1:12">1 Peter 1:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="2pe 1:20 2pe 1:21">2 Peter 1:20,21</reference>. Doubtless much which is designedly obscure to us will be clear to those for whom it was written as the time approaches. <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv168"/><hi type="bold">angel</hi> <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Heb 1:4">Hebrews 1:4</reference>")</hi>
<hi type="bold">sins</hi><div eID="gen5397" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5398" type="x-p"/> Sin. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ro 3:23">Romans 3:23</reference>")</hi>.

<hi type="bold">isle</hi><div eID="gen5398" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5399" type="x-p"/> From <reference osisRef="Rev 1:1-20">1:1 to 1:20</reference> the Seer is on the earth, looking at the vision of Christ.; <reference osisRef="Rev 2:1-Rev 3:22"> 2:1 to 3:22</reference> he is on the earth looking forward through the church-age.; <reference osisRef="Rev 4:1 11:1">4:1 to 11:1</reference> he is "in the Spirit" (<reference osisRef="Rev 4:2">Revelation 4:2</reference>; cf <reference osisRef="eze 3:12-14">Ezekiel 3:12-14</reference>) observing things in heaven and on earth.; <reference osisRef="Rev 11:1-12"> 11:1 to 11:12</reference> he is in Jerusalem with the two witnesses. <reference osisRef="11:13 22:21">11:13 to the end</reference> he is in heaven observing and recording things in heaven and upon the earth.
<hi type="bold">voice</hi> The theophanies. <reference osisRef="re 1:9-20">Revelation 1:9-20</reference>; <reference osisRef="ge 12:7">Genesis 12:7</reference>
<hi type="bold">hell</hi><div eID="gen5399" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5400" type="x-p"/> Hades, <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Lu 16:23">Luke 16:23</reference>")</hi>.
<hi type="bold">hereafter</hi><div eID="gen5400" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5401" type="x-p"/> things that are to be after these, i.e. after the churches.

<hi type="bold">angels</hi><div eID="gen5401" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5402" type="x-p"/> The natural explanation of the "messengers" is that they were men sent by the seven churches to ascertain the state of the aged apostle, now an exile in Patmos (cf) <reference osisRef="php 4:18">Philippians 4:18</reference> but they figure any who bear God's messages to a church.<div eID="gen5402" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5403" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">churches</hi> <div eID="gen5403" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5404" type="x-p"/> The messages to the seven churches have a fourfold application:<div eID="gen5404" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(1) Local, to the churches actually addressed;</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(2) admonitory, to all churches in all time as tests by which they may discern their true spiritual state in the sight of God;</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(3) personal, in the exhortations to him "that hath an ear," and in the promise "to him that overcometh";</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(4) prophetic, as disclosing seven phases of the spiritual history of the church from, say, A.D. 96 to the end. It is incredible that in a prophecy covering the church period, there should be no such foreview. These messages must contain that foreview if it is in the book at all, for the church does not appear after <reference osisRef="re 3:22">Revelation 3:22</reference>. Again, these messages by their very terms go beyond the local assemblies mentioned. Most conclusively of all, these messages do present an exact foreview of the spiritual history of the church, and in this precise order. Ephesus gives the general state at the date of the writing; Smyrna, the period of the great persecutions; Pergamos, the church settled down in the world, "where Satan's throne is," after the conversion of Constantine, say A.D. 316. Thyatira is the Papacy, developed out of the Pergamos state: Balaamism (worldliness) and Nicolaitanism (priestly assumption) having conquered. As Jezebel brought idolatry into Israel, so Romanism weds Christian doctrine to pagan ceremonies. Sardis is the Protestant Reformation, whose works were not "fulfilled." Philadelphia is whatever bears clear testimony to the Word and the Name in the time of self-satisfied profession represented by Laodicea.</item> </list> <div sID="gen5405" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">mystery</hi><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Mt 13:11">Matthew 13:11</reference>")</hi>. <div eID="gen5405" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv169"/><div sID="gen5406" type="x-p"/> <chapter eID="Rev.1"/>
<div eID="gen5406" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5407" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="2" osisID="Rev.2" sID="Rev.2"/>

<hi type="bold">angels</hi> <div eID="gen5407" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5408" type="x-p"/> The natural explanation of the "messengers" is that they were men sent by the seven churches to ascertain the state of the aged apostle, now an exile in Patmos (cf) <reference osisRef="php 4:18">Philippians 4:18</reference> but they figure any who bear God's messages to a church.<div eID="gen5408" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5409" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">churches</hi> <div eID="gen5409" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5410" type="x-p"/> The messages to the seven churches have a fourfold application:<div eID="gen5410" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(1) Local, to the churches actually addressed;</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(2) admonitory, to all churches in all time as tests by which they may discern their true spiritual state in the sight of God;</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(3) personal, in the exhortations to him "that hath an ear," and in the promise "to him that overcometh";</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(4) prophetic, as disclosing seven phases of the spiritual history of the church from, say, A.D. 96 to the end. It is incredible that in a prophecy covering the church period, there should be no such foreview. These messages must contain that foreview if it is in the book at all, for the church does not appear after <reference osisRef="re 3:22">Revelation 3:22</reference>. Again, these messages by their very terms go beyond the local assemblies mentioned. Most conclusively of all, these messages do present an exact foreview of the spiritual history of the church, and in this precise order. Ephesus gives the general state at the date of the writing; Smyrna, the period of the great persecutions; Pergamos, the church settled down in the world, "where Satan's throne is," after the conversion of Constantine, say A.D. 316. Thyatira is the Papacy, developed out of the Pergamos state: Balaamism (worldliness) and Nicolaitanism (priestly assumption) having conquered. As Jezebel brought idolatry into Israel, so Romanism weds Christian doctrine to pagan ceremonies. Sardis is the Protestant Reformation, whose works were not "fulfilled." Philadelphia is whatever bears clear testimony to the Word and the Name in the time of self-satisfied profession represented by Laodicea.</item> </list> <div sID="gen5411" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">mystery</hi><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Mt 13:11">Matthew 13:11</reference>")</hi>.

<hi type="bold">Nicolaitanes</hi><div eID="gen5411" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5412" type="x-p"/> From nikao, "to conquer," and laos, "the people," or "laity." There is no ancient authority for a sect of the Nicolaitanes. If the word is symbolic it refers to the earliest form of the notion of a priestly order, or "clergy," which later divided an equal brotherhood <reference osisRef="mt 23:8">Matthew 23:8</reference> into "priests" and "laity." What in Ephesus was "deeds" <reference osisRef="re 2:6">Revelation 2:6</reference> had become in Pergamos a "doctrine <reference osisRef="re 2:15">Revelation 2:15</reference>.<div eID="gen5412" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5413" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Nicolaitanes</hi> <reference osisRef="re 2:15">Revelation 2:15,</reference> contra, ; <reference osisRef="1pe 5:2 1pe 5:3">1 Peter 5:2,3</reference>; <reference osisRef="mt 24:49">Matthew 24:49</reference>.
<hi type="bold">angel</hi><div eID="gen5413" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5414" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Heb 1:4">Hebrews 1:4</reference>")</hi>.
<hi type="bold">angel</hi><div eID="gen5414" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5415" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Heb 1:4">Hebrews 1:4</reference>")</hi>.

<hi type="bold">The "doctrine" of Balaam</hi><div eID="gen5415" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5416" type="x-p"/> The doctrine of Balaam (CF) <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:2Pe 2:15">2 Peter 2:15</reference>")</hi> See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:jude 1:11">Jude 1:11</reference>" was his teaching Balak to corrupt the people who could not be cursed. ; <reference osisRef="nu 31:15 nu 31:16">Numbers 31:15,16</reference>; <reference osisRef="nu 22:5"> 22:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="nu 23:8"> 23:8</reference> by tempting them to marry women of Moab, defile their separation, and abandon their pilgrim character. It is that union with the world and the church which is spiritual unchastity. <reference osisRef="jas 4:4">James 4:4</reference>. Pergamos had lost the pilgrim character and was "dwelling" <reference osisRef="re 2:13">Revelation 2:13</reference> "where Satan's throne is," in the world. ; <reference osisRef="joh 12:31">John 12:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="joh 14:30"> 14:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="joh 16:11"> 16:11</reference>.
<hi type="bold">a white stone</hi><div eID="gen5416" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5417" type="x-p"/> Signifies approval.

<hi type="bold">angel</hi><div eID="gen5417" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5418" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Heb 1:4">Hebrews 1:4</reference>")</hi>. <div eID="gen5418" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv169"/><div sID="gen5419" type="x-p"/> <chapter eID="Rev.2"/>
<div eID="gen5419" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5420" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="3" osisID="Rev.3" sID="Rev.3"/>
<hi type="bold">angel</hi> <div eID="gen5420" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5421" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Heb 1:4">Hebrews 1:4</reference>")</hi>.
<hi type="bold">perfect</hi><div eID="gen5421" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5422" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Mt 5:48">Matthew 5:48</reference>")</hi>.
<hi type="bold">angels</hi><div eID="gen5422" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5423" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Heb 1:4">Hebrews 1:4</reference>")</hi>.
<hi type="bold">angel</hi><div eID="gen5423" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5424" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Heb 1:4">Hebrews 1:4</reference>")</hi>.

<hi type="bold">world</hi><div eID="gen5424" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5425" type="x-p"/> "oikoumene" = inhabited earth. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Lu 2:1">Luke 2:1</reference>")</hi>.

<hi type="bold">Father</hi><div eID="gen5426" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5427" type="x-p"/> This passage, in harmony with <reference osisRef="lu 1:32 lu 1:33">Luke 1:32,33</reference>; <reference osisRef="mt 19:28">Matthew 19:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="ac 2:30 ac 2:34 ac 2:35">Acts 2:30,34,35</reference>; <reference osisRef="ac 15:14-16">Acts 15:14-16</reference> is conclusive that Christ is not now seated upon His own throne. <hi type="bold">tribulation</hi><div eID="gen5458" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5459" type="x-p"/> The great tribulation is the period of unexampled trouble predicted in the passages cited under that head from <reference osisRef="ps 2:5">Psalms 2:5</reference> to <reference osisRef="re 7:14">Revelation 7:14</reference> and described in Re 11.-18. Involving in a measure the whole earth <reference osisRef="re 3:10">Revelation 3:10</reference> it is yet distinctly "the time of Jacob's trouble" <reference osisRef="jer 30:7">Jeremiah 30:7</reference> and its vortex Jerusalem and the Holy Land. It involves the people of God who will have returned to Palestine in unbelief. Its duration is three and a half years, or the last half of the seventieth week of Daniel. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Da 9:24">Daniel 9:24</reference>")</hi>. <reference osisRef="re 11:2 re 11:3">Revelation 11:2,3</reference> The elements of the tribulation are:<div eID="gen5459" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(1) The cruel reign of the "beast out of the sea" <reference osisRef="re 13:1">Revelation 13:1</reference> who at the beginning of the three and a half years, will break his covenant with the Jews (by virtue of which they will have re-established the temple worship, <reference osisRef="da 9:27">Daniel 9:27</reference> and show himself in the temple, demanding that he be worshipped as God ; <reference osisRef="mt 24:15">Matthew 24:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="2th 2:4">2 Thessalonians 2:4</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(2) The active interposition of Satan "having great wrath" <reference osisRef="re 12:12">Revelation 12:12</reference> who gives his power to the Beast <reference osisRef="re 13:4 re 13:5">Revelation 13:4,5</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(3) The unprecedented activity of demons <reference osisRef="re 9:2 re 9:11">Revelation 9:2,11</reference> and</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(4) the terrible "bowl" judgments of Re 16.</item> </list> <div sID="gen5460" type="x-p"/> The great tribulation will be, however, a period of salvation. An election out of Israel is seen as sealed for God <reference osisRef="re 7:4-8">Revelation 7:4-8</reference> and, with an innumerable multitude of Gentiles <reference osisRef="re 7:9">Revelation 7:9</reference> are said to have come "out of the great tribulation" <reference osisRef="re 7:14">Revelation 7:14</reference>. They are not of the priesthood, the church, to which they seem to stand somewhat in the relation of the Levites to the priests under the Mosaic Covenant. The great tribulation is immediately followed by the return of Christ in glory, and the events associated therewith <reference osisRef="mt 24:29 mt 24:30">Matthew 24:29,30</reference>.<div eID="gen5460" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5461" type="x-p"/> See "Remnant" <reference osisRef="isa 1:9">Isaiah 1:9</reference>.<div eID="gen5461" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5462" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ro 11:5">Romans 11:5</reference>")</hi>. "Beast" See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:da 9:24">Daniel 9:24</reference>" See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:re 19:20">Revelation 19:20</reference>" "Armageddon" <reference osisRef="re 16:14">Revelation 16:14</reference>. See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:re 19:17">Revelation 19:17</reference>".

<hi type="bold">kingdom of our God</hi><div eID="gen5501" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5502" type="x-p"/> The Dispensation of the Kingdom (<reference osisRef="2sa 7:16">2 Samuel 7:16</reference> refs.) begins with the return of Christ to the earth, runs through the "thousand years" of His earth-rule, and ends when He has delivered up the kingdom to the Father. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:1Co 15:24">1 Corinthians 15:24</reference>")</hi>.<div eID="gen5502" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5503" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">salvation</hi><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ro 1:16">Romans 1:16</reference>")</hi>. <div eID="gen5503" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv169"/><div sID="gen5504" type="x-p"/> <chapter eID="Rev.12"/>

<hi type="bold">rise up</hi> <div eID="gen5505" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5506" type="x-p"/> Daniel's fourth beast, <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Da 7:26">Daniel 7:26</reference>")</hi> , The "ten horns" are explained in <reference osisRef="da 7:24">Daniel 7:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 17:12">Revelation 17:12</reference> to be ten kings, and the whole vision is of the last form of Gentile world-power, a confederated ten-kingdom empire covering the sphere of authority of ancient Rome. <reference osisRef="re 13:1-3">Revelation 13:1-3</reference> refers to the ten-kingdom empire; vs. <reference osisRef="re 13:4-10">Revelation 13:4-10</reference> to the emperor, who is emphatically "the Beast."<div eID="gen5506" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5507" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Re 19:20">Revelation 19:20</reference>")</hi>.

<hi type="bold">like unto a leopard</hi><div eID="gen5507" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5508" type="x-p"/> The three animals, leopard, bear, and lion, are found in <reference osisRef="da 7:4-6">Daniel 7:4-6</reference> as symbols of the empires which preceded Rome, and whose characteristics all entered into the qualities of the Roman empire: Macedonian swiftness of conquest, Persian tenacity of purpose, Babylonish voracity.

<hi type="bold">wounded to death</hi><div eID="gen5508" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5509" type="x-p"/> Fragments of the ancient Roman empire have never ceased to exist as separate kingdoms. It was the imperial form of government which ceased; the one head wounded to death. What we have prophetically in <reference osisRef="re 13:3">Revelation 13:3</reference> is the restoration of the imperial form as such, though over a federated empire of ten kingdoms; the "head" is "healed," i.e. restored; there is an emperor again--the Beast.<div eID="gen5509" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5510" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">world</hi> <div eID="gen5510" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5511" type="x-p"/> ge = earth. <reference osisRef="joh 7:7">John 7:7,</reference> <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Re 13:8">Revelation 13:8</reference>")</hi>.

<hi type="bold">world</hi><div eID="gen5511" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5512" type="x-p"/> Kosmos, Summary: In the sense of the present world-system, the ethically bad sense of the word, refers to the "order," "arrangement," under which Satan has organized the world of unbelieving mankind upon his cosmic principle of force, greed, selfishness, ambition, and pleasure. <reference osisRef="mt 4:8 mt 4:9">Matthew 4:8,9</reference>; <reference osisRef="joh 12:31">John 12:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="joh 14:30"> 14:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="joh 18:36"> 18:36</reference>; <reference osisRef="eph 2:2">Ephesians 2:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="eph 6:12"> 6:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="1jo 2:15-17">1 John 2:15-17</reference>. This world- system is imposing and powerful with armies and fleets; is often outwardly religious, scientific, cultured, and elegant; but, seething with national and commercial rivalries and ambitions, is upheld in any real crisis only by armed force, and is dominated by Satanic principles.

<hi type="bold">he causeth</hi><div eID="gen5512" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5513" type="x-p"/> Antichrist the person is to be distinguished from the "many antichrists" <reference osisRef="1jo 2:18">1 John 2:18</reference> and the "spirit of antichrist" <reference osisRef="1jo 4:3">1 John 4:3</reference> which characterizes all. The supreme mark of all is the denial of the Christian truth of the incarnation of the Logos, the eternal Son in Jesus as the Christ <reference osisRef="joh 1:1 joh 1:14">John 1:1,14</reference>.<div eID="gen5513" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5514" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Mt 1:16">Matthew 1:16</reference>")</hi>.<div eID="gen5514" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5515" type="x-p"/> The "many antichrists" precede and prepare the way for the Antichrist, who is "the Beast out of the earth" of <reference osisRef="re 13:11-17">Revelation 13:11-17</reference> and the "false prophet" of ; <reference osisRef="re 16:13">Revelation 16:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 19:20"> 19:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 20:10"> 20:10</reference>. He is the last ecclesiastical head, as the Beast of <reference osisRef="re 13:1-8">Revelation 13:1-8</reference> is the last civil head. For purposes of persecution he is permitted to exercise the autocratic power of the emperor- Beast.<div eID="gen5515" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5516" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Re 19:20">Revelation 19:20</reference>")</hi>. <div eID="gen5516" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv169"/><div sID="gen5517" type="x-p"/> <chapter eID="Rev.13"/>
<div eID="gen5517" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5518" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="14" osisID="Rev.14" sID="Rev.14"/>

<hi type="bold">written in</hi> <div eID="gen5518" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5519" type="x-p"/> See, <reference osisRef="re 7:3">Revelation 7:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 22:4"> 22:4</reference> contra: <reference osisRef="re 13:16">Revelation 13:16</reference>.
<hi type="bold">redeemed</hi><div eID="gen5519" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5520" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ro 3:24">Romans 3:24</reference>")</hi>.

<hi type="bold">gospel</hi><div eID="gen5520" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5521" type="x-p"/> Gospel. This great theme may be summarized as follows:<div eID="gen5521" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5522" type="x-p"/> I. In itself the word Gospel means good news.<div eID="gen5522" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5523" type="x-p"/> II. Four forms of the Gospel are to be distinguished"<div eID="gen5523" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(1) The Gospel of the kingdom. This is the good news that God purposes to set up on the earth, in fulfilment of the Davidic Covenant <reference osisRef="2sa 7:16">2 Samuel 7:16</reference> a kingdom, political, spiritual, Israelitish, universal, over which God's Son, David's heir, shall be King, and which shall be, for one thousand years, the manifestation of the righteousness of God in human affairs. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Mt 3:2">Matthew 3:2</reference>")</hi>.</item> </list> <div sID="gen5524" type="x-p"/> Two preachings of this Gospel are mentioned, one past, beginning with the ministry of John the Baptist, continued by our Lord and His disciples, and ending with the Jewis rejection of the King. The other is yet future <reference osisRef="mt 24:14">Matthew 24:14</reference> during the great tribulation, and immediately preceding the coming of the King in glory.<div eID="gen5524" type="x-p"/> <list> <item type="x-indent-1">(2) The Gospel of the grace of God. This is the good news that Jesus Christ, the rejected King, has died on the cross for the sins of the world, that He was raised from the dead for our justification, and that by Him all that believe are justified from all things. This form of the Gospel is described in many ways. It is the Gospel "of God" <reference osisRef="ro 1:1">Romans 1:1</reference> because it originates in His love; "of Christ" <reference osisRef="2co 10:14">2 Corinthians 10:14</reference> because it flows from His sacrifice, and because He is the alone Object of Gospel faith; of the "grace of God" <reference osisRef="ac 20:24">Acts 20:24</reference> because it saves those whom the law curses; of "the glory" ; <reference osisRef="1ti 1:11">1 Timothy 1:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="2co 4:4">2 Corinthians 4:4</reference> because it concerns Him who is in the glory, and who is bringing the many sons to glory <reference osisRef="heb 2:10">Hebrews 2:10</reference> of "our salvation" <reference osisRef="eph 1:13">Ephesians 1:13</reference> because it is the "power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth" <reference osisRef="ro 1:16">Romans 1:16</reference> of "the uncircumcision" <reference osisRef="ga 2:7">Galatians 2:7</reference> because it saves wholly apart from forms and ordinances of "peace" <reference osisRef="eph 6:15">Ephesians 6:15</reference> because through Christ it makes peace between the sinner and God, and imparts inward peace.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(3) The everlasting Gospel <reference osisRef="re 14:6">Revelation 14:6</reference>. This is to be preached to the earth-dwellers at the very end of the great tribulation and immediately preceding the judgment of the nations <reference osisRef="mt 15:31">Matthew 15:31</reference>. It is neither the Gospel of the kingdom, nor of grace. Though its burden is judgment, not salvation, it is good news to Israel and to those who, during the tribulation, have been saved ; <reference osisRef="re 7:9-14">Revelation 7:9-14</reference>; <reference osisRef="lu 21:28">Luke 21:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="ps 96:11-13">Psalms 96:11-13</reference>; <reference osisRef="isa 35:4-10">Isaiah 35:4-10</reference>.</item> <item type="x-indent-1">(4) That which Paul calls, "my Gospel" <reference osisRef="ro 2:16">Romans 2:16</reference>. This is the Gospel of the grace of God in its fullest development, but includes the revelation of the result of that Gospel in the outcalling of the church, her relationships, position, privileges, and responsibility. It is the distinctive truth of Ephesians and Colossians, but interpenetrates all of Paul's writings.</item> </list> <div sID="gen5525" type="x-p"/> III. There is "another Gospel" <reference osisRef="ga 1:6">Galatians 1:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="2co 11:4">2 Corinthians 11:4</reference> "which is not another," but a perversion of the Gospel of the grace of God, against which we are warned. It has many seductive forms, but the test is one--it invariably denies the sufficiency of grace alone to save, keep, and perfect, and mingles with grace some kind of human merit. In Galatia it was law, in Colosse fanaticism <reference osisRef="col 2:18">Colossians 2:18,</reference> etc. In any form its teachers lie under the awful anathema of God.<div eID="gen5525" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5526" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">angel</hi><hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Heb 1:4">Hebrews 1:4</reference>")</hi>.

<hi type="bold">Babylon</hi><div eID="gen5548" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5549" type="x-p"/> Summary: The Times of the Gentiles is that long period beginning with the Babylonian captivity of Judah, under Nebuchadnezzar, and to be brought to an end by the destruction of Gentile world-power by the "stone cut out without hands" <reference osisRef="da 2:34 da 2:35 da 2:44">Daniel 2:34,35,44</reference> i.e., the coming of the Lord in glory <reference osisRef="re 19:11 re 19:21">Revelation 19:11,21</reference> until which time Jerusalem is politically subject to Gentile rule. <reference osisRef="lu 21:24">Luke 21:24</reference>.<div eID="gen5549" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5550" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">kings</hi> "Times of the Gentiles" <reference osisRef="re 16:19">Revelation 16:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="lu 21:24">Luke 21:24</reference>.<div eID="gen5550" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5551" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Babylon</hi> <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Isa 13:1">Isaiah 13:1</reference>")</hi> <div eID="gen5551" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv169"/><div sID="gen5552" type="x-p"/> <chapter eID="Rev.16"/>

<hi type="bold">Babylon</hi><div eID="gen5558" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5559" type="x-p"/> Babylon, "confusion," is repeatedly used by the prophets in a symbolic sense (<hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Isa 13:2">Isaiah 13:2</reference>")</hi> ), note 2. Two "Babylons" are to be distinguished in the Revelation: ecclesiastical babylon, which is apostate Christendom, headed up under the Papacy; and political babylon, which is the Beast's confederated empire, the last form of Gentile world-dominion. Ecclesiastical Babylon is "the great whore" <reference osisRef="re 17:1">Revelation 17:1</reference> and is destroyed by political Babylon <reference osisRef="re 17:15-18">Revelation 17:15-18</reference> that the beast may be the alone object of worship. ; <reference osisRef="2th 2:3 2th 2:4">2 Thessalonians 2:3,4</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 13:15">Revelation 13:15</reference>. The power of political Babylon is destroyed by the return of the Lord in glory. (See "Armageddon,") ; <reference osisRef="re 16:14">Revelation 16:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="re 19:17"> 19:17</reference>. The notion of a literal Babylon to be rebuilt on the site of ancient Babylon is in conflict with <reference osisRef="isa 13:19-22">Isaiah 13:19-22</reference>. But the language of <reference osisRef="re 18:10 re 18:16 re 18:18">Revelation 18:10,16,18</reference> seems beyond question to identify "Babylon," the "city" of luxury and traffic, with "Babylon" the ecclesiastical centre, viz. Rome. The very kings who hate ecclesiastical Babylon deplore the destruction of commercial Babylon.
<hi type="bold">sins</hi><div eID="gen5559" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5560" type="x-p"/> Sin. <hi type="italic">(See Scofield "<reference osisRef="Scofield:Ro 3:23">Romans 3:23</reference>")</hi>.
